The federal government says the temporary administration will help restore stability and pave the way for elected regional leadership. The TPLF has opposed the federal advance, and it remains uncertain how effectively the new administration will operate across the region.

For residents, the immediate concerns are whether salaries will be paid, schools and health facilities will function, and displaced families will be able to return safely.

In Zalambessa, Gebrehiwot said residents knew from experience what another conflict could bring.

“People are worried because we know what war means for this area. We have already suffered enough, and nobody wants to see things reach that point again,” he said.

World.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
World.content:
"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

World.title: Governments working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
World.content:
The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.

Governments and some of the world's biggest companies, including Amazon, are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws.

The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them.

Amazon was targeted in multiple attempts, which it said occurred before an embargo on the warning was lifted. It added that it was unclear how actors knew about the vulnerabilities.

A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.

"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note, external.

PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress â the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web.

World.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
World.content:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambled to contain the fallout of this discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

World.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
World.content:
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.

Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.

The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.

Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."

The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

World.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
World.content:
After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?

"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.

In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.

But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.

The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.

In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."

World.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
World.content:
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.

The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".

In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.

No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.

The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.

An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

World.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
World.content:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

World.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.

Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.

Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".

It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.

Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.

Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.

Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.

The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.

Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

World.title: Qatar, Türkiye, Pakistan, Indonesia sign Defence Industry Pact
World.content:
Qatar, Turkiye, Indonesia and Pakistan have signed a new defence industry agreement to develop and produce military equipment and defence systems collaboratively.

The Memorandum of Understanding, which seeks to strengthen defence industry cooperation among the three countries, was signed in Doha on Wednesday.

The agreement is known as the Badr Memorandum of Understanding.

The Qatari Defence Ministry said the agreement aims to “foster cooperation in the field of defence manufacturing, enhance defence capabilities among the four countries.”

The agreement comes as the war launched by the US and Israel on Iran continues to shape security calculations across the Middle East.

It had deepened concerns among countries in the Gulf about missile and drone threats. It also raised concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure and the risks of relying heavily on external powers for security.

It also comes amid increasing tension between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni rebel group, Ansar Allah, popularly called the Houthis.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Both sides have traded strikes since August. The crisis is considered a new front in the Middle East war.

According to the Qatari Defence Ministry, the new defense initiative will also “promote collaboration in technical defence training, as well as in research and development areas.”

The endgame, it noted, is also to contribute to the “creation of solutions and industries worthy of the evolution of modern defences.”

The agreement also seeks to help the three countries strengthen their domestic defence industries and develop more integrated manufacturing capabilities.

Experts say each of the four countries signed the agreement to bring its own resources and skill set to the table.

Turkiye, which has been expanding its domestic defence industry, could contribute technological expertise and a mature defence industry.

Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and their domestic markets while Qatar could provide investment potential.

World.title: 2027: Seven weeks after G100 summit, questions persist over five unity documents
World.content:
Seven weeks after six opposition parties agreed to produce five documents to guide their cooperation ahead of the 2027 general elections, questions remain over whether the documents have been completed.

Representatives of the parties have since consulted five politicians identified by G100 as presidential candidates.

G100 coordinator Salihu Lukman says they have agreed on basic terms for a working group to develop options for selecting a common candidate.

However, PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify whether the five documents proposed at the 31 August summit had been completed, submitted or adopted.

Speaking on Channels Television’s Hard Copy programme on 16 October, Mr Lukman said the parties had taken greater responsibility for the negotiations. He also acknowledged continuing distrust among parties and candidates, warning that efforts to agree on a common candidate might not succeed.

Consultations with five candidates

On 14 October, Mr Lukman announced that national chairpersons and secretaries of six opposition parties had consulted five presidential candidates over approximately two weeks.

Those consulted, according to Mr Lukman, were Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, Seyi Makinde, Adewole Adebayo and Donald Duke.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The six participating parties were the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Social Democratic Party (SDP), Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

According to Mr Lukman, the consultations were intended to advance the August summit resolutions, identify common ground and develop arrangements for cooperation.

“We have succeeded beyond some of our expectations,” he said during the Channels Television interview.

He did not announce a final agreement among the presidential candidates.

What ADC says

In a separate interview with PREMIUM TIMES, ADC National Publicity Secretary Bolaji Abdullahi confirmed his party’s involvement in the G100 discussions.

He described the talks as efforts to establish electoral cooperation, including arrangements to protect opposition votes, rather than negotiations aimed specifically at producing a single presidential candidate.

His account places the consultations within a broader coordination effort, while Mr Lukman’s remarks identify the selection of a possible common candidate as one of the issues under consideration.

Neither official confirmed an agreement requiring any participating party to withdraw its presidential candidate or support a single ticket.

Mr Abdullahi added that the parties’ national chairpersons and secretaries were leading the discussions, with Mr Lukman allowing them greater responsibility after initially bringing them together.

Kwankwaso, ADC clash over common candidate

The difficulties facing a possible common-candidate arrangement were underlined by a public disagreement between the ADC Presidential Campaign Council and Rabiu Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the NDC.

The exchange followed Mr Kwankwaso’s call for ADC presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar to step aside in favour of the NDC’s Peter Obi.

On 16 October, ADC campaign council spokesperson Kola Ologbondiyan accused Mr Kwankwaso of undermining opposition unity and advancing President Bola Tinubu’s political interests.

He said the former Kano State governor should focus on challenging the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) rather than attacking other opposition candidates.

Mr Kwankwaso rejected the allegation on 18 October.

“We will not withdraw our candidature for ADC or any other party,” he said, reaffirming the Obi–Kwankwaso ticket’s intention to contest the presidential election.

He denied working for the APC and criticised both the ruling party and the ADC, arguing that neither offered the alternative his party was presenting to Nigerians.

The ADC campaign council responded later the same day, accusing Mr Kwankwaso of directing his criticism at the ADC rather than the Tinubu administration. It challenged him to align openly with the APC if that was his agenda.

Although Mr Kwankwaso rejected withdrawing the NDC ticket, he did not announce the party’s withdrawal from G100 consultations.

The disagreement highlights the competing presidential ambitions that the proposed Roadmap to a Common Presidential Candidate would have to address.

The five documents and the timetable

At the 31 August summit, the parties proposed five working groups to prepare documents intended to guide their cooperation ahead of the 2027 elections.

The National Covenant for Democratic Renewal would establish the principles underpinning the proposed alliance, while the Single-Term Transition Charter would outline the terms and safeguards of a possible single four-year transitional government.

The National Reform Programme would identify shared policy priorities, while the Framework for Opposition Unity would define the structures and procedures for cooperation among the participating parties.

The fifth document, the Roadmap to a Common Presidential Candidate, would set out the process for negotiating and selecting a common presidential candidate.

The working groups were initially expected to complete their assignments within four weeks for consideration by the coalition leadership.

The Central Leadership Committee subsequently held its inaugural meeting on 16 September.

According to a statement reported the following day, the committee directed participating parties to submit nominees to the working groups by 18 September, with work scheduled to begin between 21 and 27 September.

It remains unclear whether the original deadline was maintained or extended, whether nominees were submitted on time or whether all five groups commenced work as planned.

During his 16 October interview, Mr Lukman referred to the nomination of representatives to the common-candidate working group as part of the process ahead.

He did not clarify whether these were outstanding nominations under the September timetable or appointments for a subsequent stage of negotiations.

Available statements also do not establish whether the working groups submitted their proposed documents for consideration by the coalition leadership.

Next steps and minimum programme

Mr Lukman said the common-candidate working group would develop recommendations and options to guide negotiations among the participating parties.

He acknowledged that distrust among political parties and their candidates could prevent them from reaching an agreement.

“For us, unless that is addressed, all these issues about coming up with a united front or a single candidate, we may not be able to achieve it,” he said during a Channels Television interview, as quoted by TheCable.

Mr Lukman said the negotiations would extend beyond the presidential contest to governorship, National Assembly and state assembly elections.

On policy, he explained that the objective was not to merge the participating parties’ manifestos but to develop a minimum programme of action reflecting priorities their candidates could endorse.

He cited petroleum subsidies as an example of an issue requiring further discussion, saying Atiku’s proposed domestic production subsidy needed a clearer implementation framework.

Mr Lukman did not indicate that the parties had adopted a common petroleum policy.

Lukman’s role

Mr Lukman had earlier suspended his ADC membership over internal disagreements, particularly concerning developments in his Kaduna constituency.

He acknowledged that his association with the party had initially raised concerns among some G100 participants.

Allowing the participating parties’ leaderships to take charge of negotiations, he said, helped address those concerns.

He did not say whether he had resumed his ADC membership.

Efforts to obtain responses

PREMIUM TIMES emailed Mr Lukman on 3 October and in subsequent correspondence, seeking clarification on difficulties in securing a common presidential candidate, possible cooperation in a presidential run-off, the progress of the five working groups and the proposed second summit.

He has not responded as of this report.

On 9 October, the newspaper contacted NDC spokesperson Osa Director with similar questions about the party’s participation in the working groups, reports received and its position on a common candidate or run-off cooperation.

Despite WhatsApp reminders and telephone calls, no substantive response was received. Mr Director answered one call and promised to respond later.

Mr Lukman’s subsequent public remarks on Channels Television did not clarify the status of the five documents.

What happens next?

Seven weeks after the summit, G100 has reported consultations with five politicians identified as presidential candidates and plans for further negotiations. However, no binding agreement on a common ticket has been announced.

The disagreement between the ADC and Mr Kwankwaso highlights the competing presidential ambitions that the proposed common-candidate framework would need to address.

With the original four-week timetable elapsed, questions remain over whether the five working groups have completed their documents, when the participating parties will consider them and whether the proposed second summit will take place.

World.title: $700,000 Fraud Trial: EFCC witness recounts arrest of two alleged impersonators of agency’s officials
World.content:
An Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) operative has told the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) High Court in Abuja how the agency arrested two men accused of posing as officials of the commission to obtain $700,000 from former Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) managing director, Mohammed Bello-Koko.

According to a statement shared by the EFCC spokesperson Dele Oyewale on Wednesday, Tanko Abubakar, the second prosecution witness, testified in the trial of Ojobo Joshua and Aliyu Hashim.

The EFCC alleges that the defendants told Mr Bello-Koko that his tenure as NPA managing director was under investigation and demanded $1 million to stop the probe.

They allegedly claimed the money was required by EFCC Chairman Ola Olukoyede and the commission’s director of operations. The amount was eventually reduced to $700,000, according to the prosecution.

The defendants were arraigned on 13 November 2024 and pleaded not guilty, according to TransparencIT, a platform that tracks corruption cases in Nigeria. They face amended four charges of impersonation, conspiracy and obtaining money by false pretence.

The defendants allegedly threatened Mr Bello-Koko with arrest and prosecution if he refused to cooperate, while claiming they could secure a “soft landing” for him through Mr Olukoyede.

Mr Abubakar told the court that he became involved in the investigation in 2024 after the EFCC’s Abuja zonal director received intelligence that the defendants were attempting to defraud the former NPA managing director.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The Abuja zonal director informed me that there is an intelligence that the first and second defendants were attempting to defraud the former MD, NPA, Muhammad Bello-Koko in the sum of $1,000,000 and one of the suspects claiming to be a personal assistant to the EFCC Chairman, Ola Olukoyede,” he said.

The witness, who is attached to the commission’s Land and Property Section in Ibadan, Oyo State, stated that Mr Bello-Koko told him that Mr Hashim had claimed to know the person posing as the EFCC chairman’s aide.

Mr Bello-Koko subsequently introduced him to Mr Hashim, whom he contacted in August 2024 to discuss the matter.

Mr Abubakar said Mr Hashim invited him to Crystal Palace Hotel on Gimbiya Street, Area 11, Abuja, where he was told they would meet Mr Joshua. They later met at the Legislative Quarters in Apo, where Mr Joshua arrived in two vehicles.

According to the witness, Mr Joshua asked whether Mr Hashim had told him how much was needed to end the purported investigation.

“The first defendant told me and Koko to bring $1,000,000. I pleaded with him that we cannot raise such an amount,” Mr Abubakar told the court.

He said he offered $300,000, but Mr Joshua rejected it. A subsequent offer of $500,000 was also turned down before Mr Hashim persuaded Mr Joshua to accept $700,000, the witness said.

Mr Abubakar said he reported the agreement to his zonal director, who assembled an investigative team comprising him, Hakeem Lasisi, Abdulhamid Wodi and Olalekan Ogunjobi.

On 28 August 2024, he informed the defendants that he had returned from Kaduna with the money and was heading to the EFCC headquarters to deliver it. Mr Joshua instead directed him to meet at an A.A. Rano filling station along Lugbe Road, Abuja.

The witness stated that Mr Joshua arrived in a Hilux and another SUV, with three armed mobile police officers in the Hilux. Mr Hashim also arrived, but the EFCC team could not make an arrest because its operatives at the scene were unarmed, he said.

Mr Abubakar said he contacted his office, which mobilised armed personnel for another attempt.

He later told Mr Hashim that the money was ready and was directed to meet him at Crystal Palace Hotel. After Mr Joshua failed to answer his calls, the witness sent him a text message confirming that the money was available. Mr Joshua subsequently called and directed him to meet Mr Hashim.

Mr Abubakar said he drove to Gimbiya Street and showed Mr Hashim the bag containing the money. EFCC operatives then moved in and arrested him.

He noted that Mr Hashim initially denied knowing Mr Joshua’s residence but later led the operatives there after Mr Joshua requested a video call to confirm that the money was ready.

According to the witness, Mr Joshua’s wife allowed the operatives into the house, where they found him inside his store and arrested him. Both men were taken to the EFCC headquarters.

Prosecution lawyer Elizabeth Alabi told the court that Hakeem Lasisi, the witness originally scheduled to testify, was unavailable because he was on an official assignment outside the country. The court allowed Mr Abubakar to testify in his place.

The trial judge Jude Onwuegbuzie adjourned the case until Thursday (today), for continuation of the trial.

World.title: Ebola: One imported case does not mean Nigeria is experiencing outbreak – WHO
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has urged Nigerians to remain calm, noting that one confirmed case of Ebola does not mean the country is experiencing an outbreak.

WHO Regional Director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, gave the reassurance in a video message posted on his X account on Wednesday night.

“One imported case does not by itself mean that Nigeria is experiencing an Ebola outbreak,” Mr Janabi said.

Mr Janabi said the agency is working with the Nigerian government and other partners to investigate the case, trace contacts, conduct laboratory testing, implement infection prevention and control, and protect health workers and communities.

He urged Nigerians to remain calm, stay informed and follow advice from public health authorities.

“There is no benefit in fear or misinformation,” he said. “What helps is early reporting, cooperation with the health authorities, and reliable information from reliable sources.”

Nigeria confirms case

Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease on Tuesday after a woman who recently travelled to the country was diagnosed at a private hospital in Abuja.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The woman developed symptoms after arriving in Nigeria and is currently receiving treatment in isolation in the Federal Capital Territory.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has activated its incident management system, while health authorities have begun contact tracing. The 44 identified contacts include healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts.

The Nigerian government said the case is currently being treated as an imported infection rather than community transmission.

WHO said Nigeria’s response demonstrates the importance of early detection and rapid public health action in preventing further transmission.

“Africa has considerable experience in responding to Ebola,” Mr Janabi said, adding that when cases are detected early, and contacts are followed closely, transmission can be stopped or interrupted.

Expert raises diagnosis concern

Meanwhile, virologist and Chairman of the West African National Academy of Scientists, Oyewale Tomori, raised concerns about the time taken to confirm the Nigerian case.

Speaking on Arise TV on Wednesday night, Mr Tomori said the gap between symptom onset and Ebola confirmation should prompt health authorities to strengthen their diagnostic response.

He said health workers should have a higher index of suspicion when treating travellers from areas where Ebola is circulating, rather than initially treating symptoms as more common illnesses such as malaria.

“If I hear somebody is coming from a country where Ebola is going on, or close to where Ebola has occurred, my first thought would be, is there Ebola?” he said.

Mr Tomori also urged authorities to prepare for the possibility that additional cases could emerge among the 44 contacts currently being monitored.

DRC outbreak continues

The Nigerian case comes amid a large Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where the Bundibugyo virus has continued to spread.

According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the DRC reported 9,552 confirmed cases and 4,602 related deaths as of 19 October, based on data up to 18 October.

The outbreak has affected 66 of 178 health zones across eight provinces, with Ituri remaining the most affected province.

Kenya has also recorded imported cases linked to the DRC outbreak, with health authorities reporting nine confirmed cases as of 20 October.

Mr Janabi said the evolving situation in the DRC is a reminder for countries across Africa to maintain strong surveillance, laboratory readiness and rapid response capacity.

World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Beyond tuition, extra school charges deepen financial strain on Nigerian parents
World.content:
By Qosim Suleiman, Aisha Yusufu, Ogalah Dunamis, Emmanuel Agbo, Manasseh Mbachii, Fortune Eromonsele, Kemi Adelagun

On the last Saturday of July, parents, teachers and pupils of Megaliy International School gathered at the Apo Resettlement Town Hall in Abuja for the school’s end-of-session and graduation ceremony.

For Mrs Kuburat, a parent at the school, the celebration came with an additional bill of almost N100,000. Three of her children were graduating at different levels. She said the school charged N20,000 for the child leaving nursery school, N25,000 for the one completing Junior Secondary School and N50,000 for the child finishing Senior Secondary School. Even in years when none of her children graduated, she said she paid N10,000 for each child towards the school’s end-of-session ceremony.

The payments reflect a broader concern among parents interviewed by PREMIUM TIMES across several Nigerian states: tuition is increasingly only one part of the cost of private education.

From Abuja to c and Benue, parents described additional bills for graduation ceremonies, textbooks, costumes, feeding, extra lessons, photographs, parties and other activities.

When the extra bills are taken together, and when they involve two or more children, parents said the additional charges are putting further pressure on household budgets.

In some schools, the payments are compulsory. In others, they are described as optional, but children whose parents do not pay may be excluded from ceremonies, activities or refreshments.

The complaints come as federal and state authorities increasingly move to curb school practices they say impose unnecessary costs on families.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In January, the federal government restricted graduation ceremonies to pupils completing Primary Six, JSS3 and SSS3 as part of education reforms intended to reduce financial pressure on parents.

Yet interviews conducted by PREMIUM TIMES suggest that additional school charges remain widespread, while regulation and enforcement vary considerably across states.

The management of Megaliy International School did not respond to PREMIUM TIMES’ request for an interview. At first, a member of the school’s management who identified herself as Mrs Udeoka said the principal lost his father and was not available for an interview. When contacted again on Tuesday, she said the school management has decided not to grant the interview request.

However, some school administrators defended the charges, saying they are to cater for the students and their parents at graduation ceremonies. They added that mandatory purchase of textbooks in schools was to maintain uniformity.

Graduation bills beyond tuition

In Lagos, Damilola Ojuolape, a caterer and mother living in Ojo, said her nine-year-old daughter’s primary school graduation became a major source of financial stress.

The school charged N45,000 for the graduation, she said, while pupils were also expected to participate in dance performances and parents were encouraged to purchase commemorative class portraits.

Beyond the school’s charge, Ms Ojuolape said she spent N154,000 preparing her daughter for the event, including buying a green dress to match the colour selected for the occasion, jewellery, a purse, sunglasses and a wristwatch.

Another Lagos parent, Tolulope Eludini, said her children attend Fluorescent Private School, where charges for graduation ceremonies and textbooks are included in the bill issued to parents at the beginning of the academic session.

Mrs Eludini said graduating pupils are also expected to pay for graduation attire, including suits and dresses, in addition to contributing towards the end-of-session celebration.

“I think the graduation fee is about N50,000,” she said, noting that the amount was separate from the cost of clothing and the graduation party.

In Katsina, the amounts can be considerably lower, but parents say the charges still matter when measured against their school fees and other household expenses.

Lawal Bishir said Maryam Majiri Memorial International School charged him N3,000 for his kindergarten daughter’s speech and prize-giving day while he was struggling to raise her N27,000 school fee.

Pupils in graduating classes paid N5,000, he said.

The school’s head of quality assurance, Ugwu Chinedu, confirmed that the payment determined who received the school’s refreshment package.

However, Mr Chinedu said the school has since stopped graduation ceremonies for nursery, primary and junior secondary pupils and now limits them to SS3 students.

Murtala Gidado, whose children attend Ayaks International School, a community-run secondary school in Katsina, said he previously paid N5,000 for an SS3 student. The amount represented one-quarter of the child’s N20,000 termly school fee.

But the proprietor, Abubakar Yunus, said the school charges a flat N6,000 per pupil per term plus N500 for examinations.

In Kaduna State, Ifeoma Habila, whose 11-year-old child attends Wusasa Children’s School in Zaria, said she paid N3,500 when her son completed primary school this year.

“My son told me that out of the N3,500 that the school is demanding, N2,000 would be used for speech and prize, graduation gown N1,000 and N500 for group picture,” Mrs Habila said.

Her second son, an eight-year-old Primary Four pupil at St Francis Academy in Wusasa, also paid N3,000 towards the school’s graduation activities, she said.

PREMIUM TIMES gathered that graduating pupils of ECWA Nursery and Primary School, Wusasa, were required to pay N8,000, while Rodah Academy in Kamazo GRA charged N5,000.

When ‘optional’ does not feel optional

Some parents said the difficulty is not simply how much schools charge, but what happens when they decide not to pay.

Mrs Eludini said the pressure at her children’s Lagos school does not always come directly from administrators.

She said the pressure sometimes comes from the children, who do not want to be left out of graduation activities.

“They don’t exactly tell you to come and pay,” she said. “But the children are already excited about the graduation and the party, so they begin to pressure you because they don’t want to be left out.”

Mrs Kuburat described a similar situation in Abuja, saying children whose parents did not make some payments could be excluded from refreshments and activities.

In Katsina, Mr Bishir said non-payment of the N3,000 charge at his daughter’s school did not affect the issuance of certificates, but the school used a headcount to determine which children would receive refreshments.

“If you pay, they will give you a refreshment package. If you don’t pay, you will not have a refreshment package,” he said.

Mr Gidado said the N5,000 graduation payment at his child’s school was described as optional, but a pupil whose parents did not pay could not attend the programme.

For him, that leaves parents weighing the financial cost against the emotional impact on their children.

“He might be affected emotionally while his contemporaries are celebrating and he is not celebrating,” he said.

The proprietor of the school Mr Gidado’s kids attended, Abubakar Yunus, said the graduation fee was for clothing, refreshments, souvenirs, invitations, venue costs and cultural activities.

He said the school eventually cancelled the ceremony when contributions proved insufficient.

Textbooks add another layer of cost

Graduation ceremonies are only one part of the additional expenses parents described. Several parents said schools also required them to buy textbooks directly from the school.

Lois Ugbede, an assistant editor at DUBAWA whose children attend a Catholic private school in Abuja, said parents are not allowed to buy notebooks or textbooks elsewhere.

PREMIUM TIMES contacted the school’s principal, Afoma Chukwu, a reverend sister, several times to seek her response to parents’ claims regarding additional charges, including alleged compulsory payments. However, the calls were not answered, and she had not responded as of the time of filing this report.

In Lagos, Mrs Eludini said parents at Fluorescent Private School are similarly required to buy their children’s textbooks from the school.

“Yes, we are required to buy the children’s textbooks directly from the school, and they don’t give us any options,” she said.

Although she had not compared the school’s prices with those charged by independent bookstores, she questioned the quality of some of the books supplied.

The two telephone numbers found for Fluorescent Private School, Lagos could not be reached for comments, despite repeated attempts.

Mr Bishir said parents of kindergarten pupils at Maryam Majiri Memorial International School in Katsina also have little flexibility.

“For those in kindergarten, it is compulsory. You must buy the pack book,” he said.

He said the school’s explanation was that pupils needed to use identical books with corresponding content and page numbers so that children would not fall behind during lessons.

For pupils in higher classes, he said, parents are encouraged to purchase from the school but some buy elsewhere to save money.

Not all the parents interviewed reported such restrictions. Mr Gidado said neither of the schools he deals with compelled him to purchase textbooks directly from them.

He estimated that he spent about N30,000 on books for one of his secondary-school children, which he sourced independently even though the school encouraged parents to buy internally.

Govt moves to reduce spending

The federal government has moved to reduce recurrent spending on learning materials.

In January, the government announced the adoption of reusable textbooks, saying the policy would allow learning materials to be used across multiple academic sessions and passed between siblings.

“This approach is intended to ensure that learning materials can be reused across multiple academic sessions,” the Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, had said.

Feeding, picnics and other bills

For some parents, the list extends beyond graduation ceremonies and books.

Emem Paul, whose children attend Ride-On Excellent Ville Nursery and Primary School on Lagos Island, said additional expenses included textbooks, a N10,000 December picnic and a feeding levy. She said pupils were not allowed to bring food from home.

“I had to insist that my children should be exempted from eating the school’s food or I would withdraw them from the school,” she said.

The school eventually granted her request and exempted her children from the feeding arrangement.

Messages reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES show that the school regularly sends parents detailed directives covering payments, pupils’ appearance and disciplinary requirements.

One notice instructed parents to pay school fees before resumption and said only pupils whose parents had completed the required advance payment would be admitted at the beginning of the term. The same notice said participation in the school’s end-of-session party was compulsory for all learners.

Such expenses, parents said, can make it difficult to determine the true cost of private schooling from tuition fees alone.

The proprietress, Latifat Ibrahim, told PREMIUM TIMES that the school lumps up the sum for textbooks alongside the school fees.

Ms Ibrahim added that payments for food and after-school lessons are compulsory.

“If children choose to bring food to the school, they won’t eat in the class because I don’t want other children looking at them,” she said.

But she stressed that the school’s extra-mural classes are optional. Only pupils whose parents opted for the lessons are allowed to participate.

On the December treat, Ms Ibrahim said parents were asked to pay because the event was organised for the pupils. She, however, noted that the payment was not compulsory and that only children whose parents approved their participation were included.

Governments move against costly graduation ceremonies

Concerns over the financial burden of school ceremonies have prompted interventions by the federal government and some state governments.

In January, the federal government announced that graduation ceremonies should be restricted to pupils completing Primary Six and students completing JSS3 and SSS3.

“Under the new guidelines, only pupils and students completing Primary 6, Junior Secondary School 3 (JSS3), and Senior Secondary School 3 (SSS3) are permitted to hold graduation ceremonies,” the government said.

The measure was announced alongside the reusable textbook policy and other reforms the government said were intended to reduce unnecessary financial pressure on families.

Some states have gone further.

In Ogun State, the government in June prohibited graduation ceremonies for nursery, kindergarten and other non-terminal classes in public and private schools.

Graduation ceremonies may be held for Primary Six, JSS3 and SSS3 pupils, but the government directed that such events should be modest and organised at no financial cost to parents or guardians.

The government also prohibited extravagant elements, including customised attire and other social displays that could create additional expenses for families.

The Anambra State Government exempted SSS3 students from the ban on graduation ceremonies, but said such ceremonies must remain optional and “must be conducted without any form of levy or financial demand on students and parents.”

The directive, issued on 24 July, applies to both public and private kindergarten, primary and secondary schools, including ceremonies described as “passing out” or “cross over.”

The government warned that schools that violate the directive could face sanctions, including closure. It said the measure was introduced to reduce the financial burden such ceremonies place on parents.

Benue State introduced similar restrictions in August 2025.

The state prohibited compulsory graduation ceremonies, particularly for kindergarten, nursery and basic school pupils, and also moved against customised educational materials that cannot be transferred from one pupil to another. The directive also prohibited compulsory extended lessons after regular school hours without parental consent.

Yet PREMIUM TIMES found that textbook charges remain part of the bills issued by some private schools in Makurdi, the Benue State capital.

One school administrator in Benue, who didn’t want to be named, expressed concerns about the impact of enforcement measures on pupils and their families, particularly where schools are sealed for non-compliance.

The administrator added that some schools were concerned about the financial implications of the policy, especially where they had already purchased textbooks for their pupils.

“When you seal a school, you also affect the children who are learning there. So, for us, what is the gap? Sealing a school, would there have been a better sanction for that than leaving the school sealed?” the administrator said.

Visits to Towering Tots School, NADI Schools, Kings Quiver and Tender Feet School in Markurdi showed that books were still included among charges presented to parents as the new academic session began. None of the schools responded to PREMIUM TIMES’ enquiries about the continued inclusion of textbook charges.

Complaints, but parents reluctant to write

In Katsina, a senior official of the state Ministry of Education familiar with the regulation of non-state schools said participation in and contributions towards graduation ceremonies must remain voluntary.

The official requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak publicly.

“You cannot force it on pupils and say everybody must contribute,” he said.

The official said the ministry had received verbal complaints from parents about graduation charges and compulsory textbook purchases.

But, according to him, many parents who complain verbally are reluctant to put their complaints in writing because they fear possible repercussions.

He said state regulations do not authorise schools to compel parents to purchase textbooks exclusively from them.

The official also said an inspection team had been deployed to examine compliance among private and community schools.

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently confirm the inspection exercise.

In Lagos and the Federal Capital Territory, officials did not provide responses to PREMIUM TIMES’ findings.

The spokesperson for the Department of Education, Federal Capital Territory Administration, Kabir Musa, directed our reporter to the Director of Quality Assurance, Hajarat Alayande.

Mrs Alayande declined to comment, saying she needed permission from the Education Secretary before speaking.

The Lagos State Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Jamiu Alli-Balogun, did not respond to phone calls and messages seeking his comments.

Private schools defend charges

Private school administrators who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES defended the additional charges, saying they cover the cost of school activities and other operating expenses.

The Vice-Principal, Academics, of St Martin de Porres Schools, Ozochi Anthonia, said graduating pupils paid between N3,000 and N3,500 to cover gowns, certificates and basic refreshments.

A private school proprietor in Kaduna, who requested anonymity, said schools depend almost entirely on internally generated revenue.

“Some private schools operate from rented buildings and have to pay rent. They also pay government taxes which are becoming overwhelming, buy school supplies and pay staff salaries,” the proprietor said.

“The running cost of a private school in Nigeria is very high. These schools receive no government funding; they fund themselves.”

The proprietor said the sale of books, uniforms and writing materials by schools could also make purchases more convenient for parents.

Customised books, the proprietor argued, could help schools maintain standards and protect parents from purchasing pirated copies.

The proprietor called on governments to provide greater support to private schools, including staff training and reductions in taxes and regulatory charges.

Mary Odiba, proprietress of Wusasa Children’s School in Kaduna State, said the charges were necessary to cover the cost of organising school activities.

She said her school charges N2,500 per child for graduation, speech and prize-giving activities and uses the money for pupils’ welfare during the events.

“If we want to organise a speech and prize-giving day and graduation, we have to rent chairs and canopies, provide refreshments for the children and buy prizes for outstanding pupils,” she said.

Mrs Odiba also said parents were encouraged to purchase books from the school for convenience and to reduce the risk of buying pirated copies.

Maureen Nwaeke-Egbim, proprietress of JPEC Chimel Academy in GRA, Zaria, Kaduna State, said graduation parties at her school are initiated by pupils and parents.

She said the school forms a committee comprising teachers and parents to plan such events.

“What the school does is to support, while the parents fund the whole thing,” she said.

On textbooks, Mrs Nwaeke-Egbim said books are available for sale at the school, but parents are free to buy elsewhere, provided they obtain the required editions.

“The aim is to avoid pirated copies and ensure pupils have the required books, so that in a class of 30 students, at least 20 to 25 have the right textbooks,” she said.

Private schools association responds

The Katsina State chairperson of the National Association of Proprietors of Private Schools (NAPPS), Mansir Sani, said compulsory graduation fees are not standard practice among most member schools.

“I won’t tell you it is 100 per cent, but the majority of our schools do not charge anything called a graduation fee,” he said.

Mr Sani said most schools charge standard examination fees rather than separate and excessive graduation fees.

“There is no compulsion in making students buy textbooks,” he said, explaining what he described as the association’s official position.

He also argued that private schools have tried to avoid increasing school fees at the same pace as taxes, regulatory charges and other operating costs.

Kano tightens regulation of private school fees

Beyond graduation and textbook charges, some states are also tightening oversight of private school fees generally.

The Kano State House of Assembly in August passed the Kano State Private and Voluntary Institutions Board (Amendment) Bill, 2026, introducing additional requirements governing school fee increases.

Among other provisions, the legislation requires consultation with parents through Parent-Teacher Associations before private schools increase their fees.

Mustapha Yahaya, director of Special Duties at the Kano State Private and Voluntary Institutions Board, told PREMIUM TIMES that the new provisions were intended to prevent schools from increasing fees without notice and consultation.

“The work of this board is to regulate private and voluntary institutions,” he said.

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify before publication the official’s claim that the governor had assented to the amendment on 4 August.

Parents feel the pressure

For many of the parents interviewed for this report, the debate over what schools need to operate ultimately meets a simpler reality: there is only so much money available to pay the bills.

Ms Ugbede said she had never defaulted on her children’s school payments, but for the first time this year, financial constraints forced her to pay their fees later than she normally would.

Mrs Eludini said her family has also had to postpone some payments.

“We’ve had to delay payment. Sometimes that’s the only option,” she said.

She recalled an occasion when parents at her children’s school collectively challenged an attempted increase in tuition.

“The parents came together and challenged it,” she said. “I think they even petitioned the Lagos State Government, and eventually the school brought the fees back down.”

But graduation fees, textbooks, feeding, clothing, parties and other charges are more fragmented and can be harder for parents to challenge collectively.

For families with more than one child, the costs accumulate quickly.

And while school owners argue that many of the charges pay for legitimate services and rising operating expenses, the experiences of parents interviewed by PREMIUM TIMES show that the financial burden of private education increasingly extends beyond the figure written beside “school fees” on a child’s bill.

World.title: Why Nigeria’s improved growth forecasts still aren’t enough, By Posi Olatubosun
World.content:
A growth rate measures the pace at which total output expands, not how evenly that growth is distributed. Nigeria’s population grows by approximately 2.5 per cent annually. With the economy expanding at just over 4 per cent, output per person increases by perhaps 1.5 to 2 per cent a year. At that rate, average income per capita would take more than three decades to double. This arithmetic explains why headline growth and household experience can diverge so sharply. Given Nigeria’s demographic profile, growth closer to 7 or 8 per cent, sustained over many years, is needed to make a decisive impact on poverty and unemployment.

Nigeria’s economy is expanding. Why, then, do so many Nigerians feel that they are making little progress? This question arises amid a week of encouraging forecasts. The International Monetary Fund has raised its projection for Nigeria’s growth in 2026 to 4.2 per cent and expects growth of 4.3 per cent in 2027. In its latest Nigeria Development Update, the World Bank projects growth of 4.3 per cent this year, rising to an average of 4.4 per cent in 2027 and 2028.

Official data indicate that the economy expanded by 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, up from 3.89 per cent in the first quarter. These are the strongest figures in years. Nevertheless, public service workers recently staged a three-day warning strike over economic hardship, while ActionAid Nigeria has described the current rate of growth as insufficient. Both perspectives can be valid simultaneously. Nigeria’s economy is growing, but not yet rapidly or broadly enough for most people to benefit from this.

The improvement merits recognition. Growth exceeding 4 per cent after years of hovering between 2 and 3 per cent indicates that reforms are beginning to yield results. The foreign exchange market is more orderly, reserves have been rebuilt, inflation has eased from its peak, and oil production has improved. Upgrades from both Bretton Woods institutions reinforce the view that Nigeria is pursuing a credible course. For investors, this credibility is significant: it reduces perceived risk and encourages long-term commitments. Precision is essential, however.

A growth rate measures the pace at which total output expands, not how evenly that growth is distributed. Nigeria’s population grows by approximately 2.5 per cent annually. With the economy expanding at just over 4 per cent, output per person increases by perhaps 1.5 to 2 per cent a year. At that rate, average income per capita would take more than three decades to double. This arithmetic explains why headline growth and household experience can diverge so sharply. Given Nigeria’s demographic profile, growth closer to 7 or 8 per cent, sustained over many years, is needed to make a decisive impact on poverty and unemployment.

The first reason economic growth has not yet been widely felt is its composition. Much of Nigeria’s expansion has been driven by services such as finance, telecommunications, and trade, as well as by a recovering oil sector. These activities are important, but they generate relatively few jobs per naira of output. Agriculture and manufacturing, which employ substantially more people, have faced challenges including insecurity, high input costs, and unreliable electricity. Growth concentrated in capital-intensive or urban sectors will increase GDP more rapidly than it raises household incomes.

What would make growth more inclusive? The World Bank’s plan to mobilise approximately $5.79 billion in private financing, with a projected 850,000 jobs, points in the right direction. Such initiatives should prioritise sectors with strong employment potential, including agro-processing, light manufacturing, construction, logistics, and digital services that extend beyond Lagos and Abuja.

The second reason is the lingering impact of past inflation. Although inflation has eased considerably, a slower rate of price increases does not reverse the earlier surge. Food, transport, and rent prices remain far above their levels of three years ago, while many salaries have not kept pace. Workers who feel poorer are not mistaken; their real incomes have eroded faster than the economy has grown. Restoring purchasing power will take time, even if prices remain stable.

The third reason is that the gains of stability have not fully reached small businesses. Manufacturers and traders need affordable credit, reliable power, and secure transport routes to expand. Until recently, interest rates were punishingly high, and many firms still find bank lending out of reach. The Central Bank’s recent rate cut may help, but transmission takes time. Without expanding enterprises, job creation will lag behind GDP growth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

What would make growth more inclusive? The World Bank’s plan to mobilise approximately $5.79 billion in private financing, with a projected 850,000 jobs, points in the right direction. Such initiatives should prioritise sectors with strong employment potential, including agro-processing, light manufacturing, construction, logistics, and digital services that extend beyond Lagos and Abuja.

Ultimately, Nigerians will judge growth by jobs, incomes, and the cost of living, not by forecasts from Washington. Four per cent growth is a foundation, not a destination. The task now is to build on it, turning stability into investment, investment into employment, and employment into rising living standards. The forecasts show Nigeria is moving in the right direction. The challenge is to move faster and bring more Nigerians along.

Public investment should focus on the binding constraints that impede these sectors. Electricity remains the most significant. Few interventions would increase productivity across the economy as rapidly as a reliable power supply. Security is equally critical. Farmers who cannot safely access their fields will not increase output, regardless of how favourable the macroeconomic environment may be. Rural insecurity has disrupted food production, increased prices, and displaced people from productive activity. Investment in security and rural infrastructure is therefore an economic policy priority, not merely a matter of public order.

Human capital is the third priority. A growing young population is an asset only if it has the skills employers need. Spending on education, vocational training and health is not a cost to be cut when budgets are tight; it determines whether Nigeria’s demographic dividend becomes a dividend or a burden. Risks remain. The IMF has warned that rising energy and food prices, global disputes and possible market corrections linked to artificial intelligence threaten the global outlook. Higher oil prices may help Nigeria’s revenue, but they also raise domestic fuel and transport costs. The pre-election period adds its own pressure. Politically driven spending, rather than productive need, could reignite inflation and undo hard-won stability.

Ultimately, Nigerians will judge growth by jobs, incomes, and the cost of living, not by forecasts from Washington. Four per cent growth is a foundation, not a destination. The task now is to build on it, turning stability into investment, investment into employment, and employment into rising living standards. The forecasts show Nigeria is moving in the right direction. The challenge is to move faster and bring more Nigerians along.

Posi Olatubosun is a UK-based academic faculty member in accounting and finance.

World.title: Nigeria’s first Ebola patient is diplomat’s wife who holidayed in Uganda — Africa CDC
World.content:
Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, for a holiday, the Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Jean Kaseya, has said.

Mr Kaseya said the woman, originally from Uganda but resident in Abuja, developed symptoms three days after returning to Nigeria on 3 October.

Providing details of the patient’s medical history, Mr Kaseya said the woman first developed symptoms on 6 October and initially sought treatment at a private hospital, believing she had malaria.

She subsequently visited another private hospital, where she was admitted on 11 October after her condition failed to improve.

“She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th,” Mr Kaseya told the BBC’s Newshour programme.

Details of patient’s travel, condition

According to a report by the BBC, Nigeria’s Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, confirmed that the 42-year-old woman spent two and a half weeks in Kampala before returning to Abuja through Ethiopia, where she had a two-hour stopover in Addis Ababa.

Mr Pate said the patient, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, was stable and responding to treatment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“She’s stable, she’s improving,” he said.

He said health authorities had identified 44 people who came into contact with the patient and were taking measures to prevent further transmission.

“Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible,” he told the BBC.

The minister explained that none of the identified contacts, including the person who travelled with the patient, had developed symptoms.

He added that the woman had remained in Abuja since returning to Nigeria.

Mr Pate said public health authorities were alerted on Monday, 19 October, after the patient’s condition failed to improve.

Her Ebola diagnosis was confirmed the following day after three laboratory tests.

Ebola has an incubation period of two to 21 days, meaning an infected person may not develop symptoms until several days or weeks after exposure.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. Symptoms can include fever, headache, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Conflicting accounts of patient’s travel history

The latest information from Nigerian authorities and the Africa CDC differs from an earlier account provided by Uganda’s Ministry of Health.

Ugandan authorities had described the patient as a Nigerian national who travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for business and only passed through Uganda while returning home.

The Ugandan government maintained that the country had no active confirmed Ebola cases and that the woman’s transit through Uganda did not establish that she contracted the virus there.

However, Mr Pate said Nigerian authorities were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the patient’s complete travel history and determine where she might have contracted the infection.

“We respect our sister nation of Uganda,” he said. “We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together.”

Mr Kaseya also called for greater information-sharing among African countries to support investigations into the patient’s movements and possible exposure.

He urged Western countries to avoid imposing travel restrictions, stressing that international collaboration and solidarity were essential to containing the outbreak.

Regional outbreak

Nigeria’s confirmed case comes amid an ongoing Ebola outbreak linked to the Bundibugyo virus in the DRC, with infections also reported in other countries.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported more than 9,500 cases and 4,602 deaths in the DRC as of 19 October.

Kenya, which confirmed its first imported case in early October, reported a ninth case on Tuesday. Its health ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster, with the eight surviving patients responding well to supportive care.

The first Kenyan patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. The development has heightened regional concerns about the movement of the virus across borders.

Uganda also recorded Ebola infections earlier in 2026 but subsequently declared its outbreak over after completing the required period without a new confirmed case.

Nigeria’s current case has renewed attention on the risks posed by international travel during an outbreak, as public health authorities work to establish the source of infection and prevent further transmission.

Health authorities have advised the public to maintain good hand hygiene, avoid contact with the bodily fluids of suspected cases and promptly report possible exposure to public health officials.

Nigeria draws on 2014 experience

Nigeria previously experienced an Ebola outbreak in 2014 after an infected traveller arrived in Lagos from Liberia.

The outbreak resulted in 20 cases, including 19 laboratory-confirmed cases and one probable case, with eight deaths.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) declared Nigeria free of Ebola transmission on 20 October 2014 after the country completed 42 days without a new case.

Meanwhile, Mr Pate expressed confidence in the country’s ability to contain the latest case, citing improvements in disease surveillance, laboratory capacity and the availability of trained epidemiologists.

He said Nigeria’s previous experience with Ebola was one reason for confidence in the current response.

“We have done it in 2014, and we have good public health institutions,” Mr Pate said.

World.title: Lawal urges Nigerians to learn to live together peacefully
World.content:
Zamfara State Governor, Dauda Lawal has stated that Nigerians must learn to live together peacefully, support one another and recognise their shared identity, regardless of ethnic or religious differences.

Lawal made the statement when he received the Igbo Community Association in Zamfara State at the Government House, Gusau, on Tuesday.

The governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to peaceful coexistence, equal treatment and cooperation among residents of diverse ethnic and religious backgrounds in the state, stressing that unity was essential for national development and harmony.

In the course of the visit, the association pledged to vote massively to return the governor to Government House to enable him to continue with the projects already started across the state.

The Igbo community delegation was led by the President-General of the association, Mr Maduka Ezemeka, who pledged massive mobilisation of the Igbo people in the state to vote for Governor Lawal in next year’s governorship election.

In his remarks, the governor recalled his long-standing relationship with members of the Igbo community, dating back to his childhood, when he interacted with Igbo businessmen and artisans who worked and lived within his ancestral home in Gusau.

He said such relationships demonstrate that Nigerians can prosper together when they embrace mutual respect, understanding and cooperation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Lawal commended the community for the visit and kind words about his administration, describing the Igbo people as brothers and partners in the development of Zamfara.

Ezemeka appealed to the government to provide financial support in the form of loans and credit facilities to support their businesses amid the prevailing economic challenges.

He also appealed for the provision of a functional bus to facilitate the association’s activities, explaining that vehicles previously provided by successive administrations were no longer in good working condition.

Governor Lawal pledged to provide the community with a bus to facilitate its activities and promised to intervene in issues affecting community members who were disengaged from teaching service in the state.

On the community’s request for business support, Governor Lawal encouraged the leadership to submit a formal proposal outlining the area of assistance required.

He said he would study the proposal with his team to determine how the government could support their businesses, including exploring possible partnerships with financial institutions and other relevant interventions.

Mr Lawal noted that access to proper documentation for landed properties could help business owners use their assets as collateral to obtain credit facilities.

He explained that his administration introduced property recertification to enable owners to regularise their documents and improve their access to financial opportunities.

On the concerns raised over disengagement of some Igbo community members who worked as teachers in the state, Lawal expressed surprise, saying he had previously directed the former Commissioner for Education to resolve the matter.

He directed the Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Abubakar Nakwada, to revisit the issue in collaboration with the Commissioner for Education and representatives of the affected teachers.

He directed the officials to investigate the facts, take necessary steps, and report back on the resolution of the matter.

World.title: Stop reacting, start protecting: Inside Nigeria’s fight to keep children safe in schools
World.content:
By Adesina Wahab, Elizabeth Osayande & Ifunanya Ndigwe

When a child leaves home in the morning with a school bag strapped to his back, the unspoken promise is simple: he will learn, grow, and return home safely. In Nigeria today, that promise is broken too often.

•From left, President, All Nigeria Confederation of Principals of Secondary Schools (ANCOPSS), Lagos State, Mr. Olushola Masheyi walls,” she said.By 2021, the Ministry of Finance (representing ANCOPSS National President, Dr Robert Okorie); Executive Director, Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism, convened a high-level meeting Mrs Alaka; Chairman, Education Writers’ Association of Nigeria (EWAN), Mr. Mojeed Alabi; Lagos State Police Commissioner, Mr Fatai with Defence, Police, DSS, Office Tijani (representing Inspector-General of Police, Mr. Tunji Disu); National Coordinator, Financing Safe Schools in Nigeria, Hajia Haliof the National Security Adviser, ma Iliya and Chairman, Nigeria Union of Teachers, Lagos State Wing, Comrade Hassan Akintoye (representing NUT National President, Mr. Titus Amba) at the 2026 EWAN National Summit on School Safety in Lagos

From Chibok in 2014 where schoolgirls were taken from their dormitories, to Dapchi, to Oriire in Oyo State, to corps members attacked in Imo, to classrooms emptied by sit-at-home order in the South-East and farmer-herder clashes in Benue, Oyo and Ogun – the classroom has become a frontline.

It was against this sobering reality that journalists, security chiefs, government officials, teachers and principals converged on Ikeja, Lagos, for the 7th Annual Summit of the Education Writers Association of Nigeria, EWAN.

The theme was deliberate and urgent: School Under Threat: From Reactive Responses to Sustainable Protection.

Chairing the summit was the Chairman, Governing Board of the National Universities Commission, NUC, Prof. Oluwatoyin Ogundipe, represented by Prof. Joseph Awoyinfa. The keynote, on behalf of the Inspector-General of Police, Mr. Tunji Disu, was delivered by the Lagos State Commissioner of Police, Mr. Fatai Tijani. But beyond titles and protocol, the message was one: Nigeria must stop waiting for the next abduction before it acts.

The Chairperson’s Warning: Don’t stop at the press statement.

Prof. Ogundipe, as chairperson, set the tone. He did not want another conference of communiques. He challenged education journalists to change the way school safety is reported.

“When authorities announce new security measures, our reporting should not end with the announcement. When funds are allocated, we should investigate whether they are used as intended, and when investigations produce recommendations, we should return to determine what has changed,” he said.

“Our ultimate objective is not to embarrass institutions. It is to ensure that they fulfil their responsibilities.”

For a country where security votes and intervention funds often disappear into vague budget lines, it was a pointed call for accountability journalism.

“Children are not safe until every school is safe”

If Ogundipe gave the framework, EWAN Chairman, Mojeed Alabi, gave the conscience.

Standing before his colleagues, Alabi began with a line that would echo through the hall all day: Children are not safe until every school is safe.

“No parent should have to choose between a child’s education and their safety. No teacher should have to teach under the shadow of abduction, and no community should have to watch its future disappear because its schools have become targets,” he said.

In a deeply personal address titled: Why Journalism Matters in the Fight Against Violent Attacks on Schools, Alabi traced the pattern Nigerians have come to know too well: an attack happens, government issues a statement, security agencies announce interventions, public outrage rises, then attention moves elsewhere – until the next attack.

“We must therefore ask: how many more warnings, disrupted school terms and grieving families will it take before school safety becomes an unquestionable national priority?” he asked.

His answer was journalism that makes the invisible visible. Not just reporting the number of children abducted, but asking whether the school had a functional emergency response system. Whether teachers had safety training. Whether there was a channel to report threats. How many school days were lost. Whether survivors returned to school. What support they got.

“Behind every school attack are human lives. Children must never be reduced to statistics or used merely to provoke sympathy. Their stories deserve accuracy, dignity, sensitivity and appropriate protection of their identities,” Alabi said.

“We cannot promise that journalism alone will end attacks on schools but journalism can ensure that warning signs are not ignored, public resources are scrutinised, failures are exposed, promises are tracked and affected communities are heard.”

It was a call for newsrooms to invest in expertise, collaborate with researchers, and use radio, television, newspapers and digital platforms to reach communities often excluded from national conversations.

The IGP’s Question: How can a child learn in fear?

When CP Fatai Tijani rose to deliver the IGP’s keynote, he came with a question that silenced the room.

“How can a child concentrate on learning when the fear of violence, abduction or other security threats is constantly present?”

For IGP Tunji Disu, school safety is no longer a peripheral police duty it is national security.
