World.title: Liberian Senate’s Own Papers Bury Its Denial
World.content:
MONROVIA – On Monday, the Liberian Senate under the leadership of Pro Temp Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, called FrontPageAfrica’s reporting on a staff salary plan “false,” “misleading” and “fabricated,” and demanded a retraction. What the Senate did not do is more telling. It did not dispute a single figure, did not challenge the authenticity of a single page, and did not say the plan does not exist.

By Rodney D. Sieh

It could not. The plan is on Senate letterhead.



What the documents say

On October 7, 2026, the Senate Committee on Rules, Order and Administration signed a “Proposal for the Standardization of Remuneration for Civil Servants and Personal Staffers of the Senate.” Six of the seven committee members signed it, including Chairman J. Gbleh-bo Brown of Maryland County and Vice-Chairman Johnathan B. Sogbe. On October 12, Senator Brown sent it to President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence. He asked for leadership’s endorsement and for the plan to be included in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget.

The numbers are the committee’s own:

* The Legal Counsel’s monthly pay rises from US$1,704 to US$2,920, an increase of US$1,216, or 71 percent.

* The HR Director rises from US$1,500 to US$2,000, and the Deputy Legal Counsel from US$1,500 to US$1,991.

* Senators’ chiefs of office staff rise from US$1,021 to US$1,500.

* The total annual cost is US$792,552. The covered payroll grows from US$1,830,648 to US$2,623,200, an increase of 43 percent.

The committee’s final recommendation asks the Senate leadership and plenary to approve US$792,552 for the 2027 budget. That is not a rumor. It is a funding request.

A denial that answers a different question

The Senate’s statement rests on one claim: the plenary never voted. That is true, and it is beside the point.

A proposal that six senators have signed, that the Pro Tempore commissioned, and that is formally headed for the national budget is news. Proposals are exactly when the public should hear about them, before the money is spent rather than after.

The statement also confirms the most important fact. It says the review was “mandated by the President Pro Tempore.” By the Senate’s own account, this plan began in the Pro Tempore’s office.

The fine print the statement leaves out

The statement describes the plan as a review “across the three branches of Government.” The documents cover only Senate staff. The other branches appear only as benchmarks for raising Senate pay.

The statement says the plan has not been “acted upon.” Yet section 2.0 of the committee’s report, titled “What Has Been Accomplished,” says the committee “has completed” standardizing fuel and gas benefits for directors, deputy directors, assistant directors, secretaries, drivers and other staff. The Senate should explain whether those benefits are already being paid.

The statement also accuses this newspaper of failing to verify the facts “through the Senate official spokesperson.” The verification is the documents themselves: the Senate’s letterhead, its committee’s signatures and its own arithmetic.

“Harmony” for whom?

The committee says the 2019 National Remuneration and Standardization Act requires the plan. It quotes the Act’s goal of narrowing “the inequality gap in government.” The tables point the other way.

The Legal Counsel’s raise alone, US$1,216 a month, is larger than the entire current salary of nine of the twelve central administration positions listed. At the bottom of the scale, the Executive Secretary gets US$96.

Today the Legal Counsel earns about three times as much as the Executive Secretary. Under the proposal, that would rise to about four and a half times. In dollar terms, the gap between them nearly doubles, from US$1,153 to US$2,273 a month.

A plan written to narrow inequality would widen it.

The comparison the Senate calls “emotional”

The Senate objects to comparisons with the national minimum wage and calls them “emotional.” They are arithmetic. Labour Minister Cooper W. Kruah has reminded employers that Liberia’s Decent Work Act sets a minimum monthly wage of US$143, and he has warned firms caught paying less.

The proposed raise for the Legal Counsel is roughly eight and a half times that minimum wage. The proposed salary is about twenty times it. That is not the language of emotion. It is the reality of a country where many families decide daily between food, school fees and medicine.

The staff have a case, and that is not the issue

Fairness requires saying this clearly: many Senate employees are underpaid, and their complaints are real. In December, staff spokesperson Roosevelt Tulay told reporters there had been no salary increment for Senate staff since 2015. He pointed out that the Senate’s own budget had grown from US$14.6 million to a proposed US$16.4 million for Fiscal Year 2026, while staff salaries stayed flat, and he warned of civil disobedience.

A serious reform would start at the bottom, with the clerks, secretaries and drivers. This plan gives its biggest dollars to the top. And the Senate’s answer to public scrutiny has been to call accurate reporting “fabricated.”

What the Senate should do

If the Senate believes the plan is sound, it should defend it in public. It should publish the full proposal and the attached spreadsheet, explain the 71 percent raise for its Legal Counsel, disclose whether the fuel benefits are already being paid, and commit to a recorded plenary vote.

What it should not do is demand that a newspaper retract a story built on the Senate’s own signed pages. FrontPageAfrica stands by its reporting.

World.title: Liberia: MCSS Students Storm Capitol Hill, Petition House Over Teacher Crisis and ‘Administrative Lapses’
World.content:
MONROVIA — Frustrated by prolonged school disruptions, students of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS) on Tuesday took their grievances to Capitol Hill, demanding urgent government intervention in the crisis affecting their teachers and schools.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Chanting, “We want to learn too,” the students petitioned the House of Representatives to enforce the implementation of a March 27 agreement between the government and MCSS, investigate allegations of intimidation and administrative interference, and increase funding for public schools.



The protest came as a 24-hour ultimatum issued by the Monrovia Consolidated School System Students Union (MCSS-SU) expired on October 20. Hours after the demonstration, the government announced that 201 outstanding volunteer teachers would be enrolled on the national payroll effective October 2026 and that eligible teachers would receive retroactive salaries following the October salary payment.

The government’s announcement marks a response to one of the central grievances underlying the dispute, but questions remain over the implementation of the agreement, outstanding teacher welfare concerns, and the broader administrative problems students say continue to disrupt their education.

Students Take Grievances to Capitol Hill

Thousands of students gathered between the University of Liberia and the Capitol Building, where lawmakers were conducting legislative business, to draw attention to the prolonged challenges confronting the public school system.

The demonstration, which lasted more than two hours, was organized under the banner of the MCSS Students Union. The students said unresolved teacher welfare issues and administrative disputes had deprived them of valuable instructional time.

In a formal petition signed at William V. S. Tubman High School on 12th Street, the union outlined four major demands and warned that it would proceed with peaceful protest action if authorities failed to respond.

The petition was received by several lawmakers, including Nimba County District No. 2 Representative Nyan Flomo, Montserrado County District No. 8 Representative Prince A. Toles, who chairs the House Committee on Claims and Petitions; River Cess County District No. 2 Representative Steve Tequah, chairman of the House Committee on Youth and Sports; and Montserrado County District No. 4 Representative Michael Thomas.

The petition was ultimately handed to Representative Flomo after the students initially rejected presenting it to Representative Toles.

Following its receipt, the petition was read during Tuesday’s plenary session of the House and referred to the Committees on Education and Claims and Petitions. The committees were instructed to report back to the plenary within one week.

Students Demand Implementation of March Agreement

At the center of the students’ demands is the full implementation of the Memorandum of Understanding signed between the government and MCSS on March 27, 2026.

The union said unresolved teacher welfare issues under the agreement continue to threaten the delivery of education across public schools in Monrovia and its environs.

The students are calling on the government to fulfill its commitments, arguing that continued delays have placed an unfair burden on learners who depend on public education.

They warned that their patience should not be interpreted as acceptance of prolonged school disruptions.

“Our patience must not be mistaken for weakness, and our commitment to peace must not be used to justify continued inaction while students’ education remains at risk,” the union stated in its petition.

Union Seeks Dismissal of MCSS Official

The students are also demanding the dismissal of MCSS Assistant Superintendent Emmanuel Kyne Robertson, accusing him of inciting students, disrupting classes and threatening learners.

The petition further alleged that individuals had been sent to attack the president of the MCSS Students Union.

The union called for an investigation into the alleged incident and measures to protect student leaders from intimidation.

The allegations against Robertson have not been independently established in the information provided for this report. He should be given an opportunity to respond to the claims.

The union also accused some school administrators of involving students in personal, administrative and political disputes within the education system.

“Students must not be used as instruments to advance anyone’s personal, administrative, or political interests,” the petition stated.

The students called for greater respect for legitimate student leadership and urged authorities to resolve internal disagreements without disrupting classes or compromising students’ safety.

Budget Increase, Better School Facilities Demanded

Beyond the teacher crisis, the union is calling for an increase in the MCSS budget and greater transparency in the use of public education funds.

While acknowledging ongoing renovations at Boatswain Junior and Senior High School, G.W. Gibson Senior High School and Matilda Newport Junior High School, the students said numerous other schools continue to face poor infrastructure, inadequate classrooms, insufficient furniture and unsanitary conditions.

They argued that addressing teacher welfare alone would not resolve the challenges confronting public education without corresponding investments in school facilities and learning resources.

The union said its demands are intended to restore teaching and learning, protect students, strengthen accountability and improve conditions across the school system.

It formally notified authorities of its intention to organize peaceful protests if its concerns remain unresolved.

Government Moves to Enroll 201 Volunteer Teachers

Hours after the students’ demonstration, the Government of Liberia issued a statement acknowledging concerns raised by MCSS teachers over employment regularization, outstanding salaries and compensation adjustments.

The government said consultations involving the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, the Civil Service Agency and MCSS had resulted in a decision to enroll the remaining 201 volunteer teachers on the national payroll effective October 2026.

According to the statement, the affected teachers will receive their October salaries as formally employed government teachers, ending their volunteer status.

The decision will bring the total number of verified MCSS volunteer teachers enrolled on the national payroll to 409.

“The Government recognizes the teachers’ invaluable contributions to the country’s educational system and remains committed to addressing their concerns through concrete administrative decisions, responsible financial measures and reforms,” the statement said.

The government also announced that retroactive salaries owed to eligible teachers would be paid one week after the October salary payment, in accordance with their respective eligibility categories.

It described the decision as evidence of its commitment to fulfilling its obligations and ensuring that affected teachers receive their compensation.

Salary Adjustments Still Under Review

On demands for salary adjustments by currently employed MCSS teachers, the government said the concerns would be addressed through an ongoing government-wide salary structure reform.

According to the statement, the proposed reform is intended to correct existing salary disparities, promote fairness and equity, and establish a transparent and sustainable compensation system across the public service.

However, the government did not provide a specific implementation date for the broader salary reform in the statement.

It appealed to public school teachers to remain calm and return to their classrooms while the relevant institutions implement the agreed measures.

The government also urged MCSS students to remain in school and continue their academic activities without interruption, reaffirming its commitment to constructive engagement with teachers and strengthening the country’s education system.

Questions Remain Over Implementation

Although the government’s announcement addresses the employment status of the 201 outstanding volunteer teachers and provides for the settlement of eligible retroactive salaries, the broader dispute involves additional concerns raised by teachers, students and school administrators.

The students’ petition places responsibility on the government and education authorities to ensure that commitments are implemented and that administrative disagreements do not continue to deprive learners of classroom instruction.

The House committees’ one-week deadline to report back to plenary could provide an opportunity for lawmakers to examine the students’ allegations, assess the implementation of the March 27 agreement and determine what further action may be necessary.

For the students who took their demands to Capitol Hill, the immediate concern remains the restoration of uninterrupted teaching and learning.

Their message was direct: while government officials and school administrators negotiate over salaries, employment status and administrative control, students should not continue to pay the price through lost instructional time.

World.title: Mpulungu Kapenta traders hail Solar-powered dryer support
World.content:
Women involved in drying Kapenta in Mpulungu District have thanked the Fish for African Caribbean and Pacific Countries Project (FISH4ACP) for supporting them with a solar-powered dryer, saying it will help improve the quality of their Kapenta.

Twazwane Women’s group chairperson Callen Nakazwe said the equipment will provide a more reliable and hygienic way to dry Kapenta, a small fish that is an important source of food and income in the area.

Mpulungu, Ms Nakazwe said traditional drying methods have for a long time left the Kapenta exposed to dust, insects and changing weather conditions, which may affect its quality.

She disclosed that the solar-powered dryer is expected to help protect the fish during the drying process and produce a cleaner, more consistent product.

‘’We are very grateful for the welcome support because it is a practical investment in our work and livelihoods as improved drying will reduce losses and help us preserve more of the Kapenta as we process it,’’ she disclosed

Ms Nakazwe explained that better-quality fish will also attract buyers and strengthen the women’s ability to compete in local markets especially during the rainy season periods when weather conditions make open-air processing difficult.

She added that the dryer will make their work more efficient while helping them maintain better standards for the Kapenta fish they sell.

The women also expressed hope that the equipment will encourage more people in their communities to adopt improved fish-handling practices.

Ms Nakazwe said they were grateful for the support and pledged to use the dryer responsibly and also called for continued training and support to help them operate and maintain the equipment effectively.

The women said the solar-powered dryer offers an opportunity to improve Kapenta quality, increase the value of their work and support their livelihoods.

FISH4ACP supports sustainable and inclusive development in fisheries and aquaculture value chains.

Its assistance to the women is intended to strengthen Kapenta processing in Mpulungu District.

World.title: Government prioritises tailings Dam safety
World.content:
The Government has identified tailings dam safety as a priority, calling for increased training of regulators and mining operators to strengthen the management of these facilities.

Minerals Regulations Commission Director Mine Inspections and Audits Elite Mhone warned that climate change and increasingly heavy rainfall heighten the risk of tailings dam failures.

Mr Mhone was speaking during a plenary session at the Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka.

He said that unlike conventional water dams, tailings facilities continue to grow as mining waste accumulates, requiring ongoing monitoring, stronger safety measures and improved regulatory oversight to protect surrounding communities and the environment.

“The size of rainfall we receive now is not the same as rainfall that was being received in 1964, right now we have got a lot of rainfall,” Mr Mhone

Mr Mhone further said that Zambia’s tailings dam management and safety standards remain inadequate, raising concerns as the country targets annual copper production of three million tonnes.

He has since called for stricter regulatory inspections, independent engineering oversight, a national tailings dam registry and greater accountability for mining companies.

And Zambia Environmental Agency (ZEMA) Acting Director Licensing and Compliance Constantino Mweembela said mining companies should strengthen water quality monitoring and engage communities to protect shared water resources in increasingly water-stressed areas.

“Environmental impact assessments must go beyond regulatory compliance to include practical measures for preventing pollution, monitoring groundwater and surface water, and detecting contamination early,” he said.

Mr Mwembela has also urged mining operators to invest in real-time monitoring systems and adhere to international tailings management standards to safeguard water resources and surrounding communities.

Meanwhile, Seed Global Health Country Director, Chikusela Sikazwe has urged mining companies to integrate health considerations into environmental and social impact assessments from the earliest stages of mining projects.

Dr Sikazwe said this will help to ensure that their investments align with government priorities.

He warned that uncoordinated investments can lead to duplication and underutilised health facilities, calling for stronger collaboration between mining companies and the Ministry of Health.

“The approach should strengthen Zambia’s health system throughout the mining lifecycle, including emergency care and preparedness for disease outbreaks, climate-related health risks and future pandemics,” Dr Sikazwe said.

World.title: President Hichilema attends SADC extraordinary meeting virtually
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema participated in the Extraordinary Summit of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Heads of State and Government virtually.

President Hichilema’s participation underscores Zambia’s resolve and commitment to supporting discussions and decisions that strengthen the SADC Secretariat, advance regional integration and promote peace, security and stability among Member States.

The Extraordinary Summit was chaired by SADC Chairperson and President of South Africa, Cyril Ramaphosa.

In his opening remarks, President Ramaphosa said the strength of SADC rests not only on political commitments but on strong institutions with the leadership, capacity and resources to translate decisions into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

He said regional integration must be measured by the extent to which it creates jobs, attracts investment, reduces poverty and improves citizens’ livelihoods, while peace and stability remain indispensable foundations for development.

Meanwhile, the Summit has elected Lesotho as the new Chairperson of the SADC Organ Troika on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation, taking over the leadership of the Organ charged with promoting peace and security in the region.

The Organ plays a central role in preventive diplomacy, mediation, conflict resolution and addressing security challenges, including the situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the threat of terrorism and violent extremism in northern Mozambique.

The Summit also appointed and swore in Treasure Maphanga as Deputy Executive Secretary responsible for Regional Integration.

Ms Maphanga’s appointment fills a key treaty position expected to accelerate implementation of the Regional Indicative Strategic Development Plan (RISDP), drive cross-border infrastructure development, expand electricity generation and transmission, and deepen regional value chains and intra-regional trade.

President Ramaphosa congratulated both Lesotho and Ms Maphanga and urged the strengthened SADC institutions to work towards building a region where peace prevails and economic opportunities expand.

Eelier, Southern African Development Community (SADC) Executive Secretary, Elias Magosi said the Extraordinary Summit was convened to conclude two matters deferred from the Durban Summit in August this year.

The first is the election of the incoming Chairperson of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation, after two member states expressed interest in the position in Durban.

He said the Summit had referred the decision pending further consultations, and consultations have since been concluded with a common position for approval today.

Mr Magosi said the Organ remains indispensable in advancing peace, security, stability, democracy and good governance in the region, as well as in providing an enabling environment for accelerating regional integration and sustainable development.

“The second item is the appointment of the Deputy Executive Secretary for Regional Integration, following a recruitment process, he added

Mr Magosi said the Deputy Executive Secretary for Regional Integration is a key pillar and driver of regional integration, overseeing progress on regional integration as guided by the Regional Indicative Strategic Development Plan (RISDP) and relevant protocols.

Meanwhile, Mr Magosi congratulated President Daniel Francisco Chapo of Mozambique for successfully hosting the inaugural International Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience in Africa in Maputo from 13th to 15th October, 2026, under the theme on strengthening governance and strategic investment for disaster resilience.

He said the conference called for accelerated implementation of disaster risk reduction commitments, strengthened partnerships and increased investment in resilience-building initiatives across Africa.

Mr Magosi also congratulated Dr Navanethem Pillay of South Africa on being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of her distinguished contributions to peace, justice, human rights and international law, describing it as a source of pride for South Africa, the SADC region and the international community.

World.title: Chinsali Council engages businesses on 2027 budget
World.content:
The Chinsali Municipal Council has engaged the business community in the preparation of its 2027 Output-Based Budget (OBB) to ensure that proposed projects and programmes reflect the development priorities of the district.

Council Public Relations Manager Lolavye Simukoko said the engagement provides a platform for stakeholders to contribute ideas and propose projects for consideration in the 2027 financial year.

Mr Simukoko said the meeting is part of the Council’s efforts to promote public participation in the budgeting process.

The council public relations manager said this in a statement released to ZANIS in Chinsali district.

He said the meeting also featured presentations on services provided by the local authority, the performance of the 2026 Council budget and the role of the Council’s Integrity Committee.

He said the engagement is also intended to ensure that proposed projects aligns with the Chinsali Integrated Development Plan (IDP), the Eighth National Development Plan (8NDP) and the national Grow Zambia Agenda.

During the meeting, stakeholders proposed the construction of an ablution block and fencing of the Council sports facility near the Zambia Army Mess, as well as the provision of waste bins in the Central Business District (CBD) to improve sanitation.

Other proposals include the construction of a transit bus station at Nambuluma Junction, additional Council houses and the rehabilitation of the community hall at the old market in Chinsali CBD.

He explained that the business community also proposed the establishment of parks and recreational spaces near Nkakula Guest House and Bread of Life Church, alongside the development of modern market infrastructure at Choshi, Mishishi and Chinsali Main Market.

Mr Simukoko said stakeholders further proposed the introduction of fire extinguisher supply and refilling services to strengthen fire safety and emergency preparedness in the district.

He said the Council will consider the submissions as part of the budgeting process, with the aim of identifying priority interventions that respond to the needs of the local community.

Mr Simukoko said stakeholder participation is important in promoting transparency, accountability and collaboration between the Council and the business community in advancing development in Chinsali District.

World.title: Kaputa health Director calls for cholera vigilance
World.content:
Kaputa District Health Director Jonathan Bwalya has urged members of the public to remain vigilant against cholera and take extra precautions to prevent the spread of the disease.

Dr Bwalya told the media in an interview that it is important for residents to observe preventive measures and remain alert to the risks posed by cholera, a waterborne disease that can spread through contaminated water and food.

He said his medical team is on the ground and working to ensure that cholera does not spread to Kaputa District.

Dr Bwalya emphasised the importance of public cooperation in preventing the disease, urging residents to take personal hygiene and sanitation seriously.

He further encouraged the public to practice proper hand washing, drink safe water, eat properly handled food and maintain clean surroundings as part of efforts to protect communities from cholera.

Residents were also urged to seek immediate medical attention if they developed symptoms such as acute watery diarrhea and vomiting, which may indicate cholera.

Dr Bwalya’s call comes as health authorities continue to emphasise the importance of vigilance and preventive measures in protecting communities from cholera outbreaks in the wake of reports of a cholera outbreak.

World.title: How long will Kalampa stay top?
World.content:
Nkana’s perfect start to the transitional Super League season is no accident.

Three games, three wins, nine points. Top of Stream A. At Nkana Stadium in Wusakile on Sunday, Elijah Tana’s side did not just beat Nchanga Rangers 2-0, they sent a statement about what a balanced team can achieve.

What is most impressive about this Nkana side is not just the results, but the method.

On one hand, there is Lazarous Kambole, a seasoned striker who knows where the goal is. His opener against Rangers, created by Kedrick Mumba’s vision from his own half, was a reminder that experience still matters in Zambian football. On the other, there is Patrick Gondwe, alert and hungry to pounce when Captain Harrison Chisala’s effort was parried by keeper Victor Chabu.

Nkana are deservedly top. Tana has blended young, energetic players with experienced heads like Kambole and Chisala, and for now, the chemistry is working. But the perfection of nine points masks a lack of clinical edge that better opponents will exploit.

This blend of youth and experience that Coach Tana has spoken about is beginning to produce results. The young, energetic players provide pace and hunger, the experienced heads provide guidance and composure. It is a formula that has served Nkana well throughout its decorated history, and it is working again.

Tana deserves credit for his honesty. “We won’t relax,” he said after the win. “We will continue pushing until the end.” That is exactly the mentality Kalampa needs. Too many times in recent seasons, Nkana have started well only to fade when pressure mounts. This transitional league is short, but it is competitive, and consistency will be key.

Now, spare a thought for Nchanga Rangers. Assistant Coach Israel Mwanza was candid enough to admit his side is under pressure after three straight defeats. Conceding early goals has become a worrying habit for Brave. Yet Mwanza insists their system is fine. Football, however, is a results business. Systems mean little if they cannot stop early setbacks.

For the league as a whole, Nkana’s resurgence is good news. A strong Nkana makes a strong Super League. When Kalampa are firing, attendances improve, rivalry intensifies, and the standard goes up. Their next test away to Konkola Blades will tell us whether this perfect start is a false dawn or the beginning of a genuine title charge in the transitional campaign.

For now, Kalampa are showing the way. The challenge is to stay there.

World.title: Zambia, Botswana, DRC recommit to strengthening regional cooperation
World.content:
Zambia, Botswana and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening regional cooperation through infrastructure connectivity, integrated value chains and cross-border industrial development.

Botswana’s Minister of Minerals and Energy, Bogolo Kenewendo, says the three countries have an opportunity to transform their mineral wealth into shared prosperity through investment, partnerships and coordinated implementation of agreed initiatives.

Ms Kenewendo adds that the African continent possesses some of the world’s most valuable minerals, as well as the talent and partnerships required to unlock their full economic potential.

The Minister was speaking in Lusaka last evening during a networking cocktail party held on the sidelines of the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment engagement.

Ms Kenewendo stressed that the continent must move beyond discussions and translate commitments into tangible projects that would benefit its people.

She said the focus should now be on implementation to ensure that the mineral resources of Zambia, Botswana, the DRC and other African countries contribute to sustainable economic growth and prosperity.

Ms Kenewendo said the discussions and engagements held over the past few days had opened up opportunities for stronger collaboration and a brighter future for African mining.

She further stressed that the continent must move beyond discussions and translate commitments into tangible projects that would benefit its people.

And Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) Minister of Mines, Louis Kabamba says African countries must take responsibility for their own development by strengthening leadership and cooperation.

Mr Kabamba said the Insaka has demonstrated the importance of African countries drawing on their own strengths, sharing experiences and exchanging best practices to accelerate development.

He said all stakeholders, including government officials, mining investors and industry leaders, had a responsibility to contribute to the continent’s development.

Mr Kabamba urged African countries to take ownership of their development aspirations and work together to build prosperous economies.

Passing a vote of thanks, Zambia’s Acting Minister of Mines and Mineral Development, Gilbert Siame, said the Insaka has come at an opportune time to showcase the mineral wealth and investment opportunities available in Zambia, Botswana and the DRC.

Dr Siame said the participation of Botswana and the DRC demonstrated the growing importance of the Insaka as a platform for regional trade and investment.

He said the meeting is also expected to facilitate business deals and joint ventures while supporting the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, particularly the target of increasing annual copper production to three million metric tonnes by 2031.

President Hakainde Hichilema officially opened the Insaka on October 19, 2026, with business expected to conclude on Friday, October 23.

The event has attracted more than 1,500 participants, including representatives of the World Bank, European Union, African Development Bank and business communities from Australia, China and the United Arab Emirates.

The cocktail party was held at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka, and brought together government officials, investors, mining companies and development partners to explore investment opportunities and strengthen regional cooperation in the mining sector.

World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema is today expected to participate in the Extraordinary Summit of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Heads of State and Government to be held virtually.

The summit will consider outstanding matters, including the recruitment of treaty positions and the election of the incoming Chairperson of the SADC Organ on Politics, Defence and Security Cooperation.

World.title: South Africa: Govt Welcomes Mid-Term Budget - South African News Briefs - October 22, 2026
World.content:
press review

Govt Welcomes Mid-Term Budget

Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni has welcomed the 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement, reports EWN. She said that it seeks to ease the cost of living. She also welcomed the temporary fuel levy reductions announced by Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana. Ntshavheni highlighted the allocation of R3.8 billion to recruit more than 3,500 social workers to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence. The social workers will help improve prevention efforts and support women reporting abuse at police stations. Discussions are continuing on measures to reduce the impact of fuel costs on consumers.

DJ Warras Murder Case Returns to Court

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Two people accused of murdering Warrick "DJ Warras" Stock are set to appear in the High Court in Johannesburg for pre-trial proceedings, reports SABC News. Hlengiwe Buthelezi and Victor Majola face charges of premeditated murder and conspiracy to commit murder. The case was previously delayed while they sought legal representation. Stock was shot dead outside the Zambesi Building in Johannesburg on 16 December last year. Armando Pacula, a Mozambican national accused of shooting Stock, has pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Businessman Suliman Carrim Faces Additional Charges

North West businessman Suliman Carrim is set to appear in the Musina Magistrates' Court after additional charges of theft and fraud were brought against him, reports EWN. The charges relate to an alleged attempt to smuggle two vehicles from Mahikeng to Musina, with Malawi as their intended destination. Police allege that Carrim and two others tried to obtain bank authorisation documents to transport the vehicles across the border into Zimbabwe. When they allegedly failed to secure the documents, they arranged fraudulent ones. Police arrested two suspects in July after they intercepted the vehicles at the Beitbridge border post.

World.title: Zimbabwe: 200,000 Zimbabweans Have So Far Fled South Africa's Anti-Migrant Protests - Cabinet Told
World.content:
JUST under 200,000 Zimbabweans have so far fled South Africa's anti-migrant protests according to government.

Cabinet was on Tuesday told that a total of 197,294 people had been repatriated and reintegrated since vigilante groups started hunting foreigners in some of South Africa's cities.

South Africa's anti-migrant protests have been led by pressure groups such as Operation Dudula, March and March and former South African President Jacob Zuma who have made it public that Zimbabweans, Somalis, Nigerians, Ethiopians, Malawians and other African nationals in their country illegally should leave.

Although efforts to flush out foreigners peaked around June 30 when the vigilante groups made a national call to chase them out, lootings, acts of violence and displacement have continuously been noted, with Durban being the latest city to do so.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Foreigners are being told to identify the nearest border from wherever they are and flee.

Of Zimbabwe's 197,294 returnees 42,553 had been repatriated through government efforts which saw buses being dispatched as far as Cape Town to collect stranded nationals at its consulate.

The other 154,741 self repatriated.

"The nation is advised that the repatriation and re-integration of Zimbabwean nationals from South Africa has significantly declined, for both Government-supported returnees and self-repatriates," reads Tuesday's briefing.

"As at 6th October 2026, a total of 42,553 returnees had been repatriated through Government arrangements. The nationals comprise 10,475 male adults, 13,631 female adults, 9,001 male minors and 9,446 female minors.

"In addition, a cumulative total of 154,741 self-repatriations have been recorded to date."

Government has involved the Joint Operations Command (JOC) in the screening of returnees, some of whom had been serving time in South African prisons.

Some 700 deportees were received from Lindela Prison Repatriation Centre in South Africa.

Added the Cabinet brief: "As at 24th September 2026, a total of 700 deportees from Lindela Prison Repatriation Centre in South Africa were received at the Beitbridge Reception and Support Centre.

"The involvement of the Joint Operations Command (JOC) remains paramount in the screening and handling process, given that some of the deportees are convicts who were serving sentences in South African prisons and are required to complete the remainder of their sentences in Zimbabwe.

"Government continues to monitor the situation and is ready to respond to any possible influx of returnees in the future."

World.title: South Africa: Bronkhorstspruit Water Crisis Exposes a National Pattern of Municipal Failure and Impunity
World.content:
The Bronkhorstspruit water crisis, which has sickened about 450 people, exposes deep-rooted failures in local government, poor oversight and a culture of non-accountability that puts public health at risk. Despite promises of disciplinary action, political patronage and weak enforcement raise doubts that officials will be held responsible or that South Africa's worsening water crisis will be resolved.

The current water crisis that has led to about 450 people in Bronkhorstspruit falling ill from drinking tap water is a microcosm of all of the problems in local government.

It shows how a culture of non-accountability has taken hold in many places, and how officials are able to evade responsibility. Even when their actions lead to serious health consequences for ordinary people, or in this case, babies.

By the time the national government announced on Monday, 19 October, that there was a problem with the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Works more than four hundred people had already fallen ill. Many of them were young children, often under the age of four.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Thankfully, at this point, no one is known to have long-lasting consequences from the gastrointestinal illness that this water is carrying.

World.title: Burkina Faso: Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty
World.content:
Chilling Message to Junta Critics Amid Sweeping Crackdowns

Burkina Faso's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code that restores the death penalty for high treason, terrorism, acts of espionage, parricide and importation of expired or prohibited products. The country had abolished the death penalty for ordinary crimes in 2018 while its last known judicial execution took place in 1988.

Reinstating capital punishment sends a chilling message to critics of the military junta and risks becoming another tool to suppress dissent. Since the September 2022 military coup, Burkina Faso's junta has steadily dismantled civic and political rights. Authorities have banned media outlets, suspended unions and civil society organizations, abolished multiparty politics, and subjected critics to arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances, unlawful conscription, and torture.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala defended the decision to reinstate the death penalty as a necessary measure to combat terrorism. He said that armed groups exploited the previous law's leniency by promising new recruits they would face no more than life imprisonment if convicted of terrorist acts.



Human Rights Watch opposes all capital punishment because of its inherent cruelty. The unfairness of death sentences in Burkina Faso would be exacerbated by the country's ill-equipped justice system. All terrorism-related cases are handled by the Specialized Judicial Unit Against Terrorism-Related Crimes, established in 2017. Human Rights Watch documented in April the special court's slow investigations and serious procedural failures that undermine defendants' fair trial rights.

A former terrorism court judge once explained to me that judges sometimes kept suspects in detention despite insufficient evidence, fearing the military might summarily execute them if released. He described the dilemma as "better to violate the right to liberty in order to preserve the right to life." With the death penalty's return, even that grim calculation may no longer hold.

Reversing course on the death penalty runs counter to a broader international movement toward abolition. The United Nations General Assembly and the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights have urged states to establish moratoriums on executions, narrow the scope of capital punishment, and progressively reduce the number of offenses punishable by death with a view to its eventual abolition.

Restoring capital punishment will not resolve Burkina Faso's security crisis. In a system already plagued by serious due process failures, the death penalty merely heightens the risk of irreversible injustice.

Close 

Ilaria Allegrozzi, Senior Sahel Researcher

World.title: Rwanda: Nine Things to Know As Refugee Appeals Tribunal Begins Hearings
World.content:
The Appeals Tribunal for Refugees and Applicants for Refugee Status has begun hearing its first cases, providing a new avenue for asylum seekers to challenge decisions rejecting their applications.

The tribunal is expected to hear at least 20 appeals in its first week. Details of the cases have not been disclosed, and hearings will be held behind closed doors to protect applicants' confidentiality.

In an exclusive interview with The New Times, Jean Damascene Ndabirora Kalinda, the tribunal's registrar, explained its mandate, how it differs from the previous appeals system, its anticipated workload and the safeguards available to applicants.

Here are nine things to know about the tribunal and how it operates.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

1. The tribunal was established in 2024, not 2026

Although the tribunal began hearing cases in October 2026, it was legally established on April 19, 2024, under Law No. 042/01 of 19/04/2024 governing the Appeal Tribunal for Refugees and Applicants for Refugee Status.

According to Kalinda, administrative preparations and other considerations delayed its operationalisation.

The appointment of the tribunal's leadership on March 4, 2026, marked a significant step towards making it operational, rather than its formal establishment.

"The tribunal has been in existence since 2024, April 19," he said, emphasising the distinction between its legal establishment and the start of operations.

2. What is the tribunal's mandate?

The tribunal is responsible for hearing appeals from asylum seekers and refugees whose applications have been rejected by the Directorate General of Immigration and Emigration (DGIE).

Asylum seekers initially submit their applications to immigration authorities, which assess their claims and determine whether they qualify for protection.

Those dissatisfied with a rejection can challenge the decision before the tribunal, which provides an independent mechanism for reviewing their cases.

Kalinda said the tribunal's mandate is distinct from that of immigration authorities, which make the initial decisions on asylum applications.

3. Why was a separate tribunal necessary?

The tribunal marks a shift from the previous asylum appeals system, which raised concerns about institutional independence.

Under the 2014 legal framework, asylum applications were initially assessed by the Refugee Status Determination Committee, comprising representatives from several government institutions.

These included the Office of the Prime Minister, ministries responsible for local government, justice, defence and environment, immigration authorities and other relevant institutions.

Applicants dissatisfied with the committee's decisions could appeal to the ministry responsible for refugee affairs, then known as MINEMA.

However, Kalinda said the arrangement raised concerns about the independence of the appeals process, particularly because the ministry handling appeals had also participated in the initial decision-making process.

The establishment of a separate tribunal under the 2024 legal framework was intended to address those concerns by creating a dedicated, independent body to review rejected asylum applications.

Unlike the previous arrangement, the tribunal's members focus specifically on hearing and determining appeals.

4. Why does the tribunal have two presidents?

The tribunal has an unusual leadership structure comprising two presidents and four other members.

Kalinda traced the arrangement to Rwanda's proposed asylum partnership with the United Kingdom, during which discussions included a proposal to have one Rwandan president and another from a Commonwealth country.

Although the UK-Rwanda asylum arrangement did not materialise, the government retained the leadership structure established under the law.

According to Kalinda, there was no compelling reason to amend the provisions solely because the proposed partnership had not proceeded.

The two-president arrangement also allows the tribunal to operate two benches, enabling it to hear cases simultaneously and potentially reduce delays.

5. How are cases heard?

The tribunal comprises six members, including its two presidents and four other members.

Depending on the applicable legal provisions, appeals may be heard by a three-member bench or a single member.

Kalinda said the structure allows the tribunal to operate two benches, each headed by a co-president, enabling parallel hearings.

He emphasised that the sensitive nature of asylum cases requires careful consideration to ensure applicants receive fair hearings.

Unlike a conventional court, the tribunal is an independent, quasi-judicial institution that reviews decisions made by an administrative authority.

Its procedures therefore differ from those of ordinary courts, although it examines both legal and factual issues arising from asylum decisions.

6. How many cases are expected?

The tribunal has not disclosed the total number of appeals it expects to receive or the size of any backlog.

However, Kalinda anticipates a substantial workload following the delay in operationalising the appeals mechanism.

He said immigration authorities did not issue rejection letters to unsuccessful applicants between 2024 and 2026 while the appeals mechanism remained unavailable.

As a result, cases may have accumulated during that period, adding to new appeals as the tribunal begins operations.

The tribunal expects to conduct at least 20 hearings in its first week, with the number potentially increasing as operations progress.

Kalinda said the two benches would help manage the caseload more efficiently.

The legal framework also allows for an increase in the tribunal's membership if necessary to cope with growing demand.

7. How can applicants submit appeals?

Appeals are submitted through a customised module of the Immigration Case Management System (ICEMS), designed to accommodate the circumstances of asylum seekers in Rwanda.

Once an appeal is received, the tribunal verifies whether the application and supporting documents are complete.

If information is missing, the application may be returned for completion, or the tribunal may contact the applicant and their lawyer to request additional documents.

The process is intended to ensure that appeals contain the information necessary for proper consideration.

8. Will applicants have access to lawyers and interpreters?

Applicants are legally entitled to representation during the appeals process, although the tribunal does not automatically cover legal fees.

Close 

Kalinda said organisations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and other partners may assist applicants with legal costs.

Interpretation services are also essential, given the diverse nationalities and languages of applicants.

According to Kalinda, applicants come from countries including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Sudan, Syria, Eritrea, Afghanistan, Chad and Ethiopia.

Some speak Arabic, while others require interpretation in different languages.

The tribunal must therefore arrange interpretation services based on applicants' linguistic needs to ensure they can participate effectively in proceedings.

9. How long will applicants wait for a decision?

The law requires the tribunal to issue a decision within six months of receiving an appeal.

Kalinda said the institution is committed to meeting that deadline and avoiding unnecessary delays.

"Justice delayed is justice denied," he said.

Applicants dissatisfied with the tribunal's decision may petition the High Court, although its role differs from that of an ordinary appellate court.

According to Kalinda, the High Court may identify legal or procedural shortcomings and recommend that the tribunal reconsider its decision.

The matter is then referred back to the tribunal, which may uphold or change its original decision following the review.

Under the governing framework, this process differs from an ordinary appeal in which a higher court directly substitutes its decision for that of a lower body.

World.title: Cameroon: Cameroon's Eseka Rail Disaster Survivors Still Waiting for Justice, 10 Years On
World.content:
A decade after Cameroon's deadliest rail disaster killed 79 people and injured more than 500, survivors are still living with serious injuries, some compensation remains unpaid and an appeal against the convictions over the crash has yet to be heard. RFI spoke to survivors still living with the consequences of the disaster and to the husband of a woman whose body has never been found.

The Camrail train was travelling from Yaoundé to Douala when it derailed near the town of Eseka, around 100 kilometres from the capital, on 21 October 2016.

That morning, traffic on the road linking Cameroon's political capital Yaoundé with its economic capital Douala was disrupted, prompting large numbers of people to take the train instead. Numerous carriages were added to cope with the influx of passengers.

An investigation later found that the train was travelling at 96 kilometres per hour on a section limited to 40 kilometres per hour. It also pointed to an overloaded train, the inappropriate addition of extra carriages and carriages with defective braking systems.



The report said Camrail management had failed to take into account concerns raised by the train driver before departure.

Students in Cameroon protest new financial requirements for French visas

Lasting injuries

Among those who survived the crash was Eugénie, now 39, who suffered several fractures, including one to her neck, and has since lost her independence.

"I remember saying three times: 'Jesus, save me.' I was trapped underneath the carriage. I started praying and shouting: 'Please, come and help me, come and help me'," Eugénie told RFI.

"There were so many people. We didn't know who would be saved and who would be left there. There was blood everywhere, people were screaming and crying."

Eugénie suffered several fractures, including one to her neck, and has since lost her independence.

"I can't do anything by myself," she said. "I always need someone to be at home with me. Since that accident, my life has ceased to exist. I'm constantly in pain, I suffer from memory loss, and my body is still in tremendous pain."

Another survivor, Arnaud, was travelling in the second-to-last carriage.

"When things had settled down and I regained consciousness, I realised there were a lot of dead bodies in our carriage and that all the seats and luggage racks had been torn away," he said.

'An invisible avalanche': what happened in Cameroon's 1986 Lake Nyos disaster?

Still searching

Among the families still seeking answers is that of Dorette Dissakè, a prominent notary in Yaoundé whose body has never been found.

"My daughter, the rest of the family and I are still waiting," her husband, lawyer Thomas Dissakè, told RFI. "On what basis can we grieve and move on? The idea doesn't even cross our minds."

Dissakè recently enlisted a team of experts, with the cooperation of Camrail and the Ministry of Transport, to examine the ground at Eseka in the hope of finding human remains.

"How is it possible that her body has never been found? The accident didn't happen at sea. Her carriage overturned at the station. They lifted it up and there was nothing. Was another carriage run over her? This mystery is still on my mind," he said.

The family's search for answers has even led to the exhumation of a body in a village in Cameroon's Centre region, but it was not Dissakè's wife.

Deadly border mine collapse exposes risks behind Central Africa's gold rush

Criminal convictions

In September 2018, Camrail and 11 of its employees were found guilty of involuntary manslaughter and causing unintentional injuries by the court of first instance in Eseka.

Close 

The company's former managing director received a six-month suspended prison sentence. Other Camrail officials received suspended sentences of between three and five months, while the train driver, who was on the run, was sentenced to five years in prison.

Camrail appealed against the ruling, denouncing the "absence of any qualified and competent expert assessment".

The appeal has still not been heard.

Lawyers representing the victims also said the compensation awarded was too low given the physical and psychological harm suffered. Some payments have still not been made.

The France-based Bolloré Group retained the Camrail railway concession after the disaster until it sold its transport activities to Italian-Swiss company MSC in 2022.

This article has been adapted from interviews in French by Richard Onanena and Jules Ntap.

World.title: Sudan: 'Many Still Missing' As Abyei Market Drone Strike Toll Rises
World.content:
Abyei — The death toll from a drone strike on Amiet market in the disputed Abyei area between Sudan and South Sudan has risen from 73 to 153, local officials say, and is expected to grow, as many people are still listed as 'missing'. The attack on Monday also forced about 8,000 people to flee, prompting condemnation from the United Nations and the UK.

The UN secretary-general has strongly condemned drone attacks in Abyei on Monday that reportedly killed dozens of civilians, including women and children, near Amiet and Todach markets, and injured many others.

A statement seen by Radio Dabanga warned that the death toll could rise as the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) continues to verify the casualties. Many people remain missing.

UNISFA deployed medical personnel, firefighting equipment and rapid-response forces after the incident to provide emergency treatment, help evacuate the injured and prevent the fire from spreading, the statement said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The secretary-general stressed that international law prohibits attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure. He called on all parties to the armed conflict to meet their obligations under international humanitarian law, including protecting civilians at all times and ensuring accountability for those responsible.

He also urged the governments of Sudan and South Sudan to take all possible steps to prevent further attacks and preserve Abyei's status as a demilitarised area.

UK calls for independent investigation

The British embassy expressed deep concern over reports of strikes on Amiet market in Abyei that caused heavy civilian casualties. It condemned attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure and called for an independent and comprehensive investigation.

Death toll rises sharply

According to Reuters, the death toll from the drone strike on Amiet market, also known as Al-Naam, has risen to 153.

The attack took place on Monday morning at Amiet market, north of Abyei town. It triggered major explosions and fires after the drone struck a fuel depot. The fires continued to burn until Tuesday, while emergency teams faced considerable difficulties recovering bodies from the rubble.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the acting information minister for the Abyei area, told Reuters that the death toll had risen sharply from the initial figure of 73 to 153. He warned that it could increase further as search and recovery operations continued.

Close 

Local authorities said the attack had displaced about 8,000 people.

South Sudan's government blamed the Sudanese Armed Forces for the strike and summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest.

A senior Sudanese military official, speaking anonymously to the Associated Press, acknowledged that the army had carried out a drone strike. The official claimed it had targeted fuel tankers believed to be intended for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), but denied that civilians had been deliberately targeted. The account could not be independently verified.

Medical teams from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said they had treated more than 20 injured people at Amiet Biek hospital, including patients with severe burns and critical injuries.

Protests were also held in Abyei on Tuesday to condemn the attack.

World.title: Africa: Africa Needs More Than Envoys to Secure the Red Sea
World.content:
analysis

The Horn's proliferating diplomatic appointments have done little to bolster African influence amid new Middle Eastern alliances.

In September, Ansarullah (the Houthis) took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, shattering the assumption that the insurgency was confined to northern Yemen. The group is now at the epicentre of the Middle East conflict and is the channel through which crises flow between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East.

Countries on either side of the Red Sea have responded asymmetrically to this shared shock. The Horn has dispatched more envoys while Middle Eastern countries, led by Saudi Arabia, are strengthening political institutions and hardwiring them with military deals. These include the newly signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) and the politically oriented 14-member Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition (MMDC).



Although the Red Sea has a history of instability, current upheavals are distinct. Ansarullah is not only at war with the Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government, but is linked to the Israel-Hamas conflict, the Israel-United States war with Iran, and escalating conflicts in the Horn. These interwoven crises require equally interlinked responses from both shores of the Red Sea.

Red Sea and bordering countries

The assertion by Iran, commentators and Ansarullah itself that its conflict is solely with Saudi Arabia is untenable. Iran's strategy of hedging its bets across the Middle East has enabled Ansarullah to evolve from an ally targeting Yemen's government into a self-tasking surrogate whose operations also serve Iran's interests. Having cultivated Ansarullah, Iran did not need to act on its earlier threat to close Bab al-Mandab.

Ansarullah's deepening ties with al-Shabaab have helped transform the Yemeni group from a transnational criminal actor involved in smuggling and illicit financial activity into a force choking a Red Sea gateway carrying nearly 15% of global trade. The two Islamist groups now run a corridor of instability, migration and economic disruption from Tehran to Nairobi and Kampala.

The Horn of Africa's four biggest conflict hotspots - Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Ethiopia - have become intertwined with Middle Eastern crises. Although conflicts on both sides of the Red Sea stem from local grievances, Middle Eastern actors are the main drivers of conflict in the Horn. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) alone is entangled with Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan and has multi-purpose investments in every country in the Horn.

In the past, the Horn's Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the League of Arab States coordinated over Somalia's crisis and conflict resolution in Sudan. But countries on either side of the Red Sea are now using markedly different tools to address their shared challenges.

In March, the AU designated former Tanzanian president Jakaya Kikwete as its High Representative for the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. Kikwete, who opted to focus on South Sudan, joined a crowded field of IGAD envoys already deployed in the Horn - covering Somalia, Sudan and South Sudan. Others include the Special Envoy for the Red Sea and Maritime Affairs, and the AU High Representative for Sudan.

A corresponding bench of envoys from outside Africa also covers the Horn - from the UN, EU, China, Germany, Japan, France, Norway, United Kingdom, Netherlands and Switzerland. While each is responsible for a piece of the interconnected conflict resolution puzzle, this 'envoyflation' adds little leverage to individual portfolios or to the Horn's stability. Instead, Horn envoys and their external partners shuttle between capitals, with little progress to show.

Source: ISS based on open-source data

By contrast, Middle Eastern countries are moving away from institutions such as the Gulf Cooperation Council and Council of Arab and African Coastal States of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, in favour of political-military frameworks. Although there are envoys in the region, they represent external powers, the United Nations (UN) and European Union (EU), not Middle Eastern countries.

The MMDC, established to safeguard freedom of navigation, was launched in Saudi Arabia on 30 July with members including Red Sea and non-Red Sea countries in Africa, the Arab world and Asia.

While it includes Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, the exclusion of IGAD highlights the Horn's limited regional control over its coastline. This was already evident from Turkey's wardenship of Somalia's maritime defence, the UAE's port expansion in the region and numerous countries' military bases in Djibouti. Eritrea's absence from the MMDC reflects its rejection of military solutions to Yemen's conflict.

Days after launching the MMDC, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled the MJDA on 7 August. Conspicuously, it excludes Horn countries but includes non-Red Sea Pakistan and Turkey. On 5 October, Saudi Arabia conducted its first military operation against Ansarullah within the MJDA framework.

Both the MJDA and MMDC exclude landlocked Ethiopia and the UAE, which could weaken these frameworks. The exclusions reflect a political dispute over which countries qualify as Red Sea states - a debate that has undermined IGAD's Red Sea efforts. Eritrea's departure from IGAD in December 2025 further limits the organisation's diplomatic leverage over the coastline.

Ethiopia, meanwhile, wants access to the Red Sea but faces opposition from Eritrea and Egypt, a founding MMDC member. This conflates Nile water disputes with disputes over the definition of the Red Sea.

The Horn has military institutions that could help secure the Red Sea. The East Africa Standby Force and Eastern Africa Fusion and Liaison Unit could have complemented IGAD's efforts, but neither has a maritime focus. Consequently, African envoys are increasingly relegated to 'managing' inland conflicts, while their external counterparts are oriented towards the Red Sea.

Close 

Envoyflation reflects IGAD and the AU's political inertia and financial weakness. Envoys are appointed in temporary posts and rely on external donor funding. In the Horn, this has led to fragmented responses and the exclusion of African actors from conflict resolution efforts. Middle Eastern states, by comparison, largely fund their own interventions.

AU and IGAD efforts to institutionalise their position on the Red Sea and engage with the League of Arab States were appropriate steps. However, the league has also been weakened by the altered context.

Going forward, the AU and IGAD should be ready to capitalise on emerging opportunities, reconceptualise their maritime mechanisms, streamline existing diplomatic efforts and work closely with their Middle Eastern partners.

Moses Chrispus Okello, Senior Researcher, Horn of Africa Security Analysis, ISS Addis Ababa

World.title: Kansas Senate rivals distance themselves from party leaders in fiery debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton repeatedly sought to distance themselves from the most unpopular elements of their respective parties Wednesday night during a contentious Kansas Senate debate.

Both candidates battled over President Donald Trump, immigration, the war in Iran and more in a race that could help determine control of the Senate.

The debate opened on a personal note, with both candidates pressed over controversies that have fueled attack ads in the closing weeks of the campaign.

Marshall was questioned about a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. The Republican defended the practice while emphasizing the millions of dollars in free care his practice provided.

GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall said. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp alleged to have been a sexual predator. Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp after an initial investigation.

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

The candidates spent much of the rest of the debate trying to define each other by their respective national parties.

Marshall repeatedly warned that electing Hamilton would help hand control of the Senate to Democrats and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, while Hamilton sought to portray himself as an independent-minded Democrat willing to break with his party.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

That divide came into focus when the moderator played footage of Trump campaigning for Marshall in Kansas earlier this week and telling voters to "pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot."

Asked whether that meant he would support every part of Trump's agenda, Marshall said no and pointed to recent disagreements involving immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Nevertheless, Marshall emphasized his support for much of Trump's agenda and urged the president's supporters to turn out for him.

"We need the Trump voters to come out," Marshall said. "If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes, then you â and you voted for President Trump â you need to come out."

Hamilton faced a similar challenge when moderators pressed him over his past support for Democrats and his campaign message of "leading from the middle."

MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

The Democratic nominee explicitly broke with former President Joe Biden over immigration.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton said. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

Hamilton also said he would not support Schumer for majority leader if Democrats win control of the Senate.

The debate did produce an unusual moment of agreement when both candidates were asked how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said.

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

SC DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS SHE WILL STAND UP TO HER PARTY AS GRAHAM TIES HER TO 'SOCIALIST DEMOCRATS'

Hamilton later said he did not want biological males competing against his 12-year-old granddaughter in sports, calling it "not a fair fight," while arguing that decisions over athletic participation should generally be handled locally rather than by the federal government.

The Kansas contest has emerged as an unexpectedly competitive Senate race in the closing weeks of the midterms. Marshall is seeking a second term in a state that has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, while Hamilton, a longtime pastor, has campaigned as a moderate Democrat.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump traveled to Kansas Monday to campaign for Marshall as Republicans work to defend the seat with control of the Senate at stake.

World.title: Angel Reese delivers another double-double as Atlanta Dream take 2–1 lead in WNBA Finals
World.content:
ATLANTA â Angel Reese helped the Atlanta Dream win a WNBA Finals game for the first time Monday. Two nights later, she helped them take their first lead in a Finals series.

ATLANTA DREAM, GOLDEN STATE VALKYRIES SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM FOR THIRD STRAIGHT WNBA FINALS GAME

Reese finished with 21 points and 12 rebounds as Atlanta beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 on Wednesday night at State Farm Arena, taking a 2â1 lead in the best-of-seven series. Reese has totaled 51 points and 28 rebounds in Atlantaâs two victories.

Reese became the youngest player in WNBA Finals history to record at least 20 points and 10 rebounds in consecutive games, joining Aâja Wilson as the only players to accomplish the feat.

And to give the Dream and their fans credit, I previously questioned whether Atlanta could fill State Farm Arena for the Finals. They answered that with a resounding yes on Wednesday night. Game 3 was a sellout, and the building was loud.

Before tip-off, both teams again left the court for the national anthem, marking their third straight absence in the series. They returned moments after the performance ended. The WNBAâs rulebook calls for players, coaches and trainers to stand and line up during the anthem, and the league has not answered OutKickâs questions about the absences.

Once the game started, Reese picked up where she left off in San Francisco. She scored Atlantaâs first basket and finished the opening quarter with eight points, including a three-pointer that pushed the Dreamâs lead to 22â12.

Golden State missed its first eight shots and didnât make a field goal until 4:38 remained in the first quarter. Atlanta led 23â15 after one.

WNBA ANTHEM CONTROVERSY SPARKS CALLS TO BAR PLAYERS WHO DON'T STAND FROM TEAM USA OLYMPIC ROSTER

Reese added another three in the second quarter and went into halftime with 15 points, matching her first-half total from Game 2. Naz Hillmon made three first-half threes of her own, helping Atlanta take a 46â40 lead into the break.

The Valkyries made a push to start the third. Cecilia Zandalasini hit two threes in the opening 68 seconds, and Golden State tied the game at 48, then again at 49.

Reese helped Atlanta answer. After Rhyne Howard put the Dream back in front, Reese made two free throws, assisted on an Isobel Borlase layup and scored on a running layup herself. That completed an 8â0 run and gave Atlanta a 57â49 lead.

Golden State cut the deficit to four, but the Dream kept scoring after Reese went to the bench with 3:31 left in the quarter. DeWanna Bonner hit a three to start a 12â2 finish to the period, scoring five points during that stretch.

ANGEL REESE DOMINATES GAME 2 AS ATLANTA DREAM EVEN WNBA FINALS WITH GOLDEN STATE VALKYRIES

Atlanta led 71â57 entering the fourth and Golden State never really threatened in the final period.

Hillmon finished with 15 points, while Jordin Canada added 8 assists. Rhyne Howard had her best offensive performance of the series, scoring 16 points.

Atlanta again held down Golden Stateâs Gabby Williams, who finished with 15 points on 5-of-18 shooting.

Atlanta entered these Finals without a win in its three previous appearances, then lost Saturdayâs opener. Now Reese and the Dream are two victories from a championship.

Game 4 is Saturday at State Farm Arena.

World.title: Mass firings vow sparks clash with Klobuchar over Walz fraud legacy

Minnesotaâs gubernatorial candidates clashed over the stateâs fraud scandals in their second debate of the week, with Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth pledging to fire all state commissioners on her first day in office and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar defending her response.

The scandals have rocked the North Star State, raising questions about how large-scale abuse of state programs went undetected and putting government oversight at the center of the governorâs race.

"Fraud unchecked here in the state of Minnesota has gone far too long, and it has finally come to the surface," Demuth said.

MINNESOTAâS ANTI-FRAUD SPENDING HAS QUIETLY BALLOONED, LEAVING TAXPAYERS TO PAY FOR FAILURE TWICE

"The thing that I will do on day one is I am going to be firing all commissioners, choosing new commissioners that are expert in their field, that will carry out the accountability and transparency that is needed in our state. We have to change the culture of fraud."

Klobuchar called Demuthâs remarks "absurd" and said she contacted U.S. Attorney Andy Luger after the fraud came to light to ask what prosecutors needed.

"He said, 'I need more prosecutors'," Klobuchar said. "I called the highest level of the Justice Department, and I got him those prosecutors."

TIM WALZ SAYS HE TAKES RESPONSIBILITY FOR MINNESOTA FRAUD BY NOT RUNNING FOR RE-ELECTION

Klobuchar also said she would have caught the fraud earlier, while criticizing Walzâs response. "Tim Walz should have caught the fraud earlier and he should have done more," she said.

She also sought to distinguish herself from the outgoing governor and criticized Demuth for not clearly separating herself from President Donald Trump. "We donât need a rubber stamp of Donald Trump in the governorâs office," Klobuchar said.



Demuth countered that Klobuchar had not identified specific policies on which she would break with Walz, whom Klobuchar has called an "incredible governor."

'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS



Beyond fraud, Klobuchar and Demuth used the debate to draw broader contrasts over the economy, taxes, public safety and the direction of the state. Both candidates have ruled out tax increases, but Demuth has argued Minnesota needs to rein in spending and regulations, while Klobuchar has emphasized lowering costs for health care, housing and child care.
