World.title: Why local officials are feeling 'on edge' as election day approaches
World.content:
Why local officials are feeling 'on edge' as election day approaches

Al Schmidt is the chief election official in the state of Pennsylvania. President Trump's insults put him in danger during the 2020 ballot count. Now Schmidt talks about preparing for the midterms.

Transcript

DAVE DAVIES, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. Our next guest, Al Schmidt, had a memorable experience in the 2020 presidential election, which Donald Trump has long claimed was stolen. Back then, Schmidt was the lone Republican on the three-member election board of Philadelphia, a Democratic stronghold in the key swing state of Pennsylvania. Schmidt helped supervise and publicly defended the integrity of the long and tedious count of hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots. The count took days and eventually gave Democrat Joe Biden the state's 20 electoral votes. But it earned Schmidt nationally reported insults from then-President Trump and threats from some of his followers.

Today Schmidt is secretary of the commonwealth, the chief voting official for all of Pennsylvania, which will again be a critically contested state in a national election with high stakes for Donald Trump. There are four competitive congressional races in Pennsylvania, which could help decide control of the House of Representatives. We thought it would be useful to get Schmidt's take on this election season and what he expects and fears from the voting on November 3 and the count and certification to follow.

Before we begin, I should note that Al Schmidt and I have known each other for a long time. I was a political reporter for many years for the Philadelphia Daily News and public radio when Al was active in local Republican politics.

Al Schmidt, welcome to FRESH AIR.

AL SCHMIDT: Great to be back with you, Dave.

DAVIES: Let's spend a moment on that harrowing experience following the 2020 election. And to remind listeners, this was the first COVID election - right? - 2020, when mail ballots, normally not common in the United States, were all over the country. Back then, Philadelphia was typically used to processing about 13,000, 14,000...

SCHMIDT: That's right.

DAVIES: ...Absentee ballots. Now there were over 370,000 mail ballots. And the state election code prevented your election workers from even opening the envelopes until Election Day, which meant it was going to take a long time. It was expected that Donald Trump would be ahead on the machine vote because he had discouraged people from using mail ballots. Tell us what it was like to try and get all those ballots counted as quickly as you could.

SCHMIDT: Yes. And to help sort of set the scene here, you're right. It was the first election that Pennsylvania had with no-excuse mail-ballot voting, meaning any voter could vote by mail. Philadelphia also had essentially new voting systems in-person at the polls that election. We also had the COVID environment possibly at its peak, and we also had civil unrest in Philadelphia. So we were trying to manage our way through all of those different challenges.

With mail-ballot voting, we had about half of our voters, probably because of the COVID environment at the time, vote by mail. That's a lot in a presidential election with predictably very high turnout. But one thing that puts Pennsylvania at a disadvantage then and now is that our counties can't begin processing mail ballots until 7 a.m. on election morning. Other states begin that process days, if not weeks, in advance.

DAVIES: They can rip open the envelopes so that you're ready to process the ballots, right?

SCHMIDT: That's right. So on election night at 8 p.m., they're ready to report the results of what they had worked on for many days, if not weeks. In Pennsylvania, that's not the case. So in 2020, obviously, we had the in-person results coming in first - those are people who voted at the polls on Election Day - followed by these waves of updates for voting by mail as they were tabulated by our counties.

DAVIES: Right. So you would give regular updates on what the count of the mail ballot showed. And what was happening was you could see that Donald Trump's lead in the state was shrinking as more Democratic votes rather than Republican were reflected in the mail ballots. It got to a point where it got ugly and personal, didn't it? I mean, threats, right?

SCHMIDT: Yes. So we had had fairly general threats prior to that, like, you're going to get what's coming to you, or things that, you know, don't really rise to a level of concern for me, especially at this point. But as it went on, they certainly got a lot more specific, naming my children, providing my address in the threats, obviously graphic descriptions of the violence.

So I really relied on law enforcement - especially the Philadelphia Police Department, which did an incredible job and I'm always going to be grateful - for really taking care of my family. Like, we were inside the convention center. We had many, many police officers and sheriffs present outside. That's probably why threats were targeting your family, right? You're not there. It's all about trying to keep you from doing your job. So we couldn't allow ourselves to be distracted from doing our job because of the threats targeting our families.

DAVIES: Was your family relocated?

SCHMIDT: My family was relocated. And then we had around-the-clock police protection for many months after that because the threats continued, certainly leading up to the certification of the presidential election many weeks later. So when I walked the dog, police were coming with us. When we took the kids sledding, the police were there. It was just a constant presence.

DAVIES: Yeah. Yeah.

SCHMIDT: Thanksgiving, Christmas.

DAVIES: I don't...

SCHMIDT: And so...

DAVIES: ...Want to be - yeah.

SCHMIDT: ...Sort of surreal. I don't mean to laugh about it, but it was a surreal environment. And we got to, you know, know them pretty well. And I - like I said, I'm grateful.

DAVIES: So you're still a registered Republican. And...

SCHMIDT: I am.

DAVIES: You're serving a Democratic governor in a swing state. So here we are. And President Trump has been very, very active in warning that there will be fraud and that mail ballots are subject to fraud. And not just talking. I mean, he's tried to do things and get the government to do things which would affect the voting in this election. Give us a sense of the kind of incoming demands you have gotten from the federal government.

SCHMIDT: Well, there have been several, primarily from the Department of Justice and from the Department of Homeland Security. The biggest, of course, was a demand that we provide Pennsylvania's voter rolls to DOJ. And not just the publicly available voter rolls but the Social Security numbers of every registered voter in Pennsylvania that we have, every driver's license number and all the rest. So that's information that we are, obviously, typically prohibited from sharing. It would not be legal for us to share. And it was clear that we weren't going to provide that information, and we declined their demand.

That information has to be safeguarded. Nothing would jeopardize election integrity more than Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers being shared with multiple government agencies with unclear control over that sort of information. So we declined. The courts ruled in our favor, as they did in more than two dozen others at this point in these lawsuits against DOJ.

DAVIES: Right. I believe also, the Department of Justice told you that there were 14,000 noncitizens registered to vote in Pennsylvania. Do I have this right?

SCHMIDT: Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security. The accusation was that we have north of 14,000 noncitizens registered to vote in Pennsylvania because of whatever data matching, using whatever datasets in whatever way that led them to reach that conclusion.

DAVIES: This came your way when? Like, two months ago? Or...

SCHMIDT: Some months ago.

DAVIES: OK.

SCHMIDT: And then we responded - rightly, I think - asking for more information on this. Like, what data was used? From what datasets? How did the matching occur? What do you consider a match and not a match? Like, I have the same name as my dad. Would we show up as a match, as the same person? Because they obviously did not have Social Security number or driver's license number, which is a unique identifier that everybody has, that would be necessary to do that sort of matching. And even when that matches, you still have to do the hard work. You still have to do the research.

And I was a Republican election commissioner in Philadelphia for 10 years. Election integrity is very important, from my point of view. And it's important to handle it responsibly and not just cry wolf every time you have some sort of data match based on garbage information.

DAVIES: And so you responded, saying, give us more information. And then what happened?

SCHMIDT: We had a virtual meeting with them where we asked more questions. The answers to those questions obviously were insufficient to provide us with any sense of security or certainty related to the reliability of their data. And that was the end of it, other than a letter from the Department of Justice saying, as you currently know, you are under criminal investigation.

DAVIES: Criminal investigation?

SCHMIDT: Yes.

DAVIES: When you're under criminal investigation, you generally know that by other means, like you get a grand jury subpoena or investigators come to you to talk to you? That...

SCHMIDT: You would. And it also doesn't usually start - as you must know, or as you know. But there's nothing certainly special about that. Every secretary who refused DOJ's demand received the same letter.

DAVIES: We'll take a break here. Let me reintroduce you. We are speaking with Al Schmidt. He is Pennsylvania's secretary of the commonwealth, the state's chief election official. We'll talk more after this short break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF ROBBEN FORD & BILL EVANS' "PIXIES")

DAVIES: This is FRESH AIR. And as we anticipate potential controversies involving the midterm election in two weeks, we're speaking with election integrity experts and an official involved in supervising elections. Our guest in this segment is Al Schmidt. He is Pennsylvania's secretary of the Commonwealth, the state's chief election official. Pennsylvania, a perennial battleground state, has four competitive congressional elections this year.

As you look forward to the election, just a little less than two weeks away, what worries you?

SCHMIDT: Well, anyone involved with an election administration worries about everything all the time. And any issue, big or small, can be exploited to undermine confidence in election results. So that's always a concern. It's never a question of things not being a concern. But obviously, now we've had to consider a lot more things than we did in the past, such as the threat of federal interference or anything like that. So we work with our counties. We do tabletop exercises with them. We work with our state partners - Pennsylvania State Police and National Guard and others - to work through different scenarios so that, should anything occur from any direction, we're all prepared and can communicate and know what everybody's roles and responsibilities are.

DAVIES: There's a lot of discussion about how common or uncommon election fraud is in the country. And you're in a better position than most people to have an opinion about this because you participated in elections not just as an election official, but as a Republican candidate running for office in a city run by Democrats. You also, when you were a city commissioner on the election board in Philadelphia, did a study of election improprieties and fraud. So what did you find? I mean, is there fraud out there?

SCHMIDT: Well, we did find evidence of cases of voter fraud, as we always have in Pennsylvania and elsewhere. It's just that it occurs extremely infrequently and has never had any impact on the outcome of an election. But that's not to shrug it off. And I made several referrals to the U.S. attorney's office and to the district attorney's office and attorney general's office and worked with all three levels of law enforcement in Pennsylvania and in Philadelphia to investigate and, when warranted, prosecute and hold people accountable who did commit acts of voter fraud. And it was always at a very local level, affecting very small races because that's where a handful of votes can really impact the outcome of an election, not necessarily President the United States or any statewide race.

DAVIES: One of the things you hear about corruption in Philadelphia is that dead people vote. You actually looked into this once, right? Tell us that story.

SCHMIDT: I did at great length. It is the easiest thing in the world to prove if it occurred. You know when a vote was cast, and you know when a voter died. You have a record of when the person died, and you have a record of when their vote was cast. So we worked comparing the Social Security Death Index against the voter rolls and narrowed it down to, in the end, it was about 10 to 12 cases that I was sure that we got. I was sure that we had identified 10 to 12 cases where a dead voter had voted. But you can't just rely on a data match and say that's evidence of anything. It was only a lead. So that's where you had to do the hard work. You had to knock on doors.

The first door I knocked on in North Philly, I remember the woman answered the door, and her record was that she was deceased. It's just that she had the same name as someone else in the same precinct or division in Philadelphia, and her record was canceled, not the person with the same name. So it showed up as a false positive. There was that, there was where people would go to vote, and someone else in the same place, usually mother and daughter or father and son, with the same name, and they would sign in the other person's spot, not in their spot. So it was never a question of more votes being cast...

DAVIES: The voter roll book that the election worker would say, sign here.

SCHMIDT: That's right. So it would be Al Schmidt followed by Al Schmidt, and they would sign where it had the one person, not the other. It wasn't a fraudulent vote or anything else like that. It was signing the poll book under the wrong person's name with the same name. And in the end, we ended up with zero out of that 10 to 12. It was kind of disappointing 'cause I thought for sure that, you know, you heard so much about all this over all these years, and you put in all that hard work. And, I mean, it was a relief knowing that you didn't have voter fraud going on. There was certainly something important to take from it all. But, you know, you end up in this search, and in the end, everything that could be done was done, and there was no evidence of it.

DAVIES: I'm wondering if the experience of 2020 has affected people's willingness to serve on election boards and assist in elections.

SCHMIDT: We track it at Department of State, and we've certainly seen an increase in turnover when it comes to the people responsible for elections, and there are many reasons for it, right? Sometimes people are just ready to retire. For others, it's because of the environment, the way that it's been around elections and also the requirements to be an election director have changed so much since I got involved in 2011 and 2012. So you have to be a lot more public facing. You have to be better at communicating. We have never had so much interest in elections. People have a lot of questions. It's just incumbent upon us to provide them with truthful answers to their questions so that they're not deceived by people who lie for a living.

DAVIES: Al Schmidt, I wish you a smooth and peaceful Election Day. Thank you for coming in and speaking with us.

SCHMIDT: Thank you, Dave.

DAVIES: Al Schmidt is Pennsylvania's Secretary of the Commonwealth, the state's chief election official.

(SOUNDBITE OF PSYCHOGRASS' "HIGH HAM")

DAVIES: On Tomorrow's show - actor Betty Gilpin, if you watched the series "Widow's Bay," you saw her Emmy-winning performance as a woman in the 1700s who realizes her new husband may be at the center of a Satanic curse. She now stars with Ethan Hawke in the new season of the FX show "The Lowdown." She also starred as Mary Todd Lincoln in the Broadway play "Oh, Mary!" I hope you can join us.

To keep up with what's on the show and get highlights of our interviews,

World.title: Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
World.content:
Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.

The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.

The unsigned order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."

It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.

Sponsor Message

As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

In January 2025, upon assuming office, Trump issued an executive order banning the use of federal funds that "promote" gender ideology. And prisoners brought a class action seeking reinstatement of the decades-long health policy. It contends that the Trump policy violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.

A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.

That's when U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and a lawyer involved in this case, said the organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in BOP custody who identify as transgender. (The BOP stopped publishing data reflecting transgender inmates after Trump took office in 2025. It only records male or female individuals incarcerated in the federal system.)

Kingdom v. Trump represents 1,000 inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis, Nowlin-Sohl explained. Of those, the ACLU believes there are about 800 who have been prescribed hormone therapy and many who are also receiving social transition accommodations, Nowlin-Sohl said.

Sponsor Message

In its request for an emergency stay on the earlier rulings, the Trump administration argued that providing this care poses several risks, including for recipients of this specialized care, who it argued would become "targets for attacks." They also said that it raises "fairness concerns" as it would "breed resentment" with other inmates.

Access to gender-affirming care is considered medically necessary to treat gender dysphoria, a medical term used to describe the deep discomfort caused by a mismatch between a person's assigned sex at birth and their gender identity. Without it, individuals can struggle severely with mental health issues such as heightened anxiety and depression, with some turning to self-harm and suicide.

Gender-affirming care can include "...hormone therapy, and gender-affirming surgeries among others," according to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. (In its filings, the Trump administration questioned WPATH's standards of care, which were developed by experts in transgender health and used by organizations across the world.)

Some people who are transgender may require hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries; others may not require any of these interventions.

The BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria since at least 1992, the ACLU said in response to the government's filings to the Supreme Court.

"Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," the ACLU wrote.

This is a "glaring omission" and appears to indicate that the government's arguments now are simply "contrived," the ACLU continued.

NPR previously covered the impact of the loss of hormone treatments on people who are incarcerated. One woman said she experienced severe physical and mental anguish when she lost access to hormone treatments.

The Supreme Court's decision is at odds with other rulings that support the Trump administration's anti-trans policy agenda.

Sponsor Message

Last June, the court ruled that states can ban transgender girls from participating in sports at publicly funded schools. And in 2025, the court upheld state laws that make it illegal for doctors and other health professionals to provide gender-affirming care for minors.

In one of his first executive orders of his second term, President Trump targeted the trans community with a declaration that his administration recognizes just two sexes, male and female. This order has been the basis for a host of anti-trans policies throughout the administration.

But at least for now, the emergency request on the prison policy was to no avail.

Waiting in the wings at the Supreme Court are other cases on transgender rights. Most prominently, the Alliance Defending Freedom, an anti-trans group, has filed an emergency petition at the court on behalf of a mother and her teenage daughter who contend that the daughter was "unknowingly" forced to face a transgender opponent in girl's high school wrestling. Later this year, the court will hear oral arguments in a case testing whether a religious preschool can receive state funding while excluding LGBTQ families. In a separate case, the justices will examine whether parents have the right to challenge a state law that allows runaway teens to receive gender-affirming care without parental consent.

NPR Legal Affairs Correspondent Nina Totenberg contributed reporting.

World.title: U.S. Embassy says Carney government brushing off 'potential interference' in midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa says the federal government is brushing off concerns about "potential interference in U.S. elections" after Prime Minister Mark Carney insisted that Canada is not getting involved in the American midterms.

U.S. officials have in recent weeks warned against what they describe as potential Canadian interference ahead of their Nov. 3 midterm elections.

In a release on Wednesday, the embassy suggested that the "Canadian government brushes off" the Trump administration's concerns. The release lists a number of statements by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and other officials as examples of attempts to influence the midterms.

Both Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.

"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.

"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."

WATCH | Carney, Ford respond to election interference claims: Carney, Ford respond to Trump administration's election interference claims | Duration closed caption 1:49 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to a fact sheet sent out by the U.S. Embassy on Wednesday claiming Canadian politicians have plans to influence American politics. 'All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers,' said Carney.

Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."

"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said last week that American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the midterms.

Hoekstra pointed to Joly's comments about the strategy behind Canadian counter-tariffs and the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Reagan ad that ran in the U.S. last year.

WATCH | Trade war a major issue in midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Wednesday's embassy release listed a number of grievances that Hoekstra raised last week but also added more, including Canada's consul general in Boston, Bernadette Jordan, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates — as well Liberal MP Anthony Housefather canvassing for a Florida Democrat during a primary vote earlier this year.

About half of the instances listed on the embassy's release occurred in 2026, and a handful point to events from last year, including a federal government billboard campaign from early 2025.

The release also alleges "Canada has the second-highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country," while listing 11 Canadians who have been charged for illegally voting in past U.S. elections.

According to the release, while the alleged offences took place between 2012 and 2024 — the 11 Canadians were all charged or sentenced this year.

Joly pushed back against Hoekstra's previous comments, telling reporters last week that Canada would never engage in election interference and would "never accept that also being done to us in Canada."

WATCH | Canada 'absolutely not' interfering, Joly says: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

Carney also told Global News last week that Canada doesn't "get ourselves involved in [foreign] elections."

Peter Navarro, one of Trump's top trade advisers, also suggested Canada could interfere in the midterms during an economic conference in Washington last month.

"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach to trade talks.

"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."

WATCH | Trump adviser issues warning to Canada: 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates running for the Senate in the two border states Navarro mentioned.

The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

Since returning to the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump has made a number of public statements backing candidates in various countries, including Argentina and Hungary.

World.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers pauses program after CBC investigation reveals more details of data leak
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto Crime Stoppers is pausing its program, effective immediately, said its chair, Sean Sportun, in a statement sent late Wednesday evening.

The news follows an exclusive CBC investigation from earlier in the day revealing that information from more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years was exposed in a massive data breach.

It was the first time precise figures were made public showing the severity of the information exposed, as well as how many Canadian tipsters were compromised.

Up until the investigation was published, the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) and individual chapters had not spoken out about the extent of the breach, only saying they awaited a detailed report from Navigate360, the U.S.-based third party company that manages its data through its platform P3.

Toronto Crime Stoppers now says it has removed the "Tip Submit” feature from its website and will no longer accept or process any new information intended for the program. It has also advised Navigate360 to immediately suspend the intake function for the Toronto Crime Stoppers chapter from its platform.

In the statement, the organization advised the public not to send tips by phone, online or through its app "until we have a safer way to protect you."

"People in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous. This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry," Sportun said in a statement.

The Toronto Police Service also announced in a statement Wednesday evening that it has "temporarily suspended its use of Crime Stoppers" until further review.

CBC found thousands of unredacted names

According to CBC's investigation, Toronto Crime Stoppers had the most tips represented in the leak of all Canadian chapters, with more than 179,000 tips.

The analysis also revealed that more than half of all Canadian tips included personally identifiable information. CBC could not determine in every instance whether the information belonged to a tipster, a victim or someone accused of a crime.

However, CBC found that in over 4,300 reports, tipsters introduced themselves with a full name, although Crime Stoppers explicitly tells the public to avoid including identifying details . Still, this represented a fraction of reports, at less than one per cent of all entries over 25 years. CBC wasn't able to verify whether all names were legitimate.

Despite hundreds of those tips containing clear staff warnings that a tipster had "self-identified" or had been "exposed," the information still appeared in the database unredacted.

WATCH | More on the investigation: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 1:52 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

Toronto Crime Stoppers' Wednesday statement reiterated that the program aims to keep tips anonymous.

"We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it," it said. "But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw. Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3."

The Toronto police statement, which was sent at almost the same time, said the news "raises serious concerns regarding the protection of confidential information provided through the Crime Stoppers program."

At the time of publication, CBC could still access a tip form using the main P3 platform.

World.title: In her riding, United Conservative Party leaders back Danielle Smith
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Premier Danielle Smith calls on separatists within her party to stand down, some party leaders in her own riding say they are on board.

Smith addressed the province shortly after Monday's referendum to outline voters' three-to-one decision against holding a formal separation vote, according to preliminary results.

Then on Wednesday, she told United Conservative Party members the result now forms party policy, and those who continue to publicly advocate for secession can "find another party" rather than risk hurting the UCP's chances in next year's election.

The party's MLAs and many local boards are "whole-heartedly, 100 per cent" behind Smith, cabinet minister Justin Wright told CBC News at a breakfast event in Medicine Hat before the premier's comments were released.

"The consensus has been very strong clear across the board," said Wright, the MLA for Cypress-Medicine Hat, located next to Smith's riding of Brooks-Medicine Hat.

"Within even the party, there's been so many [constituency] boards that have come forward, including my own, with full support for the premier, passing motions just to say we align with her and where things are going."

Wright said cabinet members met the day after the referendum, and a caucus meeting was scheduled for Wednesday.

WATCH | Alberta premier's message to separatists: Be pro-Canada or join a different party: Alberta premier's message to separatists: Be pro-Canada or join a different party | Duration closed caption 15:19 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has a message for separatists in her party: Get with the pro-Canada program, or join a different party. It comes after voters overwhelmingly chose Canada in the province's recent referendum. Power & Politics hears from Smith on how she plans to enforce that rule — and what's next for her party.

During the referendum, Smith publicly stated support for the remain option, but has been criticized by the opposition NDP for allowing the question to move ahead in the first place.

There has also been speculation that pro-independence groups would seek internal party power to continue their cause.

'We must be unified': Smith

Smith told members in a video message and then reiterated in a press conference later Wednesday that separation advocates had been heard by the party, but the issue is settled.

WATCH | UCP is not an independence party, Smith says: Danielle Smith says Alberta separatist UCP members can 'join a different party' | Duration closed caption 2:44 Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said her governing United Conservative Party must support the will of Albertans who voted overwhelmingly to remain in Canada, and that disaffected pro-separatist members are free to 'join a different party.'

Party members can form their own opinions, she said, but if they continue to publicly call for separation, they won't be welcome as candidates or members of local boards ahead of the 2027 election.

"We must be unified," she said. "If we aren't, our party will split, and Alberta will suffer terribly as a result."

This comes after the UCP riding association for Highwood passed a motion last month calling for a leadership review. At least 22 associations are needed to support the motion for it to come forward at the party's AGM in late November.

Some prominent separatists have suggested greater participation in the UCP as the next step, after their projected loss this week.

Change the channel, says former party worker

The party will have to address the separation issue quickly, said former Cypress-Medicine Hat UCP association leader Alan Rose earlier this week.

Alan Rose, a former UCP official in Medicine Hat, says Premier Danielle Smith should move beyond the separation issue. (Collin Gallant/CBC)

"It'll still be a party issue, because that's where it started," said Rose, adding that he voted against a second referendum and felt the "resounding" victory gave Smith a path forward.

"There have been factions within the UCP ... that wanted to go in a different direction, but that's not the direction that I believe most people want it to go," said Rose.

"Now, I hope the premier realizes that she has enough support to concentrate on what's actually good for Albertans."

In Monday's referendum, about 75 per cent of voters across the province cast ballots in favour of Alberta "remaining a province of Canada," according to preliminary results.

In Brooks-Medicine Hat, the "remain" figure sat at 63 per cent in unofficial results as of Wednesday evening. The Cypress-Medicine Hat portion for remain was 68 per cent.

World.title: Canada's Russian envoy returns with advice on how to hit back against Putin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's outgoing ambassador to Russia has returned with advice for crafting a response to Moscow's "cognitive warfare" campaign against the NATO alliance and why keeping sanctions on oil and gas can frustrate Vladimir Putin's struggle to finance his war machine.

Sarah Taylor's three-year tour of duty in Moscow, which ended Oct. 8, was defined by the Russian president's invasion of Ukraine from her first day in the country to her last, and that conflict, she says in a rare interview with CBC News, has all but returned the country to a Cold War mentality.

Taylor says that while many in NATO, particularly in Europe, worry about a conventional invasion of their territory by Russia, she doesn't see that happening "at least in the short to medium term."

"But I do think already we are effectively under attack in a form of cognitive warfare and we maybe don't really realize just how bad that is," she told CBC Radio's The Current, in an interview that aired on Wednesday.

LISTEN | Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow: The Current 19:08 Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow Longtime diplomat Sarah Taylor has just wrapped up nearly three years on the ground in Moscow as Canada's ambassador to Russia, her final posting before retirement. She speaks with Matt Galloway about her conversations with Russian citizens and officials as the war in Ukraine continues, and the cognitive warfare she warns is already underway.

Taylor says Russia's use of propaganda is widespread and effective because it uses its knowledge of how the West works and key language skills to ensure its campaigns will have maximum impact.

She says the large Russian dissident community, including independent journalists, that are now outside Russia could be an effective counteroffensive on the cognitive battlefield.

"I think part of Putin's power lies in an ability to sort of project inevitability and to say, 'Well, you know, it'll always be Putin and only Putin. And this is just the way it is,'" she told host Matt Galloway.

"To have an active, open discussion that's going on, particularly if some of it is in Russian and can filter back into Russia to say, 'No, Russia doesn't have to be like this. There are alternative futures.' That's really important."

Another vulnerability Taylor sees is Putin's ongoing struggle to fund Russia's war machine.

"One of their weaknesses in this war is financing it," Taylor said. "It's become a hugely expensive undertaking for them, lasting much longer than the Russians expected … and part of the way they are funding this is through their sales of oil and gas."

Frustrating Putin's war machine

She says that while some sanctions on Russia are more symbolic in nature, such as the ones targeting people who "visibly support the war," others have a deeper strategic impact — like those on oil and gas, which U.S. President Donald Trump has moved to lift with his recent diesel deal with Putin.

"I do believe, personally, that it's very important to try and maintain those as much as possible because the more you do that, the more you increase the dilemma for the Russian government about how they are going to fund this war going forward," she said.

While the cost of invading Ukraine has been steep for the Russian government, Taylor says the state has "made a huge effort to make life feel as normal as possible" in cities like Moscow and St. Petersburg.

That reality held largely true, she says, until the last six months when Ukraine began targeting oil refineries, the warehouses of Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon that some call the "Russian Amazon" and more recently, large data centres.

Smoke billows into the sky following Ukrainian drone strikes on warehouses of Russia's online retailer Wildberries, in St. Petersburg, Russia, in July. (The Associated Press)

"Those are starting to have an impact, a bit more impact on daily life," she said. "It's obviously nothing like what, say, our colleagues in Kyiv are living every day … but it does feel like you're in the middle of a Cold War."

While admitting she did not mix with a "completely representative sample of Russians" while serving in Moscow, she says support for the war is paper thin.

"I have yet to meet a single ordinary Russian who was enthusiastic about the war. And most of them just want it to end, really," she said.

But wanting, and having the capacity to do something to feed that want, are very different, she says.

"The vast majority of people who have in any way either demonstrated against the war, or even … supported Ukraine by making donations or anything of that sort are now almost all in jail," she said.

"It's very telling that there are now as many, if not more … political prisoners in Russian jails than there were in the Khrushchev era of the Soviet Union. So we're really back to a Soviet-like feeling of repression, of dissent."

World.title: Boos, heckling greet Brady Tkachuk at 1st NHL game back in Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A chorus of boos awaited former Ottawa Senators captain Brady Tkachuk as he made his return to the ice at Canadian Tire Centre Wednesday night.

It was a packed stadium of vocal Sens fans who did not hold back in letting Tkachuk know how they feel about him.

"He's a traitor, there's not much else to say," said fan Jack Kelso.

"He promised he'd give us the [Stanley Cup], but he left."

Earlier this year, the 27-year-old requested a trade to join the Florida Panthers alongside his older brother and podcast co-host, a move that was unpopular with many fans.

Nearly every time Tkachuk took the ice, or touched the puck, chants, often profane in nature, erupted through the stadium.

"I was expecting it, I just didn't think it would be this much," said fan Lesley Miller.

Senators fans Elissa Robillard, left, and Lesley Miller, right, said there was a big reaction to Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa. (Emma Weller/CBC)

A number of attendees also altered their Tkachuk jerseys to showcase their new upset with the player, with some replacing his name with that of the team's new captain Thomas Chabot.

Others chose to throw their jerseys onto the ice.

On an episode of his Wingmen podcast, Tkachuk committed to donating any Sens jerseys tossed on the ice by upset fans to the Boys and Girls Club of Ottawa.

Ottawa Senators fans wore altered jerseys of former Senators player Brady Tkachuk at the game between the Senators and the Florida Panthers in Ottawa. (The Canadian Press/Lisa Wallace)

During the game, a video tribute was made to Tkachuk, who waved to the crowd amid the chants.

Shortly after, he scored the first goal of the night in a power-play goal midway through the first period.

The Sens bounced back, winning the game 5-1.

Tkachuk focuses on fun

After the game, Tkachuk said he has no hard feeling towards anyone and just tried to enjoy the experience.

"It's new, those were my teammates not too long ago," he said.

"It was nice to be in front of this passionate fan base," he added when asked about the fan's reaction to his return.

Travis Green, head coach of the Ottawa Senators, said the game felt "as close to a playoff game as you're gonna get."

"It was very emotional, physical, was a hard fought game and I thought our team was excellent tonight," he said.

Tkachuk spent eight seasons with the Senators after being drafted fourth overall in 2018.

He is set to return to the Canadian Tire Centre on March 18.

World.title: Edmonton-based video game studio BioWare shutting down after more than 30 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Video game publisher Electronic Arts is shutting down the popular Edmonton-based game development studio BioWare after more than three decades.

BioWare announced the closure on social media Wednesday following a report by Bloomberg that also said the company is laying off 400 people, including about 50 at BioWare.

It also confirmed the upcoming Mass Effect game, the fifth in a series since 2007, has been cancelled.

BioWare was founded in 1995 and acquired by Electronic Arts (EA) in 2007.

"It's a pretty sad day," BioWare co-founder Trent Oster told CBC Radio. "I mean, 30 plus years ago we built something I think was pretty awesome. And it's pretty sad to see the end of the dream."

The Redwood Shores, California-based maker of popular titles like Battlefield and The Sims closed the $55 billion US sale of its business to Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund PIF, investment firm Silver Lake Partners and Affinity Partners, which is run by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Representatives for EA did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the layoffs.

"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember," the studio said via social media. "These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with characters, and made these worlds your own."

BioWare built its reputation on immersive role-playing adventures, from sword-and-sorcery fantasies like Baldur's Gate and Dragon Age to science fiction epics like Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect.

Oster, who is now the CEO of gaming company Beamdog, said back in its early days, BioWare was a magical place to be.

"We went from a bunch of clueless kids trying to make a game just for the hell of it to literally being the best in the world at what we did," he said. "During the time I was there, it went from six people to 420, and it was just a massive growth. Honestly, it was an amazing experience."

But the company's later effort to branch out into multiplayer shooters, 2019's Anthem, steered away from the studio's strength as a creator of compelling single-player narratives. It failed to find the sort of loyal audience that keeps online hits like Fortnite and Overwatch popular.

Meanwhile the latest installments of BioWare's two most popular original franchises — 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard — met with mixed reviews and disappointed many fans.

A new chapter of Mass Effect was in development before BioWare announced its shutdown.
