TODAY’S PICK — FREE MUSIC & ART IN CENTRO A free guitar concert in Centro, then CCBB’s collection Start at CCBB Rio on Primeiro de Março in Centro and check its current exhibitions. In the evening, walk to the Centro Cultural Justiça Federal on Avenida Rio Branco for a free Música no Museu concert at 6pm, with Mara Lúcia Ribeiro on guitar and a classic Brazilian repertoire. Check the building’s opening hours before you go. Take the VLT to Colombo or Metrô Line 2 to Uruguaiana — both put you within a five-minute walk of CCBB. For a sit-down break, cross to Confeitaria Colombo on Rua Gonçalves Dias. A coffee and a pastel de nata will run around R$25 (about US$5).

OUTDOORS — PARQUE LAGE AND JARDIM BOTÂNICO Green shade after the rain passes Parque Lage in Jardim Botânico opens at 8am and is free. The mansion courtyard is a good wet-morning cover, and the park paths are walkable once showers ease. Jardim Botânico opens at 8am daily, but on Wednesdays at 11am. Entry is R$40 (about US$8) for residents, R$80 (about US$16) for foreigners — bring proof of residency for the lower rate. Walk between the two: Parque Lage sits at the foot of the Corcovado road, and the Jardim Botânico gate is ten minutes downhill by foot.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO AND SANTA TERESA Dependable wifi and decent espresso Downtown, Curto Café on Avenida Erasmo Braga has fast wifi, long tables, and an espresso for R$9 (about US$1.8). It stays calm on Thursday afternoons. In Santa Teresa, Culto Café on Rua Almirante Alexandrino is open through the afternoon with terrace seats and reliable wifi. Good for late lunch work. For proper coworking, Centro has several spaces on Avenida Rio Branco, but a café table with a second coffee works fine on a quiet Thursday.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — MUSEU DO AMANHÃ A sci-fi cool-down at Praça Mauá If you want air-conditioning and a serious exhibition, Museu do Amanhã is open Thursday to Tuesday, 10am to 6pm. Entry is R$30 (about US$6), half price R$15 (about US$3). The museum sits at Praça Mauá, a ten-minute VLT ride from CCBB. The building itself is the main draw, and the exhibits are in Portuguese and English. This is the opposite of the free outdoor day: a structured, ticketed, indoor science museum with a strong climate-change message.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Samba at Fundição, then Lapa’s bar strip Fundição Progresso hosts Samba Independente Dos Bons Costumes at 9pm. Check the venue’s ticketing page for current prices; the venue is on Rua dos Arcos in Lapa. Doors open earlier than 9pm, so aim for 8:30pm to get a spot near the stage. The crowd is local, friendly, and the sound carries the night. After the show, walk two minutes to the Lapa arches and pick a bar. Bar da Boa on Avenida Mem de Sá has cold beer and live choro. If Fundição is too much, Rio Scenarium on Rua do Lavradio has three floors of samba and forró from 9pm, though it is pricier at the door.

ALSO ON TODAY Piaf – Eu Não Me Arrependo — Teatro Riachuelo Rio, Centro — 8pm, tickets on sale; French chanson on stage Museu Nacional de Belas Artes — Avenida Rio Branco, Centro — 10am to 6pm, free, partial reopening Paço Imperial — Praça XV, Centro — 12pm to 6pm, free, colonial art and history Real Gabinete Português de Leitura — Rua Luís de Camões, Centro — 10am to 5pm, free, ornate reading room

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô lines 1, 2 and 4 run normally today. Single journey is R$7.90 (about US$1.6) — use the Giro card or contactless card.

The VLT is the best connector between Praça Mauá, CCBB and Lapa.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: In Centro, try Tempeh on Rua do Carmo for a R$35 (about US$7) lunch plate, or Confeitaria Colombo’s buffet around R$60 (about US$12). Both are near CCBB.

Dinner: Before samba, go to Nova Capela on Avenida Mem de Sá for cabrito with rice, around R$60 (about US$12). Or split a pizza at Braz Pizzaria on Rua da Lapa for R$70 (about US$14) with a beer.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a card and some cash — small bars and street vendors often take Pix, but not all take cards. A rain shell is useful all day.

Book Fundição Progresso tickets online before going. The venue can sell out on free-music nights when locals move on afterwards.

Stay alert around Lapa’s smaller lanes after midnight, especially near the arches and Avenida Mem de Sá. Keep your phone in a front pocket.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads and new arrivals often meet at Curto Café downtown or at the Thursday language-exchange nights in Santa Teresa, which are informal and listed on Expat Rio WhatsApp groups.

For a more structured meet, check the Internations Rio group — they typically organise a monthly after-work drinque in Botafogo, with one expected in the coming week.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Flamengo host Estudiantes at the Maracanã tonight at 9:30pm in the Libertadores semifinal second leg, with the tie level at 0–0 after the first leg in La Plata.

The winner meets Palmeiras, who beat Fluminense on penalties on Wednesday, in the final on 28 November in Montevideo. Expect heavy crowds and road closures around the Maracanã in the evening.

For tonight’s match, Nova Capela in Lapa is a noisy, local Carioca viewing spot, and Boteco Belmonte in Ipanema and Bar Urca in Urca show televised games.

If you want a big-screen pub with English commentary, the Lord Jim Pub in Ipanema shows most Brazilian league matches when asked.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The market mood was mixed on Wednesday. US technology names led New York higher, while Brazilian shares eased back from recent levels.

Currency traders in Latin America saw the dollar firm against the Mexican peso, which weakened the most in the Americas session. The real held surprisingly steady.

For an expat professional, the main takeaway is a pause rather than a break: no single catalyst drove the moves. Friday brings Brazil’s IPCA-15 inflation report, and Sunday is the presidential runoff.

Reais in this brief convert at R$5.0243 per US$ (RT, 21 October).

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD FRI 23 — Warm at 26°C with a 65% chance of rain — book a table for Friday night dinner in Botafogo. SAT 24 — Hot at about 31°C with a 43% chance of rain — the best beach window of the weekend if the clouds hold. SUN 25 — Runoff election day, with polls open from 8am to 5pm; about 26°C with rain likely, so keep plans flexible. MON 26 — About 23°C with showers likely — Museu do Amanhã works as an indoor plan. TUE 27 — Check MAR in Praça Mauá — free Tuesday, open 11am to 6pm.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight: Chico Buarque, Divas Show.

Background: Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is it a good beach day today in Rio?

Not really. Showers are likely today and the high is only about 23°C. Saturday is the hot day, near 31°C, though showers are possible. Today is better for museums and Lapa nightlife.

Can I do free things in Rio today?

Yes — practically the whole day can cost very little. CCBB, Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, Paço Imperial and Real Gabinete are free. Música no Museu concerts are free; today’s is at the Centro Cultural Justiça Federal at 6pm. You only pay for transport and food.

How do I get around Centro and Lapa today?

The VLT tram is the best link. It connects Praça Mauá, CCBB, Lapa and the airport bus terminal. Metrô Line 2 stops at Uruguaiana and Carioca, both within walking distance of CCBB. Single fare is R$7.90 (about US$1.6).

Latin America's Pulse: Brazil's runoff fight dominates the mood as Lula's camp asks to annul Flávio's ticket, and the Mexican peso slides to a monthly low.

Rio Times · Latin America

Key Facts —Brazil Anxious and combative: Lula’s campaign asks the electoral court to annul Flávio’s ticket and bar him for eight years over alleged abuse of economic power. —Mexico Nervous but orderly: the peso fell about 1.4% to roughly 18.7 per dollar before Thursday’s inflation data. —Argentina Institutional hardening: Deputies voted 162-77 on 21 October for tougher penalties for rural vandalism, sending the bill to the Senate. —Colombia Regulatory caution: the CRC warns Claro would be the only fibre provider on 778 routes after absorbing Azteca’s network. —Chile Steady: the IPSA stock index rose 0.54% to 10,986 while the peso weakened. —Prediction markets Polymarket traders put Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning the 25 October runoff at 78.5% and Lula’s at 21.5%, as of 11:34 p.m. ET on Wednesday, 21 October.

The Continent’s Mood Today

The region’s biggest democracy is holding its breath. Recent polls put Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro within the margin of error.

This tightness is not just a poll number. It is a legal fight being waged through courts and platforms, and it is making the whole continent feel jittery.

Brazil – The War for the Voting Booth

The mood is raw. Lula’s campaign filed an action on 21 October asking the TSE (Brazil’s electoral court) to annul Flávio Bolsonaro’s ticket.

It asks to annul the ticket and bar him from office for eight years, alleging abuse of economic power and favouritism by Meta and X.

Mexico – Waiting for the Numbers

Mexico is waiting for data. The peso fell about 1.4% to roughly 18.7 per dollar on Wednesday, ahead of Thursday’s mid-month inflation report.

The stock market still jumped 1.4% to 70,250, so the unease is about direction, not panic. A foreigner here can still operate normally, but the currency’s slide shows the quiet anxiety underneath.

Argentina – The Iron Fist Gets a Vote

Argentina is leaning into punishment. The Chamber of Deputies voted 162-77 on 21 October to approve harsher penalties for vandalism and attacks on rural property, with sentences of up to eight years.

It now goes to the Senate.

This is about the countryside’s sense of siege and the city’s sense of chaos. The country wants order, and the bill reflects a longer shift toward law-and-order politics.

A foreigner with agricultural or land assets will find this legislation aimed at protecting them, but it also signals a more punitive social climate.

Colombia – The Small Print Fights

Colombia is feeling boxed in by its own regulators. The CRC (the telecoms regulator) warned that, after the Claro and Azteca integration, Claro would be the only fibre provider on 778 routes, and it wants strict access conditions.

The mood is one of cautious, technical survival. For foreigners, the CRC’s warning is a sign that regulators may attach strict conditions to big telecom deals, so patience is required.

Chile – Calm Markets, Softer Peso

Chile is reading the day through its markets. The IPSA stock index rose 0.54% to 10,986 on Wednesday, while the peso weakened to about 980 per dollar.

The mood is steady, with investors neither rushing in nor running for the exits. A foreigner in Chile can expect a calm backdrop, though a weaker peso raises import costs.

The Shared Mood

The shared emotion is suspicion, doped with distraction. Across the region, countries are fighting over who controls the rules: the platform, the regulator, the court, the vote.

This is not a crisis but a correction. For a foreigner living or investing here, the practical lesson is simple: assume every deal is political, and enjoy the football only until the whistle blows.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket, a prediction market where people bet real money, put Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning the 25 October runoff at 78.5 percent and Lula’s at 21.5 percent at 11:34 p.m. ET on Wednesday, 21 October. About US$191.2 million had been traded on that market.

These prices are bets by traders, not polls, and they can move within minutes of a debate or a new survey. The official result will come from Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is driving Brazil’s election anxiety on October 22, 2026?

Lula’s campaign filed an action on 21 October asking the electoral court to annul Flávio Bolsonaro’s ticket and bar him for eight years, while recent polls put the race inside the margin of error.

Why is Mexico’s mood described as nervous?

The peso fell about 1.4% ahead of Thursday’s inflation data, even as the stock market jumped 1.4%.

What does the Colombia Claro-Azteca warning mean?

The CRC regulator warned that Claro would be the only fibre provider on 778 routes, so it wants strict access conditions if the deal is approved.

01 Tech’s last word before the Fed

The S&P 500 closed at 7,757, up 0.58%, while the Nasdaq rose 1.05% to 26,703 and the Dow gained 0.69% to 52,856. The VIX fell 3.64% to 16.68, suggesting traders see less near-term risk despite a 10-year Treasury yield at 5.129%.

Gold climbed 0.28% to US$4,126 an ounce, defying the usual logic that higher yields dim bullion’s appeal. The dollar index was essentially flat at 101.647, a pause that leaves emerging-market currencies, particularly Brazil’s real, waiting for a clearer signal.

02 A Fed that cannot afford to blink

The 10-year yield’s rise to 5.129% reflects a market still pricing in restrictive policy, even as the VIX retreats. Traders are betting the Fed will tolerate slower growth rather than risk inflation becoming embedded.

For investors, the message is that long-duration assets remain vulnerable. A yield above 5% raises the discount rate on future earnings, especially for the technology names that have powered the rally this month.

03 Brazil’s tightrope between the real and Selic

Brazil’s IPCA-15 mid-month inflation report is due on Friday. Economists’ forecasts cluster around 0.4% to 0.5% for the month, and the National Monetary Council meets today.

The variable to watch is Friday’s flash PMIs, which show whether US business activity is cooling, and then the Fed’s decision on 28 October.

01 The overnight tape in one read

Wall Street ended firmly higher, with the Nasdaq gaining more than 1% and the S&P 500 and Dow also advancing. The VIX volatility index, often called Wall Street’s fear gauge, fell by almost 4%, showing investors are growing calmer.

Europe and parts of Asia firmed too. Germany’s DAX rose 1.4% and the Euro Stoxx 50 added 1.4%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 0.9%.

The US dollar barely moved against a basket of major currencies. That steadiness helps emerging markets, though Mexico’s peso weakened enough to stand out as a regional concern.

Assessment — Inflation data set the tone MEDIUM The overnight tape favors global equities, and Latin America usually follows eventually. But Wednesday’s Brazilian sell-off, led by a sharp drop in industrial names like WEG, suggests domestic investors are more worried about local interest rates than about Wall Street’s mood. If Friday’s IPCA-15 comes in near forecasts of about 0.4% to 0.5% for the month, it might ease fears and support the real. A hotter print could deepen the divergence. Watch the real first, then see if foreign flows return to Brazilian equities.

Meanwhile, the most-traded names were Petrobras and Vale, both deeply tied to global commodity prices. Heavy turnover there suggests investors were adjusting positions ahead of today’s inflation data, not abandoning the market entirely.

04 Brazil and the currencies

The real was nearly flat, a small movement that masks a bigger tension. Brazil will publish its mid-month IPCA-15 inflation index on Friday, with economists forecasting a monthly rise of about 0.4% to 0.5%.

Those numbers matter because they decide whether the central bank can keep cutting the Selic, its benchmark rate. If inflation comes in hotter than expected, the bank may pause, which would hurt local stocks and support the real at the same time.

Foreign investors are watching this carefully. The Brazilian stock exchange has seen a divergence from Wall Street, and a bad inflation print could widen that gap even further.

Mexico’s peso is the currency to watch today. It fell sharply overnight, and with inflation and unemployment data due at 06:00 Mexico City time, the peso could swing quickly. Argentina’s numbers — retail sales and consumer confidence — may also nudge the Merval, its main stock index. Also due today are Mexico’s Mid-month Core Inflation Rate and Core Inflation Rate (forecast 0.18% each, previous 0.17%), and US Initial Jobless Claims (forecast 200,000), Continuing Jobless Claims (1.72 million) and the Jobless Claims 4-Week Average (200,000), all at 13:30 Lisbon time.

05 The regional setup

Index Country Change IPSA Chile +0.54% COLCAP Colombia +1.07% IPC Mexico +1.43% Ibovespa Brazil −0.86%

The regional picture is mixed. Colombia, Chile and Mexico gained, while Brazil slipped; Argentina’s MSCI Merval rose, but local sources disagree on by how much. The cross-country gap reflects different local conditions and interest-rate expectations. Data released on Wednesday: Mexico’s retail sales rose 1.2% in August from July, beating the 0.3% forecast, according to the INEGI statistics agency. Colombia’s Balance of Trade showed a deficit of US$2.77 billion in August, against a US$2.8 billion forecast, as Imports rose 31.7% to US$7.70 billion (DANE). Argentina’s Economic Activity fell 1.7% in August from a year earlier (INDEC). Argentina’s Leading Indicator and Costa Rica’s Balance of Trade readings could not be confirmed in time for this edition.

Mexico’s IPC rose 1.4% to 70,250, but the peso’s sharp drop suggests investors are cautious before today’s inflation data. Today’s mid-month inflation data will set the tone for Mexican assets.

06 The technical picture

Brazil’s Ibovespa closed down 0.86%, about 1.2% below its record close of 209,067 on 9 October. It gave back part of Tuesday’s gain, so short-term momentum is weak, especially given that Wall Street rallied.

Mexico’s IPC jumped 1.4% on Wednesday to 70,250. The peso’s weakness is the real test: a continued slide could pull the stock index back.

Chile’s IPSA and Colombia’s COLCAP are the bright spots. Both rose on Wednesday.

The key technical line to watch is the real. If it holds near 5.02 to the dollar after the IPCA print, Brazilian assets could stabilise. If it breaks decisively higher, meaning a weaker real, the Ibovespa could retest recent lows.

Why did Brazil fall while US stocks rose?

The Ibovespa fell 0.86% on Wednesday, led by WEG (down 7.3%) and Hapvida (down 8.5%), even as US stocks rose. Investors are also waiting for Friday’s IPCA-15 inflation data.

What is the IPCA?

It is Brazil’s official consumer price index. The mid-month version gives an early read on inflation and helps the central bank decide on the Selic, its benchmark interest rate.

Why is Mexico’s peso falling?

The peso fell about 1.4% to roughly 18.7 per dollar on Wednesday, ahead of today’s inflation data.

Which markets are doing best in the region?

Colombia’s COLCAP gained over 1%. Chile’s IPSA also rose, while Mexico’s IPC rose 1.4% and Brazil slipped, as did the Argentine peso-based Merval measures that local sources report differently.
