World.title: Cyberangriffe kommen nicht nur zu Bürozeiten
World.content:
An diesem Vormittag wartet die IT-Abteilung von Babor auf einen Cyberangriff. Genauer gesagt auf das Ergebnis eines Cyberangriffs, den sie selbst in Auftrag gegeben hat: Ein Penetrationstest soll zeigen, wie gut die Systeme des Kosmetikherstellers geschützt sind. Denn die Bedrohungslage verändert sich. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie Unternehmen arbeiten, sondern auch, wie sie angegriffen werden. Phishing-Mails lassen sich heute in Sekunden auf ihre Opfer zuschneiden, Schadsoftware kann sich automatisiert an Abwehrmechanismen anpassen, und Angriffsmuster entwickeln sich schneller weiter, als klassische Sicherheitskonzepte nachziehen können. Für Unternehmen werden damit zwei Fragen immer wichtiger: Wie schnell erkennen sie einen Angriff und wie reagieren sie darauf?

Ein Härtetest für die IT-Sicherheit

Gemeinsam mit den Expertinnen und Experten von Vodafone und SITS hat das Team die eigene IT-Infrastruktur einem kontrollierten Cyberangriff ausgesetzt. Die Frage ist, wie gut die Systeme einem echten Angreifer standhalten würden und vor allem, wie früh ein solcher Angriff erkannt wird. „Das Ergebnis haben wir mit Spannung erwartet“, sagt Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor. Für die IT-Abteilung ist der Test mehr als eine technische Übung. Babor betreibt rund 200 Server am Hauptsitz in Aachen, dazu kommen weitere Rechenzentrumsstrukturen an unterschiedlichen Standorten. ERP-Systeme, Datenbanken und Kollaborationstools bilden die Grundlage der täglichen Geschäftsprozesse. Weltweit vernetzte Standorte mit Tochtergesellschaften in Europa und Nordamerika sowie mehr als 1000 Mitarbeitern machen die Infrastruktur zusätzlich komplex. Entsprechend hoch sind die Anforderungen an ihre Absicherung. Die bisher eingesetzte Sicherheitslösung stieß zunehmend an ihre Grenzen. Gesucht war ein Ansatz, der nicht nur automatisiert auf verdächtige Aktivitäten reagiert, sondern die gesamte Infrastruktur rund um die Uhr im Blick behält und bei Bedarf Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten hinzuzieht. Inzwischen ist ein solches Security Operations Center (SOC) bei Babor im Einsatz. Der Penetrationstest sollte deshalb auch zeigen, wie gut die neue Sicherheitsarchitektur im Ernstfall funktioniert.

Das Sicherheitssystem auf einen Blick

Der Moment der Wahrheit

Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.

Endlich liegen die Ergebnisse des Tests auf dem Tisch. Die Anspannung weicht der Erleichterung. „Wir waren dann aber ein Stück weit beruhigt: Der Angriff wurde in einem frühen Stadium erkannt, lange bevor Ressourcen in unserem Intranet kompromittiert werden konnten.“ Der Test zeigt damit zweierlei: Die vorhandenen Schutzmechanismen greifen und das Zusammenspiel aus automatisierter Erkennung und der Analyse durch Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten funktioniert. Gleichzeitig wird deutlich, dass IT-Sicherheit eine Aufgabe ist, die kontinuierliche Aufmerksamkeit erfordert. Denn ein Angriff hält sich nicht an Bürozeiten, und eine IT-Abteilung kann nicht rund um die Uhr vor den Bildschirmen sitzen.

Die Lösung: Security Operations Center

Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Das externe Security Operations Center übernimmt für Babor die kontinuierliche Überwachung der IT-Infrastruktur und kombiniert automatisierte Prozesse mit der Analyse durch erfahrene Security Expertinnen oder -Experten. Sicherheitsrelevante Ereignisse werden fortlaufend analysiert, Auffälligkeiten bewertet und bei Bedarf entsprechende Maßnahmen eingeleitet. Für die interne IT bedeutet das eine zusätzliche Sicherheitsebene und zugleich mehr Freiraum für andere Aufgaben. Statt sämtliche sicherheitsrelevanten Ereignisse selbst rund um die Uhr überwachen und einordnen zu müssen, kann das Babor-Team auf die Expertise der SOC-Spezialisten zurückgreifen. Auch Anforderungen, die über den reinen Schutz der IT-Systeme hinausgehen, lassen sich auf diese Weise berücksichtigen. Dazu zählen etwa Vorgaben aus dem Bereich Compliance oder Anforderungen der Cyberversicherung. Das SOC schafft damit eine Struktur, in der Sicherheitsereignisse kontinuierlich beobachtet und nach definierten Prozessen bearbeitet werden können. Für Rüdiger Mohnen, IT Leiter von Babor, macht sich die Unterstützung bereits im Arbeitsalltag bemerkbar: „Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns voll auf unser Kerngeschäft konzentrieren können. Wir wissen, dass unser Firmennetz durch eine zusätzliche Instanz zuverlässig geschützt ist und haben im Ernstfall jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite. Für mittelständische Unternehmen ist der Verzicht auf ein SOC aus meiner Sicht fahrlässig.“ Der Cyberangriff an diesem Vormittag war kontrolliert. Die nächste Attacke wird es möglicherweise nicht sein. Für Babor kommt es deshalb darauf an, Bedrohungen nicht erst dann zu erkennen, wenn sie Schaden angerichtet haben. Das SOC hilft dabei, aufmerksam zu bleiben, rund um die Uhr – auch dann, wenn in Aachen längst niemand mehr vor den Bildschirmen sitzt.

Eine zusätzliche Schutzinstanz

Drei Fragen an Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor, und Rüdiger Mohnen, IT-Leiter von Babor.

Mirella Fiebes und Rüdiger Mohnen von Babor, Quelle: Vodafone

Warum setzt Babor beim Schutz seines Firmennetzes auf ein externes Security Operations Center?

Mirella Fiebes: Für uns war entscheidend, ein durchgängiges 24/7-Monitoring sicherzustellen. Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Rüdiger Mohnen: Zuverlässiger Cyberschutz ist für uns essenziell – nicht zuletzt im Hinblick auf Compliance-Anforderungen und die Vorgaben unserer Cyberversicherung. Ausfälle infolge von Cyberangriffen würden schnell erhebliche Kosten verursachen.

Unsere Cybersicherheit muss auch an Wochenenden und Feiertagen ohne Einschränkungen gewährleistet sein.

Welche konkreten Vorteile bringt Ihnen das SOC?

Rüdiger Mohnen: Das Security Operations Center entlastet unsere IT spürbar, sodass wir uns konsequent auf unser Kerngeschäft fokussieren können. Gleichzeitig gewinnen wir zusätzliche Sicherheit durch eine unabhängige Instanz sowie durch die enge Zusammenarbeit mit den Security-Expert:innen. Im Ernstfall haben wir jederzeit kompetente Unterstützung an unserer Seite.

Warum haben Sie sich für Vodafone Business als Partner entschieden?

Mirella Fiebes: Das Angebot von Vodafone hat uns inhaltlich und konzeptionell überzeugt. Diese Entscheidung wurde sowohl in der Implementierungsphase – gemeinsam mit dem Partner SITS – als auch im laufenden Betrieb bestätigt.

World.title: Trump’s diesel deal derailed Ukraine-Russia peace progress, says Czech president
World.content:
The White House on Wednesday said Trump “successfully negotiated” the deal in order to supply the global market with “massive amounts of diesel and bring prices down.”



The deal quickly drew backlash and, at one point, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators urged Trump to rescind the deal.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media that the deal “plays into Russia’s hands” and allows Russia “to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world.” He accused Trump of using peace talks in Florida as a “smokescreen” as the administration pursued its deal with Russia.

Zelenskyy’s criticism was the latest indicator of rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Trump has repeatedly expressed frustrations with Zelenskyy, accusing him of elongating the war. By contrast, of late he has spoken warmly of Putin and said this week that “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine.”

But Pavel offered the Ukrainian president words of support on Wednesday.

“I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict,” said Pavel. “So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia.”

He added that Trump shows a more open approach to Russia than any European leader.

World.title: Far-right Italian general hunts the manosphere vote
World.content:
“It is disgusting to think you can manipulate the image of a woman for such deplorable propaganda,” the center-right junior minister in Meloni’s coalition whose image was manipulated, Matilde Siracusano, told POLITICO. “I don’t think we have ever sunk this low, especially from someone aspiring to be a national political leader.”

Vannacci’s provocations may look like familiar trolling from a politician who has built his reputation on saying the unsayable. But behind them lies a broader political project, tapping into the grievances of young men who feel alienated by feminism and progressive culture.

Emanuele Pozzolo, a National Future parliamentarian who defected from Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, believes young men have become increasingly constrained in their relationships with women.

“I think young Western men are very often almost castrated in their instinct for dealing with women,” he said, arguing that even legitimate romantic approaches risk being treated as aggression.

“The cultural problem is that sometimes everything seems to be harassment, everything abuse, everything violence,” he added, while stressing that genuine abuse must be punished.

Mediterranean patriarchy

Vannacci combines inflammatory online messaging and an alpha-male persona with a political program that promises to restore traditional roles for men and women. National Future even has a name for its preferred social order: “Mediterranean patriarchy.”

World.title: Ukraine’s foreign fighters battle Russians — and red tape
World.content:
As of August, the defense ministry said some 16,000 foreigners from 72 countries were serving in the Ukrainian armed forces, giving crucial help to a 900,000-strong military that is chronically short of recruits.

The volunteers are facing a looming deadline. The Ukrainian parliament last year passed a law mandating that foreigners serving in the military have to file paperwork by Nov. 10 to get temporary residence permits.

“If nothing changes, then after November 10, a significant number of the foreigners defending Ukraine will technically be in the country illegally,” Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan said in a social media post.

That clashes with the official recruitment information given to foreign volunteers, which says their contract "is the basis for legal long-term stay in Ukraine."

“Even though I can prove I was serving in the Ukrainian army, they still make it impossible for us foreigners; none of them have any respect for people who fight for Ukraine, and they treat us like illegal aliens,” O’Brien said.

“I have been in three different Ukrainian units, and all of them have made mistakes in my military contracts or done them in a way that is not legally correct, so when I go to immigration to apply for the residency that I fought hard for, they ended up giving me a fine that I had to pay on the spot because my information was incorrect in my contract,” O’Brien added.

World.title: Merz’s eastern nightmare is far from over
World.content:
“The behavior of the CDU parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt with regard to past and upcoming elections is completely unacceptable,” Thomas Röwekamp, a CDU lawmaker who chairs the Bundestag’s defense committee, said. The AfD “wants to annihilate the CDU in Germany” by “forcing us into a debate about how to deal with it in order to divide the party,” he added. “We must not allow that to happen.”

Under pressure from conservatives in Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt CDU leader Sven Schulze announced a plan last week to have his party’s lawmakers leave the chamber during the initial two rounds of secret voting in December, ensuring none can vote for the far-right candidate — or be suspected of doing so. It’s unclear what the party would do in a potential third round, when the AfD would only need a majority of votes cast.

AfD leaders have openly said they are seeking defections from conservative ranks, a strategy designed as much to sow division among conservatives as to win the premiership. That approach seems to be working, at least partly.

Sven Schulze, outgoing Premier of Saxony-Anhalt and member of the German Christian Democratic Union, attends the first session of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since state elections on October 6, 2026 in Magdeburg. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

State conservatives have faced intense criticism for appearing so divided and vulnerable to aiding the AfD that their leaders apparently have no choice but to avoid the vote altogether. “It’s about taking a stand and assuming responsibility, rather than shirking a decision,” Röwekamp said.

Local CDU lawmakers, however, say their approach is tactically necessary. “We have always drawn a clear line between ourselves and the AfD,” CDU state lawmaker Chris Schulenburg said. “We adhere to the principle of distinguishing ourselves on the basis of substance, but not excluding them [the AfD], because, after all, the party is not currently banned, and its parliamentarians were also democratically elected.”

AfD leaders, meanwhile, have rejoiced in the CDU’s disarray.

World.title: Tesla's profit drops as it explores a possible merger with Musk's other public company, SpaceX
World.content:
Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits on Wednesday as Elon Musk's electric vehicle maker ramped up spending on artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transport.

 

The electric vehicle maker reported third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $787 million (€701 million), or 22 cents per share, down 43% from the year-earlier period. Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy generation and storage.

Revenue was essentially flat at $28 billion (€24.9 billion), falling slightly short of the company-compiled average analyst forecast of $28.3 billion.

Excluding certain items, though, earnings per share of 48 cents beat Wall Street analyst expectations by 3 cents.

One standout for the quarter was Tesla's $1.5 billion (€1.3 billion) in free cash flow, a measure of cash generated after subtracting investments needed to keep the business running.

Given heavy spending on artificial intelligence, analysts had expected Tesla would report it had burned through cash, not generated it. However, free cash flow was still down 62% from a year earlier.

"It seems Tesla is taking a more capital-efficient approach, delaying longer-term projects to be able to self-fund their AI growth," said Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein, calling the unexpected positive cash flow the big surprise of the quarter.

Tesla is rolling back its annual spending forecast

The company also reported more than doubling capital spending from a year earlier to $4.7 billion (€4.2 billion) for the quarter, but analysts had expected a far bigger increase.

Tesla cut its full-year 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion (€17.8 billion), from more than $25 billion (€22.3 billion). Chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said the company was managing its spending efficiently and planned to fund it mainly through operating cash flow.

Besides robotaxis and AI, Tesla is investing heavily in Musk's "Optimus" humanoid robots as well as developing Terafab, a chip manufacturing project in Austin, with SpaceX.

On the positive side, Tesla reported strong demand for its paid driver-assistance software, with more than 75% of new vehicles delivered in North America including a paid subscription sign-up.

The company calls the feature Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in North America. Despite its name, the software requires active driver supervision and does not make the vehicle autonomous.

Tesla's automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, also improved. For the three months through September, it reached 18.1%, up from 15.4% a year earlier.

Tesla had previously reported delivering 486,532 vehicles last quarter, a rise from 480,126 in the prior three months, but down 2% from a year earlier.

The modest rise in deliveries from the previous quarter did not translate into higher net profit.

Musk said Tesla was aiming to produce about five million vehicles a year by around 2030, compared with approximately 1.65 million produced in 2025.

"After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth," Musk said.

The company has faced questions about the rollout of its robotaxi business, which has fallen short of Musk's earlier ambitions.

In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, more than 800 Tesla vehicles are registered for autonomous service, according to FSD Database.

Tesla shares were down 3.2% in after-hours trading after climbing 3.6% during the regular trading session.

SpaceX merger talks add to questions over Tesla's future

Questions about Tesla's future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined stock market value of about $3.5 trillion (€3.1 trillion).

In a SpaceX conference call after that company reported earnings on Tuesday, Musk said both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to explore a possible merger. He said no terms had been agreed and there was no guarantee of a deal.

Merger speculation and SpaceX's strong results helped lift shares in both companies on Wednesday. Forbes estimated Musk's wealth at $1.013 trillion (€902 billion) at 10.30am New York time, putting him briefly back above the trillion-dollar mark.

Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and satellite infrastructure, including space-based computing.

Musk declined to discuss the possible merger further on Tesla's conference call.

World.title: Kenichi Yoda, Princess of Asturias laureate: 'Ghibli is closely tied to its time'
World.content:
A former reporter for the Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun, where early in his career he covered stories on the Ghibli animation studios, it seems highly unlikely that Kenichi Yoda (born 1974) imagined he would one day go on to head the company he had focused on as a culture journalist.

 

His rise to the summit of the legendary temple of animated cinema came on 22 June, when he took over the presidency from Hiroyuki Fukuda. His interview with 'Euronews' takes place 48 hours before he accepts, on behalf of his studio, the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Communication and Humanities.

The ideas of two of its creators, the late Isao Takahata and his colleague Hayao Miyazaki, together with the work of the roughly 200 people employed by the company, remain one of the main gateways into Japanese culture for millions of people around the globe.

That was the case with 'Marco' and 'Heidi' in Spain. The anime series were broadcast between the final throes of Francoism and the Transition to democracy, at a time when Ghibli had not even been conceived by this pair of film-makers, who met in a trade union while both were working at the Toei Doga studio in the 1960s. Those series were probably, with the exception of landmarks such as Akira Kurosawa's films, the first contact an entire generation of Spaniards had with the Land of the Rising Sun.

Yoda laughs when asked whether they see themselves as a tool of soft diplomacy or Japanese 'soft power'. "I think each work exists only because its directors and animators devoted themselves to it with care. We are very happy that, as a result, people all over the world watch it. But we are not doing it for diplomacy," the president says.

Ghibli and the terrible beauty of war

In 2026 it is inevitable to ask Yoda about one of the themes that most often recurs, alongside environmental protection, friendship or the strength of his female characters, in the scripts produced by his studio: armed conflict.

Takahata, a communist sympathiser, was an outspoken defender of Article 9 of his country's constitution and a convinced pacifist, whereas Miyazaki imbibed war from childhood: his family's company manufactured parts for military aircraft on the fascist side in the Second World War.

Aspiring sincerely to an international peace based on justice and order, the Japanese people forever renounce war as a sovereign right of the nation and the threat or use of force as a means of settling international disputes Artículo 9 de la Constitución de Japón

Both men bear witness to this obsession in animation classics such as 'Grave of the Fireflies', through 'Princess Mononoke' and 'Howl's Moving Castle', and up to 'The Wind Rises'. Is it still possible today, in a Japan allocating unprecedented shares of its GDP to its Self-Defence Forces and a Defence White Paper championed by far-right politician Sanae Takaichi, to go on making pacifist films?

Yoda sidesteps the issue with finesse. "How to address war is a very important topic for Studio Ghibli. Of course, it is better if there are no wars. But what I find admirable about Miyazaki as a director is that he too has been fascinated by the weapons used in war, or by fighter planes, by their beauty as objects, as forms. Of course, he has not the slightest sympathy for war. But there is in him a feeling he cannot resist: the attraction of those things as objects. And that is, in a way, something very human," he argues.

Marco Pagot, the protagonist of Porco Rosso, is very clear about some things

We also ask him about one of the studio's most quoted lines, spoken by the lead in 'Porco Rosso' (1992), in which he pronounces in a cinema that he would rather be a pig than a fascist. Would a line like that fit into a contemporary script room, whether at Ghibli or another studio? Once again, the executive chooses to dodge the question: he says he is very pleased that one of Emmanuel Macron's favourite films (recalling a statement the French president made during an official visit to Japan) is 'Porco Rosso', according to the interviewee.

The question of artificial intelligence also hangs over the Covadonga room at the Reconquista Hotel, where the Princess of Asturias Foundation traditionally lodges its laureates. It surfaces in connection with the famous viral clip of Miyazaki (source in Spanish) from 2016, in which he cuts down two developers from another company when they try to sell the genius a kind of proto-AI to be used in his drawings. "It is an insult to life itself," he snaps at them.

"Ten years on, in every interview without fail I am asked what Studio Ghibli thinks about AI," Yoda explains with resignation. "It is very difficult to predict how it will evolve, and I think we are all living in that uncertainty. But if there is something we can say right now, and I say this also in a personal capacity, it is this. Imagine two restaurants: one where the food is made by an AI and another where it is made by people. I would undoubtedly choose the second."

His team signals that we should end the interview, but the former journalist tells us he wants to add one last point. "Listening to your questions, I have realised that Ghibli is very closely bound up with its time (...) We debate every day what the studio can do in this era and what kind of era we are living in. In that sense, I have the feeling that we are creating something with restraint," he says.

"There is great honesty towards the act of artistic creation," he continues. "It is not a business plan: it is about thinking seriously about what response the studio gives to its time. That is now the studio's day-to-day reality. And it has probably always been that way." The next decade will show whether, after Miyazaki's generational handover, still active at 85, the emblematic studio manages to maintain its creative independence and ideals, having captivated millions of children and adults far beyond the Japanese islands.

World.title: Drinking tea could lower your risk of stroke, but only if it’s not too hot
World.content:
Regular tea drinking is linked to a lower risk of vascular diseases such as stroke, coronary heart disease and heart attack, according to a new study.

 

Tea is made by steeping the processed leaves of Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub native to East Asia. All varieties —including white, green, oolong, black and pu-erh— come from this single plant, with their distinct flavours determined by how much they oxidise.

The beverage is a regular part of the diet in many cultures. From the English breakfast to Chinese tea ceremonies, it is present in the daily lives of millions of people worldwide.

Tea’s bioactive compounds, including polyphenols and flavonoids, have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and endothelial-protective properties that preserve the inner lining of blood vessels and maintain healthy circulation, all of which can help prevent vascular diseases, according to a study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Researchers followed nearly 500,000 Chinese people for an average of nine years, recording their tea consumption and any diseases that developed during that period. They found that those who drink tea regularly three or more times a week showed 11.2% lower overall risk of vascular disease. The strongest association was for ischaemic stroke with a 36.6% reduction, followed by cerebrovascular disease at 19.1%.

The protective associations varied substantially depending on how the tea was prepared and consumed, the researchers found.

Among participants, the median intake was between two and three cups a day; however, the lowest associated risk was in those who consumed six to eight cups daily.

Black tea showed the strongest and most consistent association with vascular diseases, followed by green tea. Researchers attribute this to the fermentation-derived compounds, such as theaflavins, which have anti-inflammatory and lipid-regulating properties.

The temperature and strength of the brew also made a difference. Researchers found that the best combination was moderately strong and non-scalding tea.

Surprisingly, burning hot tea was linked to the opposite effect: a 16% increase in vascular disease risk. Very hot drinks have previously also been associated with a greater likelihood of oesophageal cancer.

Tea is not a silver bullet

The protective association of habitual tea consumption was consistent across most demographic subgroups but was significantly stronger in individuals with obesity, the researchers noted.

Despite these results, the authors warn that drinking tea alone does not protect against cardiovascular disease and that it should form part of a broader healthy lifestyle and complement established prevention strategies.

“This was an observational study and other differences in people’s diets and lifestyles could help explain the findings,” said Dell Stanford, senior dietitian at the British Heart Foundation who did not participate in the study, adding that the results don’t prove “that a daily cuppa protects your heart.”

Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of illness and mortality in the European Union, accounting for one in three of all deaths and affecting an estimated 62 million people.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 22nd, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Marine Le Pen vs Alice Weidel: How the far right wants to reshape the EU
World.content:
Neither party now advocates leaving the EU. Instead, both want to reshape it into an alliance of sovereign states, with weaker institutions and reduced powers.

 

If they come to power, their plans could undermine the Franco-German partnership that has long driven European integration and reshape the future of the EU.

Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel unveiled her “New Deal for Europe” at a press conference in the European Parliament on Wednesday, a week after France’s Marine Le Pen presented her own vision at the upscale The Hotel in Brussels.

Both leaders are in strong electoral positions. After a major victory in Saxony-Anhalt's regional election last September, Weidel's AFD party is on track to lead a German State for the first time in history, and is currently leading the polls at the national level. "Our aim is to assume government responsibility after the next federal elections", Weidel said in Strasbourg.

In France, a recent Ifop poll puts Le Pen at 34% to 38% of the vote in the first round of France's 2027 presidential election, despite the recent wave of protests across the country.

Both parties oppose continued funding for Ukraine, criticise the EU’s regulatory burden, reject deeper integration and want to curb the powers of EU institutions.

But they differ on fiscal policy, energy and how far their countries should break from common rules. The AfD goes further, proposing opt-outs that would allow Germany to bypass certain EU policies.

Euronews examines the RN and AfD’s plans for Europe, highlighting the key differences and similarities between two of the continent’s leading far-right parties.

No more money to Ukraine

Both leaders agree on ending financial support for Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s war of aggression.

At her press conference last week, Le Pen argued that France’s strained public finances could no longer sustain aid to Kyiv and called for the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia.

“We obviously agreed to maintain a whole series of mechanisms to train their soldiers, to train their army, to provide them, including aid in terms of equipment, but we can no longer finance Ukraine, so this funding will stop,” she said.

Weidel said on Wednesdayshe wants a peace treaty and called for a “reasonable diplomatic approach,” which takes into account the “security interests of Ukraine and Russia.”

In a recent interview with The Economist, she argued that Ukraine had already lost the war and pledged to end Germany’s support for Kyiv.

Fiscal policy: the sharpest divide

The most significant difference lies in their approach to fiscal policy.

Le Pen wants to harmonise taxes on tobacco, alcohol and large companies at EU level to prevent fiscal dumping across Europe. She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB) revise its mandate to give more weight to economic growth, rather than focusing on price stability.

"As I have always believed, the ECB must rethink its course of action. It is essential that it take into account employment, growth, and innovation, given that the monetary easing policies pursued between 2010 and 2022 were not targeted at future investments," she said last week.

The AfD, by contrast, opposes any transfer of fiscal sovereignty to supranational institutions and claims that the ECB must strictly confine itself to its original price-stability mandate.

"There is a ban on the ECB, the European Central Bank, financing state debt. And what is the ECB doing? It's financing state debt", Weidel said.

Both parties, however, firmly oppose common EU debt and want to cut their countries’ contributions to the EU budget. Le Pen aims to cap France’s net contribution at €5 billion a year. Neither Weidel nor the AfD’s New Deal for Europe paper specifies a figure, instead emphasising the need to “end Germany’s role as paymaster.”

Energy: EU carbon border tax vs freedom to use coal

On energy and climate policy, both parties criticise the EU Green Deal and support nuclear power, but differ in their approaches.

Le Pen rejected the “climate-sceptic” label for her party, backed an EU carbon border tax and proposed tying member states’ contributions to the EU budget to their carbon emissions, thereby incentivising the transition to clean energy.

“The further a country deviates from the [Paris agreement] targets, the more it should have to contribute,” she said.

The AfD paper instead stresses total freedom to choose the national energy mix, meaning Germany must be free to use nuclear power, coal, gas and renewable energy according to the needs of its economy.

"Now we rely completely on an ideological energy transition of wind and solar power. We see this development also throughout Europe, through the implementation of the Green Deal, the building energy law, and above all the ban on combustion engines. This is a blatant disruption of the free market economy," she said.

Le Pen targets the Commission; AfD seeks to weaken Parliament too

Both parties want the European Commission to be stripped of powers and reduced to a “secretariat at the service of countries”, as Le Pen put it.

“The Commission wants to be a State, we don’t want it,” she said, rejecting any EU executive ambitions on security, diplomacy and intelligence. She also wants to abolish the European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee, two advisory bodies representing local authorities and social interests.

Weidel has a similar position. "We don't want a Commission that is not elected to intrude and disturb your private life and [Member States] decision making [process]," she said.

The AfD goes a step further, questioning the legitimacy of the European Parliament and advocating a Europe centred on sovereign nation-states.

One of the most far-reaching proposals in the New Deal for Europe states: “The EP should no longer be elected directly, but instead be composed of delegates appointed by national parliaments.”

Different strategies for change

Le Pen envisages reshaping the EU following elections in Spain, France, Italy and Poland, where far-right parties are expected to win or make significant gains.

Poland’s Law and Justice party could return to power, while Spain’s Vox could join the government alongside the Popular Party. In France, Marine Le Pen could become the country’s first far-right president.

**"**This will be our shared undertaking for the years and, the decades to come. [...] It will not simply consist of undoing what has been very badly done over the past 30 years on the European stage," she said, claiming the new "Europe of nations" will feature EU institutions not exercising any authority over the member states.

The AfD, by contrast, identifies 2029 as the pivotal year for EU reform, when the European elections could deliver a “patriotic right-wing majority in the European Parliament.”

The party also floats disruptive national options should its planned reform of the EU fail. These include making extensive use of opt-outs for Germany in areas such as free movement, defence, taxation, social policy and migration.

"If Schengen [system] is over and it doesn't work, we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," Weidel said, pointing to challenges to free movement amid episodes such as the large-scale arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta last July.

The opt-out on migration would mean that Germany "will no longer participate in any European distribution mechanisms [of migrants] or asylum quotas,” disrupting the bloc's Migration Pact. Berlin currently holds the biggest solidarity quota in the EU and is in charge of relocating 4,555 asylum seekers from frontline member states in 2026.

AFD leaves the door open for EU exit

If far-reaching reforms to the EU’s structure prove unattainable, the AfD’s plan states that "the German people should then decide for themselves," a formulation that could be interpreted as an implicit reference to a referendum on EU membership as a last resort, although Weidel did not raise this possibility at her press conference.

Le Pen, once a strong advocate of France leaving the EU, has gradually abandoned the idea, shifting towards a strategy of radically reforming the bloc from within during her 2022 presidential campaign.

Dave Sinardet, a Belgian political scientist who specialises in far-right parties, considers EU withdrawal an unrealistic scenario.

“Most radical right parties have evolved their position towards the EU in the last years,” he told Euronews, adding that after Brexit no political force is seriously considering leaving the Union.

“On this, AfD is really moving in the same direction that RN has already moved in the past. They are abandoning the ideas as Le Pen abandoned Frexit,” he said.

World.title: Canada unveils $6.2bn plan to shield manufacturers as Trump trade tariffs bite
World.content:
Canada has announced a $6.2 billion (€5.7 billion) package to protect its steel and auto industries from US tariffs, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Washington has permanently altered a trade relationship built over decades.

 

Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford jointly unveiled the plan on Wednesday, directing $3.7 billion (€3.4 billion) to steelmakers and $1.8 billion (€1.65 billion) to automakers over five years, with $1.1 billion (€1 billion) of the auto funding coming from the federal government in Ottawa.

The announcement came the same day US-owned Cleveland-Cliffs confirmed layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, underlining the human cost of the trade dispute.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage.”

The damage to the auto sector is already visible in the trade figures, as Canadian auto exports to the US have fallen more than 10 percent, while US exports to Canada have dropped more than 20 percent, a decline Carney said hurts both sides of the border.

“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” he stressed.

Carney confirmed he spoke at length with President Trump on Wednesday, covering trade, Iran and the Middle East.

He signalled no breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate. Talks collapsed in August after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€18.4 billion) in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.

For his part, Ford was direct about what the dispute has done to bilateral ties. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were,” he said.

US embassy accuses Canada of meddling in midterms

Carney has set a target of doubling Canadian exports to non-US markets within a decade, acknowledging that an integrated North American auto industry may no longer be Washington’s priority.

“Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”

Meanwhile, the day took a sharper diplomatic turn when the US Embassy issued a statement accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to influence next month’s American midterm elections.

The embassy named Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for running a US television ad featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs, the ad that prompted Trump to walk away from trade talks in October 2025.

Both leaders rejected the allegations. So did independent analysts.

“The implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, political science professor at McGill University.

World.title: El Salvador launches military operation in Haiti to free four kidnapped aviation technicians
World.content:
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele announced Wednesday that he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti, warning of a far more forceful response if they are not returned alive and unharmed.

 

The four men have been missing since Sunday, when gangs opened fire on an armoured vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince. The technicians fled the burning vehicle and have not been seen since, marking the first major attack on the international gang suppression force since it began operating in Haiti.

Addressing Haitian gang leaders directly, Bukele issued a stark ultimatum.

“Today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if they do not release the four hostages alive. And do not take our words as empty threats,” he wrote on X, sharing a video of armoured vehicles with shattered windows moving through smoke.

He added that if the men were returned safely, “everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping” but stopped short of specifying whether any further action would involve Salvadoran, Haitian or international forces.

Bukele stressed that El Salvador’s mission in Haiti is strictly non-combat. The four men are aviation technicians whose primary role is to carry out medical evacuations, he said, adding that the Salvadoran contingent “consists only of pilots and technical personnel, not to wage war.”

Haiti declares rescue an “absolute priority”

Haiti’s government responded Wednesday evening, saying the abduction of the technicians was an “absolute priority.”

A meeting was held at the prime minister’s office to assess ongoing operations and coordinate with the Gang Repression Force, according to a government statement.

“All necessary resources are being mobilised to achieve this goal,” the statement said. It was not immediately clear whether Haitian authorities had confirmed that the four men are still alive. A spokesperson for the gang suppression force did not respond to requests for comment.

The attack underscores the scale of the challenge facing international forces in Haiti, where gangs are estimated to control around 70 percent of Port-au-Prince. The country is also preparing for its first general election in more than a decade.

El Salvador is one of several countries, including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala, contributing to the multinational gang suppression force, which has more than 2,000 troops on the ground.

The UN originally approved up to 5,550 security personnel and more than 50 civilian staff for the mission in 2025. The force received at least a six-month extension through March 2027 from the UN Security Council.

In early October, El Salvador passed a law extending its own participation in the force for a year, also broadening its mandate beyond medical evacuations to allow the deployment of civilian and military personnel according to the mission’s broader needs.

World.title: Yemen: Tanks fire as fighting erupts on the outskirts of Taiz
World.content:
Yemeni government forces and allied Popular Resistance fighters clashed with Houthi fighters on the western outskirts of Taiz on Wednesday, 21 October, near the city’s old airport and Jabal Han mountain. The internationally recognised government said its forces repelled the attack, while reporting air strikes on Houthi positions, vehicles and a missile launchpad west, south and east of the city.

 

Footage showed a government tank firing towards Houthi positions as gunfire echoed across the area. The fighting comes as Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, faces mounting pressure from Houthi forces, which have largely encircled it and cut key supply routes, including the main road to Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised government.

The restrictions have also disrupted access to the city’s main landfill, leaving rubbish to pile up along major streets. Sanitation workers say they can no longer reach the dumping site because of the clashes and have resorted to burning waste in the streets.

Footage showed waste burning beside busy roads, thick smoke rising over neighbourhoods and goats feeding among the rubbish. Aid agencies said fuel shortages were also disrupting water pumps, hospitals and waste collection, deepening fears of disease outbreaks.

“If we don’t die from Houthi shelling, we’ll die from this rubbish,” one resident said.

World.title: India news: CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka released from Tihar Jail
World.content:
Skip next section CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar

10/22/2026 October 22, 2026 CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar

Das and Ranka have been seeking Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over voter-roll irregularities Image: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after a Special Executive Magistrate declined a police request to extend their judicial custody by three more days, reports said.

The two leaders at the forefront of the protests calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar following voter-list irregularities, furnished personal bonds and sureties of Rs 50,000 (€470; $530) each.

Their written undertakings promised to maintain peace and not call for protests at Jantar Mantar "till such a time that it is denotified in accordance with law."

The iconic protest site was denotified by Delhi Police earlier in October, months after CJP-led protests culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Das and Ranka were booked for "trespassing" after entering the Jantar Mantar protest site and raising the Indian flag.

The latest CJP protests have called for Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names.

World.title: Ukraine, Russia trade strikes after Witkoff talks
World.content:
Soon after Putin and Zelenskyy expressed willingness to resume US-mediated talks, Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks on each other's capitals.

Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight, authorities from both countries said on Thursday, shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.

Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding at least 15 people, eight of whom have been hospitalized, city authorities said.

The subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro river in Kyiv was also damaged, Mayor ⁠Vitali ​Klitschko ​said ​on Telegram.

Ukraine's airforce warned of Russian missiles and instructed residents to take shelter Image: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

"Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian "humanism" truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centers, and residential Areas," Ukrainian foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.

His post referred to Witkoff recently calling Putin a "humanitarian" for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday. Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces and jailed over charges of being a mercenary.

Another Russian strike killed a woman and injured four others in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram. A drone also hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the Poltava region, local authorities said without providing more details.

Meanwhile, Moscow's mayor said that 630 drones were launched towards the region overnight, wounding at least two people.

"Most of them were destroyed by air defense systems," Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on social media. Of these, 163 drones had been approaching the capital city, he added.

In western Russia's Lipetsk city, a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on Telegram.

Strikes after US attempts mediation

The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway earlier this week, followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday.

The Trump administration has attempted to mediate between the two sides to end the conflict that began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

US aims for new round of Russia-Ukraine negotiations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Putin agreed "in principle" to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. Zelenskyy, too, said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for trilateral talks at the negotiators level to be held as soon as possible.

It was "the closest we've been" to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff's meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Austrian, Swiss women kidnapped in Niger are freed — report
World.content:
An Austrian woman and a Swiss woman kidnapped in Niger have been freed after 18 months in captivity, local reports say.

Niger released two women, one Swiss and the other Austrian, after over a year of holding them captive, according to multiple reports.

The two women were flown out to Libya's eastern city of Benghazi, Libyan media outlets reported on Thursday.

The Austrian national, identified by Austrian authorities as Eva G., and the Swiss national, whom the Swiss foreign ministry has not previously named, were both abducted in Niger in 2025.

Eva G. is in her 70s, and the Swiss woman, identified by media outlets as Claudia Abbt, is 69 years old, according to reports.

Eva G. was kidnapped in the desert ⁠town of Agadez in central Niger, in January 2025. Abbt was abducted in April 2025.

It was not immediately clear which group was holding them and what demands it had made.

Libyan news channel releases video of the two women freed from captivity

In a video released by Libya's al-Masar TV , the women appeared physically weakened.

Both women thanked the deputy commander-in-chief of Libya's armed forces, Khalifa Haftar, and his son, Saddam, for their release. Haftar reportedly oversaw the operation that freed the women.

"I had been held hostage for a year and nine months," Eva G. said, while Abbt said she was "happy to be free," also thanking Haftar.

Libya and Niger share a border hundreds of miles long, cutting through the Sahara Desert and connecting with Algeria and Chad on either side. Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime ruler Moammar Gaddafi.

At the moment, two governments are vying for power there: a UN-recognized administration led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah and its rival in the east, backed by Haftar.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

Editor's note: DW has not yet independently verified the video released by the Libyan news channel that shows the two women, now freed, speaking to camera.

World.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
World.content:
The US State Department has asked some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia because of the threat of Houthi attacks on the Gulf kingdom.

At least one person was killed in a strike on a Saudi airport in the eastern city of Dammam on Wednesday, as Washington ordered some diplomats and family members to leave the Gulf country.

Saudi Arabia's revived war with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels has intensified in recent weeks, with the Yemeni rebels targeting several major Saudi airports.

Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the strike on the airport in Dammam?

The Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed one person and injured eight others.

The authority added on X that the extent of the material damage to the airport was being assessed.

It did not say who was behind the attack and the Houthis did not claim responsibility.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 said flights from the airport were being diverted as operations came to a halt.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said forces successfully intercepted a drone targeting an oil facility, but that falling debris killed two people and injured two others. Those killed were identified by the ministry as a Filipino and a Nepali national.

US State Department orders partial evacuation of Saudi mission

Meanwhile, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said his department had issued an order for the departure of non-essential staff and family members at the US embassy in Riyadh.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott wrote on X.

Both Reuters and AFP news agency cited unnamed sources as saying a similar order was also issued for other countries in the Gulf, with the AFP listing the UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain.

Pigott denied the reports, saying they were "inaccurate" and that only employees in Saudi Arabia were ordered to leave.

The US has issued similar evacuation orders on more than one occasion this year amid the Iran war and Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the US-Israeli war against Tehran.

Houthi attacks on Saudi airports raise stakes for Washington To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A four-year truce between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels collapsed amid the Iran war, with Saudi Arabia experiencing near daily attacks this month.

World.title: Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment — Vatican
World.content:
Pope Leo's lung cancer surgery last week was a success, the Vatican said. The pope broke with traditions of secrecy around papal health issues after announcing he needed surgery to remove a nodule on his lung.

Pope Leo XIV will not require further cancer treatment, his doctors announced on Wednesday, after the pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer last week.

The Vatican cited the pope's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora, as saying the pope's disease was localized and that "no further treatment" was necessary.

This confirms earlier prognoses suggesting the pope's cancer was caught early.

Pope Leo last week underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on October 13 at Rome's Gemelli hospital.

What did Pope Leo's doctors say about his health condition?

The 71-year-old pontiff's doctors said the final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during his surgery were issued on Wednesday.

"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the Holy See said.

What to know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The pope's surgeon added that there was "no clinical reason to cancel" the pope's visit to South America.

The ambitious trip, initially scheduled for November 6-17, would take the pontiff to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, involving a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and stops at high altitude.

Pope Leo's transparency around illness breaks with tradition

Leo was discharged from the hospital on Saturday, saying he would resume his activities gradually.

His illness shocked the Catholic Church, stoking concern that any potential prolonged treatment, such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy, could have affected the pope's ability to head the church.

Pope Leo first announced his condition during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, telling followers that he would be having a nodule surgically removed.

The announcement broke away from long-held traditions of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.

World.title: German youth plan France-style mass protests
World.content:
A youth-led movement in Germany has called for demonstrations in major cities of the country on October 31. The group has categorically distanced itself from the violence that took hold in France.

"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.

Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.

Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.

Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.

Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: France bans protests in parts of Paris as Macron slams Trump
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron railed against "stupid" comments made by foreign leaders for their political purposes. Plus, Paris police are set to extend restrictions on gatherings in parts of the city on Thursday.

As France braces for more protests on Thursday, Paris police said participants will be banned from gathering at the Elysee presidential palace, the Bastille Square, both houses of parliament, and several tourist areas, including the Louvre and the Champs-Elysees.

The curfew is set to apply between 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) and 8 p.m. local time.

French authorities have sought to reassure the public after the country was swept by violent unrest last weekend. The ongoing crisis started with students protesting high prices and demanding education reform, but it soon escalated, with masked rioters looting shops and clashing with police. On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted the authorities "lost control" and failed to anticipate the scale of the violence.

Violent unrest rocks France after nationwide protests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Large-scale protests are also expected in Paris this weekend. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has already pledged a "massive" security deployment for the event.

Trump blames 'migrants, jihadists, and communists' for unrest

While the European nation has seen two relatively quiet nights in a row, images of burning cars, broken store windows and ransacked buildings have been used by politicians inside and outside of France to increase pressure on the current government, led by President Emmanuel Macron.

Notably, US President Donald Trump attributed the unrest to "migrants, jihadists, and communists," saying they had "conquered, looted, and burned (France) to the ground." While campaigning for the US midterm elections, Trump also said he had warned Macron about immigration, but the French president refused to close the borders.

Macron claims images of protest manipulated, triggering 'stupid' comments

While visiting Qatar on Wednesday, Macron fired back at Trump, implying that the US leader and possibly Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were trying to gain political capital from the unrest in France. Netanyahu also spoke of an "invasion of extremist Islam" earlier this week.

"There are people who campaign at France's expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," Macron told reporters on Wednesday.

When asked if his comments were about Trump, Macron replied: "Among others."

President Macron urges distinction between protesters and vandals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He also said information about the crisis has been manipulated, including "AI-generated images depicting scenes that never actually happened." This, according to Macron, prompted comments that are "as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders."

"We've had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said.

Le Pen says Macron to blame for 'sad reality' of protests

Later on Wednesday, Macron's far-right rival Marine Le Pen sought to dismiss his account as "conspiratorial."

"The images we saw last Saturday are not generated by artificial intelligence: they show the sad reality of what France has become after 10 years of Macronist rule," said Le Pen.

The far-right leader is currently the favorite to win the 2027 presidential election in France, followed by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon.
