World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Taiwan probes organized crime links to China’s ‘transnational repression’
World.content:
Taiwan is probing organized crime’s links to Chinese efforts to carry out “transnational repression,“ a security official said on Thursday, after the island’s government said Beijing was behind an attack on a comedian who mocked Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Taiwan, which China views as its own territory over the island’s objections, has complained that Beijing is using various underhanded methods to go after Taiwanese nationals who the Chinese government views as separatists or are otherwise politically suspect.

Speaking to reporters at parliament, Taiwan National Security Bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen said the local networks that cooperate in incidents like the comedian attack are mostly criminal gangs, or private investigation firms linked to organized crime.

World.title: Japan to introduce cashless traffic fine payments from July
World.content:
The National Police Agency plans to introduce cashless payments for minor traffic violations from July 2027, allowing offenders, including cyclists, to pay fines by credit card, smartphone payment services or other cashless means, agency officials said Thursday.

The system will be rolled out nationwide in phases. The agency will solicit bids for a contractor to handle payment processing and system operations and select one by the end of the year at the earliest.

Fines are currently payable only at bank or post office counters, which are unavailable outside business hours. The agency has been considering the introduction of cashless payments to improve convenience for offenders and ease the burden on financial institutions as the government promotes the digitalization of administrative procedures.

Under the planned system, traffic violation notices, known as blue tickets, will carry QR codes that link users to a payment website when scanned with a smartphone or other device.

Offenders will enter information written by hand on the notices, including the amount due, select a payment method and complete the transaction. They will receive confirmation by email or other means.

Payment options are expected to include cashless payment apps, convenience store payment services and internet banking. Offenders will pay a processing fee of several hundred yen per transaction.

In-person payments at bank and post office counters, which carry no fee, will remain available.

The companies selected to operate the system will cover their operating costs and generate revenue from the transaction fees. The arrangement will therefore impose no additional financial burden on the police or reduce the amount of fines collected.

Companies will be selected through a competitive bidding process, taking into account factors such as the level of transaction fees and the variety of payment methods offered.

Since June 2021, the NPA has been conducting a trial program in Akita and Shimane prefectures that allows traffic fines to be paid by bank transfer through internet banking or ATMs. The utilization rate reached 14.6% last year. The agency aims to increase the rate by expanding the available payment options.

Revenue from traffic fines is first transferred to the state coffers and then distributed to local governments as special grants for traffic safety measures. The funds are used for purposes such as installing road signs. In fiscal 2025, approximately 3.85 million cases of traffic fines were issued, totaling around ¥38 billion.

World.title: Takaichi now has to prove she’s no big spender in her second year in office
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made a strong case in the year since her inauguration that she’s not a reckless spender. Now she has to prove it.

“From now on, the real test will not be words,” said Saisuke Sakai, a senior economist at Mizuho Research Institute, which operates under Mizuho Bank.

“The focus is whether the administration will really be able to convince the market with its budget, balancing fiscal discipline with growth investment, a consumption tax cut and increased defense spending.”

World.title: Most BOJ watchers expect next interest rate hike in December
World.content:
More than 80% of Bank of Japan watchers anticipate the central bank’s next interest rate increase will come in December, according to a recent survey. None expect a hike when the bank concludes its next meeting on Oct. 30.

Some 83% of economists forecast the bank will raise borrowing costs from the current level of 1.25% at its meeting ending on Dec. 18. Just last month, only 35% forecast a hike in December. In that survey, January was the most popular pick for the next rate hike.

The latest survey results also show that 67% of respondents expect the BOJ to raise rates every three months, up from 46% in the last survey. That points to expectations that the BOJ will maintain the same tempo of rate hikes after it raised rates in September for the second time in three months, the fastest pace since 1990.

World.title: Health ministry questions reliability of vasculitis drug approval data
World.content:
Japan’s health ministry said Wednesday that there may be problems with the reliability of documents submitted by Kissei Pharmaceutical for the approval of vasculitis drug Tavneos.

In its response to a series of deaths among Tavneos users, the ministry reiterated its request that medical institutions refrain from starting new patients on the drug, which is marketed by Kissei Pharmaceutical, based in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture.

The ministry plans to decide by the end of this year on administrative action, potentially including revocation of the drug’s approval.

Tavneos was launched in Japan in June 2022 after receiving approval from the ministry. Its package insert listed liver dysfunction as a serious side effect.

Kissei Pharmaceutical reported in May this year that 20 Tavneos users had died of liver dysfunction. It was later found, however, that one of the reported deaths was due to another factor.

According to the ministry, four additional fatal cases have since been confirmed, taking the total number of deaths from liver dysfunction to 23. In six of the cases, a causal relationship with the drug could not be ruled out.

The ministry approved Tavneos based on the results of a clinical trial conducted by the U.S. pharmaceutical company that developed the drug. Regulatory authorities in the United States and Europe have raised concerns about the appropriateness of the trial methodology, however.

European authorities revoked the drug’s approval in August, while U.S. authorities recommended that the approval be withdrawn.

In June, the ministry ordered Kissei Pharmaceutical to submit a report on the drug. The Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency analyzed the company’s response and compiled a report.

In the report, the agency said that the clinical trial results may have reliability issues and that it was inappropriate to use them as evidence of the drug’s efficacy. Regarding safety, it said that measures taken since May have had some effect, while noting that liver dysfunction still requires close attention.

The agency also said that it could not conclude that the drug’s benefits outweigh its risks.

Following the report, the ministry called on medical institutions to refrain from starting new patients on the drug. However, given that it is used to treat serious designated intractable diseases, the ministry asked medical institutions to make discontinuation of the drug or a switch to alternative therapies the general rule for patients already receiving it.

World.title: Japan life insurers’ bond-buying plans set to support JGBs
World.content:
Japanese life insurers are signaling they will maintain or increase purchases of domestic bonds in the second half of the fiscal year, offering a potential source of support for upcoming government debt auctions.

Japan Post Insurance said it intends to increase purchases of yen-denominated bonds, while Daido Life Insurance has raised its planned increase in domestic bond holdings, mainly through corporate debt. Meanwhile, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance plans to keep its government bond holdings roughly unchanged while switching out of lower-yielding debt into higher-yielding securities.

The plans add to signs that demand from one of Japan’s most important groups of bond investors is beginning to recover. Insurers have been net buyers of superlong Japanese Government Bonds (JGBs) for the past four months, according to Japan Securities Dealers Association data, a trend strategists say could provide a firmer anchor for upcoming auctions.

World.title: What’s holding up Washington’s $14 billion arms sale to Taipei?
World.content:
Taiwan has been waiting for months for U.S. President Donald Trump to approve a $14 billion sale of weapons and equipment, which the island democracy would use to fend off a potential Chinese attack.

Washington — Taipei’s most important security backer — has sold many billions of dollars’ worth of arms to Taiwan, most recently in December when it approved a record $11.1 billion package.

China opposes American military support for Taiwan, which Beijing claims is part of its territory and has threatened to seize with force.

World.title: Family of driver who died after truck fell into Saitama sinkhole sues prefecture
World.content:
The family of a 74-year-old driver who died after his truck fell into a sinkhole in the city of Yashio, Saitama Prefecture, last year has filed a lawsuit seeking about ¥125 million in damages from the prefectural government, sources said Wednesday.

The suit was filed with Saitama District Court in the prefecture on July 28 this year by the man’s three children, according to the complaint.

The plaintiffs claim that the road collapsed because an underground sewer pipe managed by the prefectural government had corroded due to hydrogen sulfide, arguing that the road lacked the level of safety it should normally have had.

The family claims that they suffered extreme psychological distress over an extended period because there was no clear prospect of rescuing the man.

The man was driving his truck when the center of an intersection in Yashio caved in on Jan. 28, 2025, causing him and his truck to fall into the hole. The driver’s body was recovered about three months later.

The plaintiffs also claimed that the man had carried out his daily duties with the utmost care, adding that the accident was unprecedented in its tragedy.

Saitama Gov. Motohiro Ono said in a statement that the prefectural government was reviewing the complaint and would respond appropriately.

World.title: What is the ‘cadaver skin jab’ beauty trend and does it really work?
World.content:
A growing interest among Hong Kong women in an anti-ageing injection containing human tissue has prompted a recent crackdown by health authorities, as the product, widely known in Chinese as the “cadaver skin jab”, has not been registered for use in the city.

The South China Morning Post examines why the injection has become a new beauty trend, what it claims to do and the risks involved.

1. What is a ‘cadaver skin jab’?

The “cadaver skin jab” refers to Elravie Re2O, a cadaver-derived skin injection marketed as an anti-ageing skin booster. It is commonly known by that Chinese nickname on social media.

Developed by South Korean biotech company L&C Bio and distributed by Humedix, the product was launched in November 2024.

The blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on November 26, 2025, killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents.

The judge-led panel said on Thursday that it had submitted the final report to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu.

World.title: A Tale of Two Cities, retold in style
World.content:
The opening also comes as the role of the brick-and-mortar bank branch is now very different from what it was even less than a decade ago. As everyday transactions can now be handled easily and securely through digital channels, the value of physical branches increasingly lies in conversations that benefit from professional advice, privacy and trust.

That proximity is part of the reason why OCBC has chosen the prime location of 35 Queen’s Road Central for its Central Branch. Here, clients can access wealth management services close to where they work or spend their time, in a cosy, private setting, while eligible Premier Private Clients can also access health and wellness support available in the same building. Fewer separate journeys can leave more time for work, family and life outside both.

For many of Hong Kong’s high-flying executives and entrepreneurs alike, Central is already part of their working day.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

For affluent clients, that can mean discussing investments, succession or other important financial needs face to face. OCBC’s Central Branch is taking an early lead in this direction, combining private advisory and meeting spaces with hospitality, lifestyle offerings, while selected wellness services are available to eligible Premier Private Clients.

Reimagining the branch experience

Held on September 29, the grand opening was attended by senior management, government and business leaders, partners and singer-songwriter Hanjin Tan. The occasion also marked the introduction of its new Premier Private Client Centre and the unveiling of a 3D LED display wall on the building façade.

With the addition of its newly opened second and third floors, the expanded premises give OCBC considerably more room to rethink what eligible Premier Private clients can do during a branch visit.

The approach also draws on OCBC’s Singapore origins and long presence in Hong Kong. That relationship is expressed in its latest campaign, “A Tale of Two Cities, For Your Wealth and Beyond”, which presents the two financial centres as complementary bases for serving clients whose business, wealth and families may increasingly cross borders.

A façade inspired by the Hong Kong spirit

OCBC’s 3D LED display brings a cast of animated characters inspired by Hong Kong’s entrepreneurial spirit to Queen’s Road Central. A 3D LED display wall on the branch façade introduces an original cast of animated characters inspired by qualities associated with Hong Kong people. A cat shopkeeper represents innovation and entrepreneurial spirit, while the “Wong Choi” dog embodies trust and reliability, and the “Kong Jr.” monkey represents adaptability and an ability to recognise opportunities.Reflecting the spirit of the Twin Hubs, the characters give wealth planning ideas a more playful expression. Seeking opportunities, protecting accumulated wealth and preparing for the future are represented by personalities encountered on Queen’s Road Central instead of being confined to a banking brochure.

There is an Instagrammable side to the campaign, too. Until October 31, visitors can photograph the display from a designated location outside Loke Yew Building at 50–52 Queen’s Road Central, with at least one of the cat, dog or monkey characters visible. After posting the photos on Facebook, Instagram, WeChat or Xiaohongshu with the specified campaign hashtags, visitors can redeem a limited-edition OCBC character blind box at the Central Branch, subject to terms and conditions.

The installation gives passers-by a reason to interact with the branch even without a banking appointment, while the blind box turns the digital characters into something tangible.

A Hong Kong story with Singapore roots

Singapore-born singer-songwriter Hanjin Tan brings his own tale of two cities to OCBC’s new campaign, having established his career in Hong Kong and written and composed its theme song. The same two-city idea is explored through music in OCBC’s new advertising campaign. Hanjin Tan has a tale of two cities of his own. Born in Singapore before establishing his career in Hong Kong, the singer-songwriter and Hong Kong Film Award winner embodies the connection at the centre of the campaign. He appears in the TVC and also composed and wrote its theme song.Inspired by the spirit of Hong Kong, the campaign follows aspirations at different stages of life. Creating wealth may dominate earlier years; preserving it can become increasingly important as responsibilities grow; later, succession and preparing for the next generation can become a priority.

Tan’s career has crossed the same two cities that OCBC uses for its regional proposition, allowing the campaign to talk about wealth through personal ambition, family and long-term planning instead of financial products alone. “The sense of being at home, the trust, and the peace of mind are what OCBC Premier Private Client offers,” said Tan, who is also an OCBC Premier Private Client, at the Central Branch grand opening.

Embedding wellness into the wealth journey

The new Premier Private Client Centre occupies the second and third floors of the Central Branch, with Singapore-inspired interiors, private meeting areas and a garden terrace. Through its “Navigating Your Wealth & Wellness Together” proposition, OCBC offers eligible Premier Private Clients access to personalised wealth management, wellness privileges, regional banking, lifestyle experiences and legacy planning services.

Through a partnership with Fullerton Health, eligible Premier Private Clients can access personalised one-to-one nutritionist consultations at a dedicated consultation room conveniently located within the same building, as well as cross-border medical referral services and regional healthcare support, subject to applicable terms and conditions.

[Premier Private Client Centre]

Commenting on the grand opening of OCBC’s Central Branch and the soft launch of its new Premier Private Client service in Hong Kong, Mr. Wang Ke, Head of Greater China of OCBC and Chief Executive Officer of OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong remains a key wealth management hub in Asia and an important market for OCBC. The opening of our Central Branch and the soft launch of Premier Private Client mark an important milestone in our growth journey in Hong Kong.

Mr. Sunny Quek, Head of Group Consumer Financial Services, OCBC, added, “OCBC Premier Private Client is a key offering of our wealth franchise, supporting our customers’ increasingly sophisticated wealth needs. We are now extending the experience to Hong Kong as we strengthen our Singapore-Hong Kong twin wealth hubs to capture rising Asian wealth flows.

Ms. Josephine Lee, Head of Consumer Financial Services, OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong’s affluent customers are increasingly seeking trusted advice that extends beyond investment returns to address wealth preservation, liquidity management, retirement planning, healthcare needs and legacy planning for the next generation. By bringing together personalised wealth management, wellness support and regional connectivity, OCBC Premier Private Client aims to support customers’ financial, family, lifestyle and wellness aspirations through different stages of their wealth and life journeys. This reflects our purpose to enable people and communities to realise their aspirations.”

World.title: Receivers to sell mainland developer Shimao’s 2 Hong Kong hotels for US$344 million
World.content:
Receivers of the Sheraton Hong Kong Tung Chung Hotel and the Four Points by Sheraton have agreed to sell the dual-branded complex, which together comprise the city’s third-largest hotel by room count, for HK$2.7 billion (US$344 million), Shimao Group announced on Thursday.

In a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange, the distressed mainland Chinese developer said the buyer was Oceanfront Hong Kong Limited.

The complex was seized by receivers after Shimao failed to sell it despite slashing the asking price to about HK$4.5 billion in late 2024 – down from at least HK$6 billion a year earlier.

World.title: Hong Kong ranks 24th in global rule of law index as overall score falls
World.content:
Hong Kong has been ranked 24th in the latest global rule of law index, despite slipping slightly in the fundamental rights and criminal justice categories.

The index, released by the World Justice Project on Wednesday, showed the city remained among the world’s top 10 for “absence of corruption” and “order and security”, rising to seventh in the latter category.

The organisation said the global erosion of the rule of law slowed in 2026, but the overall decline continued, with 62 per cent of the 143 jurisdictions surveyed recording falls.

The index assessed jurisdictions across eight aspects of the rule of law, scoring each on a scale of zero to one.

World.title: An AI apocalypse? Hong Kong’s real challenge is much less dramatic
World.content:
For many of us, artificial intelligence (AI) started out as something to play with. We asked it to write poems and arrange our calendars; we shared its more entertaining mistakes. Then it became something to believe in: an escape from drudgery, an assistant to every profession, even perhaps the start of a new industrial revolution. Now it is something to fear

The progression has been astonishing. Governments are scrambling to draw up AI strategies, companies are reorganising operations and investors are financing the infrastructure. The world seems to be mobilising at warp speed to join the AI rush, although there is rather less agreement about where we are going.

World.title: Hong Kong raids spark health warning over beauty jabs using dead people’s skin
World.content:
Experts have warned of the infection risks associated with an anti-ageing beauty treatment known as “cadaver-derived skin injection” amid growing interest in the treatment, as authorities crack down on beauty premises offering services with unregistered products.

The warnings came a day after the Department of Health revealed it had seized vials of an injectable product called Elravie Re20, which claims to contain human tissue, following raids on four beauty premises in the city on Friday and Tuesday.

A 38-year-old woman was arrested during the operation.

Health authorities said the product, carrying Korean packaging, was classified as a “regulated product” under the Human Organ Transplant Ordinance, as well as a “pharmaceutical product”.

World.title: Could Hong Kong’s student housing boom lure property giants off the sidelines?
World.content:
Hong Kong’s largest landlords and developers could get their first formal route into the rising student accommodation market after the government announced plans to tender land for a purpose-built student hostel this quarter, according to analysts.

Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced on Thursday the inclusion of a 1,100 square metre (11,840 square foot) site for student accommodation as one of two land tenders in the October to December quarter.

The plot – at the junction of Yuen Shun Circuit and Yuen Hong Street in Siu Lek Yuen, Sha Tin – is expected to provide 600 hostel places.

“The tender of a dedicated PBSA [purpose-built student accommodation] site could be an important catalyst for Hong Kong’s major developers to take a closer look at the sector,” said Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at property consultancy Colliers in Hong Kong.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.title: Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.content:
In 2022, I spoke with Emma, a 22-year-old Chinese student in the UK, about her experiences with dating apps. Recalling one particularly disappointing encounter, she let out a sigh. Emma had matched with a man whose profile explicitly stated that he was looking for a long-term relationship. But the day after their third date, he texted her to say he had only ever wanted casual sex, then ghosted her. Feeling betrayed and emotionally drained, Emma changed her dating profile to say she was “Not Sure” what she wanted.

Emma’s experience was far from unusual. More than two-thirds of the 40 heterosexual Chinese students I interviewed in the UK reported similarly ambiguous dating intentions — findings drawn from a longitudinal study conducted between January 2022 and March 2023 that examined how their experiences with dating apps evolved while studying abroad. Many initially joined dating apps with clear goals, whether to pursue romantic relationships, make friends, or engage in language and cultural exchange. Yet over the course of the study, 27 of the 40 interviewees became less certain about what they wanted, increasingly adopting a “go with the flow” or “I’ll just see what happens” attitude.

For some, this ambiguity opened up new possibilities. For many others, however, it became a way to protect themselves after disappointing dating experiences. Beneath their apparent uncertainty, many still longed for a stable, long-term relationship.

For some young Chinese students arriving in the UK, keeping their dating intentions ambiguous is a deliberate strategy to leave their options open. In China, traditional dating culture places considerable emphasis on long-term commitment and marriage. Expressing vague or noncommittal intentions on Chinese dating platforms can carry a social stigma, with users sometimes labeled zhanan or zhanü, derogatory terms for men and women perceived as dishonest or irresponsible in romantic relationships.

Moving abroad can change these expectations. In the UK, students encounter a dating environment where a wider range of relationship arrangements is socially accepted. Living far from their parents and the social expectations of home also gives them greater freedom to experiment. For some, dating apps offer an opportunity to explore different kinds of relationships without committing to any particular one.

This “go with the flow” mentality was particularly common among postgraduate students enrolled in one-year degree programs. Jenny, a 23-year-old master’s student, explained during our first interview, shortly after arriving in the UK, that she had deliberately avoided setting clear dating goals so she could explore unconventional relationships.

“In China, I never thought about it because I was afraid of facing stigma and judgment,” she recalled. “I want to seize this opportunity to explore different possibilities during this one-year period.”

But not everyone embraced ambiguity out of a desire to experiment. For many other students, particularly women, keeping their intentions vague was a response to negative dating experiences.

After encountering misleading dating profiles and being ghosted without warning, some students became reluctant to invest emotionally in new relationships. Julia, a 23-year-old woman who had joined dating apps hoping to find a long-term partner, described feeling “emotionally paralyzed” after repeatedly meeting men who were only interested in casual sex. She initially had a clear relationship goal, but as she grew increasingly doubtful that she would find the commitment she wanted, she changed her profile to express more ambiguous intentions. By lowering her expectations, she hoped to avoid further disappointment.

Yet the difficulties these students faced in finding long-term relationships were not only about whom they encountered on dating apps. Their status as temporary residents in the UK could also make commitment more complicated. With student visas approaching expiration, many faced uncertainty about where they would live or work after graduation. Investing emotionally in a relationship could feel risky when relocation or a return to China was only months away. Potential partners in the UK might also hesitate to commit to someone who could soon leave the country.

Chou, a 23-year-old student, summed up her approach as “No expectations, no disappointments.” She explained, “Most local daters did not want to form a long-term relationship with me because I’m only here temporarily as an international student. They worried that once I head back to China after graduation, our relationship wouldn’t have a future.” Chou thus adopted ambiguous motivations to cope with the difficulty of forming and maintaining long-term relationships as graduation approached.

Yet perhaps the most surprising finding from my study was that adopting a “go with the flow” approach on dating apps did not necessarily signal a growing preference for casual relationships. In practice, my interviewees experienced different kinds of relationships, with some remaining short-term while others had the potential to develop into longer-term partnerships. Many of them still longed for lasting love. In some cases, that desire became stronger over time, as the initial excitement of exploring different relationships began to fade.

Jack, a 26-year-old student, described this gradual shift. During our first interview, he said he found it exciting to keep his intentions ambiguous because it allowed him to “explore different types of relationships.” But when we spoke again nearly a year later, he had come to understand his desires differently.

“As I kept using dating apps, I started to realize my expectations for long-term relationships had been awakened. Trying different relationships was fun, but it gradually left me feeling empty. I really wanted a serious relationship, but I suppressed that desire because I felt it was impossible to find something long-term on dating apps.”

The word “awakened” is revealing. It suggests that Jack’s desire for long-term commitment had never entirely disappeared. Rather than simply shifting from a preference for casual relationships to serious ones, he gradually came to recognize what mattered most to him.

Eve, a 23-year-old master’s student, captured this tension through a food metaphor. She described her short-term relationships as daican, a Chinese term meaning “meal replacements.” In Chinese internet slang, the term describes a substitute that offers some comfort or satisfaction but cannot fully make up for what someone really wants.

“I feel it’s very difficult to form long-term relationships on dating apps, so I’ll just stick to some ‘meal replacements’ for now to keep me from getting hungry,” she explained. “But a meal replacement cannot replace staple food.” For Eve, these brief connections were not meaningless. They offered companionship and helped ease the loneliness of living abroad. But they were substitutes for what she really wanted. The “staple food” in her metaphor was a stable, long-term relationship.

These experiences were neither entirely positive nor entirely negative. The “meal replacement” strategy could help meet immediate emotional needs. But such relationships rarely satisfied overseas students’ deeper desire for lasting commitment. In this sense, these experiences shouldn’t be taken as defining who they were or what they wanted from intimacy.

Dating apps offer Chinese students abroad new opportunities to explore relationships beyond the expectations they grew up with. But while living overseas may change how they approach dating, it does not necessarily change what they ultimately want. For many, the desire for lasting love remains, even as the uncertainty of their temporary lives abroad shapes what they feel able to pursue.

In line with research ethics, all research participants are given pseudonyms.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.title: At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019127/At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — At China’s largest film and television production base, veteran director Zheng Zhongfu was taking his two leads through a confrontation between a prince and his wronged wife.

“In my previous life, you gouged out my heart and left me to die in the wilderness,” he recited, showing them how to deliver the line and where to look. “In this life, I will take back everything that belongs to me.”

Qi Kexin and his wife listened closely. But once the cameras rolled, they caught each other’s eye and burst into laughter, forcing Zheng to call cut. Again.

“The emotion has to land … your gaze has to focus,” he reminded them. “Whatever you do, don’t laugh. Let’s go again.”

Qi, 48, and his wife were tourists at Hengdian World Studios in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, where visitors can pay 388 yuan ($60) per person to star in a short drama of their own. Qi had booked the shoot on a whim after spotting the experience on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

The package includes costumes, makeup, and filming, with studio performers filling the supporting roles. Visitors spend about an hour in makeup and on set, sometimes longer if they add scenes or need additional coaching. Two days later, they receive a finished two-minute drama with a complete storyline.

Earlier tourist shoots required groups of three to five and at least two hours, said Wu Yizhuo, who oversees the service at Hengdian World Studios. “Individual tourists with packed schedules found that hard to accept.” His team developed shorter shoots that a single visitor could book.

Visitors can now choose from nearly 30 scripts written by staff screenwriters, drawing on themes from Chinese social media and the country’s booming ultrashort drama industry, including palace intrigue, martial arts fantasy, and romances featuring domineering CEOs.

Wu’s team asks visitors whether they want to play a hero or a villain. Most choose villains as a way to relieve stress, he said, with “satisfying revenge” stories especially in demand.

Amateur hour

Qi chose a palace intrigue script in which he plays a prince who wants to divorce his wife for another woman. His real-life wife plays the wronged spouse, who turns the tables on him with an emperor’s order and a sword.

After a nervous start, the pair began to settle into their roles as Zheng coached their dialogue and movements. Their sleeve flicks and sword draws became more assured. “You nailed it!” he called from behind the camera after one take.

By the time the shoot wrapped, Qi had a new respect for professional actors. “You have to memorize lines, vary your tone, and add emotion. You can’t attend to everything at once,” he said.

“Actors really have it hard. It truly takes skill,” Qi added. “We’re just playing around — we’re far behind the professionals.”

Zheng had spent years directing trained actors before he began filming tourists in Hengdian this summer. He breaks difficult lines into smaller pieces, sometimes splitting a sentence across three shots to ease the pressure on visitors, and aims to finish filming in about 30 minutes.

Professional crews are serious and not particularly cheerful while filming, Zheng said. With tourists, the focus is on participation and keeping the set lively. “They may not care much about the final film’s quality. The main thing is to come here and be happy.”

Zheng is open to visitors adding scenes or lines, or switching into dialect. “As long as the final film works well, it’s fine,” he said. “The more drama there is, the more fully they perform — and the more they share it on social media.”

On the day Sixth Tone visited Hengdian, Zheng moved straight from Qi’s shoot to his next performer, Zhang Zhongfeng. The 58-year-old farm owner had driven more than 2,000 kilometers from the southwestern Sichuan province with her daughter for the experience. She had never acted and was nervous when she learned her daughter had booked a shoot for her.

Zhang chose palace intrigue, and Zheng tailored a role to her age and temperament. Once filming began, her commanding presence surprised him. Onlookers mistook her for one of the studio performers.

Her daughter, Su Jing, 35, filmed a princess scene at another set the next day. “It’s a bit more complicated than filming yourself with a phone, but much simpler than a big movie — no huge number of lines to memorize, and staff guide you throughout,” she said. “It’s like an upgraded version of travel photography.”

Zheng said the experience was drawing growing numbers of visitors, particularly during holidays. Nearly 3,000 people have taken part since the package launched in July.

Around 2010, Hengdian mainly hosted big-budget films and large TV productions with long shooting schedules, Wu, who oversees the tourist service, recalled. Before one production finished, the next was already booked. “Vertical-screen short dramas have since become more common, while large productions have declined,” he said.

In recent months, cheaper AI production and cuts in platform financing have reduced live-action shoots. In Hengdian, the weekly average number of filming crews reportedly fell nearly 25% year on year in the first half of 2026.

On peak days, Wu’s team handles 30 to 40 groups of tourists. When its regular staff cannot cover the bookings, the studio calls in local part-time workers. Zheng films tourist dramas as a member of one such outsourced team.

Giovana Velasco, a tourist from Peru, first visited Hengdian last year, when the experience wasn’t available, she recalled. After spotting it on Trip.com this year, she booked a shoot and chose to play a rejected daughter seeking revenge.

She rehearsed lines in Chinese, Spanish, and English, battled nerves and laughter, and sometimes relied on body language to stay in character. Her shoot took twice as long as those of Chinese visitors. She is already planning another trip to play a scheming sister and surprise her TikTok followers.

A Shanghai tourist surnamed Xia chose a scene from the 2011 Chinese period drama “Empresses in the Palace” in which her character slaps a maid who has struck her first. She booked the shoot after seeing influencers perform in Hengdian on social media. “Just for fun, out of curiosity,” she joked.

Before she delivered the slap, the director demonstrated how to draw her hand back to make the movement look bigger on camera. The finished film arrived two days later, sooner than she expected. Xia was impressed by the picture quality, the background, and her own styling and makeup.

When she shared it with close friends, many wanted her to take them along to film one themselves. They asked, “Where’s the next episode?”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo and Xiao Chuhan; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A crew films tourists in Hengdian, Zhejiang province, September 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.title: Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019149/Chinese Satellite Constellation Extends Coverage to Arctic
World.content:
China has used a domestically developed satellite communication system to make video calls with those in the Arctic for the first time, supporting scientific data transmission, emergency medical response, and other purposes.

The breakthroughs occurred between polar research vessels on the country’s latest Arctic expedition, the country’s Qinling research base in Antarctica, and a base in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, domestic media reported Monday.

The system uses the GW constellation, the country’s first state-backed satellite internet constellation project. The constellation launched its first satellites in December 2024 and plans to deploy almost 13,000 satellites by 2035. It aims to provide broadband services to areas beyond the reach of terrestrial networks through a system of low-orbit satellites operating below 2,000 kilometers above Earth.

The expedition has transmitted and received more than 300 files totaling over 100 gigabytes and held more than 40 video conferences via the system. Connectivity reportedly remained stable in harsh conditions, including extreme cold, high altitudes, strong winds, blowing sand, and ice fog.

The first breakthrough came on Aug. 3, when the research vessel Xuelong, then in the Arctic Ocean, completed a video call with China’s Qinling Station in Antarctica, the country’s highest-latitude communication ever performed using a domestic satellite system.

On Sept. 25, as the Xuelong returned to China, its crew exchanged Mid-Autumn Festival greetings via the satellite system with researchers at the Qinling Station and those aboard the Jidi and Tansuo-3 vessels during their ongoing Arctic expeditions.

A separate video call connected the Jidi, Qinling Station, a test station on the Lhasa River in Xizang, and the North China Sea Bureau of the Ministry of Natural Resources in the eastern Shandong province.

The communication system also reportedly enabled a video consultation with medical experts in Shandong’s port city of Qingdao, who provided remote medical support for a crew member in the Arctic.

Video call lag was no more than one second, according to state media outlet CCTV. After the vessels entered ice-covered waters, files and navigation logs were also transmitted via the GW constellation, with peak one-way speeds of around 30 megabits per second, enough to download a 1 GB file in about 10 minutes.

The event also marked the first time domestically developed buoys had transmitted ocean observation data in real time via Chinese satellites rather than international satellite services, state media outlet People’s Daily reported.

“The tests have improved the ‘information isolation’ faced by polar expeditions … offering practical evidence and experience for fully domestic communications support for China’s polar expeditions and marine equipment,” Zhang Meng, a member of the expedition and an on-site tester with the North China Sea Bureau, told state news agency Xinhua.

Previously, maritime communications along Arctic shipping routes relied mainly on shore-based radio and satellite systems, but coverage was limited and signals were often constrained. Earlier media reports said Chinese polar expeditions had used satellite services including the U.S.-based Iridium and British Inmarsat systems.

China’s latest Arctic expedition departed from the northeastern Liaoning province on July 3. The Xuelong and Xuelong 2 returned to Shanghai on Sept. 29 after completing their missions.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.title: Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019141/Chinese Users Get Back at AI Male Teen, Casting Him as a Grifter
World.content:
“Xiaohai, how come your parents still aren’t here? Everyone else’s family has come to help,” a teacher asks a teenage boy preparing for a student-led product sales competition.

“I’m fine, teacher,” the boy says, sweat streaming down his face. “I can do it alone — I believe the aunties and moms out there will help me.” He then makes an at-camera plea, sweat now turned to tears, asking viewers to help him by buying a luxury face cream and saying, “Are children from poor families really not suited for this stage?”

This scene comes as videos featuring the AI-generated teen male character, “Xiaohai,” surge in popularity, with a related hashtag amassing more than 620 million views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Tuesday. The videos, marketed to older women, appear across dozens of accounts and push a range of products, from soy sauce to cosmetics.

But in response to the popularity of Xiaohai videos — in which the teen often relays fictional sob stories, likening them to elderly-targeting scams — other user-made clips portraying him as a greedy, ill-mannered troublemaker, under arrest or admitting to fraud, have also begun to emerge, domestic media reported this week.

In the original Xiaohai videos, the character addresses viewers as “aunties and moms,” asks after their health, and occasionally performs a song before marketing various products.

Many older viewers reportedly believe the AI-generated character is real. In one video in which Xiaohai donates blood, the comment section is flooded with statements that appear to reflect people’s belief that he is real, such as “You’re such a good boy,” and “Why are you so pale? Please take good care of yourself.”

Using the character to sell products has proven lucrative, according to domestic media. A report by state media outlet Shandian News found that content creators producing videos featuring Xiaohai earn up to over a half of total sales, and some creators say they earn at least 1,000 to 2,000 yuan ($140 to $280) a day from videos featuring the AI character.

In contrast, the recent wave of Xiaohai videos shifts the narrative, aiming to paint him in a light that proves he’s not worthy of viewers’ affection and to dissuade them from purchasing his products. In some videos, the boy brags about how much money he’s squeezed out of his devoted followers. In others, he smokes, drinks, insults older women, or flaunts his wealth.

In response, some commenters said they were angry they had bought Xiaohai-backed products. Others interpreted the videos as evidence that Xiaohai had accidentally gotten into trouble or been coerced into lying. “Know that your aunties and moms won’t think badly of you,” reads one comment. “This will pass … I’ll think of something; tell me your address and phone number.”

Xiaohai creates a “sense of intimacy” that can make his appeals persuasive to seniors, Yi Xiaoting, associate dean of the School of Humanities and Public Administration at Shanghai Open University, told Sixth Tone. “That sense of familiarity and intimacy can override the need to verify whether the character is real or whether the story is true,” she said.

Helping older adults navigate AI-generated misinformation means encouraging them to question seemingly trustworthy personas and to verify claims independently, even when the story feels emotionally convincing, Yi added. She also stressed the need for both digital literacy programs for seniors and increased regulation of AI-generated content.

In recent years, regulators and state media have increasingly scrutinized the use of fabricated personas and empathy-driven narratives to sell products online. In 2024, a local court in southwestern China’s Sichuan province convicted eight people for selling products online using false narratives. At last year’s Two Sessions meeting, industry experts called for legislation to curb the misuse of AI-generated deepfakes.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Screenshots of Xiaohai, an AI-generated character. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.title: Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.content:
In wildlife conservation, there are three steps to helping an injured or orphaned animal: rescue, rehabilitate, and release. “Returning” isn’t part of the plan, but try telling that to China’s celebrity seal Nana.

This 2-year-old wild spotted seal, a Class I protected species in China, was a must-see attraction this summer for visitors to Dachangshan Island, part of Dalian’s Changshan Archipelago in the northeastern Liaoning province.

Nana has been released twice far out into the Yellow Sea, with the hope he’d join a migrating colony. Both times he’s made his way back alone, once covering more than 200 kilometers in just six days.

When he first showed up on the island in June, he was wary of humans and swam away when approached. But over time, he grew braver. Tourists tempted him near with tasty fish, though this sometimes resulted in him receiving a prod or a kick, and often a startling camera flash.

Concerned for Nana’s welfare, the local government put up warning signs telling people not to feed him and to keep a safe distance, and vowed “not to use him to promote tourism.” Yet within months, a “Nana Line” shuttle service had opened, running directly from the island’s Yuanyang Port to its “best seal-watching spot,” while the local tourism bureau began working with a private business to make and sell seal-related merchandise.

For many locals, Nana’s presence has been bittersweet: he’s a cute addition to the neighborhood, but the risks to his safety outweigh the benefits, they say.

Despite the falling temperature, authorities have ruled out moving him again, much to the delight of those who feel the seal has “made his choice.” But as the tourist season ends and his steady, fan-fueled food supply dries up, others worry that Nana could face a harsh winter alone.

Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Nana comes ashore at Dachangshan Island, Liaoning, Sept. 27, 2026. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.title: Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.content:
More than 150 Chinese apps have forbidden ByteDance’s mobile AI assistant Doubao from operating them on smartphone manufacturer Nubia Technology’s newly released agentic AI smartphone.

In a list published Oct. 14 on Doubao’s official account on messaging app WeChat, its developers identified dozens of apps that prohibit its graphical user interface (GUI) automation. The technology interprets a user’s spoken command, reads what is displayed on their smartphone’s screen, and navigates across and operates apps to complete the task.

Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps.

Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually.

Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company.

Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan.

Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app.

On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan.

As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news.

Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.

Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base.

In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.title: Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.content:
SHANGHAI – Popular language-learning app Duolingo has released a Shanghainese course featuring lessons on modern culture and life in old Shanghai as well as offline activities in the city.

The course, launched Thursday, features roughly 50 lessons drawn from everyday life in Shanghai, from ordering street food and taking public transit to exchanging greetings and navigating the city’s landmarks. To access the Shanghainese course, users must first set Chinese as their display language.

Founded in the U.S. in 2011, Duolingo offers courses in over 40 languages. The launch of the company’s Shanghainese course marks its second Chinese dialect offering, following Cantonese released in 2022. China is the company’s fastest-growing and second-largest market.

The course revolves around aspects of modern life in Shanghai like workplace dynamics and coffee culture, while also featuring old Shanghai themes, such as life in the city’s longtang lane houses and local phrases for traditional games, Tan Xiuting, a senior course designer of Duolingo, told Sixth Tone at the launch event in Shanghai on Friday.

Lessons also extend beyond the screen, with offline check-in spots around Shanghai, as well as themed activities on buses and in subway stations. Duolingo has also partnered with local shops; for example, if a user orders a coffee in Shanghainese at a partner café, they will receive a gift.

Wang Chen, an official with Duolingo, said that the course underscores the company’s “long-term commitment” to the Chinese market and its linguistic diversity.

“We want to make dialects cool and help local language and culture stay alive in contemporary life through products that are digital, engaging, and easy to access,” Wang said.

Shanghainese, or the Hu dialect, is a Wu Chinese variety spoken by roughly 10 million people, primarily in Shanghai and the surrounding Yangtze River Delta region. Difficult for native Mandarin speakers to understand, it features more tones and numerous English and French loanwords due to the city’s opening as a treaty port in the mid-19th century. It also preserves many classical Chinese words and structures.

The dialect has declined in recent decades, as national policies have pushed Mandarin use in schools, workplaces, and the media. In the last decade, Shanghai has reintroduced Shanghainese in some kindergartens and on public transportation, and has held speech competitions to inspire younger generations to learn it. TV programs, films, music, and standup comedy shows in Shanghainese have also emerged in recent years.

Zhou Yuwen, a 30-year-old branding manager born and raised in Shanghai, told Sixth Tone that her generation was expected to speak Mandarin both inside and outside the classroom, but over time, Shanghainese-speaking environments decreased.

“I can understand Shanghainese, but when I try to speak it, it comes out so ‘Yangjingbang’ that I feel too embarrassed to keep going,” she said, referencing the colloquial name for the pidgin English used between European and local merchants in Shanghai in the 19th century.

Zhou said she felt “excited” by the release of Duolingo’s Shanghainese course, and shared news of the course’s launch on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, hoping to encourage others to learn. “It’s a pity that someone like me, who was born, grew up, and worked my whole life in Shanghai, can’t speak proper Shanghainese,” she said. “I absolutely love the dialect, and I hope to see it not just preserved, but truly flourish.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.title: In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.content:
“I’m pregnant. After much consideration and thorough discussions with the company and my bandmates, I have decided to temporarily leave the group to focus on rest and recovery,” reads a statement signed by Mity, one of five members of the new girl group BABYQUEEN, alongside a selfie of her wearing pink pajamas in bed.

At first glance, nothing seems out of the ordinary, except that she and the entire BABYQUEEN pop group are AI-generated.

The announcement, published Tuesday on the group’s official Xiaohongshu account, also known as RedNote, has drawn criticism for turning women’s reproductive health into entertainment, as well as jokes and incredulity about the situation’s perceived absurdity.

AI girl group accounts have proliferated on Chinese social media in recent months, with virtual idols often maintaining social media accounts where they share glimpses of their daily lives and even secure and promote brand endorsements.

BABYQUEEN, styled as a South Korean girl group, launched its Xiaohongshu account on Sept. 7. As of Friday, the account, whose IP address is located in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, has roughly 1,000 followers.

Mity’s pregnancy was initially announced on the group’s account the day before, reading, “To prioritize her health during pregnancy and prepare for childbirth, she will temporarily suspend all group and individual variety show appearances and stage performances after thorough discussions with the team.” It also urged followers not to “over-speculate about her private life.”

Since it went viral on social media, the topic has attracted more than 6 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Friday.

Many users have expressed astonishment. “AI group members can get pregnant now? I don’t understand the virtual world anymore,” one highly upvoted comment reads. Others joked that the group’s creators might be running short on tokens, implying they had to let one member go because they lacked the computing power.

Users also accused the band’s makers of using the story for views while showing little respect for women. “Using ‘pregnant and preparing for childbirth’ as a marketing hook and a sensationalized narrative trivializes real women’s reproductive experiences by turning them into entertainment,” one comment reads.

The day of the announcement, the account also released a teaser post for a new song performed by the group’s four remaining members.

In a since-deleted Tuesday post on the BABYQUEEN account, the group’s creators cited pressures of running the group as the reason for the pregnancy announcement.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” they wrote, adding that they had “not earned a single cent” from the endeavor. They also said they had experienced personal attacks and online harassment.

On the group’s official parent account, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, the creators said Mity might next “explore two possible career paths: acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: FACT CHECK: Claire Castro not removed from her post, remains Palace press officer
World.content:
The Palace press officer was still briefing reporters on the day the video was posted, while its thumbnail falsely suggests a supposed confrontation with First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos

Claim: Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary Claire Castro has been removed from her position as Palace press officer.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video posted on October 4 by “PINAS BALITA TV,” credited to “The General’s Viewpoint,” carries the claim.

Text on its thumbnail reads, “Pinatalsik! Castro sibak sa pwesto!”

(Ousted! Castro removed from her post!)

It also shows First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos appearing to confront Castro, alongside the text, “Sinira mo! Ang pangalan ng asawa ko!”

(You destroyed my husband’s name!)

The video is titled, “Heto na! Pinatalsik na sa pwesto? Ante Kler, wala ng takas, nasampolan na? Mayor Baste, rumesbak na?”

(Here it is! Ousted from her post? Ante Kler has no escape, already made an example of? Mayor Baste fights back?)

As of writing, the video has garnered more than 22,000 views and 1,300 likes.

The facts: Castro has not been removed from her post. No Malacañang statement, PCO memorandum, or credible news report has announced her dismissal or resignation.

On October 4, the same day the video was posted, Castro texted reporters on the prosecution’s decision to drop the bribery allegation against Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial. Castro said the decision was within the prosecution’s discretion but could “shortchange” Filipinos from learning the full truth.

The video does not provide evidence that Castro was supposedly removed from her post. Its commentary instead focuses on Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte’s appearance and testimony during his sister’s impeachment proceedings and criticizes Castro over her remarks about him.

Castro had said Baste Duterte elevated himself as a mayor during his testimony but appeared to throw his sister under the bus when he said that he was not aware of the Vice President’s connection to GenCorp Industries Inc.

The video’s thumbnail also gives the impression that the First Lady confronted Castro, but the video provides no evidence of such an encounter.

Castro remains: Castro did file a courtesy resignation in July 2025 when then-PCO Secretary Dave Gomez assumed office, a standard procedure accompanying a change in agency leadership. Gomez declined to accept it, and Castro has remained in her post since.

The PCO website shows several recent press briefings held by Castro. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

World.title: Tiu Laurel alleges smear campaign by rice smugglers amid import controversy
World.content:
