PROBE. Agriculture Secretary Francis Tiu Laurel attends the Senate hearing on the high prices of food and other basic agricultural commodities, on August 20, 2025.

Following reports of illegal rice imports involving a company linked to him, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. can only surmise that he is the target of an orchestrated attack by “the hands of smugglers.”

“I’m clearly under attack,” Tiu Laurel said during the budget hearing Wednesday, October 21. “For what reasons I really don’t know but I can only smell the hands of smugglers na tinira namin dati (that we took on before.)”

The “attacks” were reports about a shipment of more than 12,000 metric tons of rice from Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, aboard the M/V Tay Son 2, and its alleged links to Tiu Laurel. The shipment appeared off Davao on September 14, more than a month after the deadline (before July 31) set in the contract between Aditya Birla Global Trading and Planters Products Incorporated (PPI).

What is the connection to the head of the Department of Agriculture (DA)? The company that imported the rice was PPI. Planters Foundation Incorporated, where Tiu Laurel serves as ex officio chairman, holds a majority of PPI’s outstanding shares.

Tiu Laurel’s said he serves as ex officio chairman because of executive issuances, and that he stopped the shipment (by canceling the import permit) before it arrived.

“Imagine ako na nga ‘yung ex-officio ng PPI, alam ko na PPI ‘yan, alam ko PPI din ‘yung consignee, ako pa rin nagpahinto,” said a visibly frustrated Tiu Laurel during the hearing, where he also had printed screenshots of his messages and instructions regarding the shipment ready.

“So is doing a good thing bad? It is not. I did the right thing.”

He said he even sent a boat from their family operations in General Santos to look for the vessel and take pictures. “Talagang hinanap namin (We really looked for it).” Tiu Laurel, a fishing magnate, comes from the family that owns Frabelle.

Agriculture secretaries have served as the ex officio chairman of the foundation. As Leonardo Montemayor, himself a former DA chief, said, “It can be any secretary.”

Since 1984, when the late former president Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Letter of Instructions (LOI) no. 1428, the minister of agriculture and food held the chairmanship of Planters Foundation Incorporated. Other cabinet members make up the foundation’s board, based on the LOI.

Montemayor, along with other groups, nonetheless are calling for Tiu Laurel’s temporary leave of absence as a show of delicadeza.

“How can it be?” Montemayor told reporters Tuesday, October 21. “You are both the investigated and the one regulating imports, issuing permits, and canceling permits.”

Framed?

By the end of the budget hearing, presided over by Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan, Tiu Laurel said he was willing to be subjected to an inquiry.

“Kung kami may kasalanan, may kasalanan kami,” Tiu Laurel said. “Kung wala kaming kasalanan, masabi na para matigil na to.” (If we’re at fault, then we’re at fault. If it’s not our fault, then let it be revealed so this ends.)

And then there was a moment of sympathy in the room. Senator Pangilinan recounted his time as presidential assistant for food security during the Aquino administration, when the National Food Authority administrator “was framed by traders.”

“What you’re going through, I went through,” said Pangilinan. “And for what? Because we were going after smugglers and traders who were messing up our rice supply.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Taiwan probes organized crime links to China’s ‘transnational repression’
World.content:
TAIWAN SECURITY OFFICIAL. Taiwan National Security Bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen speaks to members of the media at the parliament in Taipei, Taiwan, October 22, 2026.

Taiwan has complained that Beijing is using various underhanded methods to go after Taiwanese who the Chinese government views as separatists or are otherwise politically suspect

TAIPEI, Taiwan – Taiwan is probing organized crime’s links to Chinese efforts to carry out “transnational repression,” a security official said on Thursday, October 22, after Taipei’s government said Beijing was behind an attack on a comedian who mocked President Xi Jinping.

Taiwan, which China views as its own territory over the island’s objections, has complained that Beijing is using various underhanded methods to go after Taiwanese who the Chinese government views as separatists or are otherwise politically suspect.

Speaking to reporters at parliament, Taiwan National Security Bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen said the local networks that cooperate in incidents like the comedian attack are mostly criminal gangs, or private investigation firms linked to organized crime.

“The National Security Bureau is more concerned with whether anyone behind them has been directed and funded by the Chinese Communist Party. How to dismantle the entire criminal group and network is a key focus for us,” Tsai said.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has not responded to previous questions on the assault on the comedian.

Other China critics in Taiwan have also been attacked, including Hong Kong singer and activist Denise Ho. She was attacked in 2019 in Taipei by a masked man who threw red paint at her.

Tsai said Taiwan might need to amend its laws to better deal with China’s activities.

“Comprehensively curbing the Chinese communists’ transnational repression in Taiwan’s democratic and rule-of-law society is also very important, and the legal framework for it has been lacking,” he added.

Taiwan’s Supreme Prosecutors Office said in a separate statement on Thursday that the public should “raise their vigilance and never assist hostile foreign forces or allow themselves to be exploited as local collaborators.”

Maritime pressure

Taiwan, whose government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, says it is facing a stepped-up pressure campaign by China, including in the waters around the island where China’s military and Coast Guard operate daily.

Tsai said Chinese Coast Guard activities to the east of Taiwan, where Beijing began what it calls “law enforcement” patrols in June, are becoming more and more routine, often taking place with Chinese research vessels.

He added that he was particularly concerned with the appearance of Chinese militia boats to Taiwan’s east and southwest.

“Generally speaking, militia fishing boats are more commonly seen in the South China Sea, so the emergence of this situation around Taiwan is significant,” Tsai said.

Earlier this month, the US State Department said China’s actions off Taiwan’s east coast are “deeply destabilising” and only worsen tension after Reuters reported the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat in those waters.

Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.

China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan’s east coast are “legitimate and lawful” given those are Chinese waters, a position Taipei’s government strongly rejects. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Escudero did not suspend House prosecutor Zamora’s law license
World.content:
Zamora faced sexist remarks over her questioning during the impeachment trial, but no revocation of her law license occurred afterwards, contrary to the claim

Claim: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Chiz Escudero ordered the suspension of House prosecutor and San Juan City Representative Ysabel Zamora‘s law license following her direct examination of a witness at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video posted on October 3 by channel “NEWS UPDATE FILES,” credited to “PH Update,” carries the claim.

Text on its thumbnail reads, “Kinarma na! Tanggal ang linsensya!” (Karma has struck! License revoked!), with the text “Hinatulan ni Chiz! Malandi kasi!” (Sentenced by Chiz! Because she’s flirtatious!). It also shows an image of Escudero holding a document stamped “SUSPENDED” alongside a photo of Zamora.

The video’s title claims that Escudero issued a judgment on Zamora and revoked her license because of her alleged flirtatious demeanor.

As of writing, the video has drawn over 12,000 views and 528 likes.

The facts: There is no order from Escudero, the impeachment court, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), or the Supreme Court suspending Zamora’s law license. No credible news outlet has reported any such disciplinary action against her.

Zamora faced online backlash from several social media users after leading the direct examination of prosecution witness Police Major Joericson Sangalang about the firearms allegedly owned by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio. Critics, including some of the Vice President’s supporters, called Zamora’s questioning style “flirtatious” and accused her of trying to act cute. (READ: Should Sara Duterte have listed all her guns in her SALNs?)

Despite this, Escudero did not issue any ruling punishing Zamora, contrary to the claim, and only called her questions “speculative.” The defense panel ultimately chose to forgo cross-examining the witness Zamora questioned.

Additionally, presiding officers in an impeachment trial do not have legal jurisdiction over administrative lawyer suspensions — disbarment and law license suspensions fall exclusively under the authority of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, with the IBP handling and investigating complaints against lawyers.

Misogynistic: While not naming names, Senator Raffy Tulfo appeared to criticize Zamora when he called out a member of the prosecution for acting cute while questioning a witness during the trial. The incident prompted advocacy groups and legal figures to cite the Safe Spaces Act and urged the Senate to maintain a professional environment free from gendered harassment.

Zamora addressed the criticism directly at a press briefing, calling the remarks misogynistic and telling detractors to “get a life,” adding, “They can’t handle sass, they can’t handle style.”

The San Juan lawmaker currently serves as one of the active prosecutors on the House prosecution panel tasked with presenting evidence in Duterte’s impeachment trial. The Vice President is facing accusations of plunder, misuse of public funds, and betrayal of public trust linked to her office’s confidential funds. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte) – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack
World.content:
The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, use an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign

A Chinese state-aligned hacking group used an AI-driven penetration testing tool to compromise IT services firm ConnectWise as part of a campaign that targeted hundreds of organizations globally, Microsoft said on Wednesday, October 21.

Based on Microsoft’s analysis and evidence available to ConnectWise, “it appears that a China state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on ConnectWise Cloud Backup,” ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said in a separate statement.

Rivelo said ConnectWise “contained the affected application connections and are restoring services in controlled phases,” and that “those actions do not remove unauthorized access that may have already been established within individual customer tenants, which require separate review.”

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said China “opposes and fights hacking activities in accordance with the law. At the same time, we oppose smears and attacks against China under the excuse of cybersecurity issues.”

The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, used an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign, Microsoft said.

There are multiple tools used to conduct penetration testing, a form of legitimate testing of the security of networks or services. ARTEX allows users to use any AI model to automate a variety of penetration testing tasks and can be configured to run autonomous tasks including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, Microsoft said.

The attack targeted organizations across a variety of sectors, including aerospace, defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, think tanks and non-profit organizations, Microsoft said.

While the majority of targeting was not successful, Microsoft said, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence — or high-level access that could continue even after cleanup efforts — at many organizations in a brief time. – Rappler.com

World.title: Government websites go dark after AI-discovered flaw sparks security scramble
World.content:
SITE DOWNTIME. A screen displays the unavailable Dutch government website, mijn.overheid.nl, as cyber agencies warn that websites may be taken offline while PHP prepares a critical fix, in Berlin, Germany, October 21, 2026.

Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts say they are bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jump to get ahead of the updates

Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday, October 21, after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.

Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately.”

With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.

Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.

AI was powering a “race to exploit,” said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet.”

PHP — a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for “Personal Home Page” — underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences.

“All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable,” said Tiffany Farriss, the interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. “This issue impacts the majority of the internet.”

Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied.

According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix.

The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue.

Even some world leaders weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a post on X said website owners should “check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix.”

Bug found with AI

The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, two cybersecurity companies said in independent reports. Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on August 1 and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said.

“Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale,” it said. “With AI, this is no longer a barrier.” Calif and Wiz said they coordinated with one another and the PHP team and OpenAI on the discovery.

In a statement, the White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday.

In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said the tech giant’s security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy “honeypot” systems on October 17, four days before public disclosure.

The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo.

More attempts followed on Wednesday by multiple actors before the embargo lifted. Amazon said it was still unclear whether any of the attempts would have worked against real websites, adding the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

Critical software

PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers.

Its ubiquity — PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs — has made experts anxious. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have proliferated in recent weeks, could wreak havoc on unpatched servers, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London.

“The scale is huge, and with AI, exploitation may happen instantly,” Olejnik said.

WordPress.com operator Automattic said users of its hosted solutions and Tumblr were safe from the bug. Risks were higher for small PHP-powered websites run by individuals or organizations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers.

Mass outages

In the Netherlands, several organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites for the country’s five largest political parties and several hospital websites.

Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform.

Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline “as a precautionary measure.”

France’s Interior Ministry said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Ginbee Go, BPI’s next president and first female CEO?
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go, who has spent more than two decades building up the Bank of the Philippine Islands’ (BPI) consumer banking business, is set to become the next president and chief executive officer of the country’s oldest bank.

BPI announced on Thursday, October 22, that Go would succeed Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco effective April 26, 2027, following the bank’s annual stockholders’ meeting and subject to necessary approvals.

Go, currently BPI’s executive vice president and head of consumer banking, is a 23-year veteran of the Ayala-led bank. She previously served as president of BPI Family Savings Bank, where she oversaw its transformation and eventual integration into BPI — a familiar career path, as Limcaoco likewise served as president of BPI Family Savings Bank before his eventual stint as head of BPI.

Before joining BPI, Go held leadership positions at Citibank, Ayala Land, and Procter & Gamble.

She is also a certified public accountant who graduated magna cum laude from the University of the Philippines Diliman and topped the 1991 CPA Licensure Examination. She later earned her MBA with honors from Harvard Business School.

If you’ve ever walked into one of BPI’s newly revamped branches, with their sleeker, more modern interiors, Go has had a hand in what you see. As head of consumer banking, she has helped modernize the bank’s branch network, expand its retail banking business, and develop digital services, including tools powered by artificial intelligence.

Her focus on consumer banking was on display last August 1, on the bank’s 175th anniversary, when she joined Limcaoco at the launch of BPI’s revamped, Disney-themed Jumpstart savings account for children.

Speaking to Rappler on the sidelines, Go explained how the bank was trying to make financial literacy more accessible to young Filipinos.

“If we want to build a stronger and more resilient economy, we must cultivate the habit of saving early,” Go said.

Go will inherit a bank serving more than 19 million customers nationwide, following five years under Limcaoco, who took the helm in 2021 and oversaw BPI’s expansion in digital banking, financial inclusion, and sustainability.

Limcaoco will remain on BPI’s board of directors after stepping down as CEO and is expected to assume senior governance roles in other major Ayala Group companies.

“I am excited for the new prospects ahead under Ginbee’s stewardship. Amidst some volatility in the global and domestic environment, there are notable opportunities, particularly as the Filipino consumer sector grows, becomes more sophisticated, and seeks a trusted partner in achieving financial stability and success,” BPI chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala expressed confidence in Go’s leadership. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Good Business] The Rags2Riches story: Woven to last
World.content:
In December 2016, Reese Fernandez-Ruiz stood before the people of Rags2Riches at their Christmas party and told them it might be their last.

“I thought we were going to close,” she recalls. “It was a very sad Christmas party.” She chose that night, she says, because nearly everyone would be in one room, and because she wanted them to hear it as soon as she knew. She had just given birth to her first child only a few months earlier and still could not walk straight. Around her were the office team and the artisans from the communities, the weavers whose hands had built the company over nine years.

Every sign pointed to closure. What she held on to, privately, was a sliver of hope.

Cinderella story

In the mid-2000s, Reese found herself in Barangay Payatas, Quezon City as part of an immersion program. This was her initial meeting with some of the community members, particularly women who wove foot rugs out of scrap cloth. These women would work all day to finish ten rugs but would only be able to take home between P12 to P16 due to the long chains of middlemen that controlled the trade. This stuck with Reese. Together with eight other individuals, they returned to Payatas with a business partnership offer for the women weavers.

Play Video

While the idea was noble, they must earn the weavers’ trust. It was quite understandable considering that the community had heard many of the same promises before. Despite this, three artisans agreed to give it a try. Thus, Rags2Riches was born. With a P10,000 donation, the founders hauled scrap cloth straight from factories and sold the rugs at school bazaars. With the middlemen gone, the three women earned far more than before. Word spread and soon enough, the original three artisans grew to 30, then 50, then 100, and by 2013, more than 900 artisans were employed across the areas of Payatas, Tondo, Caloocan, and Sucat.

The beginning of Rags2Riches can be categorized as a Cinderella story. “We didn’t start as a fashion brand,” Reese says, “and because we started with communities, we really grew with the communities. The way the artisans would weave the materials before is quite different in form from what you see right now. And we have grown alongside them to get here.” That beginning still shapes how Reese describes the company. To her, that history sets R2R apart from brands that simply buy from artisans. “Our artisans are not just suppliers or a blip in our history,” she says. “They are really part of our identity.”

She does not dismiss brands that simply buy from artisans as suppliers. A market of any kind, she says, is better than none. But she wants those relationships to go deeper than commerce, and she would rather bring such brands along than shut them out. “I’d rather be inclusive with everyone so that they can have bridges,” she says, “and then they can walk those bridges and be real partners of the communities.”

Partnering with communities, however, also meant making products people would genuinely want to buy. That pulled Reese into a world she knew almost nothing about. “I didn’t have a fashion or design background,” Reese says. “I also didn’t grow up with fashion and design around me. I was frequently on survival mode growing up, so beautiful things were just an afterthought.” Reese understood why people needed food, vegetables and gas. Fashion was different. It runs on personal taste and aesthetics, and on cycles that are hard to read. “It’s quite intimidating,” she admits, “because I didn’t know what people wanted.”

Advisers and expansion

The founders knew from the start that sympathy would not sustain sales. In fact, they saw rugs being bought only because they were useful, not because the story was moving. To make products people would actually want, the founders sought help. The breakthrough came two months after the company was formed, when the group approached designer Rajo Laurel, who agreed to help and went on to serve as an unpaid adviser. Other leading Filipino designers followed, including Amina Aranaz-Alunan, Oliver Tolentino, Olivia d’Aboville and Kenneth Cobonpue. From rugs, R2R expanded into bags, home pieces and accessories, all built around the signature R2R weave.

By 2013, R2R products were sold in Philippine stores and online, and through partners in London and Edinburgh; international sales began that February. More recent collaborations include work with artist Leeroy New and with DoiTung of Thailand, and an upcycling and sewing service with IKEA. Partners abroad took notice. In 2013 and 2014, a grant from the AirAsia Foundation funded artisan training and a push into global markets, producing exclusive R2R x AirAsia collections sold on board its flights. In 2015, R2R became the first organization in Asia, and the first outside the United States and Canada, to receive the women-owned business grant of American fashion brand Eileen Fisher.

Reese credits no single study for getting the designs right. Instead, she describes a daily discipline. The design team starts from what the artisans already know how to do. Then it listens closely to the market, especially R2R’s devoted customers, whom the company calls advocates. “They tell us their feedback in very kind ways, so we’re very grateful to them,” she says. “Because of them, we’re able to design and innovate again and again and again until we got to where we are right now.” Today, she says, R2R’s products are always sold out and its pre-order list is very long. “But that wasn’t the case from day one,” she adds. “We had to learn along the way.”

Not every lesson came from the market, though. The hardest one came from inside the company. By its ninth year, R2R had won recognition at home and abroad. Its social impact was never in doubt. Its business fundamentals were. Impact, she says, was never the hard part. “What was harder was the business metrics.” Reese says. That gap came to a head at the Christmas party of 2016. When she weighed the company’s chances that December, she saw four or five things that would all have to happen for R2R to survive the coming year. Each one seemed unlikely. She made herself a promise anyway. If they all came through, she would do whatever it took to make the company not just survive, but succeed.

Business math

All of them came through. “They were so unlikely, but they happened,” she says. “And that was on me now. After that, I was like, okay, now we have to do the work.” The whole team took on that work. Reese, however, knew her own share was personal. She had to face a belief she had carried for years: that she hated math and could never be good at it. “When you’re in business and you say you hate math and you’re not good at it, it’s very dangerous,” she says. “Business has a lot of numbers, and for the longest time, I really didn’t want to go through our numbers.” She is careful about how much blame to take. “That’s not the only reason why we almost closed,” she says, “…but that is the reason that I can be responsible for, like, 100 percent.”

She was already in her thirties and believed it was too late to learn. Anything she needed, she thought, she should have learned in school. But she would not waste the chance the company had been given. “So I said, let us try this,” she recalls. “I will have to really learn business math from scratch.” Her method was blunt. She took the financial models built by investment managers R2R had worked with over the years and reverse-engineered them. She went through all of the company’s financials and crunched every figure. “I cried for days because I couldn’t balance [the] balance sheets,” she says. “And then I just practiced and practiced, until before I knew it, I could make financial models in a few minutes.”

It is an unusual turnaround story. The company was saved, in part, because its leader agreed to become a different leader. The crisis changed the company as much as it changed its leader. “We realized that if the business is not profitable, if it’s not doing well, we can’t do this for a long time,” Reese says. “And if you can’t do this for a long time, what’s the point? Because this is a livelihood. Livelihood means you have to sustain it every single day, for as long as it is needed.” What kept the impact intact was a choice the founders had made early. Social impact at R2R does not come from a separate program. It comes from how the products are made and who makes them. “Because we have built ourselves in such a way that social impact is a direct result of our operations and supply chain,” she explains, “it didn’t become hard to still have the social impact,” while the company fixed its finances.

The system was designed around the people doing the work. Most early artisans were mothers who could not leave home for a full workday. R2R lets them weave assigned parts at home, committing to a set number of hours a day. Finished panels went to a community center for quality checks, then to a workshop for assembly. By 2013, two to three hours of work earned an artisan P350 to P500 a day. That was enough to feed a family and keep children in school, against the P12 to P16 a whole day once paid.

Pay was only the start. In partnership with CARD Bank, part of each artisan’s earnings goes straight into a savings account in their own name. For many, the bank passbook was the first they had ever owned. Micro-insurance through CARD’s CaMia covers housing and hospitalization. R2R’s Artisan Academy has run workshops on financial literacy, values formation, family counseling and nutrition, alongside skills and quality training. New artisans train for three to six months before joining production. The numbers have grown with the model. R2R also says it has kept hundreds of tons of textile waste out of landfills by upcycling factory overstock. They also kept track of how well artisans keep their savings, a sign of whether families can plan for the future.

Their impact numbers are not kept from the people who produce them. Transparency is built into R2R’s governance. Artisans, suppliers, subcontractors and employees have been represented on R2R’s board. And the Christmas party, once the scene of a near-goodbye, has become the place where Reese reports to the artisans. “They also know our annual reports,” she says. “I report them at every Christmas party. I give them the spreadsheets.” She laughs. “It’s their favorite part. It’s not, but I tell them they’ll enjoy it.”

The point, she says, is that the artisans see their work, where it goes, where the whole company is heading, and the impact they are making together. The woman who once avoided the numbers now hands them to the people whose lives depend on them. Where the company is heading, it turns out, is a long way off. Ask Reese about her vision for the next five years, and she pushes back. “For R2R, everything that we do should look at 100 years or more,” she says. The ambition behind that timescale is specific. “I want to build one of the few Philippine heritage brands,” she explains. Around the world, there are brands whose histories stretch back to the 1700s or 1800s. “But in the Philippines, we don’t have a lot of that. And I think having that has the potential to build industries and support more communities.”

Philippine heritage

A Filipino heritage brand, in R2R’s hands, is built from Filipino heritage itself. Beyond its own weave and upcycled fabric, the company works with indigenous textiles from across the archipelago. These include inabel from Ilocos, such as binakol and pinilian; ikat-based weaves from Ifugao and Kalinga; Mangyan ramit from Mindoro; and T’boli abaca weaves from Lake Sebu in South Cotabato. Some of these textiles were once used as galleon sails or traded as dowries. Many carry patterns that encode wind, waves, mountains and family bonds. Reese worried that younger T’boli were losing interest in weaving, and said R2R hoped to help keep the tradition alive. She also wanted to bring work to rural artisans so they would not have to migrate to the cities.

Keeping a heritage alive, though, requires a company that outlives the people who founded it. A century-old company cannot depend on one person, and Reese says so plainly. “Our systems and supply chain are designed in such a way that they already include the artisans,” she explains. “Even if I’m not going to be the president of R2R in the future, if somebody else will be, it’s already in the DNA. It is in the branding, it is in the systems. So it almost doesn’t matter who the leader is,” she adds. “It should be the systems in place. Otherwise, it can’t be a 100-year company if it’s just driven by one person.” The business model, the supply chain and the company policies are all designed so that the artisans are included at every step. Every product, she stresses, is handmade. “It’s not a small collection. It’s not a seasonal collection. It is literally everything we do,” she says. “And we want that to continue for the long haul.”

Reese also sees a public role for enterprises like hers. In her 2022 Tatler Asia interview, she argued that grassroots businesses help connect what happens in communities with the policies government designs, and the reverse. In that view, a company that keeps Filipino hands at work and Filipino weaves in use is part of building the nation, not only its economy. Thinking in centuries has also changed how Reese measures her own success. “When I was much younger, it was about, if we reach this milestone, if we get this award, this recognition,” she says. “But we are so far from that right now, because we have been through so much. We have really seen what it takes to build an enterprise to this level. And the goal is 100 years, so short-term success wouldn’t cut it.”

There is no longer a finish line. “My definition of success is the race that we’re running,” she says. “Are we still running the race that we wanted to run? Are we on the same path that we wanted to be on from the beginning? Are we still values-aligned? If we are, then we are successful right now.”

She admits the idea is not tidy. R2R still chases milestones, and still wants to achieve more. But she also makes room to pause and recognize that the work is good and worth continuing. And she counts the company’s habit of questioning itself as a strength. “As long as we still question what we do, because we still do, and I think that’s healthy,” she says, “…and as long as we know we still have things to do, places to go and things to achieve, I think we are on the path to success, and we are successful.”

That same patience shapes the advice she gives to young people who want to change their own communities, drawn from nearly two decades of practice. “Doing good is not a one-time thing,” Reese adds. “It’s a daily thing. It’s a habit. It’s consistency that matters. If you are only going to do good once you have a set of parameters first, then you will never get there. So do it imperfectly, but do it anyway.”

To those dreaming of their own social enterprise, she offers a narrower charge. “Do it for the right reasons,” she says. Sustainability does not have to be fully worked out on day one, but the commitment has to be consistent. Choose one path, one advocacy, and grow from there. “If you want to do too many things all at the same time, it’s going to be very difficult, and the chances for success would be lower,” she says. “And we do need to be successful, because we need more of you.”

Reese Fernandez-Ruiz, Rags2Riches FB

Every sign once pointed to closure. What Reese held on to was a small piece of hope, and a promise to do whatever it took if that hope came through. From a business proposal in Payatas to a fashion house with waiting lists, she learned that doing good only matters if it lasts. Now she continues to build a Filipino brand meant to outlive her. – Rappler.com

John Laurence Robes is a part-time lecturer under the Department of Marketing and Advertising, Ramon V. del Rosario College of Business at De La Salle University (DLSU). He completed his undergraduate degree in Bachelor of Arts in Organizational Communications at the University of the Philippines Manila, and his Masters of Marketing Communication from DLSU. Apart from being a part-time lecturer, he is also the Project and Research Assistant for the PHINMA-DLSU Center for Business and Society (PDCBS) and is an i5 Grant Competition for Innovative Pedagogy Awardee by the PRME ASEAN+ Chapter in 2023. Currently, he is pursuing his doctorate under the Doctor of Business Administration program at DLSU.

World.title: Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia
World.content:
Anyone who still thinks Russia is simply bankrolling Myanmar has the direction of money backwards. In this arrangement, Myanmar is the customer. It is preparing to buy Russian gas and, in doing so, send money into a Russian economy still financing the war in Ukraine. Russia, meanwhile, is offering technology in return: satellite navigation, communications, Earth observation and aerospace cooperation. In other words, Myanmar is not being paid to stand with Russia. Myanmar is paying Russia, while Russia trades technology for access to a new market.

In August 2026, Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing traveled to Moscow for an official visit and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The visit produced 12 agreements and memoranda covering everything from energy and culture to competition policy and space technology. Four of them are particularly interesting because the technologies involved have obvious civilian applications, but equally obvious military ones.

The four were:

Memorandum Memorandum on information and communication technologies; Memorandum satellite navigation, human spaceflight Memorandum between the Myanmar Space Agency and Bauman Moscow State Technical University on technological and aerospace cooperation.

At roughly the same time, Russia and Myanmar were also negotiating something much less futuristic: liquefied natural gas.

The interesting part is that Myanmar was not discussed only as the final customer. According to the Myanmar President’s Office, the talks also covered onward supplies of Russian LNG to China and Thailand. That changes the scale of the arrangement considerably. Russia is not simply looking for another buyer. Myanmar is being considered as a possible regional distribution point for Russian LNG into Southeast Asia.

That is where the arrangement starts to look slightly extravagant.

Myanmar already has substantial natural-gas reserves and remains a major gas exporter. Recent estimates put its proven reserves at around 22.5 trillion cubic feet, while a large share of its production is exported. It certainly does not suffer from a geological shortage of natural gas.

So why import Russian LNG?

Part of the answer may simply be infrastructure, contracts and energy shortages. Having gas underground is not the same thing as having sufficient gas available in the right place, at the right time and in the right form. But the Russian side has another obvious problem: it needs markets.

Western sanctions and the war in Ukraine have placed sustained pressure on Russia’s traditional energy relationships. Russia’s finances are under considerably more pressure than before the war. The liquid part of the National Wealth Fund on September 1, 2026, was lower than ever, at 13,194.88 billion rubles (US$159.94 billion). Russia therefore has every reason to find new buyers for what it still has in abundance. And what Russia has in abundance is natural resources.

Myanmar offers access to the Southeast Asian market. Russia offers LNG. So far, fairly conventional.

The LNG story did not begin in August. In April, Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev and Myanmar Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin were already discussing supplies of Russian LNG, petroleum products and crude oil. Myanmar’s Ministry of Electricity and Energy was quite specific about what it wanted: favorable prices, quality guarantees, secure transportation and long-term supply. The same visit produced a Memorandum of Cooperation between the Ministry of Electricity and Energy and RC-Investments. The framework was designed with Russia identifying suppliers and partners and Myanmar facilitating Russian hydrocarbon and petrochemical deliveries.

Myanmar’s LNG import system already exists. Imports resumed in late 2025 after a four-year break, with LNG loaded at the Bintulu LNG complex in Malaysia and delivered to the Thilawa floating storage unit near Yangon. So, Russia is effectively trying to insert itself into an existing supply chain. Kpler expected Myanmar to import around 0.4 million tonnes of LNG in 2026, mainly to supply the Thanlyin and Thaketa power plants. Myanmar’s own Ministry of Information confirms that LNG imports are now feeding around 500 MW of generation in Yangon.

What Russia appears prepared to provide alongside it is considerably more interesting.

The Roscosmos agreement includes satellite-navigation measurement stations, access to navigation data, a COSPAS-SARSAT ground station and an ASPOS opto-electronic telescope station. Russia will also help select and train Myanmar astronauts. According to the Myanmar Space Agency (which already took the announcement down from their website), the stated purposes include economic development, search and rescue, scientific research and monitoring hazardous objects in space. All very peaceful.

Then the cooperation expanded further. On August 19, Min Aung Hlaing met Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov. Their discussions included Earth-observation satellite imagery, a satellite-navigation measuring station, the Rassvet low-orbit communications system, nano-satellites and continued Russian assistance in developing Myanmar’s space capabilities.

None of these technologies is inherently military. That is precisely the point. They do not need to be. Remember the Chinese balloon incident in 2023? A Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed the United States before being shot down by an F-22 off the coast of South Carolina on February 4. Beijing insisted that it was a civilian airship used mainly for meteorological research which had simply been blown off course. The U.S. State Department had a rather different interpretation. A U-2 surveillance aircraft examined the balloon while it was still in the air and confirmed that it carried intelligence-collection capabilities. The U.S. government later described it as part of a broader Chinese military-linked aerial surveillance program.

Earth-observation technology works on exactly the same uncomfortable boundary between civilian and military use. The same satellite imagery that monitors forests, floods, agriculture or climate can also show roads, buildings, camps, vehicles and changes on the ground. Optical satellites provide detailed imagery; synthetic-aperture radar can observe through cloud and at night; repeated passes over the same area show what has moved, appeared or disappeared. Communications systems can connect remote communities. They can also support command and control. Radio-electronic technology can support industry. It can also support surveillance and electronic warfare. Calling the technology civilian therefore tells us very little about what it can actually be used for. A satellite looking for deforestation can look at a military base just as easily.

Below is the kind of imagery Russia can produce. These are examples from Russian Resurs-P and Canopus-V satellites:

Resurs-P4 and P5 can produce panchromatic imagery at about 1 m resolution and multispectral imagery at roughly 3-4 m. As for the Canopus-V imagery, you can clearly distinguish agricultural plots, settlements, roads and terrain. Russian Space Systems explicitly lists infrastructure monitoring among the applications of these Earth-observation systems.

And what about Rassvet? It is essentially Russia’s answer to Starlink, a low-Earth-orbit broadband communications network being built by Bureau 1440, part of Russia’s X Holding. Bureau 1440 describes the satellites themselves as “5G base stations in orbit”. The target orbit is around 800 km, with advertised speeds of up to 1 Gbit/s and latency below 70 milliseconds. The satellites communicate with each other through laser links, while user terminals can be installed on fixed sites as well as cars, ships, aircraft and trains.

Militarily, the potential is obvious. What it can potentially do is provide broadband communications in places where terrestrial networks are absent or unreliable. That could support communication between command posts, mobile units, aircraft or unmanned systems. It could also transmit satellite imagery and other intelligence quickly from one location to another.

Myanmar is an unusually important place to make that distinction.

Myanmar’s civil war is nearly as old as the country itself. Armed conflict between the central state and ethnic organizations began almost immediately after independence in 1948. The Karen conflict started in 1949, while other ethnic insurgencies developed across Kachin, Shan and other border regions. These were not temporary rebellions. They became long-running territorial conflicts over autonomy, federalism, political control and, in some cases, independence.

The Myanmar military has never been particularly effective in many of these areas. Geography is one reason. Ethnic armed organizations operate in mountains, jungles and forests along the borders with Thailand, China and India. They know the terrain, move in small units, use ambushes and landmines and often operate among populations with which they have close local connections. The Myanmar military has traditionally been much stronger in towns, on major roads and around fixed military positions.

The military is therefore not acquiring these capabilities in an abstract security environment. It is fighting an actual war.

Better Earth observation means better information about what is happening on the ground. Better satellite navigation means better positioning. Better communications mean better coordination. Better mapping means a clearer picture of roads, settlements, bases and infrastructure in territories that the military has historically struggled to control.

Russia does not need to sign a memorandum saying that it will help Myanmar locate ethnic armed organizations. No government writes agreements like that. It only needs to provide the infrastructure that makes locating them easier.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specialising in defence economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: ‘They’re Definitely Afraid of Her’: Aung San Suu Kyi’s Son Speaks Out
World.content:
Kim Aris would much rather stay out of the spotlight. But when his mother Aung San Suu Kyi was once again imprisoned after Myanmar’s military coup in 2021, he realised he could no longer remain silent. As a part of his mission to draw attention to his mother’s plight and the continuing struggle of the people of Myanmar, he came to Prague last week.

There he attended the democratic Forum 2000 Conference to remind the world that wars raging closer to home have not brought an end to those that have been devastating countries thousands of miles away for years.

His mother is now 81 and her family do not know exactly where she is being held or in what conditions. In an interview with Chechia’s Seznam Zpravy daily, he asks: if he, as her own son, does not stand up for his mother, how can he expect anyone else to do so?

When you look at Myanmar today, more than five years after the coup, what kind of country do you see?

I see a country torn apart by civil war, with people on the ground facing a very, very desperate situation. The military continues to bomb civilians regularly and refuses to stop its brutality against the population despite international pressure.

And yet, despite all this, I don’t think the situation is quite as straightforward as the rest of the world tends to portray it.

The people of Burma have shown incredible strength over the past five years, and the military is nowhere near as strong as it would like the rest of the world to believe. In fact, I would say the country is more united today than it has been for decades. It’s just very difficult for the outside world to see that at the moment.

We are witnessing something of a diplomatic rehabilitation of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing. He was warmly received in Malaysia, and the United States has begun direct talks with his government. What do you think of these developments?

I think those who are now trying to negotiate with the military are going to be very disappointed when they realise that the military is making promises it simply cannot keep.

Are you referring, for example, to American efforts to gain access to Myanmar’s rare earth mineral deposits?

Yes. But those minerals are not being mined in areas controlled by the military. Many of the promises the military is making concern things it simply cannot deliver. And even if it could deliver them, we’ve known for decades that the military frequently breaks its promises.

When was the last time you heard from your mother directly?

I’ve received just one letter from her in the past five years. That must have been about three years ago now.

This summer, photographs finally emerged showing her meeting representatives of the Red Cross. When you first saw those pictures, did they reassure you, or did they raise even more questions?

At first, I wasn’t even sure whether to believe that the meeting had actually taken place. After all, over the past five years, the military has put out a great deal of false information about my mother’s health and whereabouts.

For example, they claimed she had been transferred to house arrest, and we know that isn’t true. But when I found out that the photograph was genuine—or at least that one of them was—it gave me some hope that she was, at least, still alive.

Do you think the military is afraid of Aung San Suu Kyi herself or of what she continues to represent?

They’re definitely afraid of her. Why else would they keep her locked up?

And she really is a symbol for the people. People in Burma recognise how much she has sacrificed for them over the past 30 or 40 years. They know that she has been willing to stay in Burma, to remain with them and go through the same hardships they’ve had to endure.

Your mother remains a symbol of democracy for many people. But is there anything from her time in government that you personally disagree with? I’m thinking, for example, of the Rohingya crisis.

No, I’ve never had a problem with any of her decisions. She was in an extremely difficult position, and the international community failed to understand just how delicate that situation was.

I think it’s much clearer now that she simply wasn’t able to do everything she might have wanted to do. But I believe she did more for the Rohingya than anyone else, and people don’t realise that.

They say she remained silent on the issue, even though what she actually said about it would fill entire volumes. They say she went to The Hague to defend the military. But they say that without ever having properly listened to what she actually said there. So my advice to people is this: go and listen to what she said. Find out exactly what she did to help the Rohingya.

She initiated the establishment of the Kofi Annan Commission the day after she came to power. That was before the issue had even become a major concern for the international community. She was taking steps to help the Rohingya, and representatives of the Rohingya community I’ve spoken to have told me that she did everything she could for them.

Most people associate Aung San Suu Kyi with politics or the Nobel Peace Prize. Was it difficult growing up with someone who was both a parent and such a prominent public figure?

I grew up with it, and I think that, when you’re a child, everything just seems normal. You don’t know any other way of life, so you don’t really know what’s normal and what isn’t. From a very early age, I was aware of what she represented, but I don’t think those two things are mutually exclusive. She can be my mother and, at the same time, a very prominent political figure.

You’ve said before that you never wanted to become involved in politics, and that your mother didn’t want that for you either. Yet here you are, travelling, campaigning and speaking publicly about Myanmar. When did you realise that staying out of the spotlight was no longer an option?

When they put her in prison five years ago, I realised I had to speak out. After all, I’m her son. And if I don’t do anything, how can I expect anyone else to stand up for her?

How much of what you’re doing today is about your mother personally, and how much is about Myanmar itself? If your mother were released tomorrow, would you continue campaigning for democracy in Myanmar?

I think my mother would do a pretty good job of that herself. If I manage to secure her release, then I can feel that I’ve done my job well too.

For much of her life, Aung San Suu Kyi was seen as the daughter of Aung San, the general who played a key role in Burma’s struggle for independence from British colonial rule. Do you sometimes feel that you, too, are defined by your mother’s name?

I suppose I do, to some extent. After all, it’s very difficult not to have that image hanging over you. But at the same time, I’m doing this because I want to. I think it’s important that we all try to do whatever we can. People often don’t realise that they’re capable of doing much more than they think.

As a child, did you understand why your mother chose to stay in Myanmar rather than live a safe life with her family in Britain?

Yes, I did. I was actually with her when she was first placed under house arrest, so I saw what was happening with my own eyes. In some ways, it felt like a natural continuation of what had been happening before, because we’d been watching the situation in Burma gradually deteriorate.

I can’t say it was easy, but I think that, because I was a child at the time, I was somehow able to accept it. It’s difficult to explain. I think adults often find it harder to deal with change. And if she’d been imprisoned five years ago without my having already spent decades living with our separation, I think it would have been much harder.

What was it actually like when your mother was first placed under house arrest? Can you describe what happened?

When they first came to arrest her, they arrived with several trucks to take away the student revolutionaries who were staying in the house as well. I remember watching them being taken away. Then they put barbed wire around the entire compound, set up guard posts, cut the telephone lines and stopped us from leaving the house.

But at least we were still in her own home, and her own doctor was allowed to visit her. Even after I returned to England, I could send her parcels, and sometimes we were able to communicate. The past five years have been completely different.

You mentioned the student movement earlier. Is the revolution still visible on the streets of Myanmar today?

Yes, it is. It may not be as visible as it once was, but there is still an enormous amount of resistance across the country. In some places, like Yangon, things might appear quite normal. Other journalists I’ve spoken to who have been there have told me that everything looks remarkably normal. But it certainly isn’t. There are still huge numbers of people doing everything they can to change the situation. They’ve simply gone underground, so they’re not as visible as they used to be.

Do you ever feel that the junta has forced you into a role you would never have chosen for yourself?

Yes. I wouldn’t be doing this otherwise.

And what would you be doing?

Spending time with my children and working. I’m a trained carpenter.

How do you explain to your children what’s happening to their grandmother, and what’s happening in Myanmar more generally?

We’ve been talking about it for years, and they’ve had to come to terms with it too. They understand what’s happening in Burma. I still try to protect them as much as I can. Being in the public eye isn’t easy, and I want to keep them as far away from all that as possible.

Do you believe you’ll ever see your mother again?

Yes, I do. She’s been released before, and the situation in Burma could change at any moment. Even if the resistance doesn’t achieve victory in the near future, I think there’s still a chance that she could be released.

The interview first appeared in Czech at Seznam Zpravy. Daniela Kucerova is the new outlet’s foreign news department editor. Her main area of focus is Asia, particularly China and neighboring regions.

World.title: China Moves to Cement Myanmar Influence After U.S. Talks With Regime
World.content:
As Washington resumes direct engagement with Myanmar’s military regime, Beijing moved to cement its overarching influence last week by meeting with nine political parties in Yangon to gauge public sentiment.

The Chinese delegation was led by Peng Xiubin, director‑general of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Liaison Department. Present at the meeting were representatives of the military’s proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party, the National Unity Party, People’s Party, People’s Pioneer Party, Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party, Arakan Front Party, Kayin People’s Party, Unity and Development Party, and New Chinland Congress Party.

Participants said the Chinese side raised five key points, including Myanmar public attitudes toward China and challenges in bilateral relations.

“The Chinese side asked how the Myanmar people view them,” one participant told The Irrawaddy. “Some parties noted that sections of the public hold negative or skeptical views. They urged China to do more to show how it is helping Myanmar so that people understand.”

Anti-China sentiment in Myanmar has surged since the 2021 coup, triggered by Beijing’s support for successive military regimes, supplying them with battlefield hardware, technology and diplomatic cover. China is a key arms supplier and the biggest investor in post-coup Myanmar, propping up an embattled regime shunned by much of the international community and sanctioned by the West.

Most of the parties present at the meeting took part in Jan.-Feb. regime elections that were widely dismissed as a fraud to cement military rule.

However, leaders of the National Democratic Force (NDF) and the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD)—Htet Aung Kyaw and Sai Kyaw Nyunt—joined the talks despite their parties being dissolved for defying the regime’s electoral roadmap. One party leader said the duo attended in a personal capacity after being invited individually, rather than as representatives of their banned organizations.

The CCP delegation also asked about priority areas for cooperation, and parties’ views on peace, the economy, and domestic issues.

The meeting came as coup leader Min Aung Hlaing made progress in securing formal engagement with Washington. U.S. officials held their second round of talks with regime representatives in Tokyo earlier this month after Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance flew to Naypyitaw for talks with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in September.

“The Chinese side made no mention of the recent U.S.-Myanmar talks, focusing instead on gauging our views,” said one participant. “Some parties stressed that they prefer engagement with China, a neighbor.”

Party leaders said they also discussed trade policy and technical support for agriculture while urging China to help reopen the Muse–Mandalay highway, a vital trade corridor. After losing control of major trade routes with China in northern Shan, the regime has imposed a near total blockade on Chinese imports to starve ethnic armed organizations of tax revenue.

Saw Han Aye, chair of the People’s Pioneer Party, said: “We asked the Chinese to increase investment and reopen trade routes as soon as possible, and Beijing affirmed it wants more frequent exchanges.”

While Beijing rejects accusations of interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs, the belief that its investments prop up a military regime waging war on its own people is widespread within the country. Anti-China sentiment soared to new levels in 2024, when Beijing pressured ethnic armies to halt northern Shan offensives that were threatening the regime’s grip on power.

When China’s Asia envoy Deng Xijun called for ethnic autonomy during a Naypyitaw ceremony marking the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement’s anniversary last week, critics pointed out that northern Shan State is already controlled by ethnic armies under Beijing’s thumb.

World.title: Migrants Urge Thai Gov’t to Let Them Work Free of Myanmar Regime Extortion
World.content:
Myanmar migrants are urging the Thai government to let them work legally without so-called Certificates of Identity (CI), which they say the military regime back home is weaponizing to extort money from them.

CI, issued by the regime under a quota system for overseas laborers hired in Myanmar, allow workers to register for work permits and renew their visas in Thailand.

Starved of hard currency, the regime has recently moved to harness CI issuance to grab the hard-earned money of migrant workers, saying it will not renew the papers unless workers remit a portion of their earnings back home through official channels and pay two percent income tax.

Under remittance rule introduced in late 2023, workers must send at least 25 percent of their monthly salaries home through regime-controlled banks, which means a fixed, artificially inflated exchange rate. Traditionally workers rely on the informal “hundi” system, which offers better exchange rates.

In response, the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT) has launched a campaign calling on Thai authorities to abolish the CI requirement for visas and work permits and instead allow employment solely based on the Pink Cards issued by the Thai government to regularize the status of migrants and refugees

Since Oct. 18, workers have staged an online photo campaign to press their demands.

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government (NUG) has expressed support for the campaign.

Workers say they are not willing to pay any form of tax to the regime which does little to protect and promote their rights.

“The regime does not even provide proper passport services, so why should we pay them any money?” said a Myanmar worker in Chonburi.

The campaign began after the regime opened new CI issuing centers on Oct. 14 in Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Surat Thani, Chiang Mai and Chonburi in order to prey on migrant workers whose permit cycle expires in December. There they must show evidence that they have remitted their due share of their earnings through the regime’s banking channels.

Pouring oil on the flames, Labor Minister Maung Myint earlier this month told migrant workers in Thailand to “think of the money as a donation.”

“We are campaigning to live and work with Pink Cards only,” said Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee. “The regime’s demand for 25 percent remittance and tax payments can only be stopped by the workers themselves.”

He insisted this is not a protest against Thailand, but “simply a request to be allowed to work legally with Pink Cards.”

Workers complain that the CI centers are expensive, Byzantine and riddled with corruption in the form of demands for unofficial fees. Many laborers, who may be barely literate and speak little official Burmese, have to reply on brokers, which makes them prone to overcharging and fraud.

Campaigners have petitioned both houses of the Thai Parliament to abolish the CI requirement and crack down on brokers profiting from migrants.

MP Sia Jampatong of the House of Representatives committee said the government “must seriously review the CI center system, because the labor registration process must exist to certify status and protect rights, not be left to become a channel for officials to make a living, or provide an opportunity for the military government to exercise power over the lives of working people,” according to news outlet The Reporters.

And Senator Thewarit Maneechai pledged to bring the demand to the consideration of the Senate Labor Committee “to consider further relevant actions,” it added.

Thai activists also expressed solidarity. The Thailand Migration Reform group warned that allowing Myanmar’s regime to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the Pink Card framework used before 2009.

Until then, migrants lived and worked legally in Thailand with Pink Cards alone. “If workers could survive with Pink Cards before, why not improve that system and use it again?” said one migrant who has lived in the country for over 30 years.

According to Thailand’s Labor Ministry, there were nearly 3.5 million registered Myanmar workers with work permits in the country as of August this year, of whom only about 430,000 hold CI cards. The regime recently admitted that remittance has become a major source of foreign currency income for Myanmar.

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Kazakhstan Approves Military Reform Plan to Modernize Armed Forces
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Security Council has approved a military reform plan aimed at modernizing the Armed Forces, restructuring military management and training, and establishing a new Unmanned Forces branch, according to the presidential press service.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev chaired an Oct. 21 Security Council meeting, where he called for the creation of a modern, mobile and technologically advanced army in the shortest possible time.
