World.title: Georgia’s party ban: Court to begin hearing government case against opposition on 21 October
World.content:
At noon on 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court will begin hearing on the merits a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which is seeking to ban five opposition parties and political groups. The hearings will take place in Batumi and continue on 22 and 23 October.

Four of the five parties intend to defend their positions in court, while the fifth will boycott the proceedings. Some opposition groups also plan to hold protests in Batumi and Tbilisi alongside the hearings.

The Constitutional Court’s full bench will hear the case, meaning all its sitting judges. The court has nine seats, but only seven judges currently serve on it, with two vacancies. On 13 October, Manana Kobakhidze, one of the founders of Georgian Dream, left the court. She had previously asked to recuse herself from the case, but the court rejected her request. Kobakhidze said she had made the decision to leave the court independently and for personal reasons.

Georgian Dream MPs Archil Gorduladze, Giorgi Kakhiani, Tengiz Sharmanashvili and Tornike Cheishvili will represent the party in court.

Under the law, the court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Why is Georgian Dream seeking to ban the parties?

The claimants — 88 Georgian Dream MPs — argue that all five parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that aim to overthrow or forcibly change the constitutional order.

According to information released by the court, the claimants cite alleged human rights violations between 2004 and 2012, when one of the parties, the United National Movement (UNM), was in power. They also point to the parties’ current refusal to recognise Georgian Dream’s legitimacy. The claimants say the parties have rejected the government’s legitimacy since 2016 and are pursuing a common goal.

The claimants also accuse the parties of attempting to overthrow the government. In the case of the United National Movement, they further allege that it undermined the country’s independence and territorial integrity, citing the August 2008 war.

The opposition parties reject all these accusations.

What do the parties facing a ban plan to do?

United National Movement

The party will attend the court hearings, said Irakli Pavlenishvili, chair of its governing council. He called on members of the public to gather outside the courthouse in Batumi on the days of the hearings.

The UNM’s jailed founder and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili, has also demanded that he attend the proceedings. In a statement released on 17 October, he said he wanted the authorities to bring him to Batumi so he could “fully expose this so-called court and its master for their historic betrayal”. Much of the case against the parties concerns Saakashvili’s time in power, from 2004 to 2012.

The party’s leader, Levan Khabeishvili, who is also in prison, has likewise demanded permission to attend the hearings.

The UNM belongs to the opposition alliance and takes part in its protests.

What is the Opposition Alliance? The Opposition Alliance “Unity for Victory” was formed by nine pro-Western Georgian parties on 2 March 2026, following months of negotiations. Its members are the United National Movement, Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom, Droa, the Federalists, European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. The alliance says its goals are to end the rule of Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, restore Georgia’s Euro-Atlantic course, release political prisoners and form a coalition government after Georgian Dream loses a free election. The parties retain their ideological independence but have agreed on a joint strategy for protests and communications. The alliance’s largest rally to date took place in Tbilisi on 26 May 2026, Georgia’s Independence Day. Two other major opposition parties, Lelo and For Georgia, led by Giorgi Gakharia, have not joined the alliance. Lelo chose to operate independently, while For Georgia rejected an alliance with the United National Movement and parties that split from it.

Coalition for Change

The coalition will also take part in the hearings. Its member parties — Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom and Droa — also belong to the Opposition Alliance. On 15 October, Nika Gvaramia, leader of Ahali, announced the launch of a joint campaign by the alliance.

Gvaramia said their struggle would not be confined to the courtroom. “We will be everywhere, including on the streets of Tbilisi,” he promised.

Strong Georgia – Lelo

Lelo will attend the hearings and has asked the Public Defender (ombudsman) to submit a legal opinion on the case. As of 19 October, the ombudsman’s office had not responded.

Lelo is not a member of the alliance. The party’s political council says it has several scenarios and an action plan ready in case the court approves the ban.

For Georgia

The party announced in a statement on 20 October that it would take part in the proceedings. However, it insists that the court consider the case against it separately, rather than together with the other parties.

The party of former Georgian prime minister Giorgi Gakharia does not belong to the Opposition Alliance. It was the only one of the five parties that refused to surrender its parliamentary mandate in protest and nevertheless entered parliament.

The Federalists

The party has decided not to attend the hearings, saying it does not want to lend the proceedings a veneer of legal legitimacy.

According to party leader Tamara Chergoleishvili, the Federalists will travel to Batumi but protest against the court proceedings outside the courthouse rather than in the courtroom.

Why does it matter whether the parties attend the hearings?

The parties’ attendance could affect their chances of appealing the verdict to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg.

Sandro Baramidze, a lawyer with Transparency International Georgia, explains that the ECHR requires applicants to raise and document their arguments through domestic legal proceedings first. If a party does not attend the hearing, its application to the court in Strasbourg could therefore be declared inadmissible.

Who is organising the protests?

As Georgian Dream seeks to ban the parties listed above, the Opposition Alliance has announced a protest campaign.

The first demonstration will take place at 11:00 on 21 October in Batumi, outside the Constitutional Court. Freedom Square, a member of the alliance, is organising the protest.

At 19:00 on 25 October in Tbilisi, outside the first building of Tbilisi State University, the Opposition Alliance will launch a joint campaign aimed at organising a large demonstration in Tbilisi on 28 November.

As of 20 October, Lelo and For Georgia had not said whether they would join the protests.

What is the rest of the opposition doing?

In addition to the parties facing a ban, the Opposition Alliance includes European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. These parties are not named in the lawsuit but take part in all the alliance’s protests.

Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of Freedom Square, believes that banning the parties would create a bigger problem for Georgian Dream itself.

He says a ban will not make the country’s problems disappear. Instead, it will “close off the political path to solving these problems and guarantee an even worse end for Georgian Dream”.

Viktor Kipiani, leader of the party For Georgia First, points to the same risk:

Banning opposition parties through the courts effectively brings the political process to a standstill, while making change through elections virtually impossible.

He believes this will accelerate radicalisation in the country.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association has now issued its independent legal assessment of the case for the third time, arguing that the lawsuit aims to eliminate political competition.

What is the European Union saying?

EU institutions have reacted strongly to the Georgian authorities’ attempt to ban opposition parties:

The European Parliament adopted another critical resolution, calling for the immediate withdrawal of the lawsuit and saying it was considering personal sanctions against those who initiated the proceedings.

Christian Wigand, a European Commission spokesman, said Brussels was closely monitoring developments. He said the attempt to abolish leading political forces, alongside the Georgian authorities’ earlier statements and legislative changes, pointed to a worrying instrumentalisation of the justice system. This directly threatens democratic pluralism and fundamental freedoms.

On 20 October, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded that questioning the legitimacy of the proceedings before the court had even examined the case amounted to an attempt to pressure the court and interfere in the country’s internal affairs. The ministry urged EU representatives to refrain from statements that prejudge the proceedings.

What happens if the court upholds the lawsuit?

If the court upholds the lawsuit, the five parties will legally cease to exist. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, a total of 784,820 voters backed the five parties in the 2024 parliamentary election.

Under current legislation, the court may also, at the claimant’s request, ban people associated with the dissolved parties from engaging in political activity. The law also provides a 14-day procedure for banning a successor party.

The hearings scheduled for 21–23 October mark the first stage in the proceedings. It remains unclear how long the case will take or when the court will deliver its ruling.

World.title: Baku conference weighs digital shift in Azerbaijan’s public finance
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. A conference titled “Digital Finance Ecosystem: A New Stage in Governance” is being held on October 22, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

The event is organized by the Public Council under Azerbaijan's Ministry of Finance, with the Association of Professional Financial Managers of Azerbaijan (APFM) as its official partner and support from the Ministry of Finance.

The conference brings together representatives of government agencies, the private sector and civil society organizations, as well as professional accountants. Discussions focus on the digital transformation of public finance and its development prospects, effective financial data management, and modern approaches to strengthening transparency and accountability.

Two panel sessions are being held as part of the conference: “Digitalization of Public Finance: Inter-System Integration and a New Governance Model” and “Ensuring Resilience in Public Finance Data Management.”

The panel discussions address the transition to a unified digital public finance management model, expanded system integration, the development of national digital infrastructure, the digitalization of fiscal policy, digital payment infrastructure, and the creation of a secure and flexible settlement environment for public financial transactions.

Participants are also exchanging views on strengthening public trust in the digital finance ecosystem, applying data-driven auditing and analytical approaches to assess the efficiency of public spending, transitioning to results-oriented fiscal policy, improving databases used in public procurement, assessing competition and identifying risk indicators.

Other topics include the analysis of financial transactions and early detection of risks, establishing a reliable data ecosystem for public finance, and the role of professional accountants in this process.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan to raise social benefits for disabled, elderly from 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov has signed a decree raising several social benefits from January 1, 2027, the presidential press service said.

The decree, "On Measures to Increase the Level of Social Protection for Certain Categories of Citizens of the Kyrgyz Republic", was signed on October 21.

The state benefit for children with disabilities will rise from 8,000 soms ($91.5) to 11,000 soms ($125.8) (by 37.5%). Benefits for older persons will increase by 50%, and disability pensions will also rise.

The benefit for children who have lost both parents will rise from 6,000 soms ($68.6) to 8,000 soms ($91.5) (by 33.3%), and for children who have lost a breadwinner from 3,000 soms ($34.3) to 5,000 soms ($57.2) (by 66.7%). Pensions for children who have lost a breadwinner will also increase.

The benefit for mothers awarded the title of "Mother Heroine" will rise from 3,000 soms ($34.3) to 5,000 soms ($57.2) (by 66.7%), and their pension supplement will increase fivefold, from 1,000 soms ($11.4) to 5,000 soms ($57.2).

Monthly cash compensation will also go up for World War II participants, veterans of the war in Afghanistan, Chernobyl cleanup participants, former underage concentration camp prisoners, survivors of the siege of Leningrad and other recipients.

The Labor Ministry said compensation for World War II participants will rise from 10,000 soms ($114.3) to 11,000 soms ($125.8) and for Afghanistan veterans from 8,000 soms ($91.5) to 9,000 soms ($102.9). The press service said some payments were raised in 2025 and others had not been revised since 2010.

Additional monthly benefits for people affected by, and families of those killed in, the events in Aksy district of Jalal-Abad region and in Batken and Osh regions will rise by an average of 20%.

The press service said the measures aim to strengthen social protection for people with disabilities, children who have lost parents or a breadwinner and other groups needing state support. The payments will be financed from the republican budget. The announcement did not give the total cost.

World.title: Caspian Sea Institute says science cuts risk in Turkmen oil, gas projects
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 22. Scientific research and environmental assessments must be taken into account when designing and implementing oil and gas projects in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea, as they help improve the reliability of technical solutions, reduce risks, and ensure the predictability of long-term investments, the director of the Caspian Sea Institute, Myrat Atajanov said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

Atajanov made the statement on Thursday while speaking at the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

“Scientific research and environmental assessments are not merely an additional procedure in the implementation of oil and gas projects, but rather the foundation for making technical, investment, and environmental decisions,” he emphasized.

According to Atajanov, comprehensive scientific support is necessary at all stages of project implementation, from geological exploration and design to field operation and decommissioning. This should include studying the geological structure of the subsurface, the condition of the seafloor, hydrometeorological conditions, and shoreline dynamics, as well as assessing the state of marine ecosystems.

He paid particular attention to forecasting the possible consequences of accidental hydrocarbon spills, developing measures to prevent such incidents and mitigate their consequences, as well as assessing the cumulative impact of oil and gas infrastructure on the marine environment.

Myrat Atajanov noted that the development of Caspian resources must comply with the provisions of the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea of August 12, 2018, which provides for the exploration and development of the sea’s resources and its subsoil, while also enshrining the principles of rational resource use and the conservation of the marine ecosystem.

“The development of hydrocarbon potential and the protection of the marine environment must be viewed as interrelated tasks,” he said.

Speaking about practical measures, the institute’s director emphasized the need to take into account various scenarios for changes in the Caspian Sea’s water level when planning oil and gas activities. According to him, changes in water depths and the configuration of the coastline could affect the operation of coastal production facilities, access channels, port infrastructure, offshore platforms, and subsea pipelines.

“Under these conditions, scientific assessments must include various sea-level change scenarios, an analysis of infrastructure vulnerability, and the development of adaptation measures,” Atajanov noted.

He also highlighted the importance of the Commission on the Shallowening of the Caspian Sea, which the leaders of the five Caspian states agreed to establish on October 9 at the First Caspian Environmental Summit in the Avaza National Tourist Zone.

According to Atajanov, the commission’s work should be based on objective scientific data and coordinated approaches among all five states.

“It is of fundamental importance to ensure regular monitoring, the comparability of research results, and the practical application of scientific findings when making economic decisions,” he concluded.

Meanwhile, the second day of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) has begun in Ashgabat. As part of the event, a session is being held on the topic “Investment and development opportunities in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea.” Discussions are focusing on investment opportunities for developing the Turkmen sector, prospects for offshore exploration and production of hydrocarbons, and the development of international partnerships.

The agenda also includes existing and new production-sharing agreements (PSAs), as well as modern seismic survey programs designed to help assess resource potential and prepare promising blocks for development.

World.title: Dragon Oil sees long-term PSAs key to Turkmenistan investment
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 22. Long-term production-sharing agreements (PSAs), predictable commercial terms, and a stable partnership with the state-owned Turkmennebit concern are key factors in attracting investment to Turkmenistan’s oil and gas sector, the Vice President of Dragon Oil in Turkmenistan Michel Khammo said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

Khammo made the remark on Thursday during a session of the “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) International Conference and Exhibition in Ashgabat.

According to him, Dragon Oil has been operating in Turkmenistan for 26 years, and the extension of the company’s production-sharing agreement through 2035 demonstrates confidence in the long-term prospects for cooperation. Khammo also noted the presence of other international energy companies in the country, including Eni, Petronas, and INA.

“It is extremely important for investors to have predictable commercial terms, clear provisions in production-sharing agreements, and mutual understanding between international oil and gas companies and the government of Turkmenistan, represented by the state-owned Turkmennebit,” he emphasized.

According to Michel Khammo, effective cooperation between investors and government partners helps speed up decision-making, expand operations, and increase investment volumes.

He cited infrastructure readiness as another key condition for attracting capital. Although Turkmenistan lacks access to the open ocean, its location between East and West, as well as existing export routes, create opportunities for supplying hydrocarbons to various markets.

Furthermore, Khammo highlighted Dragon Oil’s collaboration with Turkmennebit, describing it as a partnership that goes beyond the typical investor-operator relationship. According to him, for 26 years the parties have jointly overcome operational challenges, exchanged expertise, and implemented new technologies. He also noted the support provided by the Turkmen side in recruiting local specialists and international service companies, as well as in resolving logistical issues amid a complex geopolitical situation.

“Even given the global geopolitical situation this year and in previous years, with the support of Turkmennebit, we have managed to resolve many issues related to logistics and day-to-day operations,” Michel Khammo said.

In his view, predictable operating conditions, well-developed infrastructure, and strong partnerships are of fundamental importance to investors considering projects in Turkmenistan.

World.title: Petronas plans two new Turkmen Caspian projects, drilling from December
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 22. Malaysia’s Petronas Carigali (Turkmenistan) plans to implement two new field development projects in Offshore Block 1 in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea – one for natural gas and one for oil, the CEO of Petronas Carigali (Turkmenistan), Ismadi bin Ismail said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

He made the announcement at a panel discussion on Investment and development opportunities in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian sea as part of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

According to Ismail, the company also intends to begin drilling in Blocks 19 and 20 in December 2026. He noted that the remaining resource potential of Block 1 is estimated at more than 70 trillion cubic feet (about 2 trillion cubic meters) of gas and over 200 million barrels of oil and liquid hydrocarbons. To realize this potential, the company needs to continue developing new fields and expanding its marketing capabilities.

“We are currently working on at least two new field development projects: one focused on gas and the other on oil production,” he noted.

Ismadi bin Ismail reported that Petronas Carigali (Turkmenistan) has the capacity to produce more than 500 million standard cubic feet of gas and approximately 30,000 barrels of liquid hydrocarbons per day. The company intends to increase production from Block 1 in collaboration with its partners and the state-owned Turkmengaz.

He also emphasized the need to expand sales markets to fully commercialize the remaining resources. According to him, Petronas is working with its partners and Turkmengaz to identify additional opportunities to monetize gas and other hydrocarbons.

“In order to monetize the entire volume of 70 trillion cubic feet of gas and 200 million barrels of liquid hydrocarbons, we need new markets,” Ismadi bin Ismail stated.

Moreover, he noted that in June 2026, the company signed a production-sharing agreement for Blocks 19 and 20 and expects to begin drilling there in December 2026. In addition, Petronas has signed an agreement for 2D seismic surveys in the northern offshore blocks 11, 12, 13, and 14. According to Ismail, these projects open up opportunities for geological exploration, the involvement of service companies, and the development of Turkmenistan’s oil and gas industry.

Petronas has been operating in Turkmenistan since 1996. In May 2025, the company, XRG, Khazarnebit, and the state-owned Turkmennebit signed a new production-sharing agreement for Block 1, as well as a long-term gas sales agreement with Turkmengaz. According to Petronas, the company is the operator of the block with a 57% stake, while XRG holds 38% and Khazarnebit holds 5%.

The agenda also includes existing and new production-sharing agreements (PSAs), as well as modern seismic survey programs designed to help assess resource potential and prepare promising blocks for development.

World.title: Turkmenistan offers investors 30+ Caspian blocks, customs and tax perks
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 22. Turkmenistan is offering foreign investors more than 30 licensed blocks in its Caspian Sea sector, providing for various types of contracts, tax incentives, and simplified customs procedures for companies participating in oil and gas projects, the Deputy Chairman of the state-owned Turkmennebit State Concern, Batyr Jumayev said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

Jumayev made the statement at a panel discussion on Investment and development opportunities in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian sea as part of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) in Ashgabat.

According to Jumayev, cooperation with foreign companies in the offshore sector is carried out in accordance with Turkmenistan’s Law “On Hydrocarbon Resources,” which establishes legal guarantees for investors and the conditions for conducting oil operations.

“The Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea is divided into more than 30 license blocks. If interested in one or more blocks, any potential investor may submit an official application to the state-owned concern Turkmennebit,” he noted.

After reviewing the application and verifying that the investor meets the qualification requirements, the parties may proceed to direct, non-exclusive negotiations. Based on the results of these negotiations, they may enter into production-sharing agreements (PSAs), concession agreements based on royalty and tax terms, joint venture agreements, or risk-sharing service contracts. The law also permits a combination of these forms.

Moreover, Jumayev emphasized that the tax regime entails the payment of income tax and prescribed fees for the right to use natural resources. Investors are exempt from a number of other mandatory payments and fees, as well as from customs duties on the import and export of goods, materials, and equipment necessary for oil operations. These provisions also apply to subcontractors.

In addition, investors have the right to dispose of their share of extracted hydrocarbons, including refining their share of oil at Turkmen refineries without additional taxes, licenses, or permits.

Among Turkmenistan’s current international partners in the development of offshore resources, Jumayev named Dragon Oil, Petronas, and ADNOC, which operate under production-sharing agreements.

He specifically highlighted the production-sharing agreement for the “Block 19” and “Block 20” contract areas, signed in June 2026 between Turkmennebit, the Malaysian company Petronas Carigali (Turkmenistan) Sdn. Bhd., and the state-owned enterprise Khazarnebit. According to him, this agreement marks a new phase in offshore geological exploration and production.

Another area of focus is 2D seismic surveys in licensed blocks 11, 12, 13, and 14. A corresponding agreement has been signed between Turkmennebit and Petronas Carigali. This work is intended to expand geological information on promising areas and lay the groundwork for assessing their hydrocarbon potential.

“Strategic partnerships under production-sharing agreements are a key mechanism for attracting large-scale foreign capital and technology to develop Turkmenistan’s significant hydrocarbon resources in the Caspian Sea sector,” Jumayev stated.

He added that Turkmennebit is open to dialogue with international companies based on the principles of equality and mutual benefit.

Meanwhile, the second day of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) has begun in Ashgabat. As part of the event, a session is being held on the topic “Investment and development opportunities in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea.” Discussions are focusing on investment opportunities for developing the Turkmen sector, prospects for offshore exploration and production of hydrocarbons, and the development of international partnerships.

The agenda also includes existing and new production-sharing agreements (PSAs), as well as modern seismic survey programs designed to help assess resource potential and prepare promising blocks for development.

World.title: Two years after promised change, forced adoption survivors are still waiting
World.content:
Most of us have got secrets. Things we'd rather not share.

But for some communities in Australia, secrets are particularly toxic — a poison that's seeped through generations.

In this case, the people themselves have become the secret, contributing to a lifetime of pain and suffering.

It's something felt deeply by many people in the forced adoption community — thousands of mothers who, at their most vulnerable, were hidden away by their families because of the perceived "shame" of becoming pregnant outside wedlock.

Mother forced to give up baby at 16 says she was 'treated like a cow' In the 1970s, Louise Kirk's baby was forcibly removed. Fifty years later she is coming to terms with the trauma by connecting with other women like her.

Their babies whisked away at birth before they could hold them; children given false birth certificates and denied their true identities, with some not finding out the shattering truth until later in life.

Now decades removed, some of those living with the lifelong scars say they feel uncomfortable with a perceived "secrecy" surrounding the Western Australia's government's attempt to mend that pain.

Confidential conversations

Since June last year, a group of mothers whose children were removed from them, as well as people who were adopted out as babies, has been meeting behind closed doors to advise the government on how to apply the recommendations made from the Broken Bonds, Fractured Lives report.

To prevent their mothers catching sight of them, babies were often taken straight to the hospital crèche like this one photographed in 1954. (Supplied: National Archives of Australia)

The 2023 inquiry made 39 recommendations for reform, ranging from improving mental health supports to financial redress for both mothers and adoptees.

But the 10 "lived experience" members of this group, whose identities have been kept under wraps, have had to sign confidentiality agreements, pledging not to share anything discussed at the meetings.

Briefing notes are published online, but with little detail and often weeks after the meetings take place.

"We don't know what they're doing," said Helen Driesen, a mother who, like many, wasn't allowed to see her baby, never mind hold him, after giving birth in her late teens in 1968.

Helen Driesen (second from left) is frustrated by the lack of progress. (ABC News: Claire Moodie)

"You're getting secrecy and no answers," she said.

Minister defends progress

It's been exactly two years since the government tabled its response to the inquiry. It argues steady progress is being made to implement the recommendations.

But frustrated survivors concerned about the pace of reform note it has been 16 years since WA became the first state in Australia to formally apologise for the forced adoption scandal.

Mothers and adoptees gathered on Monday at a memorial in the Perth suburb of Victoria Park to mark the anniversary.

It's over two years since the inquiry report was handed down with 39 recommendations. (ABC News: Claire Moodie)

One of them, Kaye Wilkerson, 81, wasn't confident of seeing redress in her lifetime.

"I think they're waiting for us to die," she said.

Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski wasn't available for an interview but in a statement said the confidentiality arrangements around the working group "helped create a safe environment for those impacted by forced adoptions".

And, on redress, the statement said it was "providing further consideration to the issue" given its "significance and complexity".

When Audra got married, she had no idea her mother she never met was standing right behind her Marilyn Rulyancich never gave up hope of finding her daughter — and now she's telling her remarkable story of subterfuge, detective work and sheer determination.

"Redress is just one part of the raft of recommendations made," the statement read, while work was underway on further recommendations.

New birth certificates

Earlier this week, the minister pledged to introduce laws allowing "integrated birth certificates", which list both biological and adoptive parents.

Already available in other states, the certificates would give adopted people a legal record of their birth and adoption, 14 years after a Senate inquiry recommended their introduction nationwide.

Jessica Stojkovski is WA's minister for child protection. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Speaking in parliament, Ms Stojkovski said the bill represented a fundamental change to the way adopted people would be able to choose to legally identify themselves.

"Seeing their full heritage recognised on an official document is an important step towards healing," she said.

Whilst welcomed, the legislation is well overdue, according to Albany-based adoptee Jen McRae, who led the push for the WA inquiry.

Jen McRae says the legislation for Integrated Birth Certificates is just the start. (ABC News: Claire Moodie)

"It's part of an enormous program of legislative change that needs to happen here," she said.

" We're all waiting and watching and we're not going to drop the ball on this … we're going to keep pushing. "

But having read the proposed legislation, Ms McRae said there were key issues that needed to be addressed, including allowing adoptive parents, as well as the adopted people themselves, the right to apply for the certificates.

“No-one, other than ourselves, should have the right to apply for our personal documents from Births, Deaths and Marriages,” she said.

“As adults, we must be treated as such, afforded the same rights as any other citizen."

Call for redress timeline

Ryan Dee, an adoptee who runs a support group in Perth, had hoped to influence change as a member of the behind closed doors reference group.

But the 47-year-old resigned, frustrated and upset, after the group's fourth meeting in February.

Having signed a confidentiality agreement, he cannot discuss the reasons for his departure.

Ryan Dee says survivors need a timeline for the recommendations to be implemented. (ABC News: Claire Moodie)

But now, from the outside, he is advocating for a set time-frame for the rest of the recommendations to be implemented, in particular, redress.

He says redress could help pay for the face-to-face psychological counselling and medication many survivors depend on.

"I carry it with me every day, it's like a wound … emptiness," Mr Dee said.

" It's getting worse with age, as I understand what it's taken away from me. "

World.title: 'Tireless advocate' Pat Miller to be honoured with state funeral
World.content:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

The son of a deeply respected Arrernte elder who spent her life fighting racial discrimination in the Northern Territory says the offer of a state funeral for his mother is a fitting acknowledgement of her legacy.

Patricia Ann Miller AO was born in 1946 to Milton and Polly Liddle, and described her childhood growing up on Angas Downs Station, about 300 kilometres south-west of Alice Springs, as an idyllic one.

Pat Miller on the day she was sworn in as deputy to the administrator of the Northern Territory. (Supplied: Government House)

The recipient of many honours through her life, Dr Miller was named NAIDOC Aboriginal of the Year Award in 1995, and was the NT Australian of the Year in 2004.

In 2002 she became the first Indigenous deputy to the administrator of the Northern Territory.

Dr Miller's son, Allan Miller, said it had been overwhelming to see the "genuine outpouring of heartfelt well wishes" for his family following her death.

"She was always giving," he said.

"Whether it be just time, whether it be lifts to anywhere, whether it be just being available for a kind ear, some guidance.

"She was not selfish in that way, as people attest to … [she] never sought any reward from any of that."

An incredible journey

Dr Miller's ascent to the helm of one of the Territory's largest legal organisations is inspirational.

In 1978 she joined the Central Australian Aboriginal Legal Aid Service, now known as the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency, as a filing clerk and typist.

By 1982 she had become director, a position she held for more than 30 years.

Pat Miller met King Charles in 2018. (Supplied: Government House)

Mr Miller said his mother was always a "very smart woman".

"She did a community college course through a person she worked with at the old Alice Springs Airport cafe, and they pushed her to study," he said.

"She ended up [studying], but she went back to work. Someone said to my grandpa, 'What's your daughter doing selling pies and pasties in the cafe, why isn't she working in one of these organisations?'

"So that's how it started, as a filing clerk, typist, [before she] ended up [spending] 35 years as director."

Mr Miller said his mother thrived as deputy to the administrator and was always generous with her time and energy.

"She loved meeting new people at those events … she was always the last to leave as well," he said.

"Whether it be 10 minutes more or someone catch her as she's walking out the gate, or out the door, and she'd spend 10 minutes because I just wanted to ask her some questions or meet her."

Loading...

Mr Miller said his father was his mother's "soulmate" and supported her completely. He accompanied her to many events where they rubbed shoulders with dignitaries and royals and was always able to hold his own.

"[Dad] would jovially say to his friends, 'Oh, Pat's got another function' … then he'd come back and tell us, 'Oh, I had a dinner with the King and Queen of Sweden at Uluru,'" Mr Miller said, a smile in his voice.

State funeral for woman with 'profound' legacy

Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said Dr Miller was an "extraordinary Territorian" who deserved the recognition of a state funeral.

"[Her] contribution to our community has been profound and enduring," Ms Finocchiaro said.

"Pat was a trailblazer who spent decades fighting for Aboriginal Territorians, championing access to justice and making sure people who too often went unheard had a voice."

David Miller met many dignitaries when he accompanied his wife to functions. (Supplied: Miller family)

NT Administrator David Connolly said he was "deeply saddened" by Dr Miller's death.

"A proud Arrernte woman and remarkable Territorian, Mrs Miller made history as the first Indigenous woman appointed deputy of the administrator and served the people of Central Australia with great compassion and integrity," he said.

"Her contribution to the Northern Territory extended far beyond her official duties, with a lifetime dedicated to her community and to advancing social justice, education, health and the wellbeing of others."

World.title: Schutt banned for two matches after prescription medication failure
World.content:
Australian women's fast bowler Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for failing to meet guidelines on the use of prescription medication.

Cricket Australia confirmed Schutt's suspension in a release on Thursday afternoon.

"The breach was a failure to adhere to requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication," Cricket Australia said.



"This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes."



The two-match ban applies to all international and domestic cricket.

Schutt starred in the recent three-match ODI series against Bangladesh. She had series figures of 10-71.

She has not played in a three-match T20 international series against New Zealand, which wraps up tonight at North Sydney.

Schutt released a statement acknowledging the breach and accepting the penalty.

"I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," Schutt said in her statement.

"I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received.

"While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on, and I should have adhered to these guidelines."



Cricket Australia said it would continue to provide "appropriate support" to Schutt and to reinforce standards and responsibilities expected of all involved in the game.

World.title: Colombian narcotics police 'have no record' of AFP anti-drugs taskforce
World.content:
Two police departments on the frontline of Colombia's fight against cartels say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce based in the South American nation.

In May, Commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments".

Colombia drugs taskforce concerns Questions about the Australian Federal Police's new anti-drugs taskforce in Colombia have sparked concerns it could aid the US's strikes against trafficking boats.

The team would include AFP officers in the capital Bogotá, working with Colombian, US, INTERPOL and Mexican authorities to curb the flow of drugs through the Pacific to Australia, the commissioner said.

A joint investigation by the ABC and the Colombian newspaper El Tiempo can reveal the anti-narcotics department of Colombia's National Police (PNC) has no recorded data that shows subscribed "protocols, agreements, or procedures" relating to the IJIT.

In a response to a freedom of information request filed by El Tiempo and shared with the ABC, the department said drug-related intelligence had not been shared with the AFP and no "operational activities" such as illicit substance seizures or arrests had been made in cooperation with Australian police as part of the IJIT.

The department also said there was currently only a "letter of intent" outlining a "framework for cooperation and exchange of information", which the ABC understands was signed jointly by PNC Major General Jesús Alejandro Barrera Peña and the AFP in August.

"Jungle Command" members of the Colombian National Police's anti-narcotics department. (Supplied: Instagram/@antinarcoticosponal)

"The instrument does not identify the so-called 'IJIT', nor does it establish specific functions, responsibilities or procedures for this department in relation to said mechanism," the department said.

The letter made no connection between the IJIT and joint drug seizures, destruction of narcotics production infrastructure, disruption of criminal groups or the identification of international trafficking routes, the department said.

The ABC understands the IJIT agreement was made with — and expected to be overseen by — the PNC's Office of International Relations and Cooperation (ORECI) and not the anti-narcotics department.

The AFP's joint investigations team is expected to work with Colombian, US, New Zealand, INTERPOL and Mexican police authorities. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

ORECI coordinates Colombia's international policing efforts by connecting other PNC departments to global counterparts, such as the AFP.

The department focuses on strategic decision-making and intelligence and sits above the anti-narcotics and criminal investigations agencies, which oversee frontline drug and domestic crime policing operations.

An AFP spokesperson told the ABC the IJIT was not yet operational, but an "annex" agreement was made with the PNC in August in addition to the letter of intent that would allow the taskforce to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".

The AFP did not specify when the IJIT would become operational.

In a separate response shared with the ABC, the PNC's criminal investigations department said it had no data that was able to determine whether the AFP was involved, supported, funded or shared intelligence in 174 drug trafficking investigations conducted between January 1, 2025 and October 6 this year.

The department said those figures were collated based on aggregate numbers of cases and investigations outcomes that did not list specific agencies involved.

But the department also said it had no knowledge of Colombian anti-narcotics intelligence being used to "identify, locate, track, monitor or intercept" suspected drug trafficking vessels in the Pacific Ocean or Caribbean Sea as part of the IJIT.

A Colombian police officer with sacks of fake charcoal, often created as a disguise to hide amounts of cocaine, seized in the city of Barranquilla. (Reuters: Luisa Gonzalez)

The revelations follow ABC questions posed to the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a separate Freedom of Information request.

In response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer the questions.

The AFP declined to release them, citing national security and international relations concerns, and said at the time that the IJIT was "still in the negotiation phase".

It also said publishing the information would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia, or could divulge confidential details regarding how AFP officers operate.

The AFP says 17 tonnes of illicit drugs has been seized by "local and international" police in the Pacific since January this year. (AFP)

In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.

That figure is expected to rise to $1.4 million next year, before dropping to $1.01 million and $1.03 million in the following two years.

But the budget does not detail how much is set aside specifically for the IJIT.

Commissioner Barrett said 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, have been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.

The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.

The PNC this month announced an Australian-Iranian national, Arash Ebrahimi Far, was detained in Colombia as a subject of an INTERPOL Red Notice for alleged drug trafficking and money laundering, which was not believed to be related to the IJIT.

World.title: KPMG ban on government work extended after 'serious ethical failings'
World.content:
The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February, following a review that found "serious ethical failings" by its leadership and some of its senior partners.

Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it.

In response to Mr Watt's review, which was handed down today, the department said it has agreed with the firm to a further extension to the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027.

During this period, KPMG will provide the department with an implementation plan and the first of its quarterly progress implementation reports.

The department also needs to ensure that "KPMG is engaging constructively with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) and the Tax Practitioners Board (TPB) reviews, and is committed to addressing any recommendations that have been made by those organisations".

Dr Watt said in his review the way the accounting firm had handled the whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings by some senior members of KPMG" and "significant cultural concerns within KPMG".

'Trust needs to be restored'

Dr Watt noted the review was focused on the leadership and culture of the firm "that had been warned on previous occasions about weaknesses in ethical culture, speak-up confidence and accountability, but did not deal with them with the rigour and urgency required".

Firms raise doubts about KPMG's integrity In the wake of the KPMG audit leak scandal, executives from Macquarie, Westpac, Optus and Dexus cast doubt on their faith in the auditor.

He said since March, KPMG has undergone significant change, with a new chair and a new CEO, and a number of senior personnel having left the firm.

Dr Watt said the firm had also commissioned several reviews to understand the root causes of the events.

"Trust, however, is not restored through assurances alone," Dr Watt said.

"As was often observed during review interviews, trust takes time to build, and while transparency builds trust, lack of transparency damages it."

Dr Watt said his report should not be read as a judgement on every member of KPMG.

"Virtually all of KPMG's staff had no involvement in the events that occurred," he said.

KPMG CEO John Sams and its chairman Michael Ebeid said they accepted the findings and recommendations of Mr Watt's review.

John Sams says the firm is working to revamp its internal culture. (Supplied)

"The report lays bare our failings and highlights the hard work that we must do to address them," they said in a statement.

The firm had appointed Kerry Schott to provide independent oversight and said "while we are making important progress, we know that changing culture takes longer than changing individual roles, structures or controls".

"Confidence in KPMG's suitability for Commonwealth work must be earned through evidence of effective, lasting change," the statement said.

Call to overhaul code governing bids

Dr Watt also recommended the department of finance strengthen the Commonwealth's supplier code of conduct, including tougher sanctions for suppliers breaching their obligations and more reporting pathways for potential unethical behaviour.

Whistleblowers need better protection Without whistleblowers, Australians would be kept in the dark about major corporate scandals, but evidence suggests the experience of raising alarm bells can destroy their lives.

Several states and territories have also banned KPMG from taking on public sector work pending the outcome of Dr Watt's review, or their own reviews.

They are working through their responses to the findings.

Greens finance and public service spokesperson Senator Barbara Pocock said a small extension of the freeze on KPMG contracts was not dealing with the issue.

"At a time when some of Australia's biggest corporate players like Lendlease, Macquarie Group and ANZ have sacked KPMG as auditors, why would the government consider letting them back in the fold?" she asked rhetorically.

"It should instead be setting the standard on probity amongst its contractors.

" If any ordinary worker or company was caught using confidential information for gain, cheating on an exam or mistreating a whistleblower, you'd be out on your ear, dismissed in a flash. "

Barbara Pocock says KPMG should not win new government work. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Senator Pocock said the federal inquiry into the KPMG audit leaks scandal had heard revelations of 153 reports of misconduct to regulator ASIC in the past three years in the Big Four firms, and among them 48 potential whistleblowers making complaints.

"The sheer volume is alarming and confirms there are serious problems within the Big Four in relation to misconduct, some of which have already surfaced," Senator Pocock said.

World.title: Accused 'dead set' he was not driving in crash that killed four
World.content:
A man accused of being behind the wheel of a ute that collided head-on with a van, killing four people in Western New South Wales, has told a court he is "dead set" he was not driving at the time.

Jack Bowd, 25, has pleaded not guilty to four counts of dangerous driving occasioning death over the crash on the Newell Highway, south of Dubbo near Tomingley in September 2024.

His friends Joey Urban, 19, and Lochlann Jacobs, 18, died in the crash, along with Parkes couple Sue and Graham Tait, both 57.

Taking the stand in his own defence today, Mr Bowd described his first memories after the crash.

"I remember just opening my eyes, seeing the steering wheel and then I popped the door open, went on the ground head first, and then crawled out of the side of my car," he told the court.

" I realised I had a broken leg at that point. "

Sue and Graham Tait died in a car crash at Tomingley on June 27, 2024. (Supplied: Amii Marchant)

Mr Bowd is facing a judge-alone trial in the Dubbo District Court, where the central issue is who was behind the wheel of his Toyota Hilux at the time of the crash.

Prosecutors allege Mr Bowd was driving, while the defence maintains Mr Jacobs had taken over driving before the crash.

The Crown alleges the ute was travelling more than 130 kilometres an hour and attempting to overtake a B-double truck on a bend when it collided head-on with the couple's van.

Four people died in the collision 30 kilometres south-west of Dubbo. (ABC)

Accused recounts moments before crash

Mr Bowd told the court the three friends had been pig hunting in Goobang National Park, between Parkes and Baldry, when his dog Luna was struck by his ute.

He said they were travelling to Dubbo to seek veterinary treatment when the dog's condition deteriorated near Tomingley, prompting him to pull over.

Mr Bowd told the court Mr Jacobs offered to take over driving so he could sit in the back with the injured animal.

"Lochie said, 'If she's going to die I'd rather her die with you' … so he got in the driver's seat, and I sat in the back, and then we left," he told the court.

Mr Bowd said he remembered seeing headlights moments before the crash, but could not recall what happened next.

He also maintained he told police the truth when questioned at the crash scene and during a subsequent interview with police.

Earlier in the trial, the court was shown Snapchat footage allegedly depicting Mr Bowd driving the ute while holding a can of alcohol, with the speedometer reading 160km/h.

The footage showed Mr Jacobs sitting in the middle of the back seat with the injured dog, describing it in one video as "precious cargo back here".

Another video captioned by Mr Urban read "coming in hot to the vet".

Joey Urban and Lochie Jacobs both died during a two-car crash on the Newell Highway on September 27. (Supplied)

Questions over memory

Under cross-examination, Crown prosecutor Michelle Swift questioned Mr Bowd about gaps in his memory.

"Some things I don't remember, some things I do," he told the court.

Mr Bowd conceded he could not remember seeing Mr Jacobs get into the driver's seat, but insisted his friend took over driving after they stopped near Tomingley.

"I definitely didn't get back in the driver's seat," he said.

"I'm dead set about that."

When Ms Swift suggested his memory could be fractured because of how much he had to drink, and that he had returned to the driver's seat, Mr Bowd rejected that proposition.

"I don't think it's fractured enough that I'm going to forget that. I know that I was not driving," he said.

Mr Bowd also could not remember when he learned his two friends had died, but said he knew of their deaths by the time he spoke to his mother from hospital.

"I remember telling her that I wish I kept driving, but I don't remember much else," he said.

He said he could not remember speaking to a passing motorist who stopped to help after the crash, or telling her he was "being a dickhead" when she asked him what happened.

"That's not the way I talk … I wouldn't say dickhead," Mr Bowd told the court.

"Maybe I've said it in the past, but it's not something I'd say, no."

Ms Swift suggested he began falsely denying he was driving after the witness told him his friends appeared to be dead.

"No, that is not true. I was not driving the car," he replied.

Four people were killed in the crash on the Newell Highway in September 2024. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

Snapchat witness gives evidence

A defence witness told the court he received a photo from Mr Bowd's Snapchat account on that night, taken from the back seat of a ute.

The witness said the image showed a dog resting on someone's lap with the caption, "no fishing tomorrow, big vet bills".

He told the court he believed Mr Bowd was sitting in the back because the message came from his account.

However, he conceded under cross-examination that no faces were visible and he could not identify the person sitting with the dog.

Judge Michael Smith is expected to deliver his judgment in December.

World.title: 'She became younger': Gascoigne's success at 57
World.content:
Despite her reputation today as one of Australia's most influential artists, Rosalie Gascoigne did not start exhibiting her work until she was 57.

Gascoigne, who created much of her work in Canberra and died in 1999, "hit the art world at just the right time," according to curator Deborah Hart.

"Art was starting to take different forms — there was installation art, minimalism, conceptual art," Dr Hart said.

Gascoigne held her first solo exhibition in 1976 and in 1978 was invited to have a survey exhibition at the National Gallery of Victoria.

Everyday objects are transformed to become pieces on display as part of the Rosalie Gascoigne exhibition. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

But Canberra remained the bedrock of much of her work, with many of her pieces made from materials gathered from dumps and brought back to the family home to be reshaped.

"I'm really hoping that this exhibition might generate some excitement from outside of Australia, but I wonder what they'd make of the names of the local dumps of Gundaroo, Bungendore and Captain's Flat," Dr Hart said.

'A wonderful gift'

Hester Gascoigne said the exhibition at the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra was made up of pieces she could remember her mother creating over the decades.

Gascoigne, who died in 1999, drew inspiration from the Canberra region. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"It's quite extraordinary to see it all laid out ... to be reacquainted with works which we saw being made but haven't seen for decades, and to see the progression," Ms Gascoigne said.

Ms Gascoigne said her mother "made a game" of creating art when she was growing up, as a way of engaging children in nature.

"There was always a family competition of finding the best stone when we went for picnics down the river, and the nicest line of branch and all of that," she said.

"But the trips foraging to dumps were, in many respects, very serious because it was her working material."

The exhibition is on display at the National Gallery of Australia from October 24 to February 14. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The family home was built by Ms Gascoigne's parents with the work of her mother in mind, "so there were spaces to work and place to look at things".

"The hope was we could get access to the dining room table," she said.

" I could never understand how she could create huge things like this or like that from a very crowded, confined space. "

Rosalie Gascoigne, photographed by Greg Weight. (Supplied: Art Gallery of NSW)

Gascoigne 'defined art history'

Gascoigne's husband, Ben Gascoigne, was an astronomer, and for a time the family lived at Mount Stromlo Observatory in Canberra, where the artist did not initially have a car.

"And so she's walking across the landscape, she's getting to know this place. It really is the wellspring, the foundation of her art," Dr Hart said.

The Gascoigne exhibition includes textured pieces, inspired by nature. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Gallery director Nick Mitzevich said Gascoigne's works had been a part of the collection for decades.

"The National Gallery, with the great insight of the inaugural gallery director James Mollison, made our first acquisition of Rosalie Gascoigne in 1976," he said.

He said Gascoigne was an artist who "both defined art history and encouraged us to look at art in a different way".

Rosalie Gascoigne is known for using found materials in her work. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Dr Hart said becoming a part of the NGA had been a moment of "sheer excitement" for Gascoigne.

"Suddenly she wasn't the square peg in the round hole that she felt when she brought pieces of driftwood and stones back to the mantelpiece of the house," she said.

Rosalie Gascoigne was born in 1917 and was inspired by the Canberra region. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Dr Hart quoted some of what Gascoigne had to say about her remarkable career at the exhibition's launch on Thursday:

"I think it's a basic human fear to be boxed in, and when you're an artist, you've got an expanding universe. Anything can happen."

Gascoigne continued working late into her life, retaining a youthfulness that amazed those who knew her.

"She became younger as she got older, because she grew into her true self," Dr Hart said.

The exhibition will run at the National Gallery of Australia from October 24 to February 14.

World.title: SA mother spared jail for 6yo daughter's death in car crash
World.content:
A mother who got lost on the way to church before failing to give way at an intersection – causing a crash which killed her own child – will not be sent to prison, a court has heard.

Zubeda Habonimana, 43, was driving a white van which struck a ute at the intersection of King and Penfield roads, at Virginia in Adelaide's northern suburbs, on October 5 last year.

Her six-year-old daughter Benita Ntihebuwayo suffered catastrophic injuries and died five days after the crash, while two of her other children and the driver of the ute were injured.

Father tells court children need their mother

In victim impact statements read in South Australia's District Court today, Benita's father Jason Birgirmana described the lasting impact of the loss of his daughter, but asked the court not to send his former partner to jail.

"Losing our baby was an extremely painful experience for all of us and the impact of this tragedy continues to affect our lives," he said.

Mr Birgirmana said their other children "continue to need their mother's love, care, guidance and support", particularly while coping with the loss of their sibling.

"I am capable of looking after my children, and I am a good father, but I also understand the important role and connection my children have with their mother, which can look different to what I can provide my children," he said.

The intersection at the corner of King and Penfield roads where the crash occurred. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The driver of the ute, Jason Pateman, told the court his life had "been in complete turmoil" since the crash, and that he continued to grapple with the life-changing impacts of a severe concussion.

He had been driving to Bunnings with his four-year-old daughter when they were struck.

"The sound of my daughter screaming in the car will haunt me every single day," he said.

He said while his daughter's injuries were not physical, the impact on her wellbeing had been "huge".

He said he could not forgive Habonimana, but did not wish her any harm.

"I spent weeks crying over the loss of your child. I know, it wasn't my fault, we were simply in the wrong place at the wrong time, but as a parent, it destroyed me emotionally," he said.

"I don’t want you in prison as I don't want your family to suffer further, but I do believe you should never be allowed to operate a motor vehicle again.

"The day your child passed away, you gave yourself a life sentence. No further punishment would be comparable."

His wife Tamika Pateman also detailed the lasting impacts on their daughter form being exposed to a "violent and chaotic scene".

"Things that used to be completely ordinary are now frightening to her," she said.

Habonimana previously pleaded guilty to one count of causing death and three counts of causing harm by dangerous driving.

Mother became lost on way to church

The mother of seven's defence counsel Andrew Ey said the punishment his client had suffered was "immeasurable".

"She has agonised over this, but she can't explain her gross inattention," he said.

"They missed their normal turn off, such that she was attempting to get back to her normal route to get back to the church and it's in that context that she came to be on this road – disoriented and somewhat lost," he said.

He said his client, who had since moved to Murray Bridge, had penned a letter of apology but it was not read aloud.

Ms Habonimana will be sentenced in the South Australian District Court in November. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Ey described the intersection as "notoriously dangerous" and noted a 53-year-old man had died in an unrelated crash at the same intersection earlier this month.

Prosecutor Marie Rocca said the force of impact involved in the crash was evident from the "crumpled bonnet of the ute" and the "collapsed passenger side doors" of Habonimana’s van.

She said a term of imprisonment was the only appropriate penalty for the offending, but was not opposed to it being suspended.

At the conclusion of the hearing, Judge Joana Fuller spoke directly to Habonimana, and said she would not be sending her to prison when she returns to court to be sentenced next month.

"I can tell you now that I will not be imposing a sentence that requires you to go to jail," she said.

"I don’t know what the sentence is that I will impose but I will not be separating you from your children and making you go to jail."

World.title: Seven reveals its 2027 line-up, including new hosts for I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Seven reveals its 2027 line-up, including new hosts for I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! Karl Quinn October 22, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singer Ricki-Lee Coulter and comedian Jim Jefferies have been announced as the hosts of Seven’s take on the reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! When Seven snaffled the show from Ten earlier this year, it was widely assumed it would reinstate the show’s former co-host Dr Chris Brown, who left the show in 2023 and joined Seven, and was replaced by Robert Irwin. The network has high hopes for its journey to the jungle, even if the show (developed in Britain and first aired there in 2002) has been on-air in this country since 2015. Ricki-Lee Coulter and Jim Jefferies have been unveiled as the hosts of the reborn I’m a Celebrity... Seven “Everyone always wants to talk about new, and I get it,” said Seven’s chief content officer, Brook Hall. “You can have a really reliable car that you love, but there’s something exciting about getting a new one, whether it’s better or not. Same with TV shows. [But] any new show in television inherently carries greater risk than a proven form.



“Why I love I’m A Celeb is it’s new for us, we can do something different, but it’s a proven performer. We’re going to have a different twist on it.” Related Article Australian TV Crime, comedy, an Alan Jones doco and the return of Fisk: What’s coming to the ABC in 2027 The format is “built to be talked about” said Hall. With Jefferies – who has proven a winner for the network as host of the game show The 1% Club – it has a fast-talking funnyman likely to generate plenty of headlines. And in Coulter, who has been a fixture on Australian television screens since first emerging as a contestant on the second season of Australian Idol in 2004, he’ll have a foil adept at smoothing over any rough edges. “They are two of our biggest stars, and very different types of stars, and putting them together I think already looks really different, but it’s still got the comedy and the warmth at the front there,” said Hall, who promises Seven’s version of the show – which will begin production early next year – will be “dialling up the real jungle as much as possible”. Also new to hosting an established format is Nashville-based Australian country music star Morgan Evans, who will join the Australian Idol judging panel alongside Marcia Hines and Amy Shark.



“He’s a Newcastle kid, he’s come through the system himself, and he’s genuinely interested in the process of finding Australian talent,” said Hall. “He was really passionate about it.” Australian country music star Morgan Evans joins Australian Idol. Seven Hall will also need to fill the Idol chair formerly occupied by Kyle Sandilands, whose career trajectory is looking very different thanks to the massive falling out with ARN, owner of KIIS FM, which was his principal employer until March. Seven and rival broadcaster SCA (Southern Cross Austereo) merged in January, so the option to stick it to the old rival might have been tempting. The economics of doing so, however, given the boycotts of advertisers associated with Sandilands-aligned content, might have been less so. “On radio, he was polarising, but on Australian Idol he was a different character, and I thought he was really good for the show,” said Hall. “But both parties decided, well, is this the time to freshen it up? We do that with a lot of shows, changing judges and panels.”



The merger of Seven and SCA has been a boon for both parties, said Matthew O’Reilly, head of broadcast content at the audio arm. “The cross-promotion of us running promos and commercials for the TV shows, and them doing the same to us, means their ratings are flying and our ratings are up considerably year-on-year, so I would say there’s been a good benefit for both parties,” O’Reilly said. Related Article Australian TV Today show hosts vow to restore trust as Nine reveals new MAFS expert and The Block spin-off One place that will play out is in the coverage of the Melbourne Cup next week. While Seven has the broadcast rights to most of the Spring Racing Carnival, the biggest horse-racing event of the year is on Nine (owner of this masthead). But Seven’s veteran sportscaster Bruce McAvaney will call the race as usual – only this time on Triple M for what O’Reilly called “a first-time experiment”. Hall sees plenty of cross-promotional opportunities, too, and thinks Australian Idol is the place where they will most clearly play out (Seven has not announced a return for The Voice, though that is still under active discussion). “It’s a music show so you’ll probably see things like Hit week, Triple M week,” he said. “We weren’t part of a merged company last year, so there are a few different things we can play with and I’m really excited about that.”



Chris Brown and Matt Preston on Once in a Lifetime. Seven On the drama front, Seven’s only offering is Home and Away, which remains the country’s most-watched drama with an average 1.1 million viewers per episode – about two-thirds of them watching at the time it’s broadcast. That’s an extraordinary result in this era of on-demand drama watching, and one that Hall said has caught the attention of industry colleagues overseas. “Probably because of the way it’s written, with heightened storylines all the time, people are consuming it like it’s an event,” he said. Related Article Streaming Colin From Accounts is ending. Here’s what Binge is banking on for their next hit The network is doing its best to turn the weekday staple of the game show into something like an event, too, with two new short-run series: the Matt Shirvington-fronted Stacks of Cash, which attempts to merge the frenetic excitement of Tetris with the frenzied pursuit of a pile of money, and Caught in the Middle, a knowledge-based contest hosted by Shane Jacobson. Each will run for six episodes, with Jim Jefferies’ The 1% Club returning for eight.



Though he won’t be going back into the South African jungle, and there’s no return for his makeover show My Reno Rules, Chris Brown will be back on air with Once In a Lifetime, a show in which he takes celebrities on journeys into nature around the world. “That’s his format, we know he’s passionate about nature, and he’s going to different countries,” said Hall of the show which was originally announced at Seven’s 2025 upfront but is now scheduled to air around Easter next year. “You get a bit of travel, you get a bit of nature, he’s telling his story, but he’s taking someone with him as well. So you get to see different parts there.” Returning shows to Seven in 2027 include MKR, with Manu Feildel and Colin Fassnidge hosting, The Chase, Glenn and Mick’s Celebrity Intervention and Oops I Bought a Pub. A bistro-brasserie in Parisian style, Lucette is cleverly tooled to suit the many speeds and needs of the Highlands. Viennoiserie and omelettes in the morning, baguettes at lunch, steak frites for dejeuner and dîner. Roll in for breakfast, pop in for lunch, cruise in for afternoon aperitifs (who else serves Suze in town, anyway?), or settle in for date night.

In any case, sitting here is a pleasure, either inside behind cafe curtains, or slung on mustard banquettes in the breezy terrace. But the real kicker is on the plate, where chef Guillaume Dubois (ex-Monopole) brings fine-dining nous to classics.

The peppercorn sauce with wagyu steak? Infused with shio kombu. Chicken-liver parfait? Topped with rosé jelly. Tartare has brown-butter depth, chocolate mousse has praline crunch. And then service is just the right amount of Parisian brusque to be charming. Lucette? It might just be the little light the Highlands has been waiting for.

World.title: Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants
World.content:
PoliticsFederalNACC Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants Nick Newling October 22, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
