Labor’s invite-only election grant program has “piqued” the interest of the acting head of Australia’s corruption watchdog, as departmental staff were grilled over the funding promises one legal expert says amounts to “grey corruption”. As a Senate inquiry investigates the program, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been forced to defend a “dirt file” his office disseminated about independent MP Helen Haines several weeks ago, saying it was not designed to be critical of the politician, but rather showed that “people of integrity stand up for their electorate”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spent the morning defending his office’s dissemination of a “dirt file”. Justin McManus The victim of a violent car attack on Monday, Haines has had both legs amputated and remains in a critical condition. The regional Victorian MP was a vocal critic of Labor’s use of the grant program and campaigned to establish the National Anti-Corruption Commission to investigate federal and Commonwealth agencies, programs, employees and MPs. Addressing senators on Thursday, acting NACC commissioner Kylie Kilgour said it was “impossible” to express an opinion at this time over whether corrupt conduct had occurred in the grant program, but a number of aspects had “piqued” her interest, including alterations regarding its constitutionality.



“We would not [make a determination] unless we conducted a thorough, proper investigation under the NACC Act,” Kilgour told the inquiry. Related Article Government grants ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’ Haines was critical of the Albanese government’s $560.9 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program, in which nearly three-quarters of grants were allocated to notionally Labor-held or competitive seats, according to analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity. The Marrickville Golf Club, in Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler became the centre of debate over the grant program, as it had already received five federal grants totalling almost $58,000 before Albanese promised it a $6 million grant through the program during the 2025 election campaign. Kilgour said she had yet to hear evidence that would suggest the program should fall under the jurisdiction of the NACC and, until such point, would defer to a potential investigation by the Australian National Audit Office.



She became emotional when reading the commission’s opening statement as she shared her message of support for Haines, saying the MP was “instrumental” in the establishment of the NACC. “We are deeply appalled by what has transpired, and I sent a message conveying that to her office,” Kilgour said. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Following the last election, guidelines for the grants program were republished on October 2, 2025, but they prompted by concerns that the original design released a month earlier was constitutionally invalid. The Commonwealth does not have the power to directly fund local sporting and community facilities. The scheme was subsequently changed so grants could flow through state or local governments under section 96 of the Constitution.



In a submission to the inquiry, constitutional expert Anne Twomey said politically directed grants did not necessarily deliver electoral rewards. “No, this is not about ‘being a good local member’,” she wrote. “It is about indulging in grey corruption and the misuse of public money at the public’s expense.” The inquiry will continue, with dozens of senators’ questions to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet deferred. Questions over which ministers allocated grant funding, the specifics of funding to the Marrickville Golf Club, and the administration of the ministerial code of conduct regarding conflicts of interest were taken “on notice”. Following the attack on Haines, some media outlets took the rare action of discussing and publishing a background file distributed by the prime minister’s media office regarding funding requests by Haines’ office.



Sent to journalists during public debate over the grant program, the file encourages questioning of Haines over whether “$1.8 billion worth of funding for projects she’s selected” represented value for money. Related Article Haines attack Who is Phil Haines, the soulmate who convinced Helen to run for politics? The five-page file was sent to federal politics journalists in September, suggesting questions about the due diligence Haines had performed making project funding requests, and the interests she had in organisations for whom she was petitioning. Asked to respond to the claims at the time, Haines said “the issue isn’t whether MPs advocate for their communities. Of course, we do. What I’m asking for is that all communities get a fair go.” Political parties across the spectrum regularly provide “dirt files” of damaging information collected about their political opponents to journalists. The sheets are typically provided on a “background” basis, with journalists able to test the claims but not revealing the original source.



Asked on News24 on Wednesday whether he was aware or had ordered the release of the file, Albanese said: “Helen Haines is a good local member. She put forward applications like other members do for grants, and that’s what good local members do. And Helen Haines is a very strong advocate for her community”. Facing further questioning on Thursday morning, Albanese told ABC Sydney radio the document was “a list of funding asks … just showing that people of integrity stand up for their electorate. No personal criticism of Helen”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Crown admits deportation of Sydney underworld figure was illegal
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Crown admits deportation of Sydney underworld figure was illegal Riley Walter Updated October 22, 2026 — 4:46pm ,first published 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Underworld figure Masood Zakaria’s deportation from Turkey was illegal, prosecutors have conceded, as the alleged kingpin pushes to have murder charges against him thrown out over allegations the Australian Federal Police facilitated his “kidnapping” and return to Sydney. The NSW Supreme Court heard on Thursday morning that the 31-year-old’s forced removal in late 2023 was not permitted under Turkish law because of his pending appeal against the country’s decision to deport him. He was arrested at a seaside villa earlier that year. Masood Zakaria was brought back from Turkey in December 2023. Wolter Peeters The concession looms as a significant factor in Zakaria’s unprecedented legal challenge to have a raft of serious charges, including murder, dismissed. Zakaria’s legal team is seeking a permanent stay of proceedings against him after alleging AFP officers facilitated his illegal deportation from Turkey in a recovery operation akin to a kidnapping that constituted an abuse of process. The timing of his deportation is a major focus of the legal challenge.



If their application is successful, the charges against Zakaria, including for the murders of father and son Toufik Hamze, 64, and Salim Hamze, 18, and a conspiracy to murder gangland rival Ibrahem Hamze at the height of an underworld feud in 2021, will not be prosecuted. Related Article Organised crime He’s accused of murdering a father and son. The police may have jeopardised the case Trials for those offences were last year vacated after Zakaria’s lawyers levelled the allegations at the AFP. The AFP maintains its actions were lawful. The legal saga has cast doubt on the prosecutions of several other individuals wanted by Australian authorities and returned to the country in similar circumstances. The individuals, who cannot legally be identified, were among the highest value targets for law enforcement agencies at the time of their deportations. Prosecutors on Thursday flagged that an expert in Turkish law would be called to give evidence on the legality of Zakaria’s deportation. He is being held in Goulburn Supermax, Australia’s highest security prison.



Zakaria’s application is expected to run for two weeks and hear evidence from some of the country’s most senior organised crime investigators. Zakaria – an alleged high-ranking member of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family when he fled Australia in 2021 – was returned in December 2023 onboard a chartered Airbus A319 his lawyers claim cost the AFP more than $1 million. A team of six ex-military contractors working for Hart International, a multinational security and risk management firm, escorted him back to Australia. Skytraders, an aviation company contracted by the AFP to provide the plane with which Zakaria was deported, on Thursday lost a bid for its employees to be excused from giving evidence in court. The court heard that evidence from the employees involved could incriminate them and expose them to possible criminal charges in Turkey, including deprivation of liberty, if Zakaria’s deportation and detainment are found to be unlawful. Zakaria is an alleged high-ranking member of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family. NSW Police



Opposing the application, Zakaria’s barrister, Julia Roy, SC, said there was no evidence to suggest the employees risked facing criminal proceedings or were under investigation in Turkey. Daniel Colborne, one of the pilots who flew Zakaria back to Australia, told the court that heavily armed Turkish officials kept the 31-year-old and the Hart International team onboard the plane for several days after it was grounded when it struck a flock of birds. Heavily armed officers escorted Zakaria onto a replacement plane, Colborne said. Related Article Crime Sydney underworld kingpin ‘blacklisted’ before alleged kidnapping, court told Hart International Australia’s chief executive previously told the court the company’s personnel did not restrain passengers, before being shown images appearing to show Zakaria wearing plastic restraints around his wrists. Colborne said only the captain of a flight has authority to restrain a passenger. The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard the AFP encouraged Turkish authorities to deport Zakaria weeks before his arrest on the country’s south-west coast.



In an email sent in late 2022 and read in court, then-AFP detective sergeant Scott Murphy told NSW Police investigators – whom he called “Zakaria chasers” – that the agency would engage with the Turkish National Police to have Zakaria “blacklisted” and removed from the country because his activities meant he posed too high a risk to continue residing there. The hearing before Justice Edward Muston continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCBD Sharnelle Vella quits ABC breakfast as radio exodus continues Fiona Byrne October 22, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Respected journalist Sharnelle Vella is exiting as co-host of ABC Melbourne’s breakfast radio show. Vella joined the breakfast show alongside former AFL star Bob Murphy in January 2025, just weeks after quitting Channel Seven, where she was a top reporter in the Melbourne newsroom. Bob Murphy and Sharnelle Vella. Chris Hopkins Vella, who has been on maternity leave since the birth of her daughter, Eve, in March, was expected to stay on with the ABC in 2027 and return to the co-hosting chair alongside Murphy, a former Western Bulldogs player. However, five sources with knowledge of her departure, but not authorised to speak publicly, revealed Vella had informed management in recent days that she would like to take a different path.



The sources said ABC Melbourne staff were informed on Thursday that Vella was departing. Vella’s exit continues the shake-up underway in the local radio market, with Carrie Bickmore and comedian Tommy Little calling time on their Carrie & Tommy national drive show on Wednesday. Vella joins Carrie Bickmore and Tommy Little in the radio show exodus. They will exit the Hit Network after a decade on air at the end of the year. Bickmore fought back tears while announcing to listeners, while her co-host Little said it was “certainly not how I wanted it to end”.



Meanwhile, the KIIS drive shift is up for grabs with the Will & Woody drive show, hosted by Will McMahon and Woody Whitelaw, also ending at year’s end. Vella and Murphy launched their breakfast show in 2025, taking over the highly scrutinised shift from comedian Sammy J. The pair endured a baptism of fire as their ratings dropped, sparking a storm of media criticism. In March 2025, Murphy had to apologise to Vella on air for making a “gross” joke that insinuated that she had once worked at Melbourne strip club Spearmint Rhino. The show made headlines again in April 2025 when Murphy slept through his alarm and missed most of the first hour of the program. Media commentary at the time questioned if the fledgling team would last six months.



Related Article Opinion

Fertility I’ve been on a journey of hope and heartbreak that only members of my secret club can understand Sharnelle Vella Broadcaster The show’s ratings recovered somewhat; however, in March, when Vella went on leave, the ABC’s overall share of 5.4 per cent in Melbourne constituted the largest drop of any station, with its breakfast, afternoon, drive and evening shows all losing share. Despite this, listeners responded warmly when Vella announced she and her husband, Nicholas Koutrigaros, were expecting their first child after four years of trying and numerous rounds of IVF. In making the announcement in November last year, Vella described her pending parenthood as a dream come true. “Our journey to get here hasn’t been easy, but we’re grateful for the support of our loved ones and friends. We hope our story can offer hope to others navigating endometriosis and infertility,” she said.



Richelle Hunt joined ABC breakfast in March 2026 as Vella’s maternity leave cover. Whether Hunt will stay in the role in 2027 is unclear. Both Vella and the ABC were approached for comment but neither responded. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Zenith bid goes unconditional as Forrestania builds WA gold stockpile
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Zenith bid goes unconditional as Forrestania builds WA gold stockpile Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS October 22, 2026 — 4:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Forrestania Resources has declared its takeover bid for Zenith Minerals unconditional after securing a controlling 58.99 per cent stake, clearing the way for a bigger WA gold business. The move positions Forrestania to fold Zenith’s assets into its hub-and-spoke gold strategy centred on Edna May and Lake Johnston. In a separate development, the company has also secured 400,000 tonnes of ore feed from Star Minerals’ Tumblegum gold mine, near Meekatharra. The acquisition of Zenith fits squarely into the company’s playbook, adding to its portfolio of deposits and exploration projects that can feed into its development pipeline. Forrestania Resources is building a WA gold business through two strategic processing hubs at Edna May and Lake Johnston (pictured). Forrestania’s ambitious $79 million all-scrip takeover has been anything but a quiet affair, with the company pulling off a transformational $300 million acquisition of Ramelius Resources’ Edna May gold assets just weeks after launching its Zenith bid in June. Backed by a whopping $310 million capital raising, the blockbuster deal dramatically raised the stakes, putting Forrestania on a much bigger stage in WA’s gold sector. The rapid-fire dealmaking also attracted the attention of two investors, Harvest Lane Asset Management and Ida Metal Investments, who took their concerns to the Takeovers Panel, questioning whether Zenith shareholders had been given enough information about Forrestania’s rapidly expanding ambitions.



The matter was effectively put to bed in late September when a review panel upheld its original findings and orders, leaving Forrestania’s takeover intact but imposing additional disclosure requirements to protect minority shareholders should the company secure control without achieving full ownership. Despite the regulatory detour, Forrestania confirmed it has now met the minimum acceptance condition and has declared the offer free from all remaining defeating conditions. The declaration came at the first available opportunity, following a one-week waiting period mandated by the Takeovers Panel, which concluded on October 22. While the corporate machinations of a takeover may seem dry, the strategic logic behind the company’s bid paints a far more compelling picture. The move is a central pillar in the company’s stated strategy to build a leading WA gold business through a classic hub-and-spoke development model. With the deal now a goer, Forrestania will begin issuing shares to the Zenith holders who have already accepted the all-scrip offer, within the next 14 days. With the offer extended to November 12, the company remains firmly in the driver’s seat, eyeing the 90 per cent threshold generally required to pursue compulsory acquisition and complete its broader WA gold consolidation strategy. In other notable news today, the company has added another string to its emerging gold production bow, striking a binding ore purchase deal with Star Minerals that could see up to 400,000 tonnes of gold-bearing rock trucked into its soon-to-be-in-production Edna May processing plant in Western Australia over the next two years.



The agreement covers ore from Star’s Tumblegum gold project in the Eastern Goldfields, with the first trucks scheduled to roll tomorrow. Effective immediately, the deal gives Forrestania exclusive rights to purchase Tumblegum ore meeting an agreed minimum grade threshold during the initial 24-month term, potentially adding another valuable feed source to its growing gold processing ambitions. The commercial arrangement ties the purchase price to ore grade, metallurgical recoveries and prevailing gold prices, giving Forrestania a crack at capturing upside from a buoyant bullion market. Importantly, the deal offers another potential source of mill feed for its hungry processing plants without the company having to develop a new mine of its own. It also slots neatly into Forrestania’s broader hub-and-spoke strategy, built around its Edna May and Lake Johnston processing hubs and a growing collection of gold deposits, including Tycho and Johnson Range. With the first Tumblegum trucks preparing to hit the road, the company has added another piece to its production puzzle as it pushes towards establishing a sustainable WA gold business. With the Zenith takeover now effectively locked in and a fresh source of ore in the bag, Forrestania looks to have taken further significant steps in executing its regional consolidation strategy. The focus will now likely shift to integrating the new assets and advancing its broader plan to become a significant player in the WA gold scene. World.title: Melbourne hospo powerhouse opens stunning debut Brisbane venue
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Melbourne hospo powerhouse opens stunning debut Brisbane venue High Road aims to put hotel restaurants back on the map with its beguiling dining room and a considered menu that leans hard into wood fire. Matt Shea October 22, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a tiny part of Gareth Woolcock that’s disappointed about opening High Road. “Because it’s exactly the place I’d come to,” Woolcock says, laughing. “I’d come with four or five mates, order a bunch of drinks, order a bunch of plates, and settle in. It’s such a beautiful space – they’ve achieved this balance of it feeling really open but also cosy and warm at the same time.” High Road is one of 2026’s prettiest openings. Fergus Hurst for High Road “They” is Mulberry Group, the Melbourne hospitality powerhouse that on Friday will open High Road on the ground floor of Novotel South Brisbane. And Woolcock is right – High Road is a bit of a looker. The fit-out is all dark timber panelling, marble-topped tables, vertical tiled surfaced, and burgundy and cream tones. Low kitchen counters add a sense of theatre to the place, and there’s a separate lounge area for guests wanting a more laidback experience.



Related Article Exclusive Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park Of course, Woolcock is selling himself short. Such a swish dining room would be nothing without food to eat. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Eagle Farm’s Beech Ovens has produced a 1.5-metre wide multi-level grill and custom-designed wood-fire oven that power much of High Road’s menu. It’s split into starters, steaks and items from the grill. The fit-out is all dark timber panelling, marble-topped tables, vertical tiled surfaced, and burgundy and cream tones. Fergus Hurst for High Road You might begin with a Mooloolaba prawn roll with umami mayo and cos; potato scallops with creme fraiche, black caviar and finger lime; or house-made yoghurt flatbread with Mount Zero olive oil.



The beef program features four cuts: a 220-gram pasture-fed eye fillet from Toowoomba, a 350-gram Black Angus flank from Mitchell Grass Plains in Queensland, a 300-gram Wagyu rump from Liverpool Plains in New South Wales, and a 300-gram grain-fed Riverina Black Angus sirloin from NSW. Potato scallops with creme fraiche, black caviar and finger lime. Fergus Hurst for High Road Other mains from the grill include free-range half chicken with hot sauce and labneh; a 270-gram Oria pork cutlet with salsa verde; and 500-gram slow cooked Victorian lamb shoulder with salsa verde. “It’s designed to be good, relatable food that’s had a lot of care put into it,” Woolcock says. “We have a signature burger that I’m really pleased with. We’re making the patties, the sauce in-house; we’ve tested about 15 or 20 burger buns to make sure we have that right … I’m confident it’s one of the best burgers in Brisbane.” Chargrilled tiger prawns in miso butter. Fergus Hurst for High Road



There’s also a bar menu that throws together a steak and a bunch of the starters with a couple of new dishes: karaage chicken with togarashi mayo, and flame grilled semi-cured chorizo with lime. For drinks there’s a cocktail menu that twists the classics, alongside a wine list that favours Australian producers without getting dogmatic about it, and includes a decent by-the-glass selection. High Road opens Friday, October 23. Fergus Hurst for High Road “I’m really hopeful that what we can do here is really transform the hotel dining scene … I got into hotels about 12 years ago and at that stage, hotel restaurants were starting to lose their sheen a little bit. “But we’re really lucky with the ownership group here at the hotel that they’ve really bought into the whole process.”



Open daily 12pm-3pm, 5pm-late 38 Cordelia Street, South Brisbane highroadbarandgrill.com.au

World.title: Seven reveals its 2027 line-up, including new hosts for I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Seven reveals its 2027 line-up, including new hosts for I’m A Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! Karl Quinn October 22, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Singer Ricki-Lee Coulter and comedian Jim Jefferies have been announced as the hosts of Seven’s take on the reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! When Seven snaffled the show from Ten earlier this year, it was widely assumed it would reinstate the show’s former co-host Dr Chris Brown, who left the show in 2023 and joined Seven, and was replaced by Robert Irwin. The network has high hopes for its journey to the jungle, even if the show (developed in Britain and first aired there in 2002) has been on-air in this country since 2015. Ricki-Lee Coulter and Jim Jefferies have been unveiled as the hosts of the reborn I’m a Celebrity... Seven “Everyone always wants to talk about new, and I get it,” said Seven’s chief content officer, Brook Hall. “You can have a really reliable car that you love, but there’s something exciting about getting a new one, whether it’s better or not. Same with TV shows. [But] any new show in television inherently carries greater risk than a proven form.



“Why I love I’m A Celeb is it’s new for us, we can do something different, but it’s a proven performer. We’re going to have a different twist on it.” Related Article Australian TV Crime, comedy, an Alan Jones doco and the return of Fisk: What’s coming to the ABC in 2027 The format is “built to be talked about” said Hall. With Jefferies – who has proven a winner for the network as host of the game show The 1% Club – it has a fast-talking funnyman likely to generate plenty of headlines. And in Coulter, who has been a fixture on Australian television screens since first emerging as a contestant on the second season of Australian Idol in 2004, he’ll have a foil adept at smoothing over any rough edges. “They are two of our biggest stars, and very different types of stars, and putting them together I think already looks really different, but it’s still got the comedy and the warmth at the front there,” said Hall, who promises Seven’s version of the show – which will begin production early next year – will be “dialling up the real jungle as much as possible”. Also new to hosting an established format is Nashville-based Australian country music star Morgan Evans, who will join the Australian Idol judging panel alongside Marcia Hines and Amy Shark.



“He’s a Newcastle kid, he’s come through the system himself, and he’s genuinely interested in the process of finding Australian talent,” said Hall. “He was really passionate about it.” Australian country music star Morgan Evans joins Australian Idol. Seven Hall will also need to fill the Idol chair formerly occupied by Kyle Sandilands, whose career trajectory is looking very different thanks to the massive falling out with ARN, owner of KIIS FM, which was his principal employer until March. Seven and rival broadcaster SCA (Southern Cross Austereo) merged in January, so the option to stick it to the old rival might have been tempting. The economics of doing so, however, given the boycotts of advertisers associated with Sandilands-aligned content, might have been less so. “On radio, he was polarising, but on Australian Idol he was a different character, and I thought he was really good for the show,” said Hall. “But both parties decided, well, is this the time to freshen it up? We do that with a lot of shows, changing judges and panels.”



The merger of Seven and SCA has been a boon for both parties, said Matthew O’Reilly, head of broadcast content at the audio arm. “The cross-promotion of us running promos and commercials for the TV shows, and them doing the same to us, means their ratings are flying and our ratings are up considerably year-on-year, so I would say there’s been a good benefit for both parties,” O’Reilly said. Related Article Australian TV Today show hosts vow to restore trust as Nine reveals new MAFS expert and The Block spin-off One place that will play out is in the coverage of the Melbourne Cup next week. While Seven has the broadcast rights to most of the Spring Racing Carnival, the biggest horse-racing event of the year is on Nine (owner of this masthead). But Seven’s veteran sportscaster Bruce McAvaney will call the race as usual – only this time on Triple M for what O’Reilly called “a first-time experiment”. Hall sees plenty of cross-promotional opportunities, too, and thinks Australian Idol is the place where they will most clearly play out (Seven has not announced a return for The Voice, though that is still under active discussion). “It’s a music show so you’ll probably see things like Hit week, Triple M week,” he said. “We weren’t part of a merged company last year, so there are a few different things we can play with and I’m really excited about that.”



Chris Brown and Matt Preston on Once in a Lifetime. Seven On the drama front, Seven’s only offering is Home and Away, which remains the country’s most-watched drama with an average 1.1 million viewers per episode – about two-thirds of them watching at the time it’s broadcast. That’s an extraordinary result in this era of on-demand drama watching, and one that Hall said has caught the attention of industry colleagues overseas. “Probably because of the way it’s written, with heightened storylines all the time, people are consuming it like it’s an event,” he said. Related Article Streaming Colin From Accounts is ending. Here’s what Binge is banking on for their next hit The network is doing its best to turn the weekday staple of the game show into something like an event, too, with two new short-run series: the Matt Shirvington-fronted Stacks of Cash, which attempts to merge the frenetic excitement of Tetris with the frenzied pursuit of a pile of money, and Caught in the Middle, a knowledge-based contest hosted by Shane Jacobson. Each will run for six episodes, with Jim Jefferies’ The 1% Club returning for eight.



Though he won’t be going back into the South African jungle, and there’s no return for his makeover show My Reno Rules, Chris Brown will be back on air with Once In a Lifetime, a show in which he takes celebrities on journeys into nature around the world. “That’s his format, we know he’s passionate about nature, and he’s going to different countries,” said Hall of the show which was originally announced at Seven’s 2025 upfront but is now scheduled to air around Easter next year. “You get a bit of travel, you get a bit of nature, he’s telling his story, but he’s taking someone with him as well. So you get to see different parts there.” Returning shows to Seven in 2027 include MKR, with Manu Feildel and Colin Fassnidge hosting, The Chase, Glenn and Mick’s Celebrity Intervention and Oops I Bought a Pub. A bistro-brasserie in Parisian style, Lucette is cleverly tooled to suit the many speeds and needs of the Highlands. Viennoiserie and omelettes in the morning, baguettes at lunch, steak frites for dejeuner and dîner. Roll in for breakfast, pop in for lunch, cruise in for afternoon aperitifs (who else serves Suze in town, anyway?), or settle in for date night.

In any case, sitting here is a pleasure, either inside behind cafe curtains, or slung on mustard banquettes in the breezy terrace. But the real kicker is on the plate, where chef Guillaume Dubois (ex-Monopole) brings fine-dining nous to classics.

The peppercorn sauce with wagyu steak? Infused with shio kombu. Chicken-liver parfait? Topped with rosé jelly. Tartare has brown-butter depth, chocolate mousse has praline crunch. And then service is just the right amount of Parisian brusque to be charming. Lucette? It might just be the little light the Highlands has been waiting for.

World.title: Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants
World.content:
PoliticsFederalNACC Corruption watchdog’s interest ‘piqued’ by Labor’s invite-only grants Nick Newling October 22, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Labor’s invite-only election grant program has “piqued” the interest of the acting head of Australia’s corruption watchdog, as departmental staff were grilled over the funding promises one legal expert says amounts to “grey corruption”. As a Senate inquiry investigates the program, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been forced to defend a “dirt file” his office disseminated about independent MP Helen Haines several weeks ago, saying it was not designed to be critical of the politician, but rather showed that “people of integrity stand up for their electorate”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spent the morning defending his office’s dissemination of a “dirt file”. Justin McManus The victim of a violent car attack on Monday, Haines has had both legs amputated and remains in a critical condition. The regional Victorian MP was a vocal critic of Labor’s use of the grant program and campaigned to establish the National Anti-Corruption Commission to investigate federal and Commonwealth agencies, programs, employees and MPs. Addressing senators on Thursday, acting NACC commissioner Kylie Kilgour said it was “impossible” to express an opinion at this time over whether corrupt conduct had occurred in the grant program, but a number of aspects had “piqued” her interest, including alterations regarding its constitutionality.



“We would not [make a determination] unless we conducted a thorough, proper investigation under the NACC Act,” Kilgour told the inquiry. Related Article Government grants ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’ Haines was critical of the Albanese government’s $560.9 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program, in which nearly three-quarters of grants were allocated to notionally Labor-held or competitive seats, according to analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity. The Marrickville Golf Club, in Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler became the centre of debate over the grant program, as it had already received five federal grants totalling almost $58,000 before Albanese promised it a $6 million grant through the program during the 2025 election campaign. Kilgour said she had yet to hear evidence that would suggest the program should fall under the jurisdiction of the NACC and, until such point, would defer to a potential investigation by the Australian National Audit Office.



She became emotional when reading the commission’s opening statement as she shared her message of support for Haines, saying the MP was “instrumental” in the establishment of the NACC. “We are deeply appalled by what has transpired, and I sent a message conveying that to her office,” Kilgour said. Independent MP Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen Following the last election, guidelines for the grants program were republished on October 2, 2025, but they prompted by concerns that the original design released a month earlier was constitutionally invalid. The Commonwealth does not have the power to directly fund local sporting and community facilities. The scheme was subsequently changed so grants could flow through state or local governments under section 96 of the Constitution.



In a submission to the inquiry, constitutional expert Anne Twomey said politically directed grants did not necessarily deliver electoral rewards. “No, this is not about ‘being a good local member’,” she wrote. “It is about indulging in grey corruption and the misuse of public money at the public’s expense.” The inquiry will continue, with dozens of senators’ questions to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet deferred. Questions over which ministers allocated grant funding, the specifics of funding to the Marrickville Golf Club, and the administration of the ministerial code of conduct regarding conflicts of interest were taken “on notice”. Following the attack on Haines, some media outlets took the rare action of discussing and publishing a background file distributed by the prime minister’s media office regarding funding requests by Haines’ office.



Sent to journalists during public debate over the grant program, the file encourages questioning of Haines over whether “$1.8 billion worth of funding for projects she’s selected” represented value for money. Related Article Haines attack Who is Phil Haines, the soulmate who convinced Helen to run for politics? The five-page file was sent to federal politics journalists in September, suggesting questions about the due diligence Haines had performed making project funding requests, and the interests she had in organisations for whom she was petitioning. Asked to respond to the claims at the time, Haines said “the issue isn’t whether MPs advocate for their communities. Of course, we do. What I’m asking for is that all communities get a fair go.” Political parties across the spectrum regularly provide “dirt files” of damaging information collected about their political opponents to journalists. The sheets are typically provided on a “background” basis, with journalists able to test the claims but not revealing the original source.



Asked on News24 on Wednesday whether he was aware or had ordered the release of the file, Albanese said: “Helen Haines is a good local member. She put forward applications like other members do for grants, and that’s what good local members do. And Helen Haines is a very strong advocate for her community”. Facing further questioning on Thursday morning, Albanese told ABC Sydney radio the document was “a list of funding asks … just showing that people of integrity stand up for their electorate. No personal criticism of Helen”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Crown admits deportation of Sydney underworld figure was illegal
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Crown admits deportation of Sydney underworld figure was illegal Riley Walter Updated October 22, 2026 — 4:46pm ,first published 11:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Underworld figure Masood Zakaria’s deportation from Turkey was illegal, prosecutors have conceded, as the alleged kingpin pushes to have murder charges against him thrown out over allegations the Australian Federal Police facilitated his “kidnapping” and return to Sydney. The NSW Supreme Court heard on Thursday morning that the 31-year-old’s forced removal in late 2023 was not permitted under Turkish law because of his pending appeal against the country’s decision to deport him. He was arrested at a seaside villa earlier that year. Masood Zakaria was brought back from Turkey in December 2023. Wolter Peeters The concession looms as a significant factor in Zakaria’s unprecedented legal challenge to have a raft of serious charges, including murder, dismissed. Zakaria’s legal team is seeking a permanent stay of proceedings against him after alleging AFP officers facilitated his illegal deportation from Turkey in a recovery operation akin to a kidnapping that constituted an abuse of process. The timing of his deportation is a major focus of the legal challenge.



If their application is successful, the charges against Zakaria, including for the murders of father and son Toufik Hamze, 64, and Salim Hamze, 18, and a conspiracy to murder gangland rival Ibrahem Hamze at the height of an underworld feud in 2021, will not be prosecuted. Related Article Organised crime He’s accused of murdering a father and son. The police may have jeopardised the case Trials for those offences were last year vacated after Zakaria’s lawyers levelled the allegations at the AFP. The AFP maintains its actions were lawful. The legal saga has cast doubt on the prosecutions of several other individuals wanted by Australian authorities and returned to the country in similar circumstances. The individuals, who cannot legally be identified, were among the highest value targets for law enforcement agencies at the time of their deportations. Prosecutors on Thursday flagged that an expert in Turkish law would be called to give evidence on the legality of Zakaria’s deportation. He is being held in Goulburn Supermax, Australia’s highest security prison.



Zakaria’s application is expected to run for two weeks and hear evidence from some of the country’s most senior organised crime investigators. Zakaria – an alleged high-ranking member of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family when he fled Australia in 2021 – was returned in December 2023 onboard a chartered Airbus A319 his lawyers claim cost the AFP more than $1 million. A team of six ex-military contractors working for Hart International, a multinational security and risk management firm, escorted him back to Australia. Skytraders, an aviation company contracted by the AFP to provide the plane with which Zakaria was deported, on Thursday lost a bid for its employees to be excused from giving evidence in court. The court heard that evidence from the employees involved could incriminate them and expose them to possible criminal charges in Turkey, including deprivation of liberty, if Zakaria’s deportation and detainment are found to be unlawful. Zakaria is an alleged high-ranking member of Sydney’s Alameddine crime family. NSW Police



Opposing the application, Zakaria’s barrister, Julia Roy, SC, said there was no evidence to suggest the employees risked facing criminal proceedings or were under investigation in Turkey. Daniel Colborne, one of the pilots who flew Zakaria back to Australia, told the court that heavily armed Turkish officials kept the 31-year-old and the Hart International team onboard the plane for several days after it was grounded when it struck a flock of birds. Heavily armed officers escorted Zakaria onto a replacement plane, Colborne said. Related Article Crime Sydney underworld kingpin ‘blacklisted’ before alleged kidnapping, court told Hart International Australia’s chief executive previously told the court the company’s personnel did not restrain passengers, before being shown images appearing to show Zakaria wearing plastic restraints around his wrists. Colborne said only the captain of a flight has authority to restrain a passenger. The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard the AFP encouraged Turkish authorities to deport Zakaria weeks before his arrest on the country’s south-west coast.



In an email sent in late 2022 and read in court, then-AFP detective sergeant Scott Murphy told NSW Police investigators – whom he called “Zakaria chasers” – that the agency would engage with the Turkish National Police to have Zakaria “blacklisted” and removed from the country because his activities meant he posed too high a risk to continue residing there. The hearing before Justice Edward Muston continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Exclusive NationalVictoriaCBD Sharnelle Vella quits ABC breakfast as radio exodus continues Fiona Byrne October 22, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Respected journalist Sharnelle Vella is exiting as co-host of ABC Melbourne’s breakfast radio show. Vella joined the breakfast show alongside former AFL star Bob Murphy in January 2025, just weeks after quitting Channel Seven, where she was a top reporter in the Melbourne newsroom. Bob Murphy and Sharnelle Vella. Chris Hopkins Vella, who has been on maternity leave since the birth of her daughter, Eve, in March, was expected to stay on with the ABC in 2027 and return to the co-hosting chair alongside Murphy, a former Western Bulldogs player. However, five sources with knowledge of her departure, but not authorised to speak publicly, revealed Vella had informed management in recent days that she would like to take a different path.



The sources said ABC Melbourne staff were informed on Thursday that Vella was departing. Vella’s exit continues the shake-up underway in the local radio market, with Carrie Bickmore and comedian Tommy Little calling time on their Carrie & Tommy national drive show on Wednesday. Vella joins Carrie Bickmore and Tommy Little in the radio show exodus. They will exit the Hit Network after a decade on air at the end of the year. Bickmore fought back tears while announcing to listeners, while her co-host Little said it was “certainly not how I wanted it to end”.



Meanwhile, the KIIS drive shift is up for grabs with the Will & Woody drive show, hosted by Will McMahon and Woody Whitelaw, also ending at year’s end. Vella and Murphy launched their breakfast show in 2025, taking over the highly scrutinised shift from comedian Sammy J. The pair endured a baptism of fire as their ratings dropped, sparking a storm of media criticism. In March 2025, Murphy had to apologise to Vella on air for making a “gross” joke that insinuated that she had once worked at Melbourne strip club Spearmint Rhino. The show made headlines again in April 2025 when Murphy slept through his alarm and missed most of the first hour of the program. Media commentary at the time questioned if the fledgling team would last six months.



Related Article Opinion

Fertility I’ve been on a journey of hope and heartbreak that only members of my secret club can understand Sharnelle Vella Broadcaster The show’s ratings recovered somewhat; however, in March, when Vella went on leave, the ABC’s overall share of 5.4 per cent in Melbourne constituted the largest drop of any station, with its breakfast, afternoon, drive and evening shows all losing share. Despite this, listeners responded warmly when Vella announced she and her husband, Nicholas Koutrigaros, were expecting their first child after four years of trying and numerous rounds of IVF. In making the announcement in November last year, Vella described her pending parenthood as a dream come true. “Our journey to get here hasn’t been easy, but we’re grateful for the support of our loved ones and friends. We hope our story can offer hope to others navigating endometriosis and infertility,” she said.



Richelle Hunt joined ABC breakfast in March 2026 as Vella’s maternity leave cover. Whether Hunt will stay in the role in 2027 is unclear. Both Vella and the ABC were approached for comment but neither responded. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Zenith bid goes unconditional as Forrestania builds WA gold stockpile
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Zenith bid goes unconditional as Forrestania builds WA gold stockpile Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS October 22, 2026 — 4:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Forrestania Resources has declared its takeover bid for Zenith Minerals unconditional after securing a controlling 58.99 per cent stake, clearing the way for a bigger WA gold business. The move positions Forrestania to fold Zenith’s assets into its hub-and-spoke gold strategy centred on Edna May and Lake Johnston. In a separate development, the company has also secured 400,000 tonnes of ore feed from Star Minerals’ Tumblegum gold mine, near Meekatharra. The acquisition of Zenith fits squarely into the company’s playbook, adding to its portfolio of deposits and exploration projects that can feed into its development pipeline. Forrestania Resources is building a WA gold business through two strategic processing hubs at Edna May and Lake Johnston (pictured). Forrestania’s ambitious $79 million all-scrip takeover has been anything but a quiet affair, with the company pulling off a transformational $300 million acquisition of Ramelius Resources’ Edna May gold assets just weeks after launching its Zenith bid in June. Backed by a whopping $310 million capital raising, the blockbuster deal dramatically raised the stakes, putting Forrestania on a much bigger stage in WA’s gold sector. The rapid-fire dealmaking also attracted the attention of two investors, Harvest Lane Asset Management and Ida Metal Investments, who took their concerns to the Takeovers Panel, questioning whether Zenith shareholders had been given enough information about Forrestania’s rapidly expanding ambitions.



The matter was effectively put to bed in late September when a review panel upheld its original findings and orders, leaving Forrestania’s takeover intact but imposing additional disclosure requirements to protect minority shareholders should the company secure control without achieving full ownership. Despite the regulatory detour, Forrestania confirmed it has now met the minimum acceptance condition and has declared the offer free from all remaining defeating conditions. The declaration came at the first available opportunity, following a one-week waiting period mandated by the Takeovers Panel, which concluded on October 22. While the corporate machinations of a takeover may seem dry, the strategic logic behind the company’s bid paints a far more compelling picture. The move is a central pillar in the company’s stated strategy to build a leading WA gold business through a classic hub-and-spoke development model. With the deal now a goer, Forrestania will begin issuing shares to the Zenith holders who have already accepted the all-scrip offer, within the next 14 days. With the offer extended to November 12, the company remains firmly in the driver’s seat, eyeing the 90 per cent threshold generally required to pursue compulsory acquisition and complete its broader WA gold consolidation strategy. In other notable news today, the company has added another string to its emerging gold production bow, striking a binding ore purchase deal with Star Minerals that could see up to 400,000 tonnes of gold-bearing rock trucked into its soon-to-be-in-production Edna May processing plant in Western Australia over the next two years.



The agreement covers ore from Star’s Tumblegum gold project in the Eastern Goldfields, with the first trucks scheduled to roll tomorrow. Effective immediately, the deal gives Forrestania exclusive rights to purchase Tumblegum ore meeting an agreed minimum grade threshold during the initial 24-month term, potentially adding another valuable feed source to its growing gold processing ambitions. The commercial arrangement ties the purchase price to ore grade, metallurgical recoveries and prevailing gold prices, giving Forrestania a crack at capturing upside from a buoyant bullion market. Importantly, the deal offers another potential source of mill feed for its hungry processing plants without the company having to develop a new mine of its own. It also slots neatly into Forrestania’s broader hub-and-spoke strategy, built around its Edna May and Lake Johnston processing hubs and a growing collection of gold deposits, including Tycho and Johnson Range. With the first Tumblegum trucks preparing to hit the road, the company has added another piece to its production puzzle as it pushes towards establishing a sustainable WA gold business. With the Zenith takeover now effectively locked in and a fresh source of ore in the bag, Forrestania looks to have taken further significant steps in executing its regional consolidation strategy. The focus will now likely shift to integrating the new assets and advancing its broader plan to become a significant player in the WA gold scene. World.title: Melbourne hospo powerhouse opens stunning debut Brisbane venue
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outFood Melbourne hospo powerhouse opens stunning debut Brisbane venue High Road aims to put hotel restaurants back on the map with its beguiling dining room and a considered menu that leans hard into wood fire. Matt Shea October 22, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a tiny part of Gareth Woolcock that’s disappointed about opening High Road. “Because it’s exactly the place I’d come to,” Woolcock says, laughing. “I’d come with four or five mates, order a bunch of drinks, order a bunch of plates, and settle in. It’s such a beautiful space – they’ve achieved this balance of it feeling really open but also cosy and warm at the same time.” High Road is one of 2026’s prettiest openings. Fergus Hurst for High Road “They” is Mulberry Group, the Melbourne hospitality powerhouse that on Friday will open High Road on the ground floor of Novotel South Brisbane. And Woolcock is right – High Road is a bit of a looker. The fit-out is all dark timber panelling, marble-topped tables, vertical tiled surfaced, and burgundy and cream tones. Low kitchen counters add a sense of theatre to the place, and there’s a separate lounge area for guests wanting a more laidback experience.



Related Article Exclusive Ghanem’s hefty 350-seat eatery and open-air bar arrives in Everton Park Of course, Woolcock is selling himself short. Such a swish dining room would be nothing without food to eat. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Eagle Farm’s Beech Ovens has produced a 1.5-metre wide multi-level grill and custom-designed wood-fire oven that power much of High Road’s menu. It’s split into starters, steaks and items from the grill. The fit-out is all dark timber panelling, marble-topped tables, vertical tiled surfaced, and burgundy and cream tones. Fergus Hurst for High Road You might begin with a Mooloolaba prawn roll with umami mayo and cos; potato scallops with creme fraiche, black caviar and finger lime; or house-made yoghurt flatbread with Mount Zero olive oil.



The beef program features four cuts: a 220-gram pasture-fed eye fillet from Toowoomba, a 350-gram Black Angus flank from Mitchell Grass Plains in Queensland, a 300-gram Wagyu rump from Liverpool Plains in New South Wales, and a 300-gram grain-fed Riverina Black Angus sirloin from NSW. Potato scallops with creme fraiche, black caviar and finger lime. Fergus Hurst for High Road Other mains from the grill include free-range half chicken with hot sauce and labneh; a 270-gram Oria pork cutlet with salsa verde; and 500-gram slow cooked Victorian lamb shoulder with salsa verde. “It’s designed to be good, relatable food that’s had a lot of care put into it,” Woolcock says. “We have a signature burger that I’m really pleased with. We’re making the patties, the sauce in-house; we’ve tested about 15 or 20 burger buns to make sure we have that right … I’m confident it’s one of the best burgers in Brisbane.” Chargrilled tiger prawns in miso butter. Fergus Hurst for High Road



There’s also a bar menu that throws together a steak and a bunch of the starters with a couple of new dishes: karaage chicken with togarashi mayo, and flame grilled semi-cured chorizo with lime. For drinks there’s a cocktail menu that twists the classics, alongside a wine list that favours Australian producers without getting dogmatic about it, and includes a decent by-the-glass selection. High Road opens Friday, October 23. Fergus Hurst for High Road “I’m really hopeful that what we can do here is really transform the hotel dining scene … I got into hotels about 12 years ago and at that stage, hotel restaurants were starting to lose their sheen a little bit. “But we’re really lucky with the ownership group here at the hotel that they’ve really bought into the whole process.”



Open daily 12pm-3pm, 5pm-late 38 Cordelia Street, South Brisbane highroadbarandgrill.com.au

World.title: 'Not a consideration': Who picks up the phone on election night?
World.content:
Audio player for " The rise of AI politics, who gets on the phone November 8, & National's front bench risk " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2087485%2Fnot-a-consideration-who-picks-up-the-phone-on-election-night

The rise of AI politics, who gets on the phone November 8, & National's front bench risk Caucus Download MP3 47m

Analysis: It's one of the defining questions of Election 2026 - will Opportunity get the opportunity to help form a government for the next three years?

The fledgling party has left its mark on the political landscape, regardless of how it polls on election day, ushering in seldom-heard conversations about bipartisanship and long-term planning.

We know from the past month of intense campaigning that Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong, should her party cross the five percent threshold and hold the balance of power, promises to talk first to the party with the most seats.

We know Labour leader Chris Hipkins is happy to take that call and that National leader Christopher Luxon is not, but if that remains everyone's position on 8 November, what happens then?

Wong rings Luxon "and it goes straight to voicemail", deputy political editor Craig McCulloch jokes in this week's episode of RNZ's politics podcast, Caucus.

The great question is whether Luxon actually does pick up the phone and negotiate, or not.

On this week's Stuff Leaders' Debate, Luxon made the Mitre 10 Mega of all rulings-out - or at least, he appeared to.

He said he had ruled out joining a coalition with Opportunity in the same vein as having ruled out a coalition with Labour or Te Pati Maori.

He listed all the parties he wouldn't work with.

"I don't know how much clearer I can be," he has taken to saying over and again.

"I am serious about it," Luxon told debate moderator Paddy Gower. "It's not a consideration."

It's unusual for a prime minister to be so definitive, because if he was to U-turn on that position after the election, he would be a laughing stock, but McCulloch says Luxon immediately undermined his tough line by refusing to promise to quit, rather than pick up the phone.

"If he really meant what he's saying, he would have no issue staking his job on it."

The political reality is that, if Luxon refused to make that call, his caucus would decide for him by rolling him.

As RNZ political editor Jo Moir says: "The National Party base is not going to accept that as the conclusion at the end of all of this."

It highlights the fact that if these leaders hold fast, coalition negotiations could be incredibly unstable and jobs could be lost.

For Wong, there are no set rules, but she has suggested she won't run parallel negotiations with both major parties, as New Zealand First has done in the past.

Moir says that's inexperience showing and McCulloch says, "In a negotiation, surely you want to see all the options available to you" - but it may be Wong's way.

"We'll genuinely try and do good-faith negotiating with the largest party first," she told Newstalk ZB. "I think that's the fair thing to do, but if we feel like we have to walk away because we're compromising too much, then we would go to the other side and see what they've got."

There's wriggle room, however, a willingness to see what the other side has to offer and Labour will almost certainly be willing to offer more.

As Wong faces questions about the negotiations and bottom-lines, you can't help but notice she seems less comfortable with the core policies being pitched by the existing coalition parties.

Moir has asked her about this on the campaign trail.

"She pointed out ACT's policy to freeze the minimum wage, New Zealand First's and ACT's policies to abolish the Waitangi Tribunal, National's policy to drug testing beneficiaries... all the examples she used were from centre-right parties. She didn't put up anything from the centre-left that she fundamentally disagrees with."

"Qiulae Wong is having to walk quite a fine line in her messaging to court both that left and right vote," says McCulloch. arguing that if Opportunity went with the centre-right, it would represent the change within government without needing to change the prime minister.

Going right, "she sees the party's role as being very much a handbrake".

Then there's Labour. There's no rule saying it has to play the wallflower.

"Labour definitely picks up the phone," Moir says. "They've never said, 'we're not picking up the phone'.

In the final two weeks of the campaign, expect more questions about phone calls and what might transpire from 8 November.

World.title: 'Potentially catastrophic': Westland's Waiho River changing course years ahead of forecasts
World.content:
Experts say Westland's Waiho River is changing course three or four years earlier than expected, posing a serious threat to people's lives and property in Franz Josef.

At a public meeting on Wednesday night an independent technical advisory group called for councils to urgently secure central government funding and prepare for a managed retreat before disaster strikes.

The group of river scientists, appointed by the West Coast Regional Council, had previously recommended releasing the river's southern stopbanks within 10 years to allow the Waiho (Waiau) River to fan out naturally.

That would submerge local farmland, require the relocation of State Highway 6 and the town's wastewater treatment ponds and lead to the abandonment of the local aerodrome.

Group spokesperson Professor Ian Fuller said the rapid river changes meant the timeline had effectively brought that reality forward.

Professor Ian Fuller. (File photo) Ian Fuller / Supplied

Without action there was a "potentially catastrophic" risk to life, he said.

"It's not just a question of water flowing over the stopbanks. It's a question of water and sediment - coarse debris, essentially gravel - moving across what is currently protected land," he said.

"I don't think Aotearoa New Zealand can afford a disaster occurring in this area."

Fuller stressed that councils would not be able to manage or pay to ward off the threat on their own.

"This can't be done by the local community or the local or regional council. It has to be addressed at a government level. There has to be central government funding involved," he said.

Westland mayor Helen Lash said locals were understandably angry and frustrated to learn that millions spent on river protection work could be undone.

"I'm not surprised by it because I've been watching it happen, as has all of Franz Josef. They did say some time ago that the river would migrate over to the Tātare [tributary] and it's done just that," she said.

"The last [technical advisory group] report was done in 2023 and it indicated that with the extension or the expansion of the current stopbanks, that would give us another 10 years. That 10 years has disappeared in three," she said.

"Bearing in mind that these ratepayers have poured huge sums of money into river protection work, which they're now told might have to be removed to let the river go and take their land. It's a bitter pill to swallow."

Lash said she had formed a multi-agency working group, which aimed to have a formal proposal ready for ministers early next year.

"We don't go to the government and say, 'Look, we need this money, where the hell do we start spending it?' We've got to do the hard graft," she said.

Fuller said affected landowners would need to be properly compensated.

Authorities needed to move before it was too late, he said.

World.title: Enrolment rate still short of last election with three days left
World.content:
Enrolment as a percentage of the population remains below that of 2023, although the total number of enrolments is now higher.

The latest enrolment figures from the Electoral Commission out on Thursday came with another reminder to get on the roll before voting starts on the long Labour weekend.

At 92.1 percent, the percentage of eligible voters who are enrolled remained below the 94.7 percent of the last general election in 2023.

However - because of a larger population - the total number of people enrolled (3,729,667) had surpassed the final number of voters in that election (3,688,292).

Those aged 18-24 remained the least enrolled at 302,475 or 68.6 percent of eligible voters in that group.

On 21 October 2026, with three days to go before the enrolment close, 3,729,667 people were enrolled to vote. Supplied to RNZ

Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne said there was still time for people to enrol or update their details before the cutoff this weekend.

"You must be enrolled by midnight this Sunday 25 October for your vote to count," he said.

"This weekend, we'll be at events around the country to help people enrol or check their details. You can also drop off an enrolment form at one of our hubs. Locations and hours are available on vote.nz."

With the rules now restricting voting to those who enrolled at least two weeks before election day, a former polling booth manager has warned people who did not know about the change who could become angry.

The Commission said its staff were trained to assist voters while remaining neutral, respectful and mindful of people's privacy.

Le Quesne said delivery of EasyVote cards - which sped up voting but were not a requirement - by email and post was on track for when voting starts on Monday.

"Voting places will be open before election day in convenient locations including shopping areas, transport hubs, marae, community halls and tertiary institutions, to make it easy for people to vote as they go about their daily lives," he said.

"There will be 207 voting places open on Monday 26 October offering 1,437 hours of voting. The days and hours that advance voting places are open vary, so check before you go to vote. The number of voting places will increase as we head towards election day. On election day Saturday 7 November, more than 2,300 voting places will be open from 9am to 7pm."
