Tech.title: Ruggable’s Washable Rugs Are Worth It and Now on Sale (2026)
Tech.content:
It’s a great time to buy a rug. The floors are getting cold, and you need to be prepared for your winter hibernation. Fall is also hosting season, which means making your place more presentable for the holidays. Maybe you’ve moved, as many do at this time of year, and are still furnishing your new space. Fortunately, home goods sales are plentiful right now.

Ruggable’s October Hosting Sale is one of my favorite excuses to redecorate, with up to 30 percent off select styles. It runs through October 25, so your window is closing as I type. Keep reading for more reasons I love Ruggable, plus a few of my favorites currently on sale.

For People Who Make Messes

I adore Ruggable. The entire WIRED Reviews team adores Ruggable. I have the Pamir Moroccan Flatwoven runner under my kitchen sink, and it's gorgeous, but I don’t panic when spills and stains happen. In fact, I welcome them. The beauty of a washable rug is that you can actually live on it, which feels almost radical when so much home decor seems designed for childless, pet-free people who never eat or drink.

WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz has a toddler and a cat, both of whom have peed on his hallway rug. Both times, he was grateful he could toss it in the washing machine and dryer and move on. Commerce executive director Cooper Fleishman was debating between the Wendel Ochre Rug by Anthropologie, the bohemian Yara Navy & Bronze Rug, and the Berber-inspired Enya Multicolor Rug for his office. Reviewer Simon Hill has the Santiago Persian Tufted Rug in his home in Scotland (yes, they ship to the UK and Europe) and recommends the Mandalore Tufted Rug for any Star Wars fans out there.

Tech.title: Apple Limitis iPhone Duo Purchases to 2 Foldable Phones Per Person
Tech.content:
If you were hoping to score multiple iPhone Duo devices from Apple when the new foldable becomes available on Friday, we have some bad news for you: The tech giant is limiting sales of the phone to two per person.

As reported earlier this week by MacRumors, when we attempted to add more than two to our bag on the Apple Store, we got the following message: “A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out.”

Screenshot by Corinne Reichert/CNET

The limit of two foldables per purchase will presumably also apply to those shopping in-store when the phone finally launches on Friday.

More from CNET

While preorders are backed up until the end of January — our estimated delivery when adding two to our bag is Jan. 25, as of the time of publication — Apple will have limited stock of the iPhone Duo in stores, though you may have to wait in line overnight to be one of the few people able to get their hands on one (or two).

While companies may limit the number of devices in each order, especially for stock-scarce products like game consoles, it’s been a while since Apple has restricted how many phones people can buy at once. Nearly two decades ago, the company launched the original iPhone to great fanfare in September 2007, but limited buyers to two per order (later easing it to five by the holidays). The restriction returned in 2012, when Apple limited orders to two iPhone 5 preorders per customer.

If you do want to buy more than one iPhone Duo, we found that we could add multiple to our carts while shopping at Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and Best Buy, though all of those purchases require you to 

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, entering the mobile niche that Samsung and Motorola have been fighting over since 2020, with Google entering the fray with the first Pixel Fold in 2023. Chinese phonemakers like Huawei and Xiaomi have also released their own foldables, though none have been sold widely in the US.

Despite refined devices like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Ultra 2026 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold releasing earlier this year, analysts predict that Apple’s new device will carve out a significant chunk of the market: The International Data Corporation expects the Duo to amount to 31% of the foldable share of the phones market by the end of the year, growing to 40% in 2027.

Customer preorders seem to have followed those predictions, though we’ll have to wait and see whether that appetite continues throughout the holidays and into the new year. Early reviews have been positive, with CNET Senior Reporter Abrar Al-Heeti noting that despite some downsides attributable to a first-generation device, the Apple foldable’s finer details make the experience feel fluid and cohesive.

“Personally, I have no plans of switching back to a slab phone anytime soon,” Al-Heeti said in her review.

Tech.title: A Privacy Company Just Saved the Clearest Flock Surveillance Map I’ve Seen
Tech.content:
A powerful, free Flock surveillance-tracking platform is now hosted by Proton, the creator of Proton Mail and Proton VPN. The move provides extra technical and legal protection for the interactive mapping tool, which Flock has repeatedly attempted to shut down through legal threats.

The deal, announced on Wednesday, gives the public access to a free database of Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and AI surveillance cameras across the US.

Security researcher Joshua Michael first published the interactive map in September before facing a swift trademark complaint from Flock. Despite Flock’s demands for its removal, the map remains publicly accessible.

More from CNET

Flock’s surveillance networks capture license plates, vehicle details, human physical characteristics, and audio signals such as gunshots or shouting. While law enforcement agencies use this data to track and search suspects, privacy advocates warn that the technology enables widespread, unchecked tracking.

Proton also says the map shows far more Flock cameras are active than Flock currently says it has. Flock said this summer that it operates more than 120,000 cameras nationwide, but the tool says there are more than 214,000 Flock devices in service, with more than 80,000 in the planning stages.

A representative from Flock Safety didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The map is one of the most usable Flock tools I’ve seen. Proton’s Flock tool has better visual clarity, faster search responses and a more intuitive interface than other sites I’ve tried and is available without a subscription to other Proton services.

I searched my own city, which canceled its Flock contact over a year ago. The map accurately reported that no active Flock cameras are currently present, but correctly located decommissioned Flock cams. Since the data is based on Flock’s own reporting, I place more trust in it than in crowdsourced tools like the Deflock app, which are subject to errors or misrepresentation.

Proton’s tool is striking to look at and simple to use. Proton

“My research on FlockSurveillance.org documents cybersecurity failures with national-security consequences,” map creator Joshua Michael told CNET. “My research argued that Flock Safety could not detect exports of their data and that because they hold data on nearly every American and their pattern of life, they are a national security threat to our country and people.”

Michael said Flock has “promised to take every measure possible to take my research offline,” he said, offering that as one reason why Proton moved to preserve the map in its Swiss servers. Switzerland enforces some of the world’s strongest privacy laws. Proton’s site notes that under Swiss data protection regulations, the company isn’t required to comply with requests that are not supported by a Swiss court order. Flock is a US-based company.

Camera locations are constantly changing, meaning a surveillance map could rapidly become dated.

“If new and reliable data becomes available, then we will update the map,” a Proton spokesperson told me. “We’re committed to keeping the public informed of all forms of surveillance where reliable data can be sourced.”

Another surveillance mapping option

While Proton’s map provides a specialized, point-in-time look at Flock Safety’s network, the Atlas of Surveillance offers a broader, historical catalog of the sweeping technologies US law enforcement agencies have quietly adopted over the years.

Powered by a network of volunteers who analyze public data and official government records, the Atlas database tracks everything from automated license plate readers to cell-site simulators and body-worn cameras. The project continuously updates its findings.

Tech.title: EA Shutters BioWare, Creator of Mass Effect, Dragon Age, KOTOR and More
Tech.content:
Video game publisher Electronic Arts is closing the venerable studio BioWare, maker of legendary series like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, it announced on Wednesday.

Recent years have seen record layoffs across the gaming industry as companies scaled back expansion during the COVID-19 pandemic, disrupting tens of thousands of careers and closing many studios. The shuttering of BioWare is a symbolic and substantial blow, presumably ending multiple fervently adored game series and carrying implications for the industry at large. The closure reportedly involves around 400 layoffs, about 50 of which were at BioWare, according to Bloomberg.

EA confirmed in a blog post Wednesday that the closure of BioWare accompanies the choice to stop development on the next game in the Mass Effect series, which BioWare first teased on Nov. 7, 2020 — otherwise known as N7 Day to fans, an in-universe reference that has become an annual day to share appreciation for the sci-fi roleplaying series.

More from CNET

It hasn’t been lost on fans that the shuttering of the 31-year-old studio comes just weeks before N7 Day, and social media has been awash with mourning for the many franchises that came out of BioWare.

The studio made a name for itself with Baldur’s Gate in 1998, its sequel Baldur’s Gate 2 and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic before branching into original game series with Jade Empire in 2005, the first Mass Effect in 2007 and Dragon Age: Origins in 2009.

BioWare found its niche in roleplaying games with well-written narratives and deeply detailed characters. The studio was lauded for developing rich arcs for “companion” characters with varied sexualities, some of whom the player could romance. Its queer representation earned the studio a devoted fanbase.

It’s worth noting that BioWare was shuttered shortly after EA closed a deal in August to be acquired by a business consortium that includes Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia has criminalized homosexuality and transgender expression, imprisoning people and reportedly sentencing them to punishments including fines, flogging and death. The oil-rich country has also invested heavily in real-world sports, including boxing, golf and soccer, and EA’s blog post mentions “deepening” its core of sports games, which include the annual EA Sports FC and Madden NFL games.

“We believe we can use our experience building interactive entertainment, together with our relationships in sports, to create entirely new ways for fans to engage with the teams, athletes and sports they love,” the company said. “These will be disciplined investments that only scale when they demonstrate real potential.”

The business consortium that acquired EA for $55 billion also included the equity company Silver Lake and investment firm Affinity Partners, which is headed by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of President Donald Trump.

BioWare’s rocky recent years amid a changing industry

After a lengthy development, Dragon Age: The Veilguard launched in 2024 to favorable reviews, but its sales were far below expectations. EA

As the news went out, BioWare fans took to social media to remember the studio’s formative games, but few of its recent ones.

Backlash over the controversial ending of 2012’s Mass Effect 3 led the studio to develop a new trajectory for the series with Mass Effect: Andromeda in 2017, which got a lukewarm reception from fans. While Dragon Age: Inquisition was a hit in 2014, its sequel was reportedly mired in development difficulties and was reworked into the 2024 title Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which met with favorable reviews but a poor reception from fans, and fell short of EA’s sales expectations, IGN reported. Between those, the studio’s attempt at an action-adventure live-service game, 2019’s Anthem, launched in a flawed state, and its road to recovery of updates was cut short in 2021 when the studio stopped development.

BioWare’s last decade saw departures of people who had headlined the games that fans grew up playing, and the more recent missteps led to a cooling of the studio’s beloved reputation. But plenty of things changed in the larger games industry over that span, too, with development time extending from a few years to five or even longer, increasing the costs of making every game. That puts more pressure on new games to be big hits, selling millions of copies to float ever-longer development cycles. When they don’t, it has increasingly led to studio closures.

EA’s blog post announcing the BioWare departure reflects this new era of gaming, and perhaps changing tastes. It’s no surprise to hear the publisher is refocusing on “core areas” and thinning out existing teams, as any business does during an industry contraction. These seem to be shooters like Battlefield 6, action-adventure games like the upcoming Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game (presumably referring to Respawn’s sequel to Jedi Survivor), EA’s sports franchises, The Sims and its skateboarding series, Skate. BioWare’s closure is nestled between those updates, and notably absent is any mention of other RPGs.

But amid recent years of gaming layoffs and shuttered studios, it’s hard to see BioWare’s closure as anything but a swan song for an era of gaming long passed on a new road paved by more laid-off developers and headed toward uncertainty. It’s not as much of a surprise, as analysts confided their worries about the future of EA-owned franchises to Polygon when the business consortium first announced its intent to acquire in September 2025.

There’s a dim hope that private ownership will liberate EA from shareholder pressure to try new risky gaming ideas, but the loss of BioWare is deeply felt among gamers who grew up playing risks that paid off for a time — and ensconced stories and characters in their hearts.

Tech.title: Tons of People Are Apparently Asking Meta’s Muse AI Agent to Shop for Them
Tech.content:
We’re about to be immersed in the busiest shopping season of the year, and if Mark Zuckerberg has his way, people will completely hand over the responsibility of buying stuff to their own personal AI agent. In fact, according to the Meta CEO, that is already happening.

During the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, Zuckerberg said that over a quarter of Meta Muse‘s engaged users — now totaling more than 10 million — were using the AI agent for shopping, with an “average purchase size of over $200.”

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to financial services company Plaid, which facilitates payments between stores and buyers. He added that, due to higher-than-expected volumes, Meta had to work with payment app Stripe to raise credit limits to meet the shopping demand by Muse users.

More from CNET

Now that the AI agent has achieved what Zuckerberg referred to as a “product-market fit,” the name of the game for Muse in the long term is that we may be living in a reality where you have your own personal AI agent communicating with a business’s AI agent to complete transactions without you ever needing to speak with someone directly.

“Billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together,” Zuckerberg said, painting a picture of what a large-scale Muse network could look like.

One of the goals is to get Muse to scale up its revenue, which he believes will eventually surpass the earnings of Meta’s combined existing family of apps: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads and Messenger.

‘The Muse network’

Then there’s the coming integration of Muse into Meta’s smart glasses, which will launch next month. Soon, you’ll be able to access Muse on the go, without having to pull out your smartphone to use it.

“Having your personal superintelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience,” Zuckerberg said.

How will all this work together? That remains to be seen, but during the call, Zuckerberg referenced something called “the Muse network,” which he said is Meta’s plan to, if I understand things right, gamify the whole personal AI agent experience.

A Meta spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

“It’s not just a kind of single-player game where you have your Muse, but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses],” Zuckerberg said, before bringing the conversation back to shopping, “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent.”

Meta announced third-quarter revenue of $64.6 billion, a 26% jump from the $51.2 billion announced this time last year. Costs were significantly higher, however, up by 68% to $51.6 billion due in large part to the company’s “agreement with 52 attorneys general to resolve litigation related to teen mental health and social media, which provides for payments of up to approximately $18.59 billion.” Net income was up by 264% year-over-year to $9.9 billion for the quarter.

Tech.title: AI and Data Centers Will Impact Midterm Voting, According to Experts
Tech.content:
As far as public opinion goes, artificial intelligence is not a bed of roses. With the Nov. 3 elections looming nationwide, an issue that was barely a blip a year ago has become a full-blown backlash and a likely spoiler in the midterm elections.

A new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

More from CNET

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

Reading the room

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

Tech.title: Google Chrome Will Notify You If You’re on a Scam Website
Tech.content:
Google’s Chrome will start showing alerts for suspicious or dangerous websites when Enhanced Protection mode is on.

Google’s Chrome browser is adding several new features to help guide people away from websites known for scamming visitors, including sites that try to trick people into opening their computers to vulnerabilities.

In a Tuesday blog post, Google outlined a series of new features that can kick in as long as Enhanced Protection mode is enabled.

If the browser detects you’re on a suspicious website, Chrome displays a clear, “This site doesn’t seem right” pop-up warning. That warning will show as an overlay over the content, with the option to instead mark the site as safe. But that’s just if the site is suspicious. For websites that Google deems as dangerous, meaning that they’re commonly associated with causing harm, a full red page showing the warning will appear. It will direct the user away from continuing.

More from CNET

The new feature focuses on helping users avoid fake antivirus and browser update scams, even creating a scam likelihood score.

Chrome will also fight against ClickFix scams, in which a website tricks someone into copying and pasting code into their computer, often under the pretense of fixing a fake vulnerability. When Chrome detects that someone is being tricked into copying code on such a site, it will clear the clipboard and display a warning message. This is meant to help stop the practice in real time since, if successful, it could allow a scammer to gain full access to one’s device.

To use these features, users must opt into Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode via the browser’s privacy and security settings.

The security suite provides real-time defenses—such as blocking “ClickFix” social-engineering attacks—in exchange for sharing additional browsing data with Google. Users should weigh this enhanced protection against the expanded data collection before enabling the feature.

Tech.title: Lawsuits Allege Delivery Robots Recorded Biometric Data Without Permission
Tech.content:
Food delivery robots might not just be carrying burritos. They could be taking a measurement of your face.

Two proposed class action lawsuits in Chicago accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of collecting biometric information without consent and using it to train their artificial intelligence systems. The Cook County residents allege that the companies violated Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires companies to provide written notice of the types and purposes of data collection, obtain prior written consent, and maintain set retention and deletion schedules.

Plaintiff Mitchell Breidinger said that even though he hadn’t chosen robot delivery for his DoorDash groceries, a Coco robot showed up at his home in September 2025. Breidinger said that while he was entering a pickup code, the robot’s cameras captured his face, head and hands and that lidar — a type of 3D imaging technology — measured the geometry of those body parts. Breidinger also alleged that a Coco remote operator watched the delivery on video and that the company didn’t notify him in writing of its intent to collect his biometric data or how long it would retain it.

More from CNET

The other plaintiff, Barry Schain, said he received three Serve Robotics deliveries with his Uber Eats orders even though he hadn’t selected robot delivery.

The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, plus other unspecified relief. Both companies have denied the claims, saying they don’t record the biometric data of customers or people who walk by the robots on the street.

A Serve Robotics spokesperson said in a statement to CNET that its robots “use cameras and sensors to navigate the sidewalks of Chicago safely. Serve does not use that data to identify individuals, and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.”

Coco Robotics didn’t respond to a request for comment, but a company spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company collects only navigational data “to make sidewalks safer for all users” and that it does “not share data from the beginning or end of delivery trips under our data sharing partnerships.”

The robot privacy pitfall

Robotic deliveries have expanded significantly since Starship Technologies’ inaugural package delivery nearly a decade ago. Starship said it surpassed 10 million deliveries globally by midyear.

Coco Robotics now operates about 1,000 robots for deliveries in Chicago, Los Angeles, Washington, DC and Miami. Serve Robotics has more than 2,000 in Los Angeles, Atlanta, Dallas-Fort Worth, Miami, Chicago and Alexandria, Virginia. Both companies primarily deliver food for DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub.

According to most projections, global robotic delivery will expand rapidly over the next several years. One forecast estimates that the US market will grow from $252 million in 2025 to $3.1 billion by 2035. And it won’t just be food and groceries. Deliverables could include medicine, industrial parts and a wide variety of retail goods, and there could also be a rise in delivery by drone and boat.

As fear and anger mount over technology increasingly encroaching on people’s everyday lives, delivery robots — which use AI, cameras and lidar to navigate sidewalks — are advancing rapidly. Just as the backlash against other AI surveillance tools and Flock Safety cameras has cropped up all across the US, there’s a growing pushback against potential privacy violations from delivery robots, which have been punched, kicked, tipped over and defaced, according to a recent story by The New York Times.

Privacy experts and digital rights activists also raise concerns that autonomous courier technology will eliminate delivery jobs and be used by the government or corporations to track people’s activities.

Tech.title: The 3-in-1 Alloop Wearable Could Replace Both Your Wellness Wristband and Ring
Tech.content:
This wearables industry has become increasingly saturated with smart rings and wrist-based fitness trackers, so any company that wants to compete in the space has to get creative. Enter Alloop, a modular, AI-native health wearable announced on Wednesday.

According to a press release, Alloop can be worn in three ways. The company calls this the Trio.

As part of the Trio, there are four pieces of hardware. There’s a wristband, a ring, the Cube — a compact sensor system that collects your health data — and Halo, which offers tap-to-speak, light, color patterns and haptic feedback to communicate reminders, device information, your wellness status and more.

More from CNET

You can wear the wristband with both the Cube and Halo for extra feedback and to log with your voice; the wristband with just the Cube for a lighter, more discreet wrist-based design; or snap the Cube into the ring for the most compact version of the wearable, ideal for sleep.

What Alloop measures

The Cube’s sensors measure resting heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, breathing rate and temperature. You can also log your meals and supplements using photos, voice or text. Collectively, this allows Alloop to provide a sleep score and information about nutrition, activity, strain, recovery and health trends.

Compatible with iOS and Android, the Alloop app’s health dashboard brings key data into a unified view.

There’s also Bio Age, which uses 18 measurements across six health categories, including nutrition, bodily signals and lifestyle, to determine your biological age and show the factors contributing to it. As opposed to one’s chronological age, biological age estimates how you’re supposedly aging at the cellular level.

Even after removing the Halo hardware, you’re still left with the Cube to track your health metrics. Alloop

Alloop AI

The Alloop Trio was built around a personal AI health agent. You can log your meals, symptoms, feelings and more using text, voice and images, while Alloop AI connects that information to the health data collected by the Cube’s sensors and then uses it to offer guidance, proactive insights, personalized plans and more.

This is similar to how AI agents created by other wearable companies work.

It uses Google Gemini and ChatGPT, an Alloop spokesperson said.

Subscription-free

Alloop described the Trio in its press release as an open health platform, as, unlike other fitness trackers, its app doesn’t require a subscription. However, there will also be an optional Pro plan with usage-based access levels, costing about $5 per month.

While the free plan will serve the vast majority of people for everyday health management and light conversational AI use, the Pro plan will provide more in-depth health-related research and enhanced personal agent capabilities.

“By drawing on a user’s longer-term data, health goals, daily behaviors and interaction context, Pro will support deeper insights and more personalized planning,” the Alloop spokesperson said.

Supported integrations include the ability to import data from medical records, lab tests, continuous glucose monitors and third-party wearables and health apps, including Apple Health and Google Health.

Privacy

According to the press release, Alloop “specifies health data protection across collection, transfer, storage and management, with controls that let users review, delete and export their data.” The company’s privacy policy adds that it doesn’t sell personal information and that health and wellness information isn’t used for advertising or marketing.

“Our policy is to keep US users’ data within the United States, without transferring it overseas,” said the Alloop spokesperson.

The company is developing its privacy and security practices to meet the requirements of the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation and the California Consumer Privacy Act, with the goal of completing a SOC 2 examination and obtaining ISO/IEC 27001 certification. SOC 2 is a voluntary compliance standard for safeguarding customer data, while ISO/IEC 27001 is a global standard for information security management systems.

However, you should always exercise caution and read the fine print before sharing your health data with any company or AI agent.

Community

There will be a community feature that allows you to share your progress and see others’ across workouts, meals, daily life and health routines and protocols. You can also create groups, take part in shared challenges and chat with each other in the Alloop app.

Alloop’s privacy policy states that when you use the community features, the company collects profile information, follows, posts, images, comments, reactions, feed activity and messages, which can help it respond to reports, enforce community rules and protect you from spam, abuse and security threats. Depending on the feature and visibility settings, the information you publish may be visible to others.
